JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Imam Nakhmatullaev; Svjatoslav Jakovlev; Eric Juergens; Jaan Juergens; Ilja Karunas; Juri Karunas; Jason Onoufrienko; Renek Tiku; Vladislav Turaskin; Kevin Valdhans; Vjatseslav Zogolev (members of a Russia-based transnational criminal organization controlling nominee-owned DME companies); Hong Yuen Mak a/k/a 'Joe Mak' (pharmacy owner); Boris Manaev (owner, BB Medical Equipment Inc.); Mujjahid Huq (licensed pharmacist and pharmacy owner); Joseph Tony Brown-Arkah (owner, American Medical Centers Suboxone clinic)
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County; New York - Erie County (Buffalo); New York - Nassau County (Lynbrook); New York - Suffolk County (Halesite); Florida - Broward County (Plantation)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Supplemental Insurers (private health insurance companies); Medicaid
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Device, DME; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: In the lead 'Operation Gold Rush' case, a Russia-based organization bought dozens of existing DME companies through paid foreign-national nominee owners and fabricated corporate records to hide true control, then used stolen identities and personal information of more than one million Americans to rapidly submit over $10.6 billion in false DME claims to Medicare and Medicare Supplemental Insurers, collecting about $900 million from supplemental insurers and $41 million from Medicare before laundering the proceeds through U.S. bank accounts, shell companies, overseas banks and cryptocurrency; approximately $27.7 million has been seized. Four other separately charged EDNY defendants in the same takedown allegedly paid gift-card kickbacks for fake OTC-card transactions (over $1 million, guilty plea), billed $8.2 million for medically unnecessary DME, billed Medicare/Medicaid $2.1 million for drugs never dispensed while concealing pharmacy ownership, and billed $85 million for Suboxone-clinic services provided by unlicensed or excluded providers with prescriptions written sight-unseen plus associated lab testing.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, CMS-855S ownership fields list foreign-national nominee owners whose identity documents repeat across dozens of unrelated supplier NPIs. Newly acquired supplier NPIs jump from dormant to top-decile DMEPOS claim volume within weeks of a PECOS change-of-ownership filing. Beneficiary HICN/MBI identifiers on the claims span states far outside the supplier's PECOS service area with no prior utilisation history. Multiple supplier NPIs share one bank routing and account number on the CMS-588 EFT authorisation record. Suboxone and lab claims carry rendering NPIs whose state licence board file shows lapsed licensure or an OIG LEIE exclusion match.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Post-acquisition volume spike: on supplier NPI x week, compute billed DMEPOS charges divided by the provider's trailing 26-week median in the 12 weeks after a PECOS ownership-change date; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 2) Shared payment-instrument degree: on bank account number from CMS-588, compute the count of distinct billing NPIs and distinct TINs mapped to it; fires when that count exceeds one without a disclosed common-ownership record; action prepay edit plus site visit. 3) Rendering-provider registry mismatch: on claim line, compare rendering NPI against the state licence board active-licence file and OIG LEIE on the date of service; fires on an exact exclusion or expired-licence match; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
SchemeSummary: Annual summary press release, not a single case: the office reports charging dozens of defendants for health care fraud causing billions in intended losses to Medicare and other federal programs, involving fraudulent billing, kickbacks, and diverted or adulterated pharmaceuticals, with unspecified criminal forfeiture and restitution ordered. No individual defendant, amount, or conduct period is identified.
WaysToIdentify: This item is an annual enforcement summary rather than a single case, so no specific claim, provider NPI or adjudication point is identified. Without dates of service, billed codes or a payer file, no prepay signal can be derived from it. The nearest non-claims route is tracking the named defendants from the published charging documents into PECOS and OIG LEIE for enrolment revocation.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is an automated feed of DOJ charging announcements matched to NPPES and PECOS records to trigger enrolment review and exclusion listing.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Jerome Sydney Heyward (North Charleston City Councilmember); Sandino Savalas Moses (North Charleston City Councilmember); Mike A. Brown (North Charleston City Council Member); Donavan Laval Moten (founder of Core4Success Foundation); Aaron Charles-Lee Hicks; Hason Tatorian "Tory" Fields; Rose Emily Lorenzo; Michelle Stent-Hilton (non-profit affiliate and personal assistant to Heyward)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Three North Charleston city councilmen and five associates were charged in bribery, extortion, kickback and money laundering schemes: a councilman extorted a businessman for payments in exchange for official action; councilmen Heyward, Brown and Moses solicited/accepted bribes from Hicks and Fields (acting for a company) in exchange for supporting rezoning of the Baker Hospital site; and Heyward conspired with nonprofit operators Moten and Stent-Hilton to kick back to him a portion of City violence-reduction grant funds awarded to their nonprofits, laundering the kickbacks through intermediary Rose Lorenzo. WaysToIdentify: This is municipal bribery and grant embezzlement, so there is no health care claim and no adjudication point. No provider NPI, HCPCS code or date of service exists to edit against. The nearest detection route is grant subrecipient audit comparing nonprofit disbursement ledgers to bank transfers reaching officials or intermediaries.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Michael Procopio (leader of South Philadelphia's '10th and O Crew')
SchemeSummary: Procopio obtained prescription oxycodone pills from area doctors' offices and unlawfully distributed them on Philadelphia streets through a network of intermediaries; he admitted distributing approximately 14,925 milligrams of oxycodone, and a search of his home found oxycodone and Adderall hidden in a safe concealed in a hollowed-out dictionary.
WaysToIdentify: This is street diversion of pills obtained from physician offices, so there is no submitted claim and no adjudication point. The pills were taken from office stock rather than dispensed under a billed NDC. The nearest detection route is state PDMP and DEA 222/ARCOS reconciliation of office-stock oxycodone acquisitions against documented administrations. Office inventory shrinkage reported on DEA Form 106 loss reports gives a second non-claims signal.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is an ARCOS-to-PDMP reconciliation on DEA registrant number computing acquired controlled-substance dosage units minus dispensed and administered units.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Community Options, Inc. (New Jersey not-for-profit providing oversight and centralized billing); Community Options New York, Inc. (New York not-for-profit provider of Day Habilitation services)
State_County: New York - New York County (Manhattan); New York (statewide); New Jersey
SchemeSummary: Defendants billed the New York Medicaid Program for Day Habilitation services for adults with developmental disabilities that were not delivered or documented in compliance with OPWDD requirements (inadequate policies and employee training led to deficient documentation), and after non-routine internal reviews identified Medicaid overpayments, they failed to report and return them. Resolved by a $5,016,626.11 total FCA settlement ($2,148,540.37 federal, $2,868,085.74 to New York State) plus an HHS-OIG Corporate Integrity Agreement, arising from a sealed qui tam suit the government joined.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Day Habilitation units billed exceed the attendance hours recorded in the OPWDD service documentation and daily attendance log. Self-identified overpayments appear in the provider's internal review files but no matching claim void or adjustment reaches the payer's remittance history. Billed units per beneficiary per day exceed the maximum authorised in the person-centred service plan on file. Staff-to-participant ratios implied by billed units exceed the employees on the payroll register for that date of service. The 60-day report-and-return clock elapses with no credit-balance submission for known overpaid claim control numbers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Unreturned self-identified overpayment: on provider NPI x claim control number identified in an internal review, compute days between the review completion date and any voided or adjusted claim in remittance history; fires when the gap exceeds 60 days; action postpay audit. 2) Units versus attendance: on beneficiary x date of service, compute billed Day Habilitation units minus documented attendance units in the OPWDD log; fires when the difference is positive; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Staffing capacity: on provider NPI x date of service, compute total billed service hours divided by direct-care hours on the payroll register; fires when the ratio exceeds the programme's authorised staffing ratio; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Sanjeev Kumar (gynecologist)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a Memphis gynecologist performed medically unnecessary gynecologic procedures on patients using reused 'single use' or improperly reprocessed devices held in insanitary conditions, then billed Medicare and Medicaid as if the procedures were medically necessary and as if a new or properly reprocessed device had been used for each procedure.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, procedure claim volume for the gynecologic CPT codes far exceeds the single-use device units the practice purchased per wholesaler and distributor pedigree invoices. The same disposable device HCPCS is billed fewer times than the procedures that require it on matching dates of service. Procedure counts per rendering NPI per day exceed the room-time hours physically available in a 24-hour period. Beneficiaries show repeat post-procedure infection diagnosis claims clustered on one rendering NPI within 30 days. State licence board and accreditation survey files record insanitary-condition or infection-control deficiencies at the practice address.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Device-purchase reconciliation: on provider NPI x quarter, compute count of procedure claim lines requiring a single-use device minus device units on wholesaler pedigree and 340B/purchase invoices; fires when the difference is positive; action postpay audit plus documentation request (ADR). 2) Same-day procedure capacity: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of CMS work-time minutes for all billed procedures; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Post-procedure infection rate: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the share of procedure beneficiaries with an infection diagnosis claim within 30 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Mi Ok Song Bruining (clinical social worker and supervisor at Recovery Connections Centers of America, Inc.); Recovery Connections Centers of America, Inc. (RCCA)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other private health insurers
SchemeSummary: As a supervisor at an addiction treatment center, Bruining billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for 45-minute psychotherapy/counseling sessions when patients were actually seen for only 5-10 minutes (sometimes a one-question conversation), and directed staff to record 45-minute intervals without AM/PM designations and to copy-and-paste prior visit notes so the volume of impossible same-hour sessions would not be apparent, yielding more than $3.5 million in fraudulent claims.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, summed timed-psychotherapy minutes for CPT 90837 and 90834 per rendering NPI per date of service exceed 24 hours. Session start times recorded in the encounter record repeat at identical clock intervals with no AM/PM designation across many beneficiaries. The provider bills 90837 at a share of all psychotherapy lines far above same-specialty peers in the remittance history. Progress notes attached to ADR responses are byte-identical to prior visit notes for the same beneficiary. Facility staff roster hours on payroll records are fewer than the counselling hours billed under supervised NPIs that day.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible clinician day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of CPT-defined minimum minutes for all timed psychotherapy lines; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) High-intensity code share: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute 90837 lines divided by all psychotherapy lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Note duplication: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the count of consecutive encounter notes with identical text hashes in submitted documentation; fires when that count exceeds one; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Sola, Inc. (operator of adult residential group homes)
PayerName: Medicaid (Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services)
SchemeSummary: Sola, Inc., which operated adult residential group homes, allegedly billed Virginia Medicaid (DMAS) for skilled and other nursing services in units of time that exceeded the hours actually worked by its nurses as documented on their time sheets, overbilling $641,396.11 for services impossible to have been performed; it paid $2 million to resolve the civil claims.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed nursing time units per date of service exceed the aggregate nurse hours on the facility's payroll timesheets. A single licensed nurse NPI appears on claims totalling more than 24 hours in one calendar day. Billed nursing units exceed the staffing hours reported to the state licensing agency for that group home census. Nurse licence numbers on the claims do not appear on the state board of nursing active file for the service dates. Units per resident per day exceed the level authorised in the DMAS service authorisation record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Payroll-hours ceiling: on provider NPI x date of service, compute billed nursing time units converted to hours minus nurse hours on the payroll timesheet file; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit. 2) Single-nurse day limit: on nurse licence number x date of service, compute total billed service hours across all facilities; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Authorisation overage: on beneficiary x date of service, compute billed units minus service-authorisation units on file; fires when positive; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Aesculap Implant Systems, LLC (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Aesculap sold the VEGA Knee System to physicians and hospitals while knowing bone cement did not properly adhere to the implant, causing premature loosening and revision surgeries, and failed to record or report adverse events, resulting in Medicare and Medicaid claims for devices that were not reasonable and necessary; it also paid a Georgia orthopedic surgeon consulting fees, free international travel and entertainment to induce use of the Vega, and separately distributed two devices (ELAN-4 Air Drill and JS Series SterilContainer S2) without FDA clearance after an employee forged clearance documents.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, revision-arthroplasty CPT claims within a short interval of the index implant cluster on one device catalogue number and UDI. The implant UDI on the hospital claim maps to a device with no FDA clearance record in the GUDID and 510(k) databases. Surgeons with the highest use of the implant appear in Open Payments with consulting fees and travel from the manufacturer. Adverse-event volume in MAUDE for the device is far below the payer's observed revision counts. Prior-authorisation records show the same surgeon NPI concentrating one manufacturer's device far above peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Early revision rate by device: on device catalogue number or UDI, compute the share of implant claims followed by a revision CPT within 24 months; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus other implants in the same product category; action postpay audit. 2) Clearance-registry mismatch: on claim line, match the billed device UDI against the FDA GUDID and 510(k) clearance file on the date of service; fires on an exact absence of clearance; action prepay edit. 3) Payment-linked device concentration: on surgeon NPI x manufacturer, compute the share of implants from that manufacturer alongside Open Payments transfer-of-value totals; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Aesculap Implant Systems LLC (medical device manufacturer/distributor)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Aesculap sold its VEGA Knee System prosthetic implants to U.S. physicians and hospitals while knowing bone cement did not properly adhere and the device would loosen and fail prematurely at a higher than acceptable rate, causing claims for non-reasonable/necessary implants and revision surgeries to be billed to Medicare and Medicaid; it also paid a Georgia orthopedic surgeon consulting fees, free international travel and entertainment to induce use of the Vega, and separately distributed two devices (ELAN-4 Air Drill and JS Series SterilContainer S2) after an employee forged FDA clearance documents (employee previously pleaded guilty and was imprisoned). Whistleblowers Marien and McGee receive $4,475,000 of the $38.5M settlement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, index implant claims for one device catalogue number show revision surgery within 24 months at rates above comparable knee systems. The implant UDI on hospital claims has no matching clearance entry in the FDA GUDID or 510(k) file. Open Payments records show consulting fees, travel and entertainment from the manufacturer to the highest-volume implanting surgeon NPIs. MAUDE adverse-event counts for the device are far below the revision volume observed in paid claims. Prior-authorisation files show one surgeon NPI selecting a single manufacturer's implant far above same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Device-level early failure: on device catalogue number or UDI, compute revisions within 24 months divided by index implants; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer implants in the same category; action postpay audit plus coverage review. 2) Unlisted-device edit: on claim line, match billed UDI to the FDA clearance registry active on the date of service; fires on exact registry absence; action prepay edit. 3) Transfer-of-value concentration: on implanting NPI x manufacturer x year, compute manufacturer share of implants and Open Payments dollars received; fires when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Agendia, Inc. (molecular diagnostics company); Knoxville Comprehensive Breast Center, PLLC; Knoxville Dermatopathology Laboratory, LLC
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; other government payors
SchemeSummary: Agendia allegedly caused referring providers to order MammaPrint breast-cancer genomic tests through standing/automatic orders that were not reasonable or medically necessary, and induced referrals with extravagant dinners, improper honoraria, gift cards, per-referral and monthly flat-rate payments, then billed Medicare, Medicaid and other government payors; KCBC and KDL allegedly participated in generating the tainted referrals. Settlements total at least $3,250,000 (Agendia), $322,500 (KCBC) and $207,500 (KDL), with possible additional payments if Agendia is sold.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the genomic assay CPT is ordered by one referring NPI in identical volume every month, consistent with a standing order rather than per-patient decisions. Orders arrive without an intervening E/M or oncology encounter claim between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary. A small set of ordering NPIs accounts for a disproportionate share of one laboratory's test volume. Those same ordering NPIs appear in Open Payments with honoraria, meals and gift-card-equivalent transfers from the laboratory. Test claims lack a supporting breast-cancer diagnosis code meeting the payer's coverage policy on the date of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Standing-order signature: on ordering NPI x HCPCS x month, compute the coefficient of variation of monthly order counts and the share of ordered tests lacking a prior E/M encounter with the same beneficiary; fires when order counts are near-constant and the no-encounter share exceeds the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Referral concentration: on laboratory NPI, compute the share of test volume from the top ordering NPIs plus Open Payments dollars those orderers received from the lab; fires when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Coverage-diagnosis match: on claim line, compare the submitted diagnosis to the payer's coverage policy list for the genomic CPT; fires on exact absence of a covered diagnosis; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Cody Lee Anderson (designated personal representative of the estate); Thomas Allen Bateman, Jr. (co-conspirator, named sole beneficiary)
SchemeSummary: Anderson conspired with Bateman to have an 88-year-old Aiken woman, who investigators found lacked the mental capacity to make an informed decision, execute a will leaving her entire estate of roughly $20 million to Bateman, with Anderson named personal representative in line for a 5% fee; both men pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and neither has been sentenced.
WaysToIdentify: This is estate and bank fraud against an incapacitated individual, so there is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point. No NPI, HCPCS code or date of service exists to edit. The nearest detection route is bank elder-financial-exploitation monitoring of large beneficiary changes and fiduciary fee arrangements.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a financial-institution rule comparing testamentary or account beneficiary changes for customers over 80 against recent capacity-related medical or guardianship records.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Cody Lee Anderson (designated personal representative of the estate); Thomas Allen Bateman, Jr. (sole beneficiary named in the will)
SchemeSummary: During the pandemic a will was executed by an 88-year-old Aiken woman who lacked the mental capacity to make an informed decision, purporting to leave her entire estate (worth approximately $20 million) to Bateman, with Anderson named personal representative in line for a 5% fee of about $1 million; both men were convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud and each sentenced to 24 months in prison plus three years of supervision.
WaysToIdentify: This is estate and bank fraud, with no claim submitted to any health plan and no adjudication point. No provider, code or service date exists that a payer could edit against. The nearest detection route is SAR filing by the bank on abrupt beneficiary designation changes benefiting a non-relative.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a bank monitoring rule computing the dollar share of an elderly customer's estate redirected to a single non-relative payee within a short window.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Tommie Robinson (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: An Alabama doctor working with telemedicine companies signed pre-populated doctors' orders for DME and cancer-risk genetic testing generated from telemarketing calls to Medicare beneficiaries, without any contact with or medical relationship with the patients; DME suppliers and labs then billed Medicare over $6 million for the medically unnecessary, kickback-tainted orders.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on the L-code brace and genomic test claims has no prior E/M encounter with the beneficiary. One ordering NPI signs orders for beneficiaries across many states within a single week. The beneficiary's other claims show no telehealth encounter claim from that ordering NPI near the order date. Order signature timestamps cluster in bursts far exceeding a plausible per-order review time in a workday. Ordered volume routes to a small closed set of supplier and laboratory NPIs sharing an address in PECOS.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M or telehealth claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer geographic dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct billing supplier NPIs on ordered claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Orderer-supplier closure: on ordering NPI, compute the share of ordered DMEPOS and lab claims billed by supplier NPIs sharing a PECOS practice address; fires when that share exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Tommie Robinson (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Robinson, an Alabama doctor, signed pre-populated doctors' orders generated from telemarketing calls to Medicare beneficiaries he never examined or spoke with, authorizing medically unnecessary DME and cancer-risk genetic testing; DME suppliers and labs then billed Medicare over $6 million on those kickback-tainted orders.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, brace and genetic test claims carry an ordering NPI with no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with the beneficiary. That ordering NPI's daily signed-order count exceeds the number of patient contacts possible in a 24-hour day. Beneficiaries on the orders reside in states far from the ordering physician's NPPES practice location. No telehealth encounter claim exists from the ordering NPI within the coverage-required window before the order date. Ordered claims concentrate in a handful of supplier and laboratory NPIs paying per-order arrangements not disclosed in PECOS.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) No-encounter order edit: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the gap in days to the nearest qualifying E/M or telehealth claim with the same beneficiary; fires when none exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Signing-capacity ceiling: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries on newly ordered DMEPOS and lab claims; fires when the implied per-patient time falls below a physically possible visit length in 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Orderer-to-supplier concentration: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the share of ordered volume billed by the top three supplier or lab NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Muhammad Adil Quraish (former Air Force dentist); at least four unnamed co-conspirators
PayerName: Small Business Administration (PPP and EIDL pandemic relief programs)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Quraish and at least four co-conspirators submitted PPP and EIDL loan applications for several entities with inflated employee counts and payroll figures, supported by fabricated payroll records and falsified IRS tax forms falsely certified as filed, netting $1,471,599 in relief funds that were partly invested in cryptocurrency.
WaysToIdentify: This is pandemic small-business loan fraud with no health care claim and no payer adjudication point. The falsified artefacts are IRS payroll forms and bank applications, not claim lines. The nearest detection route is matching applicant-reported employee counts and payroll to IRS Form 941 filings and state unemployment wage records before disbursement.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a loan-underwriting check on applicant EIN comparing claimed payroll to IRS 941 transcripts and state wage-base filings, and shared bank accounts across affiliated applications.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: West End Services, Inc. (pharmacy); Christopher Leon (owner-pharmacist)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy and its owner-pharmacist allegedly billed Medicare for prescription drugs - including Latuda, Humira, Abilify, Invega Sustenna, Seroquel, Acyclovir, Flovent and Truvada - that were never actually dispensed to Medicare beneficiaries, and agreed to pay $825,000 based on ability to pay.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, dispensed NDC units billed exceed the pharmacy's purchased units in wholesaler pedigree and 867 acquisition data for the same period. Beneficiaries show no corresponding office visit or prescriber encounter claims supporting the high-cost NDCs billed. Refill intervals for Invega Sustenna and Humira are shorter than the days-supply previously paid in remittance history. Prescriber NPIs on the claims report no prescribing relationship in the state PDMP or the plan's prior-authorisation records. Beneficiaries reside far outside the pharmacy's service radius shown in NPPES with no delivery documentation.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed dispensed units minus units acquired per wholesaler pedigree invoices; fires when the difference is positive; action payment suspension. 2) Early-refill impossibility: on beneficiary x NDC, compute days between fill dates minus days supply on the prior paid claim; fires when the gap is negative beyond the plan's refill tolerance; action prepay edit. 3) Prescriber-relationship gap: on claim line, compute the count of prior encounter claims between the prescribing NPI and the beneficiary in the lookback window; fires when zero for a high-cost specialty NDC; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Courtesy Transport Services, LLC; Melanie Burger (owner); Dr. John Milanick (owner)
SchemeSummary: Courtesy Transport Services billed Medicare and Florida Medicaid for basic life support, non-emergency ambulance transports that were not medically reasonable and necessary, where patients did not require ambulance transportation, or that were never actually provided; resolved via qui tam settlement totaling $900,000 across the company and its two owners, with the relator receiving about $171,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, BLS non-emergency transport claims lack a Physician Certification Statement supporting bed-confined or medically necessary status. Origin and destination modifiers pair residence to a destination with no same-day facility or treatment claim for the beneficiary. Loaded mileage HCPCS A0425 units do not match the road distance between the billed origin and destination ZIP codes. The beneficiary's other claims show ambulatory status, such as outpatient therapy or self-transport-consistent visits, near the transport dates. Repeat round-trip transports for one beneficiary exceed the frequency same-specialty ambulance peers bill for that condition.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Destination corroboration: on claim line, compute the count of facility or professional claims for the same beneficiary at the destination on the transport date; fires when zero; action prepay edit. 2) Mileage geometry: on claim line, compute billed A0425 units minus computed road miles between origin and destination ZIP centroids; fires when the difference exceeds the mapping tolerance; action claim suspension. 3) Repeat non-emergency intensity: on beneficiary x supplier NPI x month, compute the count of paid BLS non-emergency transports; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. David Antonio Becerril (licensed Washington physician); Health First Urgent Care (urgent care clinic, Richland and Pasco, WA)
State_County: Washington - Yakima County (Selah/Yakima); Washington - Benton County (Richland); Washington - Franklin County (Pasco); Washington - Spokane County (Spokane)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: This roundup release covers two health care matters: (1) Dr. David Becerril was convicted at trial on 16 counts for signing false orders in a telemarketing scheme for medically unnecessary genetic tests and back/knee/shoulder/ankle braces for Medicare beneficiaries he never saw or spoke to - including deceased patients and patients with no limbs - being paid per order signed, resulting in over $3.2 million billed to Medicare (sentencing set for January 2026); and (2) Health First Urgent Care agreed to pay $2,807,729 under the False Claims Act for 'unbundling' PCR respiratory and urinary tract infection panel tests and billing each component test individually, plus billing Washington Medicaid for more expensive, medically unnecessary panels.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on brace and genomic test claims has no prior encounter claim with the beneficiary. Dates of service fall after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File and the payer's eligibility file. Limb-specific brace HCPCS are billed for beneficiaries with prior amputation diagnosis or amputation procedure codes in claim history. Component respiratory and UTI PCR CPT codes are billed separately on the same date instead of the correct panel code. Panel testing volume per rendering NPI far exceeds same-specialty urgent-care peers for the same diagnosis mix.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Death and anatomy edits: on claim line, compare date of service to the Death Master File date and compare limb-specific HCPCS to prior amputation diagnosis history; fires on an exact registry or anatomical contradiction; action prepay edit. 2) Per-order signing volume: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute distinct beneficiaries with new DMEPOS or genetic test orders and the count lacking any prior E/M; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Panel unbundling: on rendering NPI x beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of individual PCR component CPT codes billed where a single panel code exists; fires when the count exceeds the panel's component threshold; action prepay edit and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Rodolfo Rivera (Amtrak employee); Kevin Frink (Amtrak employee); Quinton Johnson (Amtrak employee); David McBrien (Amtrak employee); Gregory Richardson (Amtrak employee); Michael Toal (Amtrak employee); Damany Walker (Amtrak employee); Timothy Bogen (Amtrak employee); Dion Jacob (Amtrak employee); David Lonergan (Amtrak employee); Punson Figueroa (acupuncturist); Michael DeNicola (podiatrist)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Amtrak employees took cash kickbacks from health care providers (including an acupuncturist and a podiatrist) in exchange for letting the providers bill the Amtrak employee health plan for services that were never rendered and were not medically necessary; Rivera also recruited other employees whose plan IDs were used for the false claims. Claims tied to Rivera, his dependent and his recruits caused over $2 million in plan payments, and the overall conspiracy caused over $11 million in fraudulent payments; co-defendant acupuncturist Figueroa received 34 months in prison while Rivera awaits sentencing and nine co-defendants remain charged.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a small cluster of plan member IDs from one employer worksite accounts for a disproportionate share of one provider's billings. Treatment dates for those members overlap with shifts recorded in the employer's timekeeping and duty-roster files. Members show identical service code sequences and visit counts across unrelated providers, suggesting scripted billing. Members and their dependents receive services at a frequency far above the plan's same-employer peer distribution. Providers bill members residing far outside the practice's NPPES service area with no referral record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Member-provider concentration: on member ID x rendering NPI, compute the count of paid visits and that member's share of the provider's annual claim volume; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Shift conflict: on member ID x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between billed service times and the employer timekeeping record; fires when overlap is positive; action claim suspension. 3) Recruiter cluster: on rendering NPI, compute the count of distinct members sharing a worksite code who each exceed the calibrated visit percentile; fires when that count exceeds the peer baseline; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Anthony Saloka (Amtrak employee/insurance beneficiary); Punson Figueroa (acupuncturist); Michael DeNicola (podiatrist)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Saloka, an Amtrak employee, took thousands of dollars in cash kickbacks from providers (including an acupuncturist and a podiatrist) in exchange for letting them use his personal and health insurance information to bill the Amtrak health plan for services never rendered or medically unnecessary; the plan paid over $11 million on fraudulent claims tied to the scheme's providers. Co-conspirator Figueroa was sentenced to 34 months; DeNicola's sentencing is pending.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a single member ID appears on acupuncture and podiatry claim lines from unrelated rendering NPIs on the same dates. Claim service dates fall on days the member's employer timekeeping file shows the member on shift far from the provider ZIP. The provider bills an implausible count of services per member per year versus plan norms in the remittance history. No referral or E/M encounter from any other treating NPI precedes the sustained treatment series in the member's claim history. A small cluster of members from one employer group accounts for most of the provider's paid volume in the plan enrolment file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Member super-utiliser: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the count of paid visit lines per rolling 90 days from claim history; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Employer-cluster concentration: on rendering NPI, compute the share of paid dollars attributable to a single employer group ID over distinct members; fires when concentration exceeds the provider's own trailing baseline; action postpay audit. 3) Shift conflict: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between billed service times and employer timekeeping shift hours; fires when overlap is greater than zero; action prepay edit.

State_County: New Jersey - Essex County (Newark); New Jersey - Burlington County (Willingboro); New Jersey - Monmouth County (Hazlet); New York - Queens County (Rockaway Park)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Amtrak employees took thousands of dollars in cash kickbacks from health care providers (including acupuncturist Punson Figueroa and podiatrist Michael DeNicola) in exchange for allowing their Amtrak employee health plan to be billed for services never rendered and not medically necessary; the plan paid over $11 million in fraudulent claims. Figueroa was previously sentenced to 34 months; sentencings of the five employee defendants remain pending.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, members show recurring acupuncture and podiatry lines with identical CPT sequences repeated on fixed weekly cadence across many dates. The rendering NPI's paid population is drawn almost entirely from one self-insured employer group in the plan eligibility file. Members' claim histories show no supporting diagnosis, imaging, or E/M encounter from any other NPI. Service dates conflict with employer timesheet and travel records for the member. Provider paid volume rose from near zero to top-decile within weeks of the first member enrolling, per remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cadence repetition: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the count of identical CPT-modifier line sets billed at regular intervals over 12 months; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Single-employer dependence: on rendering NPI, compute the ratio of paid dollars from one employer group to total plan dollars; fires when above the provider's trailing baseline; action postpay audit. 3) Attendance conflict: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between billed encounter time and employer timeclock hours; fires when overlap exceeds zero; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Alaska
FraudEntity: Dr. Claribel Tan (rheumatologist, clinic owner/operator); Daniel Tan (husband, office and management work for the clinic)
PayerName: More than 10 health insurance plans (not individually named)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; Upcoding; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: A rheumatologist and her husband billed more than 10 insurance plans for full injections of costly injectable medications while actually underdosing patients, substituting free samples, expired, or other patients' medication - claiming 4,829 units billed against only 369 units purchased - and also billed for longer office visits and services never provided, causing about $12.5 million in losses; they then overstated clinic drug expenses on 2014, 2015 and 2017 tax returns and failed to file returns for 2018-2021, costing the IRS about $4.25 million. Figures cover both defendants jointly, who each pleaded guilty and agreed to forfeit $10,471,106, pay $6,300,849 toward restitution and $1,855,144 in False Claims Act civil settlement; a linked release notes the doctor was later sentenced to 78 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, J-code units billed across all payers exceed units the practice purchased per wholesaler pedigree and 340B/distributor invoice data. Claim lines show the same infusion HCPCS at full-vial units for every patient with no JW drug-wastage or partial-dose variation. E/M levels billed by the rendering NPI skew to 99214/99215 far above same-specialty peers in remittance history. Some infusion dates of service conflict with the beneficiary's other claims placing them elsewhere. Manufacturer free-sample distribution records list the practice as a sample recipient for the same NDCs billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Purchase-to-billed reconciliation: on provider TIN x NDC/HCPCS per quarter, compute billed units minus units acquired from wholesaler pedigree data; fires when billed units exceed acquired units; action payment suspension and postpay audit. 2) E/M level skew: on rendering NPI, compute the share of 99214 and 99215 among all office E/M lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit on high-level codes. 3) Dose uniformity: on ordering NPI x J-code, compute the distinct-value count of billed unit quantities across beneficiaries; fires when that count is one despite varying patient weights; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Northwest Anesthesiology and Pain Services (NWAP) (anesthesiology service provider); Donald Carmichael (former president); Stacey Green (independent contractor manager); Remedy Physician Solutions (contractor company)
SchemeSummary: NWAP paid approximately $1.8 million in 'productivity' bonuses to its independently contracted pain management practices that were actually calculated from lab referral revenue minus costs, allegedly functioning as thinly veiled kickbacks for lab referrals, creating improper financial relationships under the Stark Law and tainting Medicare reimbursement claims; NWAP self-disclosed and paid $999,999.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment and credentialing, CMS-855A/855B ownership and contracting fields show pain practices under contract with the referral-receiving laboratory entity. Physician compensation schedules tie bonus amounts to laboratory referral volume, visible in Stark financial-relationship disclosures. At adjudication, contracted practices' referral rates for toxicology and clinical lab panels exceed same-specialty peers sharply. Lab claims cluster to a narrow set of ordering NPIs all sharing one corporate TIN in NPPES and PECOS. Ordering volume per practice moves in step with quarterly bonus payment dates in the entity's ledgers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral concentration graph: on laboratory NPI, compute the share of paid lab dollars originating from ordering NPIs sharing common ownership per CMS-855 fields; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action postpay audit. 2) Ordering intensity by affiliation: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute lab tests ordered per 100 patient encounters; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Stark disclosure mismatch: on provider TIN, compute the count of financial relationships present in contracts but absent from enrolment disclosure fields; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension pending enrolment correction.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Armand Ntchana (APRN, owner); Integrated Procare Services, LLC (psychiatric medication management practice); Brookside Residential Care Home, LLC; 134 Franklin Street Extension, LLC; Riverview Residential Care Home, LLC; 92 Lexington Avenue, LLC
State_County: Connecticut - Wethersfield; Connecticut - Danbury; Connecticut - New Haven
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Falsify certificate; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: Ntchana and his psychiatric medication management practice billed Medicare and Connecticut Medicaid listing Ntchana as rendering provider for services never provided - impossible hours per day, while he was out of the country or absent, for hospitalized or deceased patients, and for staff-called medication refills - creating false or no medical records; they also billed for patients seen by an unlicensed individual and billed both E/M and psychotherapy for visits where only E/M was provided. Settlement of $614,427.51 plus interest covers Ntchana and his related entities, with a two-year DSS suspension and permanent withdrawal from Connecticut Medicaid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, summed timed-service minutes for the rendering NPI on one date of service exceed 24 hours. Dates of service fall inside inpatient stays shown on the beneficiary's institutional claims for the same days. Some dates of service postdate the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File. Service dates coincide with border-crossing or travel records showing the rendering physician outside the country. Claim lines pair an E/M code with an add-on psychotherapy code on nearly every encounter, above same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total billed service minutes from CPT time definitions; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Inpatient and decedent conflict: on claim line, compute whether the date of service falls inside an inpatient admit-discharge span or after the Death Master File date; fires on any overlap; action claim suspension. 3) Psychotherapy add-on saturation: on rendering NPI, compute the ratio of E/M lines carrying 90833/90836 add-ons to total E/M lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (District of Maryland)
FraudEntity: James Vincent Campbell (CEO and founder of Axim Fringe Solutions Group, LLC); Axim Fringe Solutions Group, LLC (employee benefits processor)
SchemeSummary: Campbell's company processed employee benefits for federal contractors, receiving client funds meant for health insurance premiums and 401(k) contributions and pooling them in a master trust account before forwarding them to carriers and retirement accounts. Instead of taking only the contractual $40 per employee per month fee, he allegedly made 135 unauthorized withdrawals totaling $2,486,905 from the trust account, spending the money on big game hunting trips, taxidermy, jewelry, casino gambling, and payments to his girlfriend; eleven money laundering counts accompany the ERISA theft count.
WaysToIdentify: There is no claim submitted to a payer and no adjudication point, because the loss occurred inside a benefits trust account before premiums reached carriers. The nearest detection route is reconciliation of client remittance deposits against carrier premium receipts and 401(k) custodian postings for the same period. Carrier lapse and non-payment notices for covered employees are the earliest external symptom of diverted funds. Bank-level review of withdrawals from the master trust against the contractual per-employee-per-month fee schedule shows unauthorised transfers. Form 5500 filings and ERISA plan audits disclose trust balances inconsistent with participant contributions.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Trust reconciliation: on bank account x month, compute deposits received minus premiums remitted to carriers minus the contracted per-employee-per-month fee times enrolled headcount; fires when the residual is positive or withdrawals lack a matching carrier payment; action postpay audit by the plan fiduciary and referral to EBSA.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Kevin Lamorris McKenzie (Chief Operating Officer then CEO of Apache Behavioral Health Services); Corina Martinez (co-defendant, controlled Evolved Health Care Inc.); Helping Everyday Youth (HEDY); Evolved Health Care Inc. (EHI)
State_County: Arizona - Pima County (Tucson); Arizona - White Mountain Apache Tribe
SchemeSummary: As COO and then CEO of Apache Behavioral Health Services, McKenzie used two sham vendor contracts to divert tribal healthcare funds to himself: ABHS paid over $35 million to Helping Everyday Youth, which under a secret side agreement kicked back roughly $16 million to a shell company McKenzie controlled, and ABHS paid about $16.5 million to co-defendant Corina Martinez's Evolved Health Care Inc. under phony employee-referral contracts under which no employees were ever referred and no services performed, with proceeds split between them (cash, $800,000 of McKenzie's credit card bills, a $128,000 Rolls Royce and a $928,000 home). Figures reflect the combined scheme; the $33,155,701 restitution and forfeitures were ordered against McKenzie.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim and no adjudication point, because the loss occurred through vendor contracts paid from tribal healthcare grant funds. The nearest detection route is vendor-master screening comparing payee TINs and addresses against officer and executive home addresses in corporate registry filings. Accounts-payable analysis showing a single new vendor receiving an outsized share of disbursements without deliverables is the earliest symptom. Grant-recipient single audits under Uniform Guidance should test contracts for competitive procurement and documented services rendered.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Related-party vendor match: on bank account x payee TIN, compute the count of exact matches between vendor addresses or beneficial owners and organisation officers in state corporate registry and payroll files; fires when the count exceeds zero; action payment suspension and postpay audit by the grantor.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Alexandra Gehrke (owner of Apex Medical LLC and Viking Medical Consultants LLC); Jeffrey King (co-owner of graft application company); Apex Medical LLC; Viking Medical Consultants LLC
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial insurance plans
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gehrke's companies paid medically untrained sales reps kickbacks to find elderly and hospice patients with wounds and order oversized (4x6 cm or larger) amniotic wound grafts from a specific distributor, from which Gehrke received over $279 million in kickbacks; patients were then referred to King's company, whose nurse practitioners were directed to apply all ordered grafts regardless of medical necessity, and $1.21 billion in claims were billed to Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers, which paid $614.99 million. Restitution figures span both defendants ($614,990,420 and $605,690,110) plus over $410 million in agreed forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Q-code skin-substitute graft units per beneficiary and per wound far exceed same-specialty peer norms for the same wound size. Billed graft square centimetres exceed documented wound surface area on the ordering NPI's assessment records. Beneficiaries are concurrently on the hospice benefit per the hospice election record, making the graft duplicative. A small set of rendering NPIs order exclusively the largest-size grafts from one distributor NDC/HCPCS, with no size variation. Sales-representative payments and distributor rebate flows appear in Open Payments and CMS-855 ownership disclosures.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Graft area versus wound: on beneficiary x wound episode, compute total billed graft square centimetres from Q-code units divided by documented wound area; fires when the ratio exceeds one; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Size uniformity: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute the distinct-value count of graft sizes billed and the share of the largest size; fires when the largest size share is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 3) Hospice overlap: on claim line, compute whether the date of service falls inside an active hospice election period; fires on any overlap; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Mary Blakley (principal of medical clinic business, self-described 'Doctor Mary'); Fred Blakley (principal); Janmarie Lanzo (clinic worker/product seller)
State_County: Arizona - Lake Havasu City (defendants' base); clients throughout the United States
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: The Blakleys ran clinics charging clients nationwide roughly $300, usually in cash, for sham 'full body scans' performed on conventional ultrasound machines that they falsely claimed contained Mary Blakley's 'smart chip technology' capable of diagnosing, treating and curing cancer and other diseases; based on the bogus scan results they and Lanzo sold supplements, the cosmetic cream Aetheion, and the veterinary dewormer fenbendazole as human cancer treatments, bolstered by fabricated credentials (a nonexistent Karolinska Institutet Ph.D.) and concealment tactics such as claiming to be doing only research, using coded language, keeping no records, and requiring membership/confidentiality agreements. All three pleaded guilty; Fred Blakley also pleaded guilty to felon-in-possession of firearms.
WaysToIdentify: There is no insurance claim and no adjudication point, because patients paid roughly $300 in cash for the purported scans. The nearest detection route is state licence board and NPPES verification of the claimed doctoral credential against the issuing institution's registrar. FDA and state health department complaint intake on unapproved diagnostic devices and drug claims is the practical trigger. Sale of a veterinary anthelmintic for human cancer treatment is detectable through distributor purchase records and marketing content.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Credential verification: on rendering NPI or practitioner record, compute exact-match count between claimed degrees and issuing-institution registrar and state licence board files; fires when the match count is zero; action site visit and referral to state licensing authority.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Kevin Paul McMains (Army veteran, benefits claimant)
PayerName: Medicare; Department of Veterans Affairs; Social Security Administration
SchemeSummary: Over nearly 14 years McMains obtained more than $779,000 in VA disability benefits by submitting fabricated documents and making false statements to the VA and to medical professionals that post-traumatic stress left him unable to work or care for himself, and by falsely claiming he had been awarded a Purple Heart as proof of service-connected injury; the false disability status also qualified him for Social Security disability benefits and Medicare coverage. He was ordered to repay $378,380.82 to VA, $357,847.80 to SSA, and $43,451.56 to CMS.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the claimed Purple Heart award has no matching entry in DD-214 and service department award records. Medicare entitlement derives from an SSA disability determination that itself rests on the unverified VA rating, visible in the cross-agency eligibility file. Submitted supporting documents show altered fonts, duplicated letterhead, or issuing-office numbers absent from VA document registries. Claimed total inability to self-care conflicts with the beneficiary's own Medicare claims history showing no corresponding care utilisation. Earnings reported to SSA payroll records conflict with the sworn inability to work.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Award registry mismatch: on beneficiary claim file, compute exact-match count between claimed decorations and the service department award registry; fires when the count is zero; action claim suspension pending verification. 2) Utilisation-versus-severity gap: on beneficiary x year, compute the count of paid claims consistent with the certified disabling condition; fires when zero while a total-disability rating is in force; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Earnings conflict: on beneficiary x quarter, compute reported wage earnings from SSA payroll data during certified unemployability; fires when earnings exceed the program threshold; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: John R. Manning (licensed medical doctor)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Dr. Manning worked for multiple 'telemedicine' companies and signed doctor orders/prescriptions for durable medical equipment, topical creams, and cancer genetic tests based on only a brief conversation with patients or no conversation at all, in exchange for over $812,000 in kickbacks; the orders caused at least $41 million in false Medicare claims, of which Medicare paid over $19 million. He was ordered to pay $19,780,565.44 restitution plus $812,303.41 forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI has no prior or contemporaneous E/M claim with the beneficiary before the DME, cream, or CGx order. One ordering NPI signs orders for beneficiaries across dozens of states within a single week per claim ZIPs. Ordered items span unrelated categories - braces, topical compounds, and hereditary cancer panels - from unrelated supplier NPIs. Telehealth encounter durations, where billed, sum to more than 24 hours in a day for that rendering NPI. Beneficiaries have no cancer diagnosis in claim history supporting hereditary cancer panel orders.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days since the last E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states, distinct supplier NPIs, and distinct HCPCS categories ordered; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) CGx indication check: on beneficiary x CPT 81162-series line, compute the count of cancer or family-history diagnoses in 12-month claim history; fires when the count is zero; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Athira Pharma Inc.; Leen Kawas (former CEO)
PayerName: National Institutes of Health; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Athira Pharma failed to disclose to NIH and the HHS Office of Research Integrity allegations that its former CEO had falsified and manipulated scientific images in her dissertation and published papers, which were cited in NIH grant applications (including a grant NIH funded in 2019) and in progress reports and institutional assurances; the company paid $4,068,698 to resolve FCA claims brought by a qui tam whistleblower who received $203,434.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, because the funds were NIH research grant awards rather than reimbursed services. The nearest detection route is comparing images in grant applications and progress reports against prior published figures using duplication-detection software at peer review. Institutional assurance certifications should be cross-checked against Office of Research Integrity inquiry and misconduct disclosures for named key personnel.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Research-integrity disclosure check: on grant application x key-personnel identifier, compute the count of open or resolved ORI and institutional misconduct allegations not disclosed in the certification fields; fires when the count exceeds zero; action award suspension pending inquiry.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: press release announcing the appointment of Michael DiGiacomo as U.S. Attorney for the Western District of New York; it only mentions health care fraud among his past prosecution areas generally.
WaysToIdentify: There is no fraud allegation, no claim, and no adjudication point in this document. It is a personnel announcement naming a United States Attorney, not a case with a payer or loss amount. No detection route exists because no billing conduct is described.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Austin Emergency Center, LLC; Austin ER, LLC; AEC ER 4, LLC; Pahala Ventures, LLC; AEC Physicians, PLLC; AEC Pflugerville, LLC (collectively 'Austin Emergency Center', operator of standalone emergency medical facilities)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Austin Emergency Center allegedly charged FEHBP more for certain COVID-19 tests than it charged cash-paying patients (June 18, 2020 - April 2, 2021) and up-coded evaluation and management services billed for drive-through COVID-19 screening (April 13, 2020 - April 2, 2021), collecting inflated reimbursements from the federal employee health program.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the billed charge for the COVID-19 test HCPCS exceeds the facility's cash price posted under the hospital price transparency file. E/M levels billed alongside drive-through screening skew to high levels despite place-of-service indicating parking lot or off-campus screening. Encounter documentation lacks the history, exam, and decision elements required for the billed E/M level. The facility's E/M level distribution shifted sharply upward from its own trailing pre-pandemic baseline. Nearly every test claim carries an accompanying E/M line, above same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cash-price parity: on claim line x HCPCS, compute billed charge minus the provider's published cash price for the same test; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit and repricing. 2) Screening E/M upcode: on rendering NPI x place of service, compute the share of level 4 and 5 E/M lines paired with a COVID-19 test code; fires when above the provider's trailing baseline and above same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Bundled E/M rate: on provider TIN x month, compute the ratio of E/M lines to test lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer facilities; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Mark Malone (pain management doctor, founder of Advanced Pain Care); Advanced Pain Care and related entities including Mark Malone M.D., P.A., Round Rock Surgery Center, LLC, APC-Amarillo Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Killeen Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Waco Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Southwest Surgical Operating Company, LLC, Shoal Creek Pharmacy Operations, LLC, Palo Duro Pharmacy Operations, LLC, APC Pharmacy, LLC, Advanced Anesthesiology, Advanced Health Holdings, LLC, Advanced RX Pharmacy, APC Investments LLC, APC360 LLC, 6000 South Mopac APC LLC, MMJ Partners, LP, MMC Holdco, LLC
State_County: Texas - Austin, Amarillo, Waco, and Houston areas
PayerName: Medicare; Texas Medicaid; TRICARE; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: The government alleged the pain practice billed Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and FEHBP for concurrent presumptive and definitive urine drug tests on the same patient on the same date of service without reviewing presumptive results to determine whether definitive testing was medically necessary, and billed the VA for definitive drug testing using separate CPT codes for individual analytes (CPT 803XX series) rather than appropriate codes, between January 3, 2017 and December 31, 2021.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, presumptive (80305-80307) and definitive (G0480-G0483) urine drug test codes appear for the same beneficiary on the same date of service. Definitive testing volume per patient shows no reduction following negative presumptive results in the beneficiary's claim history. The VA claims use individual analyte CPT 803XX codes instead of the definitive drug class code set, an unbundling pattern. Every patient of the ordering NPI receives the same maximum analyte panel, with no distinct-value variation. Definitive test frequency per patient per year exceeds same-specialty peer norms for pain management.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Same-day reflex violation: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of presumptive and definitive UDT codes both present; fires when both appear without a documented reflex justification; action prepay edit. 2) Analyte unbundling: on claim line, compute the count of individual 803XX analyte codes billed for one specimen; fires when that count exceeds one where a definitive class code exists; action prepay edit and rebundle. 3) Panel uniformity: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute the distinct-value count of analytes ordered across beneficiaries; fires when panel size is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Thomasina E. Amponsah (unlicensed individual posing as registered nurse/licensed practical nurse)
State_County: Maryland - Baltimore County; Maryland - Baltimore City
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Amponsah, who never held any nursing license, used stolen Maryland and Florida nursing license numbers and duplicated license images belonging to two identity victims, plus fabricated resumes and false claims of a Florida State University nursing degree, to be hired as an RN/LPN at no less than 40 Maryland facilities (mostly skilled nursing facilities, plus nursing homes and a Baltimore City public school) directly and through a staffing agency; the facilities billed Medicare and Medicaid for services she purportedly rendered and she earned at least $100,000 in wages. She also forged a physician's signature on a controlled-substance form for Tramadol faxed to a pharmacy and falsified medical records after failing to administer prescribed medications. A later release in the document notes she was sentenced to 38 months.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, the presented nursing licence number in the state board file resolves to a different name and date of birth than the applicant. The same licence number appears simultaneously in staffing rosters at facilities in two states on overlapping shift dates. Submitted licence images are pixel-identical duplicates of another licensee's card in the board's verification portal. Claimed nursing degree has no matching record in the university registrar or National Student Clearinghouse. Controlled-substance faxes to the pharmacy carry a prescriber signature not matching the DEA registrant's on-file specimen.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence identity match: on staff credential record, compute exact-match count between licensee name, date of birth, and licence number in the state board file; fires when any field mismatches; action claim suspension for services attributed to that staff member. 2) Concurrent-licence use: on licence number x date, compute the count of distinct facility NPIs reporting shifts and total scheduled hours; fires when hours exceed 24 or facilities are geographically impossible; action site visit. 3) Prescriber signature verification: on pharmacy claim x prescriber DEA number, compute match between the faxed order signature and the registrant's on-file specimen and prescribing history for that drug; fires on mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Thomasina E. Amponsah (unlicensed individual posing as registered nurse/licensed practical nurse)
State_County: Maryland - Baltimore County; Maryland - Baltimore City
SchemeSummary: Amponsah used two stolen nursing license numbers and duplicated license images, plus fabricated resumes and educational histories, to obtain employment as an RN/LPN at no less than 40 Maryland facilities (mostly skilled nursing facilities) and a Baltimore City public school, earning over $145,000 in wages; the facilities billed Medicare and Medicaid for the services she purportedly provided. She also forged a physician's signature on a Tramadol prescription faxed to a pharmacy and falsified medical records to conceal unadministered medications.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, primary-source verification against the state board licence file returns a different licensee name for the presented number. The same licence number is reported by multiple unrelated facility NPIs on overlapping payroll periods in staffing agency records. Uploaded licence images match another licensee's document byte-for-byte in the verification portal. Claimed nursing education has no confirming record at the named school registrar. Medication administration records show documented doses with no matching pharmacy dispensing or eMAR scan event.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Primary-source credential mismatch: on staff credential record, compute exact-match count of name, licence number, and expiry against the state board file; fires when any field mismatches; action payment suspension for affected service lines. 2) Licence concurrency: on licence number x week, compute the count of distinct employer NPIs and total reported hours; fires when hours exceed physically possible working hours; action site visit. 3) MAR-to-dispense gap: on beneficiary x drug x date, compute documented administrations minus pharmacy dispensed units; fires when administrations exceed dispensed units; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Matthew Hightower; Davon Carter (shooter); Clifton Mosley (accomplice)
SchemeSummary: Hightower, then under federal indictment for a health care fraud scheme and a murder, conspired from jail to kill a federal witness who had given law enforcement information about the health care fraud scheme; the hired shooter killed the witness's neighbor, Latrina Ashburne, by mistake. The document provides no details of the underlying health care fraud billing, payer, or amount.
WaysToIdentify: The document describes witness retaliation and homicide, with no billing detail, payer, or adjudication point disclosed. No claim field, code, or date of service is available on which a payer edit could act. The nearest non-claims route is payment suspension on the underlying indicted provider's NPI under the credible-allegation-of-fraud authority once charges are filed.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Indictment-triggered suspension: on provider NPI, compute the count of pending federal health care fraud indictments matched from court and OIG exclusion feeds; fires when the count exceeds zero; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Samrat Mukherjee (licensed paramedic falsely posing as a medical doctor)
State_County: Louisiana - East Baton Rouge Parish (Baton Rouge)
PayerName: Medicaid (Louisiana); Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: A licensed paramedic created a fake medical degree and residency match letter to pose as a physician, obtaining physician privileges and badges at hospitals and at Acadian Ambulance, then called in and wrote prescriptions for himself and others while falsely claiming to be two doctors (including forging an oncologist's signature on an Ondansetron-ODT prescription), causing pharmacies to submit reimbursement claims to Medicaid and BCBSLA.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, the presented medical degree and residency match letter have no matching record with the school registrar or NRMP. At claim adjudication, the prescriber NPI on the pharmacy claim has no active state medical licence or DEA registration in the board file. Prescriptions written by the impersonated oncologist's NPI originate from a pharmacy and fax number outside that prescriber's practice location in NPPES. The prescriber NPI appears on the pharmacy claim while the drug class is far outside that NPI's historical prescribing mix. The same individual is listed as prescriber for himself as the beneficiary on dispensed claims.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber licence verification: on pharmacy claim line, compute match between the prescriber NPI and an active state licence and DEA registration for the drug schedule; fires on any registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Self-prescribing: on claim line, compute whether prescriber NPI identity matches the beneficiary identity fields; fires when they match; action claim suspension. 3) Prescribing-mix anomaly: on prescriber NPI x drug class, compute the share of scripts outside the NPI's trailing 12-month therapeutic mix; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Med-Surg Physician Group Inc. (medical practice); Oluyemisi Sangodeyi, M.D. (owner)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (West Virginia Medicaid / Bureau for Medical Services)
SchemeSummary: Med-Surg routinely appended HCPCS code Q3014 (telehealth originating site facility fee) to Medicare and Medicaid claims for telehealth visits where the patient was at home, a location for which the facility fee is not payable, collecting $76,191.35; the practice and its owner also falsely certified compliance with program requirements and agreed to pay $152,382.70 to resolve FCA allegations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, HCPCS Q3014 appears on claims whose paired professional line carries place of service 10, patient home. The originating-site facility fee is billed by an entity that is not the site where the patient was physically located per the encounter record. Q3014 lines appear on nearly every telehealth encounter for the billing TIN, above same-specialty peers. Q3014 volume rose from zero to steady state after the telehealth expansion date in the provider's remittance history. The provider's compliance certification on enrolment conflicts with the sustained non-payable code pattern.
