FeaturesToCreate: 1) Originating-site place-of-service conflict: on claim line, compute whether Q3014 is billed with a paired telehealth professional line coded place of service 02 or 10; fires when the home place of service is present; action prepay edit. 2) Facility-fee attachment rate: on provider NPI x month, compute the ratio of Q3014 lines to total telehealth encounters; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 3) Recovery scope: on provider TIN, compute the sum of paid Q3014 dollars where the paired encounter place of service is non-facility; fires when the sum exceeds zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Miguel Saravia (CEO of Dana Group Associates; former COO of Prime Behavioral Health)
SchemeSummary: Saravia directed untrained staff to enter CPT codes for therapy services that were never provided and to upcode psychotherapy visit codes, submitting false claims to health care benefit programs for treatment not rendered or more complex than delivered; he was sentenced to 3.5 months in prison and ordered to pay $561,141.89 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare psychotherapy minutes billed under CPT 90837, 90834 and 90832 per rendering NPI per date against a 24-hour day. The rendering NPI on the claim line is not held by a licensed clinician in the state licence board file. Session codes cluster almost entirely at the highest-duration code versus same-specialty peers in remittance history. Beneficiaries show no corroborating claims such as medication management or referral encounters around the billed session dates. Requested progress notes on ADR lack timed start and stop entries matching the billed duration code.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible therapy day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed billed minutes implied by CPT 90832/90834/90837/90853 plus E/M time; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or the licensed clinician's scheduled hours; action prepay edit. 2) Duration code skew: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the share of psychotherapy lines billed at 90837 over all timed psychotherapy lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR), then postpay audit. 3) Unlicensed renderer: on claim line, match rendering NPI against the state licence board file and NPPES taxonomy for the billed CPT; fires on exact registry mismatch or expired licence at date of service; action claim suspension.designs

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Hemal Patel
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Patel allegedly received kickbacks for referring home care patients to home care agencies, forged physician signatures on eligibility certification forms, and used individuals' personal identifying information without their knowledge to enroll them for home care services while they were living out of the country; Medicaid was billed roughly $1,069,384 for home care services never provided.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, cross-check dates of service against border-crossing or absence indicators plus zero other in-state claims for the beneficiary in that window. The certifying physician NPI on the plan of care has no E/M claim with that beneficiary before the certification date. One certifying NPI signs plans of care for beneficiaries clustered at a handful of referring agencies. EVV visit records are absent or show identical clock-in times across many beneficiaries on the same day. Beneficiaries deny enrolment when contacted from the payer's own beneficiary-verification mailing tied to remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Absent-beneficiary billing: on beneficiary x month, compute the count of paid home-care visit lines while the beneficiary has zero other claims of any type for consecutive months; fires when visit lines exist with no corroborating utilisation across the lookback; action claim suspension, then postpay audit. 2) Certifier-encounter gap: on ordering NPI x beneficiary, compute days between plan-of-care certification date and the nearest E/M claim between them; fires when no encounter exists in the required lookback; action prepay edit. 3) Referral concentration: on certifying NPI x agency TIN, compute the share of that certifier's home-health certifications going to one agency; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Ulma Form Works, Inc. (manufacturer and supplier of concrete formwork, shoring and temporary scaffolding systems)
SchemeSummary: Ulma Form Works applied for and received a $2 million PPP loan in January 2021 by falsely certifying it had no more than 300 employees, when counting its affiliates and their foreign-based employees it exceeded the limit; it then obtained full forgiveness of the loan plus accrued interest, and resolved the resulting FCA qui tam suit for $2,902,795 (relator share $290,279).
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point in this loan-forgiveness scheme. The nearest detection route is matching the borrower's SBA employee-count certification against IRS Form 941 payroll filings and state unemployment wage records. A second route is linking the borrower EIN to parent and affiliate EINs through Dun & Bradstreet or SEC ownership data to aggregate worldwide headcount before forgiveness.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a pre-forgiveness affiliation check: on borrower EIN, compute aggregated employee counts across all commonly owned EINs from payroll filings and corporate ownership records; fires when the aggregate exceeds the programme size standard; action loan-forgiveness hold and audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Delaware
FraudEntity: BioReference Health LLC, formerly BioReference Laboratories Inc. (clinical laboratory); OPKO Health Inc. (parent company)
SchemeSummary: The government alleged that BioReference routinely performed and billed federal health care programs for the more expensive complete blood count (CBC) with automated white blood cell differential test when providers had actually ordered the cheaper CBC without differential, making the tests billed medically unnecessary and unordered. Resolved via a $704,349 False Claims Act settlement from a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $112,694.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare the CPT billed, 85025, against the test actually ordered on the referring provider's electronic requisition or order record. A single laboratory NPI bills 85025 for nearly all CBCs while peers show a mix with 85027. The ordering NPI's other laboratory orders never include differentials, contradicting the code billed on its behalf. Differential lines appear without any diagnosis on the claim supporting a white-cell evaluation. Remittance history shows a step change in the 85025 share immediately after a laboratory information system or billing vendor change.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-to-code mismatch: on claim line, compare the billed CPT (85025 versus 85027) against the ordering NPI's requisition record for that accession; fires on exact mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Differential saturation: on laboratory NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of 85025 lines to all CBC lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers and above the lab's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Orderer contradiction: on ordering NPI x laboratory NPI, compute the share of CBCs billed with differential versus that orderer's rate at other labs; fires when the gap exceeds the calibrated percentile; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Armen Muradyan (owner/operator of Genex Laboratories Inc.); Genex Laboratories Inc.
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Muradyan, barred by Medicare from submitting claims, paid a long-time friend $2,000/month to pose as owner of his Burbank blood-testing lab Genex Laboratories and to file the Medicare enrollment paperwork; Medicare reimbursements for blood testing were wired to bank accounts in the nominee's name but controlled by Muradyan, and Genex income was reported on the nominee's returns, evading about $11.2 million in taxes on roughly $23.9 million of unreported income. He also obtained a $99,900 SBA EIDL loan by falsely claiming his entity GenMed had employees and $800,000 in 2019 income.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, screen the CMS-855B owner and managing-employee names against the OIG LEIE and CMS preclusion and revocation files. The listed owner's SSN and address on the CMS-855B match an excluded individual's known addresses in prior enrolment records. The lab's electronic funds transfer bank account has previously received payments for a revoked provider NPI. The nominee owner has no prior laboratory ownership, licence or PECOS history consistent with running a clinical lab. A site visit finds the enrolled owner absent and the excluded party directing operations at the listed address.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Nominee owner graph: on bank account and address, compute the count of distinct enrolled provider NPIs and owners sharing the same EFT account, phone or practice address across CMS-855 records; fires when any linked party appears on OIG LEIE or a revocation list; action claim suspension at enrolment. 2) Excluded-party proximity: on owner SSN x enrolment, compute exact matches to LEIE, preclusion and prior-revocation identifiers including former addresses; fires on any exact registry match; action enrolment denial and site visit. 3) New-lab ramp: on laboratory NPI x month, compute paid amount growth against the provider's own trailing baseline since enrolment; fires when growth exceeds the calibrated percentile for newly enrolled labs; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Danielle Molinari
SchemeSummary: Molinari joined a conspiracy to obtain medically unnecessary oxycodone prescriptions, filled them, and then resold the pills to another individual for cash, distributing approximately 4,665 oxycodone pills between February 2019 and March 2023.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute morphine milligram equivalents per beneficiary per day across oxycodone NDCs on paid pharmacy claims. The beneficiary fills the same oxycodone NDC at multiple pharmacy NPIs within overlapping days-supply windows. Prescriptions come from one prescriber NPI whose oxycodone share exceeds same-specialty peers in the payer's remittance history. Fills are cash-and-carry or early refills with the gap in days far below the prior days supply. Pharmacy purchase volumes in ARCOS or wholesaler pedigree data exceed dispensed claim volume for the same NDC.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Overlapping opioid supply: on beneficiary x opioid NDC class, compute overlapping days-supply across distinct pharmacy NPIs and prescriber NPIs in a rolling 90 days; fires when overlap days exceed zero with more than one prescriber; action prepay edit. 2) Early refill gap: on beneficiary x NDC, compute days between fill date and prior fill date minus prior days supply; fires when the gap is negative beyond the plan's refill tolerance; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Prescriber opioid concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute share of paid prescriptions that are Schedule II opioids and mean daily MME; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Belinda Jo Juarez (majority owner and CEO of Superior Home Health Service); Superior Home Health Service
SchemeSummary: The owner/CEO of a San Antonio home health company continued deducting health insurance premiums from employee paychecks after she stopped remitting payments to the insurers (leading insurers to cancel coverage), without telling employees their coverage was inactive, and also withheld federal payroll taxes from paychecks without remitting them to the IRS. She was ordered to pay $617,738.65 restitution to former employees and $3,667,098.88 restitution to the IRS, plus a $20,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim submitted to a payer and no adjudication point in this payroll-remittance scheme. The nearest detection route is reconciling insurer premium receipts against the employer's payroll deduction records and IRS Form 941 filings. A further route is the group insurer's own lapse notice file, which shows coverage cancelled for non-payment while member enrolment remained active.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a coverage-lapse notification rule: on employer group policy, compute days between premium due date and receipt plus the count of active members; fires when a policy lapses with active members, triggering direct member notice and IRS payroll-deposit referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
FraudEntity: Jacobo Melcer (owner/operator of two durable medical equipment companies)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Melcer owned two DME companies that billed Medicare $5,885,382 (paid $3,479,303) for orthotic braces, paying over $227,000 in kickbacks to companies for referrals of Medicare beneficiaries and DME prescriptions signed by physicians with no legitimate doctor-patient relationship or examination; he also sold the two DME companies to a co-conspirator to place them under a nominee owner and conceal true ownership from Medicare after the co-conspirator was suspended as a provider.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on the L-code brace claims has no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. Beneficiary residence ZIPs sit far outside the supplier's service area declared on its CMS-855S enrolment. At enrolment, the new CMS-855S owner is linked by address, phone or bank account to a suspended or revoked supplier NPI. A small set of ordering NPIs accounts for nearly all of the supplier's brace orders across many states. Marketing-company payments appear as the graph link between referral-source TINs and multiple supplier NPIs in ownership disclosures.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when none exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Ownership-change succession: on supplier NPI, compute the count of shared identifiers (address, phone, EFT bank account, managing employee) with previously revoked or suspended supplier NPIs in CMS-855 records; fires on any exact match; action claim suspension and site visit. 3) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Athira Pharma, Inc. (Bothell, WA biopharmaceutical company); Leen Kawas (former Chief Executive Officer)
PayerName: National Institutes of Health (NIH) / U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Athira Pharma allegedly obtained NIH research grants for age-related cognitive decline studies (including a grant funded in 2019) while failing to disclose to NIH and the HHS Office of Research Integrity, in grant applications, Research Progress Performance Reports, Small Business Organization Statements and annual reports, that its then-CEO Leen Kawas had allegedly falsified and manipulated scientific images in her doctoral dissertation and in published papers cited in those applications. The company paid $4,068,698 to resolve False Claims Act allegations raised in a qui tam suit, with the relator receiving $203,434.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no claim adjudication point in this research-grant scheme. The nearest detection route is matching key-personnel names in grant applications and Research Performance Progress Reports against ORI misconduct findings and PubPeer or journal retraction notices. A second route is automated image-duplication screening of figures in publications cited in the application and in the PI's dissertation before award or continuation funding.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a pre-award integrity screen: on grant application x key-personnel name, compute matches to ORI findings, retraction databases and image-forensics hits on cited publications; fires on any match; action award hold pending institutional certification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Niranjan Mittal (cardiologist, operator of Brooklyn medical clinic)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Mittal disguised kickbacks as office-space 'rent' payments to other providers to induce patient referrals to his Brooklyn clinic, then had staff order unnecessary diagnostic tests and office visits and fabricate patients' recorded symptoms to justify medically unnecessary peripheral vascular interventional procedures; insurers paid over $40 million between 2016 and 2023 for claims tied to those referred patients.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute each referring NPI's share of the clinic's peripheral vascular procedure volume and compare against rent payments disclosed in ownership and lease records. The clinic's ratio of diagnostic angiography to therapeutic atherectomy CPT lines per beneficiary exceeds same-specialty peers. Repeat interventions on the same limb and vessel recur within short intervals for many beneficiaries. Documentation obtained on ADR shows identical templated symptom language across unrelated beneficiaries. Non-invasive vascular study results in prior claims do not meet the severity thresholds required by the payer's coverage policy.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral-payment graph: on referring NPI x clinic TIN, compute the count of referred beneficiaries alongside the existence of a lease or rent payment between the two entities from ownership disclosures; fires when both are present and referral count is above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit. 2) Repeat revascularisation: on beneficiary x limb-laterality modifier, compute the count of atherectomy or angioplasty CPT lines and the gap in days between them; fires when repeats occur inside the payer's medically expected interval; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Intervention conversion rate: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of therapeutic interventions to diagnostic vascular studies; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Zakia Khan (owner of Happy Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., a home health care fiscal intermediary, and Tanwee Services Inc.); Seema Memon (employee); Amran Hashmi (employee)
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn), Coney Island
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Khan owned two Coney Island social adult day care centers and a home health fiscal intermediary; she and her marketers paid cash kickbacks and bribes to Medicaid recipients to enroll, then billed Medicaid roughly $68 million for social adult day care services that were either never provided or were induced by the kickbacks, laundering the proceeds through multiple business entities (including Tanwee Services Inc.) to generate the cash for the bribes. Khan agreed to forfeit $5 million including properties and over $300,000 in seized cash and gold; two employee co-defendants also pleaded guilty and eleven others await trial.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute daily attendance units billed per centre against the licensed capacity on the state adult-day-care licence file. Attendance rosters and sign-in sheets requested on ADR show identical signatures or times across many enrollees. Enrolled beneficiaries live far outside plausible travel distance from the centre address in NPPES and eligibility files. The same beneficiaries appear simultaneously on home-care EVV visit records and adult-day-care attendance on the same hours. Ownership disclosures link the centre, the fiscal intermediary and marketing entities to shared owners and bank accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Capacity overflow: on centre NPI x date of service, compute distinct beneficiaries with billed attendance units against licensed capacity in the state licence file; fires when count exceeds capacity; action prepay edit. 2) Concurrent-service overlap: on beneficiary x date, compute overlapping minutes between adult-day-care attendance units and EVV-recorded home-care visits; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero; action claim suspension. 3) Common-control network: on owner identity, compute the count of distinct billing NPIs and shared bank accounts across centres, intermediaries and marketing TINs; fires when the graph degree is above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action site visit and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Avanish Kumar Jha (co-owner, Dhrishti Pharma International); Rajnish Kumar Jha (co-owner, Dhrishti Pharma International); Dhrishti Pharma International
SchemeSummary: Two brothers operating Dhrishti Pharma International in India advertised prescription drugs online to U.S. buyers and shipped counterfeit and adulterated medicines, including vials labeled as the cancer drug Keytruda that actually contained over-the-counter heartburn medicine and no active ingredient; payments came via wire transfers, direct money exchanges and U.S.-based intermediaries collecting cash, with packaging designed to evade customs detection. Each brother was sentenced to 30 months and fined $50,000 (total $100,000), with $81,596 restitution to Merck to be considered later.
WaysToIdentify: There is no US payer claim and no adjudication point for these direct-to-consumer counterfeit shipments. The nearest detection route is customs and international mail screening for parcels from the seller's shipper accounts, matched to manufacturer serialisation and DSCSA pedigree data for the branded NDC. A second route is manufacturer surveillance of online pharmacy advertising plus payment-processor and money-transfer records tied to the seller's US intermediaries.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a serialisation check: on package serial number, compute a match against the manufacturer's DSCSA pedigree and issuance file; fires when the serial is unissued or duplicated, triggering seizure and manufacturer alert.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Willie F. Murray, Jr. (registered agent and manager of Lab Tess, LLC); Lab Tess, LLC
State_County: Florida - Broward County (West Park); Florida - Charlotte County (Punta Gorda); Florida - Palm Beach County (Belle Glade, South Bay)
PayerName: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) COVID-19 Uninsured Program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Murray used Lab Tess, LLC, which provided no actual COVID-19 testing, to submit more than 126,000 fraudulent reimbursement claims to HRSA for COVID-19 testing of uninsured individuals, using personal identifying information of Florida state prisoners, deceased persons, and people falsely reported as tested at homeless shelters and electrical substations, collecting about $5,671,611 that he partly used to buy South Florida real estate.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, match each claimed patient identifier against the Death Master File for a date of death before the date of service. Claimed patients' identifiers match state department-of-corrections incarceration rosters covering the service dates. Service-location addresses on the claim resolve to non-clinical sites such as shelters or utility substations in address validation. One newly enrolled laboratory NPI submits claim volumes far above same-specialty peers within weeks of enrolment. The lab holds no CLIA certificate covering the COVID-19 test procedure billed at those dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Deceased and incarcerated patients: on claim line, compute whether the date of service falls after the Death Master File date of death or inside a corrections incarceration span; fires on any exact registry match; action prepay edit. 2) Testing-volume implausibility: on laboratory NPI x day, compute distinct beneficiaries billed against CLIA-certified testing capacity and staffing on file; fires when count exceeds documented capacity or above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action payment suspension. 3) Non-clinical service address: on claim line, compute geocode match of the service facility address to residential, shelter or utility parcels; fires on exact mismatch with the enrolled practice location; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Favorite Home Care, LLC; Larry Sakson (co-owner); Olena Radionovsky (co-owner); Marina Sakson (employee/manager); Michael Radionovsky (employee/manager)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the owners and managers of Favorite Home Care each personally placed electronic visit verification calls attesting they were delivering home care services to clients when they were not present, after which the company billed Medicaid and a Medicaid MCO and received payment for services never rendered.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare EVV caller telephone numbers and device IDs against the caregiver of record in the agency's staff roster. EVV clock-ins for many beneficiaries originate from one phone number within overlapping minutes. The attesting caregiver is a listed owner or manager in the agency's CMS-855 and state Medicaid provider file. GPS or caller-ID location on the EVV visit record does not match the beneficiary's address on file. Billed visit units exceed the EVV-verified minutes for the same beneficiary and date.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) One-phone many-visits: on EVV caller phone number x date, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with clock-ins and any overlapping visit minutes; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero or distinct beneficiaries exceed a physically feasible daily route; action claim suspension. 2) Owner-as-caregiver: on rendering caregiver identity x agency NPI, compute exact matches to owners and managing employees in CMS-855 and state enrolment; fires when the attesting caregiver is an owner and visit volume is above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) EVV-to-claim reconciliation: on claim line, compute billed units minus EVV-verified minutes converted to units; fires when the difference exceeds zero; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Arkan Fadhel (owner, Queen City Transportation, Inc.); Queen City Transportation, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Fadhel, owner of a non-emergency Medicaid transportation company that drove beneficiaries mainly to methadone clinics, submitted false attestation records to Medical Answering Service claiming rides that never occurred and billing group rides as if each passenger had been transported separately, causing a Medicaid loss over $250,000. He was sentenced to three years supervised release with 12 months home incarceration, 400 hours community service, $781,186.80 forfeiture and $250,000 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare trip attestations in the transportation broker's record against the beneficiary's same-day methadone or clinic encounter claims. Multiple beneficiaries share identical pickup times and destinations yet are billed as separate single-passenger trips. Driver-level trip counts per day exceed feasible driving hours given mileage and trip durations on the attestation file. Vehicle and driver licence records show the assigned driver unlicensed or the vehicle uninsured on the service date. Billed mileage exceeds the point-to-point distance between the beneficiary address and the clinic address.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Group-ride unbundling: on vehicle ID x date x time window, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries billed as separate trips with overlapping pickup minutes and identical destination; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented separate trip; action prepay edit. 2) No-clinic trip: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the existence of any clinic or provider encounter claim on the trip date; fires when no destination encounter exists; action claim suspension. 3) Driver-hours impossibility: on driver NPI or driver ID x date, compute summed trip durations and mileage-implied drive time; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or licensed duty limits; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Maureen Holleran (workers' compensation claims handler for Insurance Company 1)
PayerName: Insurance Company 1 (unnamed Canadian-headquartered workers' compensation insurer)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: As a remote workers' compensation claims handler, Holleran entered more than 1,200 fabricated claims (fictitious lost wages, medical supply and copay reimbursements) each kept under her $2,000 no-approval authority, using fake claimant email accounts to register in the insurer's client portal and route roughly $2.37 million in payments to her own bank accounts; she failed to report about $1,592,095 of the embezzled funds on 2020-2022 tax returns, with about $545,792 in tax due, and was sentenced to 18 months for filing a false tax return.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute the distribution of payment amounts per handler against the individual approval-authority threshold in the claims system. Many claimant records share one bank account or routing number in the disbursement file. Claimant portal registrations use email domains and IP addresses that repeat across unrelated claim numbers. Paid reimbursement claims have no matching employer first-report-of-injury or provider invoice in the claim file. One adjuster's paid-claim count and dollar total exceed the trailing baseline of same-role peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Threshold clustering: on adjuster ID x month, compute the share of approved payments falling just below the individual authority limit; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-role peers; action payment suspension. 2) Shared payee account: on bank account number, compute the count of distinct claimant IDs and claim numbers receiving disbursements; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented common payee; action prepay edit. 3) Orphan reimbursement: on claim line, compute the existence of a matching provider invoice, NPI or employer injury report; fires when none exists for the payment; action documentation request and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Zaven Yeghiazaryan (business owner)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: Defendant used shell companies and false identities to defraud the SBA's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program and the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance program, and also participated in a scheme to defraud Medicaid; he pleaded guilty to 13 counts including conspiracy, health care fraud, wire fraud and money laundering, with restitution of $334,905.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, screen the applicant's identity and business EIN against Secretary of State registration age and the Death Master File for stolen identities. Shell entities share addresses, phones and bank accounts across multiple provider enrolments and loan applications. The Medicaid billing NPI submits claims from an entity with no licensed staff listed in state licence board files. Loan and unemployment applications reuse the same routing and account numbers as the Medicaid EFT record. New provider claim volume ramps abruptly with no prior remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Shared-identifier shell graph: on bank account, address and phone, compute the count of distinct enrolled NPIs, EINs and benefit applications sharing each identifier; fires when the count exceeds one without documented common ownership; action claim suspension and site visit. 2) Synthetic identity screen: on CMS-855 applicant SSN, compute exact matches to the Death Master File and to entity registrations dated after the application; fires on any match; action enrolment denial. 3) New-provider ramp: on billing NPI x month, compute paid amount versus the provider's own trailing baseline since enrolment; fires when growth is above the calibrated percentile for new enrollees; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Zaven Yeghiazaryan (business owner)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendant used shell companies and false identities to defraud government programs, including the SBA's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance, and also admitted participating in a scheme to defraud Medicaid; proceeds were laundered. Ordered to pay $118,205.94 restitution plus $151,300 in fines and assessments.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, match the applicant identity on the CMS-855 against the Death Master File and stolen-identity indicators before an NPI is allowed to bill. Multiple shell entity enrolments share one EFT bank account or mail-drop address in the payer's disbursement file. The billing entity has no licensed practitioners listed in the state licence board file for the services billed. Claims begin immediately after enrolment with no prior remittance history for the NPI. The same account receives both Medicaid remittances and government benefit disbursements.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Shell-entity linkage: on EFT bank account, compute the count of distinct provider NPIs, TINs and benefit programme payees sharing it; fires when the count exceeds one without documented common ownership; action payment suspension. 2) Identity registry mismatch: on enrolment application, compute exact matches of applicant SSN, name and address to Death Master File and known mail-drop address lists; fires on any match; action enrolment denial and site visit. 3) No-licensed-staff biller: on billing NPI x claim type, compute the count of rendering NPIs with an active state licence for the billed service; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: C.R. Bard, Inc.; Liberator Medical Supply, Inc.; Liberator Holdings; Rochester Medical Corporation
SchemeSummary: Bard and its Liberator affiliates allegedly gave urology practice groups discounts, excessive free samples and cost savings on in-office urological supplies to induce them to adopt Bard's 'Link' prescription form as the standard form for intermittent catheters, steering patients' catheter prescriptions to Bard products and to Bard's own DME subsidiary Liberator Medical, which billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE. Resolved for $17 million following a qui tam suit by a former 180 Medical employee.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute the share of a urology practice's catheter prescriptions (A4351, A4352, A4353) routed to one supplier NPI. Prescription steering follows the adoption date of a manufacturer's standardised order form visible in requisition metadata. The supplier's parent manufacturer also supplies free in-office samples recorded in Open Payments or practice purchase records. Beneficiary catheter brand mix at that practice diverges sharply from same-specialty peers in remittance history. Prior-authorisation files show no clinical rationale for the specific brand or product code selected.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Supplier steering concentration: on prescribing NPI x HCPCS A4351/A4352/A4353, compute the share of orders going to a single supplier NPI or its corporate parent; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Remuneration linkage: on practice TIN x manufacturer, compute the sum of Open Payments transfers, sample value and discounts alongside referred DMEPOS paid dollars; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit. 3) Form-adoption step change: on prescribing NPI x month, compute the change in single-supplier order share against the prescriber's own trailing baseline; fires when the jump exceeds the calibrated percentile; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: American Psychiatric Centers, Inc., d/b/a Comprehensive Psychiatric Services (CPS) (behavioral medicine provider)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Medi-Cal); TRICARE; Veterans Affairs health care programs; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
SchemeSummary: CPS billed government health care payors using psychotherapy 'add-on' CPT codes 90833 and 90836 alongside evaluation and management visits where its providers either never performed the psychotherapy services described or failed to sufficiently document them; CPS will pay $2,615,569.32 to the United States and $134,430.68 to California.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute the share of E/M claims by each rendering NPI carrying psychotherapy add-on CPT 90833 or 90836. Add-on minutes plus E/M time summed per rendering NPI per date exceed a 24-hour day. Documentation returned on ADR lacks the separately timed psychotherapy note the add-on code requires. Add-on billing rate jumps against the provider's own trailing baseline after a billing-system or template change. Same-day beneficiary claims show no diagnosis or treatment plan supporting psychotherapy alongside the medication visit.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Add-on attach rate: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of 90833 and 90836 lines to eligible E/M lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers or above the provider's trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Impossible clinical day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed minutes implied by E/M plus psychotherapy add-on codes; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or contracted clinic hours; action prepay edit. 3) Undocumented add-on: on claim line, compute whether a timed psychotherapy note with start and stop times exists in the submitted or requested record; fires when absent; action claim suspension, then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Advoque Safeguard LLC (mask manufacturer); Jason Azevedo (owner/manager); Andrew Stack (owner/manager); Paul Shrater (owner/manager); JDM Supply LLC (distributor); Daniel Motha; Jeffrey Motha; Jason Colantuoni
SchemeSummary: Advoque Safeguard manufactured facemasks that were falsely represented as NIOSH-approved N95 respirators and JDM Supply sold hundreds of thousands of them to a Massachusetts hospital during the early COVID-19 pandemic; NIOSH lab testing showed filtration efficiency of only 83.94%-93.24%, below the 95% N95 requirement, and the hospital paid for but never used the masks. Figures span multiple corporate and individual defendants (fines totaling about $1.03 million); one defendant also pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit price gouging.
WaysToIdentify: At purchasing, the respirator model and TC approval number on the invoice has no matching entry in the NIOSH Certified Equipment List. The supplier NPI or vendor TIN has no FDA establishment registration or device listing for respiratory protective devices. Unit price on the purchase order exceeds the payer's trailing pre-pandemic median price for the same HCPCS by a large multiple. The manufacturer named on packaging differs from the NIOSH CEL approval holder for that TC number. Vendor appeared in the payer's remittance history only after March 2020 with no prior device supply activity.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) NIOSH approval registry match: on purchase order line, compare the TC approval number and model string against the NIOSH Certified Equipment List and FDA device listing; fires when there is an exact registry mismatch or missing entry; action prepay edit. 2) Pandemic price spike: on vendor TIN x HCPCS, compute the ratio of unit price to the payer's trailing 12-month median unit price for that HCPCS; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-commodity peers; action claim suspension. 3) New-entrant PPE surge: on vendor TIN, compute the count of prior-year paid device invoices and the current-quarter paid dollars; fires when prior count is zero and current dollars exceed the calibrated percentile versus peer suppliers; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Advoque Safeguard LLC (mask manufacturer); Jason Azevedo (owner/manager); Paul Shrater (owner/manager); Andrew Stack (owner/manager); JDM Supply LLC (distributor); Daniel Motha; Jeffrey Motha; Jason Colantuoni
SchemeSummary: Advoque Safeguard LLC manufactured facemasks and, with distributor JDM Supply LLC, sold hundreds of thousands of them to a hospital in spring 2020 falsely represented as NIOSH-approved N95 respirators; NIOSH lab testing showed filtration efficiency of only 83.94%-93.24%, below the 95% N95 requirement. The company and three owner/managers pleaded guilty to misbranded-device charges; a second company and three other individuals pleaded guilty earlier, one to conspiracy to commit price gouging.
WaysToIdentify: At procurement, the TC approval number printed on the respirator has no matching record in the NIOSH Certified Equipment List. The distributor's pedigree documentation does not trace back to a manufacturer holding that NIOSH approval. The manufacturer TIN has no FDA establishment registration or device listing for N95 respirators. Invoiced unit price sits far above the buyer's trailing remittance history for the same respirator HCPCS. The distributor NPI or vendor record was created within months of the first large PPE invoice.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Approval-holder chain match: on invoice line, compare the labeled manufacturer against the NIOSH Certified Equipment List approval holder for the cited TC number; fires when the two do not match exactly; action prepay edit. 2) Unregistered device manufacturer: on manufacturer TIN x device category, compute the count of active FDA establishment registrations and device listings; fires when that count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Price-to-baseline ratio: on vendor TIN x HCPCS, compute unit price divided by the trailing 12-month median paid unit price; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-commodity vendors; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Adam Wayne Owens (owner of marketing companies)
SchemeSummary: Owens used California marketing companies to identify Medicare beneficiaries and pass their personal and medical information to cancer genetic testing (CGX) companies, which mailed at-home test kits and billed Medicare; Owens received $1,700-$2,000 per reimbursed test, routed through a New Zealand company under a sham marketing contract and false hourly invoices to disguise the kickbacks, causing over $10 million in Medicare losses.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on the CGX CPT lines has no prior evaluation-and-management claim with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI signs cancer genetic panels for beneficiaries spread across many states in a single week. The specimen collection date precedes any oncology diagnosis in the beneficiary's other claims history. The laboratory NPI's paid volume for CGX CPT codes jumps from near zero to peer-top-decile within weeks. The laboratory's CMS-855B ownership and marketing-contract disclosures name entities that also appear on other flagged labs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the CGX date of service and the nearest E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer geographic dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the distinct count of beneficiary states and distinct laboratory NPIs on ordered CGX lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Lab CGX concentration: on laboratory NPI x month, compute the share of paid dollars from CGX CPT codes and the growth ratio versus the provider's trailing baseline; fires when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Central District of California
FraudEntity: Juan Carlos Esparza (owner of House of Angels Hospice); Petros Fichidzhyan; Karpis Srapyan; Susanna Harutyunyan; Mihran Panosyan; House of Angels Hospice
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Valley Village/greater Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants operated four sham hospice companies that billed Medicare nearly $16 million for hospice services that were medically unnecessary and never provided, using foreign nationals' identities as nominee owners to open bank accounts, enroll with Medicare, sign leases, and obtain cell phones; proceeds were laundered through shell company accounts and assets (Esparza bought a $90,000 vehicle). Figures span multiple co-defendants; Fichidzhyan received the longest sentence, 12 years.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855A owner listed on the hospice application has an SSN or passport tied to a person with no U.S. entry or address history. Multiple new hospice NPIs share a practice address, phone number, or bank routing and account on their EFT forms. The attending physician NPI certifying terminal illness appears on Death Master File or has never billed hospice-related services. Beneficiaries on the hospice election continue to receive curative Part A and Part B claims during the election period. Newly enrolled hospice NPIs reach peer-top-decile paid dollars within their first billing quarter.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Shared identity graph: on hospice NPI, compute the count of other enrolled NPIs sharing bank account, address, phone, or owner SSN across CMS-855A and EFT records; fires when that degree exceeds one without disclosed common ownership; action site visit before enrolment approval. 2) Certifying physician validity: on claim line, match the certifying NPI against NPPES status, state licence file, LEIE, and Death Master File; fires on any exact registry mismatch or date-of-service after date of death; action prepay edit. 3) Curative-care conflict: on beneficiary x hospice election period, compute the count of paid curative inpatient, chemotherapy, or surgical claims; fires when that count is above zero; action claim suspension and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California
FraudEntity: Mihran Panosyan (money launderer); Petros Fichidzhyan (co-defendant)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Winnetka/greater Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Co-defendants used identities of foreign nationals who had left the U.S. to set up and operate sham hospice companies, then billed Medicare roughly $16 million for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill and never requested or received care; Panosyan laundered over $4.6 million of the proceeds through accounts of the purported foreign owners, the sham hospices, and shell corporations to buy real estate, private school tuition, and personal expenses. Co-defendant Fichidzhyan previously pleaded guilty and received 12 years.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855A owner's identity documents belong to a foreign national with no current U.S. residence or SSA activity. Several new hospice NPIs route payments to bank accounts controlled by the same signatory on EFT enrolment forms. Beneficiaries on hospice election have no prior claims history consistent with terminal illness in their Part A and Part B records. The certifying physician NPI has no prior hospice certification history and no encounter claim with the beneficiary. Paid hospice dollars are swept from the provider account into shell company accounts within days of remittance.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Nominee-owner verification: on hospice NPI, compare CMS-855A owner identity data against SSA and immigration status records at enrolment; fires on an exact mismatch or absent U.S. presence; action site visit before approval. 2) Bank account fan-in: on bank account number, compute the distinct count of enrolled provider NPIs receiving EFT payments; fires when that count exceeds one without disclosed common ownership; action payment suspension. 3) Terminality evidence gap: on beneficiary x hospice election, compute the count of prior-year claims with qualifying terminal diagnoses and the count of encounters with the certifying NPI; fires when both are zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Petros Fichidzhyan (controlled sham hospice entities and a home health care agency)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Granada Hills / greater Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Fichidzhyan and co-schemers controlled sham hospice companies that billed Medicare for hospice services never provided and not medically necessary, using foreign nationals' PII to open bank accounts, enroll with Medicare and sign leases, and misappropriating the identities of several doctors (two deceased) to submit claims; Medicare paid nearly $16 million, of which he received about $7 million with $5.3 million laundered through a dozen shell/third-party accounts, plus over $1 million to his home health agency using a doctor's name to falsely certify beneficiaries.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the certifying physician NPI on hospice and home health claims has a date of death preceding the certification date in the Death Master File. Newly enrolled hospice and home health NPIs share owner identities, addresses, and bank accounts across CMS-855A filings. The certifying NPI submits no other claims of its own while appearing on thousands of certifications. Beneficiaries billed for hospice show no hospice election consistent diagnoses in their other Medicare claims. Payments are swept from provider accounts to a dozen unrelated third-party accounts shortly after remittance.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Deceased or dormant certifier: on certifying NPI x date of service, compare against Death Master File date of death and the NPI's own billing activity; fires when the service date follows death or the NPI has zero self-submitted claims; action prepay edit. 2) Common-control cluster: on owner SSN, address, and bank account, compute the distinct count of linked hospice and home health NPIs from CMS-855A and EFT data; fires when that count exceeds one without disclosed common ownership; action payment suspension. 3) Certifier volume impossibility: on certifying NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries certified divided by documented face-to-face encounter claims; fires when encounters are zero or the ratio exceeds a 24-hour workday equivalent; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: American Furniture Rentals, Inc. (furniture rental company, Pennsauken, New Jersey)
SchemeSummary: AFR applied for and received a $2 million PPP loan in January 2021, falsely certifying eligibility despite having more than 300 employees (the eligibility cap at the time), then obtained full forgiveness of the loan plus accrued interest; the False Claims Act qui tam matter settled for $2,907,703.
WaysToIdentify: This is an SBA loan certification matter with no health claim and no adjudication point. The nearest detection route is comparing the borrower's certified employee count on the PPP application against IRS Form 941 payroll filings and state unemployment wage records. A second route is matching the borrower EIN against affiliate EINs in SAM and corporate registries before forgiveness is granted.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll-count reconciliation: on borrower EIN, compute the difference between certified employee count on the PPP application and the headcount reported on the four preceding IRS Form 941 filings; fires when the filed headcount exceeds the program cap; action claim suspension of the forgiveness decision.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Krishna Gidwani (co-owner/operator of DME company); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Gidwani and Sharma allegedly owned and operated a DME company that paid telemarketing companies for orthotic brace orders (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then shipped braces Medicare beneficiaries did not need or want and billed Medicare over $4 million; the doctors whose signatures appeared on the orders often never treated the beneficiaries or prescribed the equipment.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on the L-code brace claims has no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI signs brace orders for beneficiaries in many distant states within a single week. The same beneficiary receives multiple different L-code braces from the supplier on nearly the same date of service. Beneficiary residence ZIPs fall far outside the service area declared on the supplier's CMS-855S enrolment. Supplier paid volume rises from near zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the brace date of service and the most recent E/M claim linking that NPI and beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Brace stacking: on beneficiary x supplier NPI, compute the distinct count of L-code body regions billed within 30 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the distinct count of beneficiary states and supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Krishna Gidwani (DME company owner/operator); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator, DME company owner/operator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Gidwani and co-conspirator Raju Sharma owned and operated a DME company that paid telemarketing companies for orders for orthotic braces (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then billed Medicare over $4 million for braces beneficiaries did not need or want; the doctors whose signatures appeared on the orders often never treated the beneficiaries or prescribed the equipment.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, no evaluation-and-management claim exists between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary before the brace date of service. A small set of ordering NPIs accounts for nearly all of one supplier's paid L-code volume. Beneficiary ZIPs cluster far outside the service area on the supplier's CMS-855S enrolment record. Multiple brace HCPCS covering different joints are delivered to the same beneficiary within days. The supplier's paid dollars per week rise sharply above its own trailing baseline after a marketing contract begins.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the days between the brace date of service and the nearest prior E/M encounter claim with that beneficiary; fires when none exists; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer concentration: on supplier NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid L-code lines attributable to the top five ordering NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty suppliers; action postpay audit. 3) Multi-joint brace bundle: on beneficiary x supplier NPI, compute the count of distinct anatomic L-code categories billed within 30 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Krishna Gidwani (owner/operator of DME company); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Gidwani and co-conspirators owned and operated a DME company that paid telemarketing companies for orders for orthotic braces (ankle, wrist, knee, back), then billed Medicare over $4 million for braces beneficiaries did not need or want, using DME orders bearing signatures of doctors who often never treated or prescribed for those beneficiaries.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the signing physician NPI on the DME order has no claim history with the beneficiary in any setting. One ordering NPI's DMEPOS order count per day exceeds any feasible clinic schedule of 24 hours. Beneficiary residence states span far beyond the supplier's CMS-855S declared service area. Delivery dates on brace claims precede or immediately follow the order date with no fitting encounter. Supplier's ordering-physician graph shows the same NPIs shared with other suppliers flagged for telemarketing.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the brace date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action prepay edit. 2) Signer throughput: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with DMEPOS orders divided by a 24-hour day; fires when implied per-patient time falls below a feasible visit length; action payment suspension. 3) Shared-orderer graph degree: on ordering NPI, compute the distinct count of supplier NPIs billing its orders in a rolling 90 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Eric Strom Holland (operator of unlicensed virtual pain clinic)
SchemeSummary: Holland ran an unlicensed, entirely virtual pain clinic and recruited temporary doctors by falsely telling them the clinic had a physical location, that patients had been physically examined by nurse practitioners, that patients had standing relationships with long-term physicians, and that abuse safeguards such as urine screens were in place; the deceived doctors issued more than 900 prescriptions for over 100,000 oxycodone tablets (street value over $4 million), and Holland routinely failed to pay the doctors as promised.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, the clinic's listed practice address on CMS-855B and state licence records is not a licensed clinical site. At claim adjudication, no place-of-service 11 encounter claim precedes any Schedule II oxycodone prescription attributed to the clinic. Prescriber NPIs rotate rapidly at one clinic address in the state PDMP dispensing file. No urine drug screen CPT lines appear in the beneficiaries' claims history alongside chronic opioid prescribing. PDMP data show high morphine-milligram-equivalent per prescriber-day concentrated in a handful of pharmacy NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber turnover at a site: on practice address x quarter, compute the distinct count of prescriber NPIs writing Schedule II prescriptions in PDMP records; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action site visit. 2) Missing baseline evaluation: on beneficiary x prescriber NPI, compute the count of in-person E/M claims and urine drug screen CPT lines preceding the first oxycodone fill; fires when both counts are zero; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Opioid MME throughput: on prescriber NPI x date of service, compute total oxycodone MME dispensed divided by distinct patients seen; fires when implied encounter time exceeds a 24-hour workday; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Fouodzing Mbord (home health aide/caregiver)
SchemeSummary: No billing scheme; a home health aide providing 24-hour care to a bedridden stroke victim was captured on home security cameras striking the vulnerable adult on two occasions in November 2023 and threatening to do it again. He pleaded guilty to abuse of a vulnerable adult and received a 180-day jail sentence suspended in full with one year of probation; the case was investigated in part by the D.C. OIG Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.
WaysToIdentify: This is a patient-abuse prosecution with no false claim and no adjudication decision point. The nearest detection route is cross-matching aide identity in EVV visit records against state abuse-registry and licence-board disciplinary files at hiring. A second route is trending beneficiary emergency-department and injury-diagnosis claims against the aide assigned in EVV during the same period.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Aide-linked injury signal: on aide identifier x beneficiary, compute the count of injury-diagnosis emergency claims during weeks with EVV visits by that aide; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer aides; action site visit and referral to the state abuse registry.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Carson Tahoe Health System (owner of Carson Tahoe Physician Clinics and Carson Tahoe Continuing Care Hospital); Carson Tahoe Physician Clinics; Carson Tahoe Continuing Care Hospital
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Carson Tahoe Health System and two affiliated entities obtained four Paycheck Protection Program loans in May 2020 and February 2021 totaling $5,077,011 plus a $2 million second loan, and had them forgiven, despite allegedly being ineligible because their combined size under SBA affiliation rules exceeded program limits; the forgiven principal, interest and lender fees cost the government $7,267,009, resolved by an $8,876,475.45 False Claims Act settlement arising from a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: This is an SBA loan eligibility matter with no health claim and no claim adjudication point. The nearest detection route is applying SBA affiliation rules to the borrower EIN against parent and sibling EINs in corporate filings and Medicare cost report ownership schedules before forgiveness. A second route is comparing certified headcount to combined IRS Form 941 filings for all affiliated EINs.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Affiliate headcount roll-up: on borrower EIN, compute the sum of employees on IRS Form 941 filings across all commonly controlled EINs identified in Medicare cost report Worksheet S-2 and state corporate registries; fires when the total exceeds the program size standard; action claim suspension of the forgiveness decision.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Catholic Health System, Inc. (CHS) and its affiliated hospitals
SchemeSummary: CHS and its affiliated hospitals allegedly maintained compensation arrangements with non-employee physicians for administrative services that were not commercially reasonable or exceeded fair market value; those physicians then referred laboratory testing, hospital services and medical supplies to CHS, which billed Medicare for the referred services in violation of the Stark Law. Resolved by a $3,293,122.66 civil settlement following a qui tam suit by relator Gary Tucker.
WaysToIdentify: At claim adjudication, hospital claims carry referring NPIs who also hold paid administrative contracts disclosed in the system's financial relationship records. Per-hour administrative compensation to those physicians sits above independent fair-market-value benchmark surveys for the specialty. Referral volume from contracted physicians exceeds their own trailing baseline after the contract effective date. Designated health service lines billed for those referrals lack a Stark exception attestation in the hospital's arrangement database. The same physician NPIs appear as referrers on hospital laboratory, imaging, and DME lines at disproportionate share.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Compensated-referrer share: on hospital NPI x referring NPI, compute the count and dollars of designated health service claims where the referrer holds a paid administrative agreement; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile versus peer hospitals; action postpay audit. 2) FMV rate variance: on physician contract, compute hourly administrative rate divided by the specialty benchmark median from published survey data; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty benchmarks; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Post-contract referral lift: on referring NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of DHS referral dollars after contract start to the referrer's trailing baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of New York
FraudEntity: Centers Healthcare (operator of 44 related skilled nursing facilities)
State_County: New York - Albany, Essex, Fulton, Jefferson, Oneida, Onondaga, Otsego, Rensselaer, Schenectady, Ulster, Warren, and Washington counties; Rhode Island; Kansas; Missouri
SchemeSummary: Centers Healthcare admitted that Medicare cost reports submitted for 44 commonly owned/controlled skilled nursing facilities contained false statements or omitted material information about transactions with related organizations, which SNFs must disclose at the lower of actual cost or market price; management reviewed the reports and knew or should have known of the falsities. Resolved for $6,063,500 under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: At cost report settlement, related-organization costs on Worksheet A-8-1 are absent while CMS-855A ownership discloses common control of the vendor. Vendor TINs paid by the facility match owner TINs listed in the PECOS ownership and change-of-information records. Reported per-bed costs for management, therapy, or rent exceed peer facility medians under common ownership. Identical vendor names appear across dozens of commonly owned facility cost reports without related-party flagging. Lease and management fees exceed the market benchmark for the same county in the payer's cost report database.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Undisclosed related party: on facility provider number x vendor TIN, compare vendor TIN against owner and officer TINs in CMS-855A and PECOS ownership records; fires when a match exists but Worksheet A-8-1 shows no related-party adjustment; action postpay audit. 2) Chain vendor concentration: on vendor TIN, compute the distinct count of commonly owned facility cost reports listing that vendor as unrelated; fires when that count exceeds one across the same ownership group; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Cost-to-market ratio: on facility x cost center, compute reported per-bed management, rent, or therapy cost divided by county peer median; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-size peers; action claim suspension of interim rate.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Cemhan "Jimmy" Biricik (sole member and CEO of Fast Lab Technologies, LLC); Dr. Martin Perlin (Medical Director and ordering physician); Fast Lab Technologies, LLC
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; TRICARE; private health insurers
SchemeSummary: Fast Lab operated a website offering "free" COVID-19 tests and harvested visitors' insurance information, then billed Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and private insurers for antigen and PCR tests across multiple dates per beneficiary, falsely representing that antigen tests were observed by medical professionals, that saliva samples were collected, and that PCR testing was performed - none of which occurred; claims were often submitted before kits were even delivered, and Dr. Perlin was listed as ordering physician without any treating relationship. Over $500 million billed, more than $50 million paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the COVID test claim's date of service precedes the shipping carrier delivery date recorded for the kit. A single ordering physician NPI appears on essentially all of one laboratory's test claims with no encounter claims. The same beneficiary is billed multiple antigen and PCR CPT lines on overlapping dates by the same laboratory NPI. Beneficiary residence states span nationwide while the laboratory's CLIA certificate covers one site. The laboratory's CLIA certificate scope does not include high-complexity molecular testing for the PCR CPT billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Service-before-delivery: on claim line, compute the gap in days between the billed date of service and the carrier delivery date for the associated kit shipment; fires when the date of service precedes delivery; action prepay edit. 2) Sole-orderer dependence: on laboratory NPI x month, compute the share of paid test lines attributable to the single most frequent ordering NPI and that orderer's count of E/M encounters with the beneficiaries; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile and encounters are zero; action payment suspension. 3) CLIA scope match: on claim line, compare the billed CPT complexity against the laboratory's CLIA certificate type and specialty in the CLIA registry; fires on exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Cashmir Chinedu Luke (CEO, sole owner and billing representative of Four Corners Health LLC); Four Corners Health LLC
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Tulare County; California - Merced County; California - Mariposa County; California - Madera County; California - San Francisco County; California - Contra Costa County
PayerName: Department of Veterans Affairs (Veterans Community Care Program)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Retention of Overpayment
SchemeSummary: Luke, sole owner of Four Corners Health LLC, submitted roughly 10,000 false claims to the VA's third-party benefits administrator under the Veterans Community Care Program for in-home care hours never rendered - duplicate claims, days caretakers were not present, hours beyond those worked, and care for veterans who had already died - collecting $7 million into a bank account he solely controlled, then spending it on personal expenses or transferring it across accounts in Asia and Africa while deceiving the administrator's recovery efforts.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed in-home care dates of service fall after the veteran's date of death in the Death Master File and VA enrollment file. Claimed hours per caregiver per day exceed 24 hours when summed across veterans. Submitted claims duplicate the same veteran, date, and hour range already paid in remittance history. Billed hours exceed caregiver timesheet and EVV visit-record hours for the same date. A single provider's paid dollars concentrate in one bank account with rapid outbound foreign transfers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Post-mortem service: on claim line, compute the gap in days between date of service and the veteran's date of death from the Death Master File and VA eligibility file; fires when the date of service is later; action prepay edit. 2) Caregiver hour impossibility: on caregiver identifier x date of service, compute the sum of billed care hours across all veterans; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Duplicate and EVV variance: on veteran x provider NPI x date, compute billed hours minus EVV-verified hours and the count of overlapping paid claims; fires when the difference is positive or the overlap count exceeds one; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Gary Cox (CEO of Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)); Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs; VA; other insurers
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cox operated DMERx, an internet platform that generated fraudulent doctors' orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces and pain creams for Medicare beneficiaries recruited via mailers, TV ads, and offshore call centers; telemedicine companies paid doctors to sign orders without examinations, and DME suppliers and pharmacies paid kickbacks for the orders and billed Medicare and other insurers over $1 billion, of which more than $360 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on brace and compounded-cream claims has no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with that beneficiary. A small set of telemedicine ordering NPIs generates orders billed by dozens of unrelated supplier and pharmacy NPIs nationwide. Beneficiary residence states fall far outside the supplier's CMS-855S declared service area. The same beneficiary receives multiple L-code braces and topical pain cream NDCs within one month from different billers. Supplier and pharmacy paid volume jumps from near zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of platform onboarding.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer-to-biller fan-out: on ordering NPI x month, compute the distinct count of supplier and pharmacy NPIs billing its orders and distinct beneficiary states; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Cross-biller saturation: on beneficiary x 30 days, compute the distinct count of L-code braces and compounded topical NDCs paid across all billers; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Gary Cox (CEO of Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)); Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami); Arizona - Maricopa County
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs (including VA); other insurers
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cox operated DMERx, an internet-based platform that generated false doctors' orders falsely representing that physicians had examined Medicare beneficiaries, when telemedicine companies paid doctors to sign orders after brief or no patient contact; Cox connected DME suppliers, pharmacies, and marketers with these telemedicine companies in exchange for kickbacks, and the suppliers billed Medicare and other insurers over $1 billion for orthotic braces, pain creams, and other items, receiving over $360 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the signing telemedicine NPI has no evaluation-and-management claim with the beneficiary before the order date. One prescriber NPI's daily order count implies less than a feasible minute per patient in a 24-hour day. Suppliers and pharmacies sharing the same ordering NPI pool have no geographic or ownership relationship in PECOS. Beneficiary ZIPs are dispersed nationwide while the supplier's CMS-855S service area is local. Paid volume for the supplier begins immediately after enrolment with no prior remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the days between order date and the nearest prior E/M encounter claim with that beneficiary; fires when none exists; action prepay edit. 2) Prescriber throughput impossibility: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute distinct beneficiaries ordered for divided by 24 hours; fires when implied per-patient contact time falls below a feasible telehealth visit length; action claim suspension. 3) Shared-orderer network degree: on ordering NPI, compute the distinct count of unrelated supplier and pharmacy NPIs billing its orders in 90 days from PECOS ownership data; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Gary Cox (CEO of Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)); Power Mobility Doctor Rx, LLC (DMERx)
PayerName: Medicare;TRICARE;Department of Veterans Affairs health programs;other insurers
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Cox ran DMERx, an internet-based platform that generated false doctors' orders falsely representing that physicians had examined Medicare beneficiaries recruited via misleading mailers, TV ads and offshore call centers; he connected DME suppliers, pharmacies and marketers with telemedicine companies that took kickbacks to have doctors sign orders without regard to medical necessity, and the suppliers and pharmacies then billed Medicare and other insurers more than $1 billion, collecting over $360 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, brace and pain-cream claims cite ordering NPIs with no prior encounter claim for that beneficiary. Telemedicine ordering NPIs cover beneficiaries across dozens of states within a single billing week.
