FeaturesToCreate: 1) Diagnosis substantiation: on claim line, compare the diagnosis code on a restricted-formulary NDC against the program's approved diagnosis list and the beneficiary's medical claim history; fires on absence or exact mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Missing authorisation: on beneficiary x NDC, compute whether an approved treatment authorisation request exists in the payer prior-authorisation file for fills lacking an approved diagnosis; fires when none exists; action claim suspension. 3) Store-level bypass rate: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute restricted-drug claims paid without diagnosis substantiation divided by all restricted-drug claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus chain peers; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jacquelyn Farrish (Medicaid Consumer Directed Care Program recipient/timesheet approver)
SchemeSummary: Farrish enrolled in Virginia Medicaid's Consumer Directed Care Program and listed her estranged husband A.L., who lived in another part of the state, as her paid personal care attendant; she then submitted and approved fraudulent timesheets using his personal information claiming 9,819 hours of personal care services that were never provided, causing $116,536 in Medicaid losses.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the attendant's home address in the enrollment packet sits hundreds of miles from the member's service address on the claim. EVV visit records show no GPS or telephony check-in matching the timesheet hours submitted for those dates of service. The consumer-directed enrollment form lists the same person as both employer of record and approver of the attendant's timesheets. Paid hours per attendant NPI or SSN per day exceed 24 when summed across all timesheets in the fiscal agent file. State vital and address registries show the attendant residing in a different locality than the plan of care service county.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Attendant-member distance: on attendant ID x member ID, compute the road miles between attendant address in the fiscal agent enrollment file and member service address; fires when distance exceeds a same-program calibrated percentile without documented relocation; action prepay edit. 2) Self-approval loop: on timesheet record, compute a match count between the member/employer-of-record identifier and the approver identifier; fires when the identifiers are identical; action claim suspension pending documentation request (ADR). 3) EVV corroboration gap: on attendant ID x date of service, compute paid timesheet hours minus EVV-verified visit hours; fires when the gap is above zero for consecutive pay periods; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jacquelyn Farrish (Medicaid Consumer Directed Care recipient)
SchemeSummary: Farrish enrolled in Virginia Medicaid's Consumer Directed Care Program and listed her estranged husband, who lived hundreds of miles away, as her paid personal care attendant, then submitted and approved fraudulent timesheets using his personal information for 9,819 hours of personal care/respite services never rendered, causing $116,536 in Medicaid losses; sentenced to five years' probation with 12 months home detention and $116,536 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: At claim adjudication, timesheet hours for the attendant have no corresponding EVV check-in or check-out record for those dates of service. The attendant's residential address in the fiscal agent enrollment record is hundreds of miles from the member's service address. The same individual appears as both the consumer-employer approving hours and the beneficiary receiving personal care and respite. Cumulative paid hours per attendant across a year exceed plausible full-time limits set in the consumer-directed program rules. Respite hours are billed on the same dates and clock times as personal care hours for the same member.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Zero-EVV payroll: on attendant ID x pay period, compute the ratio of EVV-verified minutes to timesheet-claimed minutes; fires when the ratio is below the calibrated program percentile; action claim suspension. 2) Annual hour ceiling: on attendant ID x rolling 12 months, compute the sum of paid personal care and respite hours; fires when the sum exceeds hours physically available given 24-hour days across all members served; action postpay audit and payment suspension. 3) Approver-recipient identity: on timesheet record, compute whether the approver identifier equals the member identifier in the fiscal agent file; fires on exact match; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Moktar Hassan Aden (owner, Brilliant Minds Services LLC); Mustafa Dayib Ali; Khalid Ahmed Dayib; Abdifitah Mohamud Mohamed (operator, Foundation First Services LLC); Christopher Adesoji Falade (operator, Faladcare Inc.); Emmanuel Oluwademilade Falade (operator, Faladcare Inc.); Asad Ahmed Adow (owner, Leo Human Services LLC); Anwar Ahmed Adow (owner, Liberty Plus LLC)
State_County: Minnesota - Ramsey County (St. Paul); Minnesota - Hennepin County (Brooklyn Park); Minnesota - Anoka County (Blaine); Minnesota - Ramsey County (Roseville)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Eight defendants operating four Minnesota Medicaid Housing Stabilization Services providers (Brilliant Minds ~$2.3M, Faladcare ~$2.2M, Leo Human Services ~$2.7M, Liberty Plus ~$1.2M) obtained beneficiary names from addiction treatment centers and other facilities, then submitted inflated and fabricated reimbursement claims for housing consultation, transition and sustaining services that were largely never provided; one owner also had employees manufacture false service notes to survive potential DHS audits, and proceeds were diverted to employees/co-conspirators, real estate, luxury car leases and personal AmEx charges. Figures span four companies and eight defendants.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, housing transition and sustaining claims list beneficiaries whose only other claims come from a single addiction treatment facility roster. Billed service units per staff NPI per day exceed the hours physically available in a 24-hour day. Newly enrolled provider entities reach top-decile monthly billing within months of their CMS-855 or state DHS enrollment date. Service notes produced under documentation request share identical text blocks across unrelated beneficiaries and dates of service. Payment bank accounts on the provider enrollment file are shared across several distinct provider TINs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staff-day impossibility: on rendering staff ID x date of service, compute total billed service units converted to minutes across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 1440 minutes; action prepay edit. 2) New-enrollee ramp: on provider NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by months since state enrollment effective date; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-service peers; action prior-authorisation requirement and site visit. 3) Shared payee graph: on bank account number, compute the distinct count of provider TINs and NPIs receiving remittance; fires when that count exceeds one; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Live Wire, LLC (Vermont-based defense contractor)
SchemeSummary: Live Wire, LLC sold electronic communications headsets to the U.S. Army under government contracts and submitted claims for payment for headsets that had not been tested to the required military specifications and were non-compliant; the company self-disclosed the testing failure and agreed to pay $628,328 under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point in this procurement matter. The nearest detection route is contract-level: compare delivered lot numbers against required military specification test certificates in the contractor's quality file. Government source inspection and DCMA acceptance records would show missing first-article and conformance test reports before invoice payment.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on contract line item x delivery lot, require matching specification test certificate identifiers in the acceptance record before invoice release, with payment withheld on any lot lacking a certificate.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Adrienne Ponzo (loan application preparer); unnamed co-conspirators (recruiters)
State_County: New Jersey - Camden County (Camden); Delaware - New Castle County (Bear)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Ponzo's co-conspirators recruited owners of shell or barely-operating companies, and Ponzo prepared and electronically submitted fraudulent PPP and EIDL applications to the SBA and PPP lenders, fabricating bank statements and tax returns to support them; 14 loans totaling nearly $1.5 million were obtained and Ponzo kept a share of the proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point because the funds are SBA loans, not reimbursements. The nearest detection route is loan underwriting: match applicant payroll figures against IRS Form 941 and state wage filings before disbursement. Bank statements and tax transcripts submitted with applications can be verified directly with the IRS Income Verification Express Service. One preparer IP address or email domain appearing across many unrelated applicant EINs is visible in the lender portal logs.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on preparer IP address or submitter email, compute the distinct count of applicant EINs filed within a rolling 30 days and hold disbursement when that count exceeds the lender-calibrated percentile pending IRS transcript match.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (Civil Division)
FraudEntity: More than 600 unnamed defendants in over 280 enforcement actions, including multiple nursing home operators
SchemeSummary: Annual report summarizing DOJ elder fraud and abuse enforcement: more than 280 actions against over 600 defendants, domestic and transnational, who stole or attempted to steal over $2 billion from more than one million older Americans, and actions holding nursing home operators accountable for grossly substandard care billed to Medicare and Medicaid. No single scheme mechanics are described.
WaysToIdentify: This is an aggregate enforcement summary with no single scheme and no identifiable claim to adjudicate. The nearest payer-side route for the nursing home component is linking CMS survey deficiency and staffing data to paid per-diem claims. Payroll-Based Journal staffing hours far below the facility's case-mix expectation while claims are paid in full is observable before payment cycles close.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on facility CCN x quarter, compute PBJ nursing hours per resident day against MDS case-mix expected hours and route facilities below the calibrated percentile to survey and postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General / Office of Public Affairs
FraudEntity: More than 20 unnamed doctors and clinics that performed transgender medical procedures on children
SchemeSummary: DOJ announced it issued more than 20 subpoenas to doctors and clinics that performed transgender medical procedures on children, as part of investigations into potential health care fraud and false statements; no billing mechanics, amounts, or defendants are identified.
WaysToIdentify: This is an investigative announcement with no charged billing conduct and no adjudicated claim described. The nearest detection route is comparing procedure and diagnosis code pairs on submitted claims to the payer's own coverage policy and prior-authorisation file. Consent and medical-necessity documentation would be obtained through documentation request rather than any automated prepay signal.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on claim line, compare the billed CPT and ICD-10 pair against the plan's written coverage policy and route non-covered pairs to documentation request before payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs (Civil Division; Criminal Division, Fraud Section)
SchemeSummary: Announcement of a new DOJ/DHS cross-agency Trade Fraud Task Force to pursue importers who evade tariffs and customs duties and smuggle prohibited goods, using Tariff Act collection actions, False Claims Act suits, and parallel criminal prosecutions; no specific defendant, health care service, or fraud amount is identified.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point in this customs and tariff initiative. The nearest detection route is import entry data: compare declared HTS classification and country of origin on CBP Form 7501 against manifest and supplier records. Transshipment patterns are visible in Automated Commercial Environment entry summaries before duty liquidation.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on importer of record x HTS code, compute declared unit value against the trade-lane median and hold liquidation when the deviation exceeds the calibrated percentile.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Forefront Dermatology S.C. (owner/operator of Henghold Dermatology); Henghold Surgery Center LLC (ambulatory surgery center, wholly owned by William B. Henghold, M.D.)
SchemeSummary: A dermatology practice and affiliated ambulatory surgery center allegedly billed Medicare for wound repairs following Mohs micrographic skin cancer surgery using inaccurate, higher-paying codes - coding linear repairs as flap repairs and smaller flap repairs as larger flap repairs. Resolved for $847,394 under the False Claims Act following a qui tam suit by a former employee, who receives $152,531.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ratio of adjacent-tissue-transfer flap codes to simple and intermediate repair codes following Mohs CPT 17311 series is far above dermatology peers. Flap repair CPT codes billed carry defect sizes in square centimeters that exceed the Mohs stage count and lesion size documented on the same claim. The same rendering NPI reports large-area flap codes at a rate above its own trailing baseline after a coding vendor change. Operative notes obtained by documentation request describe linear closure while the claim line reports adjacent tissue transfer. Facility and professional claims for the same encounter report inconsistent repair code families for the identical anatomic site.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Repair mix ratio: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute flap and adjacent-tissue-transfer CPT lines divided by all post-Mohs repair lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Defect-size coherence: on claim line, compute the billed flap code's square-centimeter band minus the lesion size and Mohs stage count on the linked surgical line; fires when the repair size exceeds the excised area; action prepay edit. 3) Professional-facility mismatch: on encounter key of beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of differing repair CPT families between the ASC and physician claims; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension pending postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Genetic Technological Innovations, LLC (GTI) (diagnostic laboratory)
SchemeSummary: GTI paid a purported infection-prevention/marketing company $4,000-$4,500 per month per long-term care facility under a sham Marketing Services Agreement as disguised payment for laboratory test referrals; the company swabbed nursing home residents for COVID-19 and GTI then 'stacked' medically unnecessary respiratory pathogen panels on the same specimens for every resident regardless of symptoms, billing Medicare at roughly 10 times the COVID-19 test reimbursement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, respiratory pathogen panel CPT 87633 is billed on the same specimen date as COVID-19 testing for nearly every resident of a facility. Ordering NPI on the panel claims has no encounter claim with those long-term care beneficiaries around the date of service. Panel claims carry no symptomatic respiratory ICD-10 diagnosis, only screening or exposure codes. The laboratory's payment ledger shows fixed monthly per-facility payments to a marketing entity that is not an enrolled provider. Panel-to-COVID test volume ratio for the lab is far above same-specialty laboratory peers in the same states.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Panel stacking rate: on facility address x date of service, compute the share of residents with CPT 87633 billed alongside a COVID-19 test code; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile versus peer facilities; action prepay edit. 2) Symptom support: on claim line, compute the count of respiratory-illness ICD-10 codes present on the panel claim and the beneficiary's claims within the prior 7 days; fires when the count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Marketing-payment concentration: on laboratory TIN x referring facility, compute the ratio of fixed monthly vendor payments to referred test volume from the lab's general ledger obtained on audit; fires when payments track referral counts; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
FraudEntity: Patients Choice Laboratories (PCL) (diagnostic laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: PCL allegedly paid a purported infection prevention company $5,000/month under a sham Marketing Services Agreement (about $1.86 million total) and paid 1099 sales representatives at least $372,000 in volume-based commissions in exchange for laboratory test referrals; the company swabbed long-term care residents for COVID-19 and PCL used the same specimens to bill Medicare over $6 million for thousands of medically unnecessary respiratory pathogen panels at 43 facilities, sometimes billing RPPs without performing any COVID-19 test.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, CPT 87633 respiratory pathogen panels are billed for whole long-term care rosters without any accompanying COVID-19 test code on the same specimen. Ordering NPIs on the panels have no evaluation-and-management claim with the beneficiaries near the date of service. Panel claims lack symptomatic respiratory diagnoses and appear on the same collection date across dozens of facilities. The lab's contractor payment file shows flat monthly fees and per-test commissions to non-enrolled sales entities. Distinct facility count served per week jumps far above the laboratory's own trailing baseline after the marketing agreement start date.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Roster-wide panel saturation: on facility x collection date, compute the fraction of residents with a paid CPT 87633 line; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer facilities; action prepay edit. 2) Missing index test: on claim line, compute whether a COVID-19 test code exists for the same beneficiary and specimen date; fires when absent while the panel is billed; action claim suspension. 3) Facility footprint growth: on laboratory NPI x week, compute the distinct count of long-term care facility addresses on paid claims; fires when above the lab's trailing 26-week baseline; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section and U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Done Global Inc. (California digital health company); Mindful Mental Wellness P.A. (Florida medical practice); Ruthia He (founder and CEO of Done Global, previously convicted); David Brody (former clinical president of Done Global, previously convicted)
SchemeSummary: Done Global operated a subscription-based 'digital health' ADHD platform in which members paid a monthly fee and prescribers were instructed to issue Adderall and other stimulant prescriptions without legitimate medical purpose - often with no examination, no pre-existing practitioner-patient relationship, and sometimes based only on a short video/audio contact or none at all - resulting in over 40 million pills prescribed and more than $100 million in revenue. Done Global and Mindful Mental Wellness allegedly deceived pharmacies (incorporating MMW to bypass pharmacies that had blocked Done-affiliated prescriptions) and conspired to submit false claims to Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers, plus altering and destroying records after a grand jury subpoena; the company defendants are charged while founder Ruthia He and clinical president David Brody were previously convicted.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, stimulant NDC fills trace to prescriber NPIs whose only claim with the member is a single brief telehealth code. Prescriber NPI writes Schedule II stimulant prescriptions at a volume far above same-specialty telepsychiatry peers in PDMP data. Telehealth encounter durations billed are below the minimum time threshold for the CPT code reported. Pharmacy claims show members switching to a new dispensing chain immediately after prior pharmacies blocked the prescriber group. The prescribing entity's NPI cluster shares one corporate TIN and address on NPPES across dozens of prescriber NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Stimulant per-prescriber rate: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the count of Schedule II stimulant NDC fills divided by distinct patients; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Encounter-fill linkage: on beneficiary x prescriber NPI, compute the count of qualifying evaluation encounters before the first stimulant fill; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit on the pharmacy claim. 3) Corporate prescriber cluster: on TIN, compute the graph degree of prescriber NPIs sharing the NPPES practice address writing the same stimulant NDCs; fires when above the calibrated percentile; action payment suspension and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey; U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Diopsys Inc. (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Diopsys allegedly caused eye-care providers to bill Medicare and Medicaid for medically unnecessary electroretinography (ERG) vision testing using its NOVA device, which the FDA had cleared only for visual evoked potential testing, and made substantial unapproved changes to the device without required FDA submission. Resolved by a qui tam civil settlement of $1,225,000 guaranteed plus up to $13,025,000 contingent payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, ERG CPT 92273 and 92274 lines are billed by practices whose device inventory is FDA-cleared only for visual evoked potential testing. Ordering NPIs bill ERG on nearly every patient encounter regardless of retinal diagnosis on the claim. ERG volume per optometry NPI is far above same-specialty peers concentrated among practices using one manufacturer's device. The FDA 510(k) clearance database shows no ERG indication for the device model listed in the practice's purchase records. Beneficiaries receive repeat ERG testing at intervals shorter than the payer's local coverage determination allows.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Indication coherence: on claim line, compute whether a retinal-disease ICD-10 code supported by the LCD accompanies CPT 92273 or 92274; fires when absent; action prepay edit. 2) ERG penetration: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute ERG lines divided by total distinct patients seen; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Repeat-interval gap: on beneficiary x ERG HCPCS, compute days between successive paid tests; fires when the gap is shorter than the coverage policy minimum; action claim suspension.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Diopsys, Inc. (medical device company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Diopsys allegedly caused eye-care providers to bill Medicare and Medicaid for medically unnecessary electroretinography (ERG) vision tests performed with its NOVA device, which was FDA-cleared only for visual evoked potential testing, and made substantial device changes never submitted to FDA. Resolved by a qui tam settlement with $1,225,000 guaranteed and up to $13,025,000 contingent payments (total up to $14.25 million).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, electroretinography CPT lines are submitted by eye-care NPIs whose testing device holds FDA clearance only for visual evoked potential. Claims lack any retinal or glaucoma diagnosis meeting the payer's coverage determination for ERG. A small set of practices sharing one manufacturer's device account for a disproportionate share of national ERG volume. ERG billing at each practice begins abruptly within weeks of the device purchase date in supplier records. Repeat ERG intervals per beneficiary fall below the coverage policy minimum.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Device-clearance mismatch: on rendering NPI x HCPCS, compute an exact match between the billed test type and the FDA 510(k) cleared indication for the device model on file; fires on mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Onset spike: on rendering NPI x month, compute ERG line count against the provider's trailing 12-month baseline; fires when the count rises above that baseline immediately after device acquisition; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Diagnosis support: on claim line, compute the count of LCD-listed covered diagnoses on the ERG claim; fires when zero; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: James Rausch (director of operations and sales, Northeast region, mobile medical diagnostics company)
State_County: Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); New York - Suffolk County (Port Jefferson Station)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Rausch and co-conspirators at a mobile medical diagnostics company paid doctors cash and check kickbacks based on the volume of transcranial doppler brain scans they ordered, disguising the payments as fair-market-value space rental and administrative service agreements; the medically unnecessary TCD scans generated about $70.6 million in Medicare claims, of which Medicare paid about $27.2 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, transcranial doppler CPT 93886 and 93888 volumes per ordering NPI are far above same-specialty peers. Ordering physicians receiving space-rental or administrative payments from the testing company appear as the sole referral source for that mobile entity. Beneficiaries have no cerebrovascular diagnosis or prior neurologic workup in their claim history before the scan. Scans are billed on the same date across an entire clinic panel, indicating batch testing rather than clinical indication. The mobile company's CMS-855B ownership and address records show no fixed imaging site matching the place of service billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Orderer concentration: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute TCD scan counts divided by distinct patients and compare to same-specialty peers; fires when above the calibrated percentile; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Referral-payment graph: on testing company TIN x ordering NPI, compute the ratio of rental or administrative payments in the vendor ledger to ordered scan volume; fires when payments correlate with volume; action payment suspension. 3) Batch-date clustering: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute the distinct beneficiary count with TCD scans; fires when above the provider's trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Farrukh Jarar Ali (owner of ProMD Solutions); Cle'Esther Davenport (owner, Davenport House LLC); Ira Denny (nurse practitioner); Tyler Kontos; Joel "Max" Kupetz; Jorge Kinds (nurse practitioner); Gina Palacios (nurse practitioner)
State_County: Arizona - Maricopa County (Phoenix, Peoria, Surprise, Mesa, Scottsdale)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS); TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial insurers
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Seven Arizona defendants charged in related takedown cases: Ali's Pakistan-based billing/credentialing firm enrolled 41 sham substance-abuse clinics with AHCCCS and billed ~$650M for addiction treatment never provided to homeless and Native American patients, creating false therapy notes for audits ($564M paid, $24.5M to Ali personally); Davenport took ~$739,000 in kickbacks for referring sober-home residents to Tusa Integrated Clinic (~$1.58M paid by AHCCCS); and Kontos, Kupetz, Kinds, Denny and Palacios billed Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers over $1 billion (plus $209M and $59M respectively for Denny and Palacios) for medically unnecessary amniotic wound allografts applied to elderly and hospice patients by nurse practitioners at the direction of untrained sales reps paid via kickbacks. Amounts span multiple defendants; $7.2M in crypto and bank accounts seized.
WaysToIdentify: At enrollment, dozens of distinct clinic NPIs share one offshore billing agent, contact email and bank account in the CMS-855 and state Medicaid files. At adjudication, billed treatment hours per rendering clinician per day exceed 24 across the sham clinic cluster. Skin-substitute Q-codes are billed in square centimeters far above the wound sizes documented for elderly and hospice beneficiaries. Beneficiaries concurrently enrolled in hospice receive high-cost wound allograft applications from unrelated NPIs on overlapping dates. Sober-home operators appear as payees in provider ledgers while their residents' claims concentrate at a single clinic NPI.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Shared-infrastructure cluster: on bank account and billing agent ID, compute the distinct count of enrolled provider NPIs sharing them in enrollment records; fires when the count exceeds one; action prepay edit and site visit. 2) Clinician-hour impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total billed therapy and application minutes; fires when the total exceeds 1440 minutes; action claim suspension. 3) Allograft size outlier: on rendering NPI x Q-code, compute mean billed square centimeters per application against same-specialty peers; fires when above the calibrated percentile; action prior-authorisation requirement and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: John Patterson, M.D. (physician); Nursemind Home Care Inc. (hospice); Zenia Chavez (owner of Nursemind Home Care, Inc.)
SchemeSummary: Dr. Patterson allegedly accepted kickbacks from Nursemind Home Care Inc., an El Paso hospice, in exchange for certifying patients as eligible for hospice services when they were not, causing false claims to be submitted to Medicare; he agreed to pay $468,626 to settle FCA allegations, while hospice owner Zenia Chavez pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit illegal remunerations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one certifying physician NPI signs hospice election certifications for a disproportionate share of a single agency's admissions. Live-discharge and long-length-of-stay rates for beneficiaries certified by that NPI exceed hospice peer benchmarks. Certified beneficiaries lack any prior encounter claim with the certifying physician before the CTI date. The hospice's general ledger shows medical director or consulting payments to the same certifying NPI unrelated to documented hours. Terminal diagnoses on the hospice claim are unsupported by the beneficiary's prior Part A and Part B claim history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Certifier concentration: on certifying NPI x hospice NPI, compute the share of that hospice's certifications signed by the physician and the count of other hospices served; fires when concentration is above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Live-discharge rate: on certifying NPI x rolling 12 months, compute live discharges and revocations divided by total certifications; fires when above the calibrated percentile; action postpay audit and payment suspension. 3) Pre-certification encounter gap: on beneficiary x certifying NPI, compute days between the certification date and the most recent face-to-face encounter claim; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Ali Rashan (medical doctor, CEO and founder of ClearMD); ClearMD (COVID-19 testing provider)
State_County: New York - New York County (New York City)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Unbundling; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Rashan allegedly directed his COVID-19 testing company ClearMD to bill insurers for thousands of evaluation and management services never performed and to bill two to four COVID-19 testing codes when only a single test was administered; when insurers requested documentation, staff wrote software to auto-generate fabricated medical records that were submitted to justify retaining roughly $24 million in payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, evaluation-and-management CPT lines accompany nearly every COVID-19 test claim from a testing-only entity with no clinician staff in credentialing files. Multiple COVID-19 test HCPCS codes are billed for one specimen collection date and one accession number. Rendering NPIs on the E/M lines are the same handful of clinicians across thousands of daily encounters. Records supplied on documentation request share identical templated narrative strings across unrelated members and dates. The entity's E/M-to-test ratio is far above same-specialty testing peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) E/M attachment rate: on billing TIN x month, compute E/M lines divided by distinct COVID-19 test encounters; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Test code multiplicity: on beneficiary x collection date, compute the distinct count of COVID-19 test HCPCS codes billed; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented reflex protocol; action claim suspension. 3) Clinician-day impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute billed E/M minutes summed from CPT time thresholds; fires when the total exceeds 1440 minutes; action payment suspension and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Duane Dixon (doctor); Wendell Lewis Randall (former doctor); Charles Wilson Adams, Jr. (falsely held out as trained medical professional); Debra Shaffer (nurse practitioner); John Gregory Barnes (L5 owner); Jennifer Adams (former COO); L5 Medical Holdings, LLC d/b/a Pain Care Center
State_County: Virginia - Lynchburg; Virginia - Madison Heights (Amherst County); Virginia - Christiansburg (Montgomery County); Virginia - Blacksburg (Montgomery County); Virginia - Woodlawn (Carroll County)
SchemeSummary: At L5 Medical Holdings pain clinics, Dr. Duane Dixon pre-signed dozens of blank prescriptions that clinic staff filled out for Schedule II opioids (fentanyl, oxycodone) and gave to patients who never saw a qualified provider, and shared his DEA registration number so unauthorized providers could prescribe Suboxone; to obtain insurance payments he also approved and signed patient files, including another doctor's records, for patients he had not treated. Dixon received 40 months, a $35,000 fine and $200,000 forfeiture; co-defendants Randall (18 months) and Charles Adams (24 months) were also sentenced, and the owner, COO and L5 itself pled guilty awaiting sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Schedule II opioid pharmacy claims list a prescriber NPI with no corresponding office-visit claim for that patient near the fill date. One DEA registration number appears on prescriptions written across multiple clinic locations on the same day in PDMP data. Buprenorphine prescriptions cite a prescriber whose waiver and licence status in the state board file does not cover that clinic site. Signed patient records supplied on audit carry one physician's signature over another clinician's documented encounter. Opioid morphine-milligram-equivalent volume per prescriber NPI is far above same-specialty pain peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Fill-without-visit: on beneficiary x prescriber NPI, compute days between the controlled-substance fill date and the nearest E/M claim from that prescriber; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit on the pharmacy claim. 2) DEA geographic spread: on DEA number x date, compute the distinct count of clinic addresses on prescriptions in PDMP records; fires when the count exceeds one where travel time makes attendance impossible; action claim suspension and site visit. 3) MME concentration: on prescriber NPI x month, compute total morphine milligram equivalents dispensed per distinct patient; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Alexander Baldonado, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: A Queens physician took cash kickbacks from two related New York laboratories and from a DME supplier to order medically unnecessary cancer genetic and other lab tests and orthotic braces for Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries he never treated - many recruited at COVID-19 testing events at assisted living facilities, adult day care centers and a retirement community - and also billed Medicare for lengthy office visits he never provided, causing over $24 million in claims and more than $2.1 million in Medicare payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one ordering NPI authorizes hereditary cancer panel CPT 81162-series tests and L-code braces for beneficiaries with no prior E/M encounter with him. Ordered beneficiaries cluster at assisted living, adult day care and retirement community addresses rather than the physician's practice ZIP. The same physician bills prolonged office-visit CPT codes on dates when total billed minutes exceed a 24-hour day. Genetic testing orders lack any personal or family cancer diagnosis code required by the coverage determination. Two related laboratory NPIs and one DME supplier account for nearly all of the physician's ordered volume.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on beneficiary x ordering NPI, compute days between the genetic test or brace date of service and the most recent E/M claim between them; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer-supplier concentration: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the share of ordered lab and DMEPOS dollars going to the top three supplier NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension. 3) Visit-minute impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed CPT time-threshold minutes for all billed E/M lines; fires when the total exceeds 1440 minutes; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal grand jury in California)
FraudEntity: Violetta Mailyan (doctor, owner and operator of Healthy Way Medical Center); Healthy Way Medical Center
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Superseding indictment alleges the owner of Healthy Way Medical Center billed Medicare more than $45 million for Botox injections that were medically unnecessary or never provided, including claims for dates when she or the beneficiary was traveling internationally, when the beneficiary was in federal prison, and when the clinic was closed; she also allegedly produced falsified medical records in response to a grand jury subpoena.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare J0585 Botox unit counts per rendering NPI per date against clinic staffing and appointment capacity. Cross-check dates of service against beneficiary incarceration files and CMS inmate eligibility flags before payment. Match rendering-provider dates of service to international travel records surfaced during any investigation or to clinic closure days with zero other claim types. Compute the drug units billed versus wholesaler purchase pedigree for onabotulinumtoxinA acquired under that TIN. Look for identical chart language and cloned diagnosis strings across submitted records in ADR responses.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Toxin purchase reconciliation: on provider NPI x quarter, compute billed J0585 units minus units purchased per wholesaler pedigree invoices; fires when billed units exceed purchased units; action payment suspension. 2) Ineligible-date service: on claim line, compute overlap of the date of service with incarceration or Death Master File periods for the beneficiary; fires on any overlap; action prepay edit. 3) Impossible day volume: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total injection sessions times minimum documented session minutes; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Gabriel Alejandro Hernandez-Roman (emergency room resident doctor)
State_County: Iowa - Linn County (Cedar Rapids); Iowa - Johnson County (Iowa City)
SchemeSummary: A resident ER doctor knowingly accessed the protected health information of multiple women who were not his patients at two Iowa hospitals under false pretenses, asked one victim to falsely tell the hospital she had consented, shared a patient photograph via SnapChat with no medical purpose, and made false statements to the Iowa Board of Medicine; no billing or payer loss was involved.
WaysToIdentify: There is no claim submitted and no adjudication point, so no payer edit could have intervened. The nearest detection route is EHR access-audit logging comparing each user's record opens against the treatment relationship in the ADT and scheduling feed. State licence board complaint records and NPPES-linked disciplinary files support credentialing-time screening at the second hospital.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside claims: on user ID x patient MRN, compute the count of record opens with no matching encounter assignment in the ADT feed within the access window; fires on any unmatched open; action privacy investigation and credentialing hold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: David M. Young M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Young signed thousands of prescriptions and medical records for orthotic braces and cancer genetic tests for over 13,000 Medicare beneficiaries (including undercover agents) he never saw, spoke to, or treated, falsely certifying medical necessity, diagnoses and plans of care; brace suppliers and labs used these prescriptions to bill Medicare more than $70 million while Young was paid about $475,000 for signing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on L-code brace and CGx claims has no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI signs orders for beneficiaries across dozens of states within a single week. The same beneficiaries appear on both brace supplier claims and genetic lab claims sharing one ordering NPI. Ordered volume for that NPI jumps from near-zero to peer-top-decile with no matching office-visit claims. Beneficiary residence ZIPs sit far outside the ordering physician's practice location in PECOS.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days since the last E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct billing supplier or lab NPIs on ordered claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Cross-product overlap: on ordering NPI x beneficiary, compute the count of both a DMEPOS L-code and a CGx panel ordered within 30 days; fires when the ratio of such beneficiaries exceeds the trailing baseline; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Wendell Lewis Randall (physician, sole owner of National Institute of Toxicology, PLLC); National Institute of Toxicology, PLLC
SchemeSummary: Randall, sole physician/owner of National Institute of Toxicology, prescribed opioids and other controlled substances without regard to medical necessity and required every patient to submit to definitive urine drug tests at each visit, run by his in-house lab, billing Medicare and NC Medicaid at the highest-reimbursing code for nearly all Medicare/Medicaid patients; he obtained $753,446.70 from Medicare and $1,296,300.77 from Medicaid and used proceeds for purchases including a $97,000 building near his home.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the share of visits billing definitive urine drug testing G0483 at the highest analyte tier approaches one hundred percent per ordering NPI. The ordering NPI and the performing lab share the same TIN and address in PECOS, showing in-house self-referral. Every patient with a controlled-substance prescription on the PDMP file has a same-day definitive test claim rather than presumptive testing first. The count of drug classes billed per specimen exceeds documented clinical indication in the medical record. Payment per beneficiary per year for toxicology exceeds same-specialty peer distributions.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Definitive-test saturation: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of definitive UDT claims to total patient visits; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Highest-tier default: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute the share of toxicology claims at the top analyte-count code versus lower tiers; fires when that share exceeds the provider's trailing baseline and peer distribution; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Self-referral loop: on ordering NPI x performing lab TIN, compute the fraction of the lab's revenue traced to one ordering NPI sharing its PECOS ownership; fires when the fraction exceeds the calibrated peer percentile; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Alexander Baldonado, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Physician took cash kickbacks from two New York laboratories to order expensive cancer genetic tests and other lab tests for Medicare beneficiaries recruited at COVID-19 testing events held at assisted living facilities, adult day care centers and a retirement community, without treating, examining or even speaking to them; he also billed Medicare for lengthy office visits never provided and took cash bribes from a DME supplier for signing prescriptions for medically unnecessary orthotic braces, causing over $24 million in claims and $2.2 million in Medicare payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, high-level E/M codes are billed on the same days the physician's ordered CGx tests cluster at congregate facility addresses. Beneficiary addresses on claims map to assisted living or adult day sites rather than the ordering NPI's PECOS practice location. The ordering NPI has no prior claim history with the beneficiaries whose CGx and L-code claims he signs. Two unrelated laboratory NPIs share the identical ordering-NPI referral concentration, indicating a paid referral channel. E/M claim minutes summed per rendering NPI per date exceed a working day.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Congregate-site clustering: on ordering NPI x facility address, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with CGx claims sharing one service address in a rolling 30 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 2) E/M time impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of typical-time minutes for billed E/M codes; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Referral concentration graph: on laboratory NPI, compute the share of CGx revenue attributable to its top ordering NPI plus that NPI's degree across multiple labs and DME suppliers; fires when above the calibrated peer percentile; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (DOJ-HHS False Claims Act Working Group)
SchemeSummary: Not a specific fraud case: DOJ and HHS announced the creation of a joint False Claims Act Working Group and listed priority enforcement areas (Medicare Advantage, drug/device pricing and rebate arrangements, network adequacy, kickbacks tied to drugs/devices/DME, defective devices, and EHR manipulation driving utilization).
WaysToIdentify: This is a policy and enforcement-priority announcement, not a case, so there is no claim and no adjudication point. The nearest non-claims route is qui tam intake and risk-adjustment data validation audits in the named priority areas. Enrolment and ownership data in CMS-855 and PECOS support targeting of the listed kickback and pricing arrangements.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside claims: on Medicare Advantage contract x HCC, compute the share of risk-adjusting diagnoses unsupported by any encounter claim in the same year; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer contracts; action targeted RADV audit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (Office of Public Affairs)
FraudEntity: Peter Roussonicolos (silent-partner owner of five DME suppliers); unnamed co-conspirators serving as nominee owners
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Roussonicolos secretly owned and operated five durable medical equipment suppliers through paid nominee owners and falsified Medicare enrollment forms and bank records to hide that his felony convictions made him ineligible to enroll; the companies submitted roughly $61.5 million in claims for medically unnecessary DME (paid about $26.7 million), with beneficiary referrals obtained through kickbacks and bribes paid to patient recruiters. Restitution of $21,195,540.18 and forfeiture of $2,514,040 were ordered against him.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855S owner and managing-employee fields fail exclusion and criminal-history screening against OIG LEIE and background files. Multiple supplier NPIs list distinct nominee owners but share bank routing and deposit account numbers on EFT authorisation forms. The same practice address, phone, or billing agent appears across several separately enrolled supplier NPIs in PECOS. Newly enrolled suppliers reach top-decile L-code billing within weeks with no corresponding ordering-physician encounters. Beneficiaries appear on claims from several of the linked suppliers for overlapping DME items.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Shared bank account graph: on bank account number, compute the count of distinct enrolled supplier NPIs and TINs receiving EFT payments; fires when the count exceeds one without disclosed common ownership on CMS-855S; action payment suspension and site visit. 2) Nominee owner screen: on CMS-855S owner and managing employee, compute exact-match hits against OIG LEIE and prior revoked-NPI ownership records; fires on any registry match; action enrolment denial and prepay edit. 3) New-supplier ramp: on supplier NPI x week, compute paid DMEPOS dollars divided by weeks since PECOS effective date; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty new enrollees; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut

The nearest detection route is cross-lender matching of EIN, address, and bank account across PPP and EIDL application records. IRS transcript verification of the attached tax returns and quarterly 941 filings would contradict the stated payroll.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside claims: on applicant EIN, compute reported employee count and wages versus IRS Form 941 filings and state wage records; fires on any mismatch beyond filing tolerance; action loan disbursement hold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana

SchemeSummary: Annual FY2024 collections release: after a trial and guilty verdict, the office's Monetary Penalties and Recovery Unit collected approximately $3.7 million in restitution to Medicare from hospice owner Shiva Akula, restraining and turning over his assets including hospice licenses; separately it forfeited approximately $34,570 in proceeds from Michelle Andre, who pleaded guilty to distributing misbranded injectable contraceptives to patients. For the drug component, wholesaler pedigree and FDA misbranding registries identify product not traceable to a licensed supply chain.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Tajul Shams Chowdhury (physician, owner of Center for Pain Management); Mohammad Imtiaz Chowdhury (purported pharmacy marketer, son)
SchemeSummary: A physician referred prescriptions for costly compounded drugs from his Edinburg pain management clinic to local pharmacies, and the pharmacy paid $6.6 million in kickbacks to his son, who posed as a pharmacy marketer.

Average paid amount per compounded prescription for that pharmacy sits far above same-specialty peer distributions. Pharmacy payroll or 1099 records show payments to a marketer sharing a surname and address with the top prescriber. Compound formulations repeat identical ingredient mixes across unrelated patients regardless of diagnosis on the claim. Refills continue without any intervening E/M encounter between prescriber NPI and beneficiary.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber-pharmacy concentration: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI, compute the share of that prescriber's compounded-drug claims filled by one pharmacy; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) High-cost compound mix: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute mean paid dollars per compounded claim and the distinct-formulation count; fires when cost is above peer percentile while formulation diversity is below it; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Marketer payment link: on pharmacy TIN, compute the count of vendor or payroll payees sharing surname, address, or bank account with a top-decile referring prescriber; fires when the count exceeds zero; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Carrie Musselman (chiropractor)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor billed Medicare and private insurers for services falsely represented as performed by physicians when they were actually delivered by nurse practitioners and physician assistants (triggering higher reimbursement), billed placement of electroacupuncture devices as surgically implanted neurostimulators, and billed for neurostimulators and allergy injections never provided (patients instead received unapproved 'experimental' oral drops). Convicted at trial of health care fraud and five wire fraud counts; a related release notes she was later sentenced to 20 months and ordered to repay more than $2.3 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claims bill under a physician NPI on dates when only nurse practitioners or physician assistants are on the practice's staffing roster and timesheets. The practice bills CPT codes for surgically implanted neurostimulators without any facility, anesthesia, or operating-room claim on the same date. Place of service on the neurostimulator claims is an office rather than a surgical setting permitted by the code descriptor. Allergy injection HCPCS units far exceed antigen vials purchased under that TIN per wholesaler pedigree. Rendering NPI specialty in NPPES is chiropractic, outside the scope of the procedure codes billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Incident-to identity mismatch: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute claims billed under a physician NPI minus documented physician presence in payroll or scheduling records; fires when the difference exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 2) Implant without procedure context: on claim line, compute the presence of a matching facility, anesthesia, or device HCPCS claim for the same beneficiary and date; fires when the neurostimulator code appears with no such companion claim and office place of service; action claim suspension. 3) Scope-of-licence edit: on rendering NPI x CPT, compute exact match of the billed code against services permitted by the state licence board file and NPPES taxonomy; fires on any mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Carrie Musselman (chiropractor)
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor billed Medicare and twelve other insurers for services as if performed by medical doctors when they were actually performed by mid-level providers (triggering automatic higher reimbursement), billed for allergy injections never given (patients instead received unapproved experimental oral drops), and billed placement of an electroacupuncture device as a surgically implanted neurostimulator, a service that otherwise would not have been payable.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, services bill under a physician NPI although the practice's rostered clinicians that day are mid-level providers only. Allergy injection code units exceed antigen doses purchased under that TIN per wholesaler invoices. Neurostimulator implantation codes appear with an office place of service and no anesthesia or facility claim. NPPES taxonomy and state licence board file show the billing provider is licensed as a chiropractor, not a physician. Patient complaint records and remittance history show repeated identical code combinations across all beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Supervising-physician presence: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute physician-billed line count minus documented physician on-site hours from payroll records; fires when the difference exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 2) Supply reconciliation: on provider TIN x quarter, compute billed allergen injection units minus units purchased per wholesaler pedigree; fires when billed exceeds purchased; action payment suspension. 3) Code-to-licence match: on claim line, compute exact comparison of the billed CPT against the scope permitted by the rendering NPI's state licence and NPPES taxonomy; fires on mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Darius Moore (patient recruiter / "body broker")
SchemeSummary: Moore worked as a "body broker," conspiring with sober living home/addiction treatment facility owners to refer patients for drug addiction treatment; the facilities billed the patients' private insurance for the treatment and paid Moore a share of the insurance proceeds, totaling nearly $500,000 in kickbacks. He was also convicted of a separate firearms offense committed while on pretrial release.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, admitted members cluster by a small set of referral sources and out-of-state home addresses far from the facility's licensed location. The same member cycles through multiple treatment facility TINs with repeated detox admissions within short intervals. Facility claims show premiums recently paid by a third party rather than the member, visible in the plan's premium payment file. Urine drug testing volume per admitted member vastly exceeds peer facilities' per-member counts. Marketing or consultant payments in the facility's vendor ledger track proportionally to admissions per referrer.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral-source concentration: on facility NPI x referral source identifier, compute the share of admissions attributable to one non-clinical referrer; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer facilities; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Member recycling: on member x 12 months, compute the distinct count of treatment facility TINs billing residential or detox levels of care; fires when the count exceeds the plan's clinically supported readmission baseline; action claim suspension and documentation request (ADR). 3) Third-party premium linkage: on member, compute whether the premium payer bank account matches an account also paying premiums for other members admitted to the same facility; fires when the shared-account degree exceeds one; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Alabama
FraudEntity: Exactech Inc. (medical device manufacturer, Gainesville, Florida)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: Exactech allegedly knew as early as January 2008 that its finned tibial tray knee-replacement component failed prematurely at an unacceptable rate, and as early as January 2019 that the polyethylene component in its Logic and Truliant knee systems did likewise, yet continued marketing and selling them for total-knee replacement surgeries on Medicare, Medicaid and VA beneficiaries, causing claims for devices that were not reasonable and necessary. Resolved via $8 million settlement ($7,640,000 federal share, $360,000 state share) in Chapter 11 bankruptcy, arising from qui tam suits in Alabama and Maryland.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, revision-surgery CPT claims tied to one device model's implant registry entries show early failure well before expected device life. Device identifier fields on hospital claims link implants to the specific tibial tray and polyethylene lots at issue. FDA MAUDE adverse-event counts and manufacturer recall notices name the same catalogue numbers being billed. Time from index arthroplasty to revision per device model is far shorter than peer models in the payer's own claims history. Continued billing of the model after the recall date is visible in remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Early-revision rate by device: on device catalogue number, compute revision arthroplasty claims divided by index implant claims within a fixed post-implant window using UDI fields; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer device models; action postpay audit and coverage review. 2) Recall-date billing: on claim line, compute exact match of the billed UDI or catalogue number against FDA recall and manufacturer notification registries with date of service after the notice; fires on any match; action prepay edit. 3) Time-to-failure gap: on beneficiary x device model, compute days between index implant and revision; fires when the median gap for that model falls below the peer-model baseline; action coverage determination and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Michael Roberts (executive director and co-owner of Progressive Alternatives); Larry Keith Gildersleeve III (co-owner/purchaser)
State_County: Ohio - Lake County; Ohio - Ashtabula County
SchemeSummary: Roberts, executive director and co-owner of Progressive Alternatives, an in-home care business serving people with developmental disabilities, withheld payroll taxes from employees' wages (reflected on paychecks and W-2s given to employees) but never filed W-2 forms with the government or remitted the required quarterly employment tax payments to the IRS; the scheme surfaced when an employee preparing to retire in 2017 found the payroll taxes had not been paid. Restitution figures combine Roberts ($322,718.56) and co-owner spouse Gildersleeve ($692,697.50), each sentenced to 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, since the loss falls on the IRS rather than a payer. The nearest detection route is IRS matching of Forms W-2 issued to employees against employer 941 filings and deposits. State wage-reporting files also show wages paid with no corresponding federal deposit for the same EIN.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside claims: on employer EIN x quarter, compute wages reported on employee W-2 and state wage files minus wages reported and deposited on Form 941; fires when the difference exceeds zero; action IRS employment-tax examination.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Dafud Iza (executive vice president of an insurance brokerage firm)
PayerName: Affordable Care Act federal premium subsidies (federal government/ACA insurance plan)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Iza and accomplices at an insurance brokerage submitted false ACA plan applications that inflated the incomes of ineligible, often homeless or substance-affected consumers (and used mismatched addresses and Social Security numbers) so the federal government would pay premium subsidies; the brokerage collected millions in commissions from the insurer, and the government paid at least $133.9 million in subsidies. Street marketers paid bribes to induce enrollment.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, stated household income on ACA applications fails income verification against IRS and SSA data hub responses. One broker National Producer Number appears on applications for an implausible count of enrollees relative to peer brokers. The same mailing address or phone number recurs across many unrelated applicant households on the enrolment file. Applicants show projected income clustered just above the Medicaid threshold with zero subsequent utilisation claims. Applicant SSNs mismatch names in the SSA verification response yet the plan remains effectuated.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Income-hub mismatch: on application, compute the difference between attested projected income and IRS or SSA reported income from the data hub; fires when attested income clears the subsidy threshold while verified income does not; action subsidy hold pending documentation. 2) Broker enrolment concentration: on broker NPN x month, compute the count of enrolments and the share with zero claims in the first 90 days; fires when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus peer brokers; action commission suspension and enrolment audit. 3) Shared contact graph: on mailing address or phone number, compute the distinct count of unrelated applicant households enrolled; fires when the count exceeds one without documented relationship; action enrolment verification and prepay subsidy edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Eye Consultants of Pennsylvania, PC (ECOP) (ophthalmology practice)
SchemeSummary: ECOP billed Medicare Part B for Evaluation & Management services on the same date of service as bilateral eye injections for beneficiaries, contrary to Medicare billing rules, and agreed to pay $790,000 to resolve False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, an E/M code appears on the same date of service as an intravitreal injection CPT for the same beneficiary and rendering NPI. Modifier 25 is appended on nearly every such paired claim rather than exceptionally, visible in the claim line modifier field. The provider's rate of same-day E/M with injections exceeds same-specialty peer distributions in remittance history. Documentation submitted on ADR lacks a separately identifiable service beyond the injection's inherent evaluation. Bilateral injection modifiers and E/M pairing repeat across consecutive monthly visits for the same beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Bundled same-day E/M: on claim line, compute whether an E/M code and a same-date injection CPT for the same beneficiary and rendering NPI both pay without a supported modifier 25 basis; fires on any such pairing; action prepay edit. 2) Modifier 25 saturation: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the share of injection encounters carrying a paired E/M with modifier 25; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Repeat pairing per beneficiary: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the count of consecutive months with both an injection and same-day E/M; fires when the count exceeds the provider's trailing baseline; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Office of Public Affairs)

Soleyman Cohen-Sedgh, Farid Pakravan, Farhad Manavi; Hemisphere GNSS (USA) Inc.; Andrew Maloney and Capstone Diagnostics; Provista Health LLC and Patrick Britton-Harr (owner); CityMD entities (City Medical of the Upper East Side PLLC, Summit Medical Group P.A., Summit Health Management LLC, Village Practice Management Company LLC); Sikorsky Support Services Inc. and Derco Aerospace Inc.; Austal USA LLC; Insect Shield LLC and Estate of Richard Lane; Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia Tech Research Corp.; Guidehouse Inc.; Nan McKay; Insight Global LLC; Gen Digital Inc. (formerly Symantec Corp.); City of Los Angeles; Hilcorp San Juan L.P.; XTO Energy Inc.; Hahn Air Lines GmbH and Hahn Air USA Inc.; Consolidated Nuclear Security LLC; AECOM

SchemeSummary: Annual DOJ report: False Claims Act settlements and judgments exceeded $2.9 billion in FY2024 (over $1.67 billion health care related) across 558 resolutions and 979 new qui tam suits, spanning opioid over-dispensing and unlawful prescribing (Endo/Opana ER, Rite Aid controlled substances, Dr. Gerber), billing for medically unnecessary or never-provided services (Grand Health Care therapy quotas, Acadia inpatient behavioral health, Crossroads billing exams for check-ins, Walgreens prescriptions never picked up, unnecessary respiratory panel and cancer genomic tests), kickback and Stark Law arrangements (Community Health Network above-FMV physician pay, DaVita, Oak Street Health agent payments, Paksn medical directorships, RDx commissions/MSO payments, Innovasis surgeon inducements), Medicare Advantage and rebate-reporting misconduct, retained overpayments (Gentiva hospice, USFHP plans), plus pandemic PPP/COVID-testing and cybersecurity, procurement and royalty matters.
