JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Helen Zervas (optometrist, owner of Family Eye Care)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Optometrist billed Medicaid (300+ claims) and Medicare (30+ claims) for insertion of amniotic membrane to the eye surface when the treatment was never provided or was not medically necessary; she then conspired with a senior state Office of Policy and Management official and a state representative, paying them through Family Eye Care to pressure state employees to interfere with the Medicaid billing audit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, amniotic membrane codes V2790 and CPT 65778 billed per beneficiary exceed the eye-surface anatomy plausible in the date-of-service series. Claim volume for a single high-cost graft HCPCS concentrates in one rendering NPI far above same-specialty peers in the state file. Purchase invoices and lot numbers for the amniotic tissue do not reconcile with the units billed on paid remittance history. Chart notes lack a documented corneal defect diagnosis on the ICD fields supporting membrane placement. Payments from the practice TIN to state officials appear in the CMS-855 ownership and managing-employee disclosures and in Open Payments-style vendor records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Tissue-product inventory reconciliation: on provider NPI x HCPCS x quarter, compute units billed for amniotic membrane codes minus units evidenced by supplier purchase invoices and lot numbers; fires when billed units exceed purchased units; action prepay edit. 2) Graft frequency per eye: on beneficiary x provider NPI, compute the count of amniotic membrane placements per laterality modifier in a rolling year; fires when count exceeds the documented defect episodes; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Single-code concentration: on provider NPI x quarter, compute the share of allowed dollars from the top one high-cost HCPCS; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Donald Calvin Saunders (organizer/leader); Vanessa Ragin-Boatright; Dajuan Strickland; Cynthia Jenkins Harris; Latarsa Hitchcock; Stephanie Corbett; Karen McClary; David Corey Hill; Crystal Sherrell Jackson (owner, Jackson Consulting Services LLC); Nirvana Hyperbaric Institute, LLC; Roger Hunter (owner); Dr. Herminia De Guzman Ferreras; Steven Osbey (clinic co-owner); Benson I. Ejindu (DME business operator); LabXperior Corporation; Tina Ball (owner)
State_County: North Carolina - Mecklenburg County (Charlotte); South Carolina
PayerName: South Carolina Medicaid; North Carolina Medicaid; Medicare
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Eight defendants were charged with conspiring to bill South Carolina Medicaid more than $21 million for behavioral health services that were inflated or never rendered, buying and selling Medicaid beneficiaries' personal identifying information (including fictitious beneficiaries created by investigators), paying kickbacks for providers' NPI numbers (some obtained by tricking professionals with fake job applications), creating fictitious service notes, and laundering proceeds disguised as consulting contracts and payroll. Separately, Crystal Jackson allegedly billed NC Medicaid over $1.9 million (paid $1.6 million) through Jackson Consulting Services for psychotherapy and high-level urine drug tests that were unnecessary or never provided, using beneficiary identities including more than a dozen incarcerated or deceased persons; the release also reports civil False Claims Act resolutions totaling about $5.1 million (Nirvana Hyperbaric $200,000, Steven Osbey $4.7 million judgment for phantom physician home visits, LabXperior/Tina Ball $235,000) plus a filed complaint against a DME operator for billing more expensive supplies than provided.  Figures span multiple defendants and separate schemes.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, dates of service post-date the beneficiary's date on the Death Master File or fall inside a state incarceration roster window. Rendering NPIs appear on claims from a billing TIN with no employment or affiliation record in NPPES or the state provider file. Sentinel fictitious beneficiary identifiers created by investigators appear on submitted claims, an exact registry mismatch. High-complexity urine drug testing codes are billed alongside psychotherapy for nearly every beneficiary of one group. Service notes across a rendering NPI share identical text blocks and identical minute counts across dates of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Ineligible-beneficiary status: on claim line, compute the gap in days between date of service and the Death Master File date or incarceration admission date; fires when the service date follows either date; action prepay edit. 2) NPI-borrowing detection: on rendering NPI x billing TIN, compute the count of claim lines where no NPPES affiliation or payroll record links the pair; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Test-with-therapy pairing: on billing TIN x month, compute the ratio of definitive urine drug test claims to distinct psychotherapy beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Sanjeev Kumar (gynecologist)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a Memphis gynecologist performed medically unnecessary gynecologic procedures using single-use medical devices that he stored in unsanitary conditions and reused on patients instead of disposing of or properly reprocessing them, then billed Medicare and Medicaid as though the procedures were medically necessary and a new or properly reprocessed device had been used each time; charged with 27 counts of adulteration/misbranding of medical devices.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, procedure claims using single-use device codes exceed the practice's documented device purchases on wholesaler and distributor pedigree records. One rendering NPI bills the same gynecologic procedure CPT for an implausible share of his panel per year. Device-supply HCPCS or revenue-code charges are absent on claims that require a disposable instrument, indicating no new unit consumed. Procedure counts per rendering NPI per date of service imply more room-minutes than a 24-hour day allows. State licence board file and accreditation survey records show unresolved infection-control deficiencies at the practice address.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Disposable-device reconciliation: on provider NPI x quarter, compute procedures billed requiring a single-use instrument minus units purchased in distributor pedigree data; fires when billed procedures exceed purchases; action postpay audit plus site visit. 2) Procedure saturation per panel: on rendering NPI x year, compute the share of distinct beneficiaries receiving the target gynecologic CPT; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Day-capacity check: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of procedure typical-time minutes across all billed lines; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: George Nathaniel Boykins (Qualified Mental Health Professional)
State_County: Virginia - Richmond; Virginia - Chesterfield County (North Chesterfield)
SchemeSummary: Boykins, a Qualified Mental Health Professional, caused his multiple employers to submit Medicaid claims for Mental Health Skill-Building Services he never provided - including on dates he was outside the United States, for different recipients at the same date and time across employers, and once while he was being interviewed by law enforcement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the same rendering NPI bills overlapping service minutes for different recipients at the same date and time across separate billing TINs. Claimed service dates fall inside international travel windows shown in border-crossing or payroll absence records. Daily billed service units for one staff member exceed 24 hours across all employers combined. EVV visit records or timesheets carry no GPS check-in matching the recipient address on the claim. Mental health skill-building units per recipient sit above the state service plan authorization on the prior-authorisation record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cross-employer overlap: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute overlapping service minutes across all billing TINs using start and stop times; fires when any two lines overlap by more than zero minutes; action prepay edit. 2) Daily hour ceiling: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of billed units converted to hours; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) EVV corroboration: on claim line, compute the count of matching EVV visit records within the billed time window at the recipient address; fires when the count is zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Precious Cruse (owner and operator of Caring Through Love, a prenatal care coordination company); Caring Through Love
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Cruse recruited pregnant women and young mothers into her prenatal care coordination company by offering free baby items (car seats, pack 'n plays, diapers, wipes) as inducements, then used their personal information to bill Medicaid for prenatal care coordination services that were never provided; proceeds funded luxury travel, designer clothing and an $18,000 custom diamond necklace and bracelet.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, prenatal care coordination claims lack any corresponding prenatal or obstetric claim from any provider for the same beneficiary. One provider NPI bills care coordination for a count of distinct pregnant enrollees far above same-specialty peers in the state. Care coordination encounter dates cluster on identical calendar days across many unrelated beneficiaries with identical unit counts. Beneficiary contact information on enrollment forms repeats one phone number or address across dozens of member records. Gift and incentive expenditures appear in the provider's cost reports without corresponding beneficiary-signed acknowledgement in the case files.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota

PayerName: Minnesota Medicaid (Minnesota Health Care Programs/Minnesota DHS); UCare; USDA Federal Child Nutrition Program (via Feeding Our Future/MDE)

SchemeSummary: Hassan enrolled Smart Therapy LLC as an EIDBI autism provider (concealing co-owners, one excluded by DHS), recruited Somali-community children by paying parents $300-$1,500 monthly cash kickbacks, used a QSP to get every child qualified for autism services, staffed 'behavioral technicians' with untrained teenage relatives, and billed Minnesota Medicaid/DHS and UCare for the maximum authorized ABA therapy hours - including services never rendered and claims bearing forged provider/QSP signatures - collecting over $14 million, some of which was wired abroad to buy real estate in Kenya. WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, CMS-855 and state ownership disclosures omit a co-owner who appears on the DHS exclusion list and OIG LEIE. Billed ABA hours equal the maximum authorized units on the prior-authorisation record for almost every member every month. Behavioral technician rendering NPIs lack the required state credential or training registry entry on the licence board file. Provider and QSP signatures on treatment plans repeat as identical image files across unrelated member records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Hidden ownership screen: on provider NPI x owner SSN or EIN in CMS-855 disclosures, compute exact matches against OIG LEIE and the state exclusion file including prior addresses and affiliated entities; fires on any exact registry match; action claim suspension plus site visit. 2) Authorization-ceiling billing: on provider NPI x month, compute the share of members billed at exactly 100 percent of authorized ABA units; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Single-diagnoser funnel: on diagnosing NPI x provider NPI, compute the share of that provider's members whose autism qualification originates from one assessor; fires when above the peer percentile; action prior-authorisation requirement.

Supplier billing concentrates in a handful of ordering NPIs supplying almost all beneficiaries.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida

State_County: Florida - Pinellas County (Pinellas Park, St. Petersburg); Florida - Pinellas County (Palm Harbor)

SchemeSummary: Gulfcoast Eye and a third-party TCD provider performed trans-cranial doppler ultrasounds on thousands of patients and billed Medicare/Medicaid hundreds of dollars per test, pre-assigning patients a qualifying diagnosis (occlusion and stenosis of cerebral arteries) before results were received even though nearly no patient had that condition; Gulfcoast Eye paid the TCD provider based on the volume/value of tests ordered and referred patients to the provider's preferred radiology group, violating the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Diagnosis code appears on the claim with a date of service preceding any interpreting radiologist report in the record. The ordering practice's payment history shows per-test remittance to an outside testing entity, visible in CMS-855B contracted-supplier and reassignment fields. Almost all downstream imaging referrals from the practice route to a single radiology group TIN. Test volume per beneficiary exceeds specialty peers with no confirmatory follow-up vascular study in the beneficiary's other claims.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Pre-assigned diagnosis rate: on rendering NPI x CPT for cerebral doppler studies, compute the share of lines carrying occlusion/stenosis ICD-10 codes; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Referral concentration: on ordering NPI, compute the share of imaging referrals paid to a single radiology TIN and the graph degree of distinct receiving TINs; fires when concentration is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 3) Confirmation absence: on beneficiary x doppler CPT, compute the count of follow-up vascular or neurology claims within 180 days; fires when that count is zero for a provider whose positive-diagnosis rate is top-decile; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Pinellas Eye Care, P.A. d/b/a Gulfcoast Eye Care (ophthalmology practice)

SchemeSummary: Gulfcoast Eye and a third-party TCD provider performed trans-cranial doppler ultrasounds on thousands of patients and billed Medicare and Medicaid hundreds of dollars per test, pre-assigning patients a qualifying diagnosis (occlusion and stenosis of cerebral arteries) before results were available even though nearly all patients did not have that condition; Gulfcoast paid the third-party provider based on the volume/value of tests ordered and referred patients to its preferred radiology group, implicating the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Settlement of $615,000 ($602,046 federal, $12,953 Florida), with $116,850 to the qui tam whistleblower.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, nearly every trans-cranial doppler line from one practice carries the same cerebral occlusion or stenosis ICD-10 code. The qualifying diagnosis appears on claims dated before any interpreting report exists in the medical record produced on ADR. Per-test payments from the practice to an outside testing vendor appear in CMS-855B contracted-entity and reassignment disclosures. Downstream imaging referrals from the practice concentrate on one radiology group TIN in the beneficiary's other claims. Beneficiaries show no confirmatory carotid or cerebrovascular study after a positive doppler result.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Diagnosis saturation: on rendering NPI x doppler CPT, compute the proportion of lines bearing occlusion/stenosis diagnosis codes; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Referral graph concentration: on referring NPI x quarter, compute the share of imaging dollars flowing to the single largest receiving TIN; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 3) Volume-based vendor payment exposure: on practice TIN, compute the ratio of paid doppler tests to distinct beneficiaries seen; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: OHM Pharmacy Services, aka "Benzer," aka "Auburndale" (Florida-based pharmacy)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy dispensed the high-priced naloxone auto-injector Evzio and, to obtain insurer coverage, completed and signed prior authorization forms in place of prescribing physicians (sometimes without authorization), making it appear physicians submitted them, and included false statements that patients had already tried and failed Narcan/naloxone. Resolution combined a criminal guilty plea with $82,000 restitution plus one year probation and a $1,018,000 False Claims Act civil settlement (whistleblower share $285,040).
WaysToIdentify: At prior authorisation, the submitting fax number and IP on the Evzio PA form trace to the dispensing pharmacy NPI rather than the prescriber's office. The prescriber signature block on PA forms is identical in image across many different prescribing NPIs. Step-therapy attestation claims prior Narcan trial, yet the beneficiary's Part D history shows no naloxone NDC ever dispensed. One pharmacy NPI accounts for a dominant share of the plan's total Evzio NDC claims. Prescribing NPIs on those claims have no other dispensing relationship with that pharmacy in remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) PA origin mismatch: on prior-authorisation record, compare the submitting fax/NPI on the form against the prescriber NPI of record in NPPES; fires on exact mismatch to the dispensing pharmacy NPI; action prepay edit. 2) Step-therapy contradiction: on beneficiary x high-cost naloxone NDC, compute the count of prior naloxone NDC fills in the Part D claim history; fires when the PA asserts prior failure and that count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Single-NDC concentration: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of paid dollars from one branded NDC and the count of distinct prescriber NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: OHM Pharmacy Services, aka "Benzer," aka "Auburndale" (Florida-based pharmacy)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy dispensed the high-priced naloxone auto-injector Evzio and, to obtain insurer coverage, completed and signed prior authorization forms in place of prescribing physicians (sometimes without physician authorization), making it appear a physician submitted them, and included false statements such as that patients had previously tried and failed Narcan/naloxone, causing Medicare Part D and other insurers to reimburse the claims. Resolution includes $82,000 criminal restitution plus $1,018,000 False Claims Act civil settlement, of which the whistleblower receives $285,040.
WaysToIdentify: At prior authorisation, Evzio PA forms arrive from a fax number and sender registered to the dispensing pharmacy, not the prescriber's practice address in PECOS. Identical prescriber signature images repeat across PA forms bearing different prescriber NPIs. The asserted prior Narcan failure is contradicted by the absence of any naloxone NDC in the beneficiary's Part D history. One pharmacy NPI submits an outsized share of a plan's PA requests for a single high-cost NDC. Prescribers named on PA forms disclaim any dispensing relationship when contacted during credentialing verification.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Pharmacy-originated PA: on prior-authorisation record, compute whether the submitter identifier equals the dispensing pharmacy NPI rather than the prescriber NPI in NPPES; fires on exact mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Step-therapy evidence gap: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the count of prior naloxone fills in the 24-month Part D history; fires when the PA asserts prior failure and the count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Signature reuse: on pharmacy NPI, compute the distinct-count of prescriber NPIs sharing one identical signature image hash on submitted PA forms; fires when that count exceeds one; action payment suspension.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Sehrelina Tardo (senior accountant at a car dealership)
SchemeSummary: As senior accountant at a New Orleans car dealership, Tardo embezzled customer cash down payments and deposits for herself and concealed the theft with fake journal entries of customer transactions in the employer's books; she agreed to pay $535,750.77 restitution to the dealership. No health care service or payer involved.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point in this scheme, only employer cash receipts. Detection belongs to the dealership's bank reconciliation, comparing deposit slips against posted customer deal jackets and receipts. Segregation-of-duties review would show one accountant both receiving cash and posting the offsetting journal entries.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Deposit reconciliation gap: on employee ID x day, compute the difference between customer down payments recorded on deal jackets and the amounts deposited to the bank account; fires when any unexplained non-zero difference exists; action internal postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Yolanda Dupont (nominee owner of Allstar Medical Supply Corp.); Allstar Medical Supply Corp.
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Dupont acted as nominee owner of Allstar Medical Supply Corp., a purported New Hampshire DME company, to conceal the true owners and falsely certified no false claims would be submitted; she and co-conspirators billed Medicare approximately $3.3 million for orthotic braces that were medically unnecessary and often unwanted, collecting at least $1.6 million.

Brace claims list ordering NPIs with no prior E/M encounter with the beneficiary. Beneficiary residence ZIPs lie far outside the supplier's declared service area on the CMS-855S. Supplier billing rises from zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of initial PECOS enrolment. Beneficiary contact confirms no delivery, contradicting the proof-of-delivery documents supplied on ADR.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Nominee-owner linkage: on CMS-855S owner SSN, compute the distinct-count of supplier NPIs where that person is listed as owner or officer in PECOS; fires when that count exceeds one for a new enrollee; action site visit before billing privileges activate. 2) New-supplier ramp: on supplier NPI x month since enrolment, compute paid DMEPOS dollars and distinct beneficiary count; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-vintage peers; action prepay edit. 3) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days to the nearest prior E/M claim with that beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Georgina Exposito (owner of 3rd Party Services of Florida); 3rd Party Services of Florida
SchemeSummary: Exposito and her company allegedly altered patients' medical diagnoses in prior authorization requests submitted on behalf of pharmacies, including PerforMix Specialty Pharmacy, a compounding pharmacy in Amherst, NH, causing false claims to be submitted to Medicare and TRICARE; she agreed to pay $400,000 under the False Claims Act following a whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: At prior authorisation, the diagnosis code on the PA request does not appear anywhere in the beneficiary's prior claim history from that prescriber. A single PA-submission vendor identifier appears across requests for multiple unrelated pharmacy NPIs. Compound drug PA approval rates for that submitter far exceed peer submitters for the same drug classes. The prescriber NPI on the PA form has no other claim contact with the beneficiary near the request date. Diagnosis codes on PA forms shift to covered indications immediately after a plan coverage policy change.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) PA diagnosis corroboration: on prior-authorisation record, compute whether the asserted diagnosis code appears in the beneficiary's claim history within the lookback window; fires on exact absence; action prepay edit. 2) Submitter concentration: on PA submitter identifier, compute the distinct-count of pharmacy NPIs and the approval rate for compounded NDCs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer submitters; action claim suspension. 3) Prescriber-beneficiary linkage: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary, compute the count of encounters within 90 days of the PA date; fires when that count is zero; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Julian Lopez (seller of Medicare beneficiary information); One Medical Services (durable medical equipment company)
SchemeSummary: Lopez obtained Medicare beneficiary identification cards and sold beneficiaries' personal information to One Medical Services, a sham DME company, which used the data to bill Medicare over $3.2 million for orthotic braces that were never provided and were medically unnecessary.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, brace claims for one supplier NPI show no ordering NPI encounter with the beneficiary in the claim history. Many billed beneficiaries share a common enrolment or address cluster inconsistent with the supplier's CMS-855S service area. Beneficiaries appear on this supplier's claims while showing no other Medicare utilisation for years. Some dates of service post-date the beneficiary's date in the Death Master File. Proof-of-delivery documents supplied on ADR share identical signature images across different beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dormant-beneficiary billing: on beneficiary x supplier NPI, compute the count of other Medicare claims in the 12 months before the brace date of service; fires when that count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Post-death service: on claim line, compute days between date of service and Death Master File date; fires when the service date is on or after death; action prepay edit. 3) Delivery-proof reuse: on supplier NPI, compute the distinct-count of beneficiaries sharing one identical proof-of-delivery signature image hash; fires when that count exceeds one; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Shekhar Thakur (physician, owner of Parkside Medical)
SchemeSummary: Physician at his own Battle Creek clinic routinely prescribed Schedule II opioids, benzodiazepines and other controlled substances without legitimate medical purpose - no physical exam, records review or verification, and despite failed urine drug screens indicating abuse or diversion - resulting in a Controlled Substances Act civil suit resolved for $705,075 and permanent surrender of DEA registration.
WaysToIdentify: In PDMP and Part D data, one prescriber NPI writes Schedule II opioids with benzodiazepine overlap at rates above same-specialty peers. Controlled-substance prescriptions issue on dates with no corresponding E/M claim for the same beneficiary. Urine drug screen results in the record show illicit substances or absent parent drug, yet opioid fills continue afterwards. Beneficiaries travel unusually long distances from residence ZIP to the clinic's practice address in NPPES. High-MME prescriptions cluster on days where the prescriber's billed encounter count exceeds feasible clinic hours.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescription without encounter: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary x fill date, compute days to the nearest E/M claim by that prescriber; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit on the pharmacy claim. 2) Opioid-benzodiazepine overlap: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the share of patients with overlapping Schedule II opioid and benzodiazepine days supply and mean daily MME; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Encounter-hours feasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed typical-time minutes of billed E/M codes; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire; Justice Department Tax Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Andrew Park (co-founder and CEO of a startup technology company)
SchemeSummary: As CEO responsible for company finances, Park withheld Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from employees' wages from 2014 through Q3 2021 but never paid them over to the IRS, also failing to pay the employer's matching share, and did not file his own individual returns from 2013-2020 despite a ~$250,000 annual salary, causing over $14 million in tax loss. He was ordered to pay $639,821.78 restitution plus a $15,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the loss is unremitted employment tax. Detection sits with IRS matching of Forms W-2 withholding totals against Forms 941 filed and deposits actually made. A second route is matching W-2 wage reporting for a named officer against the absence of a filed Form 1040 for the same years.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Withholding remittance gap: on employer EIN x quarter, compute the difference between W-2 reported withholding and Form 941 deposits received; fires when the difference is positive for consecutive quarters; action IRS trust fund recovery examination.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Andrew Park (co-founder and CEO of a startup technology company)
SchemeSummary: As CEO of a startup software company, Park withheld federal, state and local payroll taxes (including Social Security and Medicare withholdings) from employees' wages from 2014 through Q3 2021 but never paid them over to the IRS, using the funds as capital for the business, and also failed to file personal returns from 2013-2020 despite a ~$250,000 annual salary, causing over $14.7 million in tax loss; ordered to pay $639,821.78 restitution plus a $15,000 fine.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point here, only unpaid payroll trust fund taxes. Detection belongs to IRS reconciliation of Form W-2 withholding totals against Form 941 filings and actual deposits for the same EIN. Officer non-filing is detectable by matching reported W-2 officer wages to the absence of a Form 1040 for those tax years.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Trust fund shortfall: on employer EIN x quarter, compute W-2 withholding reported minus federal tax deposits received; fires when positive across consecutive quarters; action IRS trust fund recovery penalty assessment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
FraudEntity: Pamela J. Kahut (former Chief Financial Officer, Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission)
PayerName: Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission self-funded health care benefit program (health benefit trust account)
SchemeSummary: As CFO, Kahut controlled the employer's self-funded health benefit trust account and wrote checks/withdrew approximately $211,083 from it between October 2014 and September 2020, including a $2,812.85 check for her spouse's long-term care insurance premium, plus paying off her pension loans and credit card bills.
WaysToIdentify: There is no provider claim and no payer adjudication point, since disbursements came directly from a self-funded trust bank account. Detection belongs to the plan's TPA reconciliation, comparing trust account disbursements against adjudicated claim payments and premium remittances. Checks payable to individuals or to insurers unrelated to the plan, such as a long-term care carrier, have no matching adjudicated claim record.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Unmatched trust disbursement: on health benefit trust bank account x month, compute the sum of debits with no corresponding adjudicated claim or premium invoice identifier; fires when any unmatched debit exists; action postpay audit and dual-signature requirement on the account.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
