Federal grant single-audit testing of allowable fringe benefit costs would surface payees unrelated to any plan participant claim.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payee registry mismatch: on trust account disbursement, compute whether the payee matches an enrolled participant, provider NPI, or contracted carrier on the plan roster; fires on exact registry mismatch; action postpay audit and payment suspension on the account.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jennifer Adams (Chief Operating Officer and practice manager, L5 Medical Holdings d/b/a Pain Care Centers); John Barnes (owner, L5 Medical Holdings); L5 Medical Holdings d/b/a Pain Care Centers; Dr. Wendell Randall (practitioner)
State_County: Virginia - Woodlawn; Virginia - Lynchburg; Virginia - Madison Heights; Virginia - Blacksburg; Virginia - Christiansburg
SchemeSummary: As COO of pain clinics owned by a non-medical former mortgage broker, Adams directed non-medical staff to override providers' medical decisions on opioid and Suboxone prescribing, knew the clinics used doctors' DEA prescribing credentials to issue Suboxone prescriptions for patients those doctors never saw, and implemented urine drug-testing policies that improperly inflated bills to medical insurers.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, buprenorphine prescriptions carry a prescriber DEA/NPI with no corresponding E/M or OTP encounter claim for that beneficiary. Definitive urine drug testing panels bill a high distinct-analyte CPT count on every patient at every visit. Presumptive and definitive drug testing codes are billed together routinely rather than on confirmatory exception. The clinic's ownership disclosed on CMS-855B lists no licensed practitioner among managing controllers. Testing dollars per patient encounter far exceed same-specialty pain and addiction clinic peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescription without visit: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary x prescription date, compute days to the nearest billed encounter by that prescriber; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Definitive testing intensity: on clinic TIN x beneficiary x month, compute the count of definitive drug test analytes billed and the ratio of definitive to presumptive tests; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Reflex-testing violation: on claim line, compute whether a definitive test line has a paired presumptive result documented as positive; fires when definitive testing is billed on every encounter regardless of presumptive result; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Jariatu Jalloh (community support worker)
SchemeSummary: While employed as a community support worker for a D.C. Mental Health Rehabilitation Service provider, Jalloh submitted encounter notes claiming an hour or more of community support services for Medicaid beneficiaries she never met or met only briefly, causing D.C. Medicaid to pay over $234,500 on fraudulent CSW claims.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one rendering NPI's summed community support unit-minutes on a single date of service exceed 24 hours. Encounter notes submitted on ADR repeat identical narrative text across different beneficiaries and dates. Billed service dates fall while the beneficiary has an inpatient or institutional claim elsewhere. The worker's billed hours exceed payroll timesheet hours held by the employing provider agency. Beneficiaries show no corroborating clinical contact from the agency, such as an assessment or treatment plan update, near the billed dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Hours-per-day feasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed billed units converted to minutes across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 2) Note text duplication: on rendering NPI, compute the share of encounter notes whose text hash matches another note for a different beneficiary; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus agency peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Conflicting-location overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between community support units and any inpatient or residential claim span; fires when overlap exceeds zero minutes; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Wendy Nicole Villatoro (former D.C. Homeland Security Commissioner and former USDA employee)
PayerName: Small Business Administration (PPP/EIDL); private financial institutions
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Villatoro submitted eight PPP loan applications to financial institutions and 15 EIDL applications to the SBA containing materially false statements, including loans on behalf of fake businesses and inflated employee counts, payroll, revenue and cost of goods sold; she attempted to obtain between $2.6 million and $5.5 million and received over $844,000, which she spent on student loans, a BMW SUV and luxury goods.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since these are SBA loan and grant applications. Detection sits with cross-application matching at the SBA, comparing applicant EIN, address, and bank account across multiple PPP and EIDL submissions. IRS Form 941 and W-2 filings for the claimed EIN would contradict the asserted payroll and employee counts. Secretary of State registration dates would show entities formed after the eligibility reference period.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Cross-application identity linkage: on applicant SSN and deposit bank account number, compute the distinct-count of PPP and EIDL applications and the summed requested amount; fires when the count exceeds program limits or the account is shared across unrelated EINs; action disbursement hold pending IRS payroll verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Sandra Jackson (former Delaware nurse practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner digitally signed hundreds of pre-populated orders for genetic testing and durable medical equipment for Delaware Medicare beneficiaries she never examined and had no relationship with, signing within seconds of opening and providing no follow-up care; Medicare paid about $520,000 on the resulting claims. Resolved as a civil False Claims Act settlement with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on genetic testing and DMEPOS claims has no E/M encounter claim with the beneficiary. Electronic signature audit logs show seconds between order open and signature across hundreds of pre-populated orders. One ordering NPI orders for beneficiaries clustered in a state distant from the practice address in NPPES. The same ordering NPI appears across multiple unrelated laboratory and supplier NPIs in a short window. No follow-up claim from the ordering NPI appears after the ordered test or device.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the nearest E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Signature velocity: on ordering NPI x day, compute the count of signed orders and the median seconds between order open and e-signature in the portal audit log; fires when order count is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Orderer-supplier fan-out: on ordering NPI x month, compute the distinct-count of billing laboratory and supplier NPIs and distinct beneficiary states; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, Fort Worth Division
FraudEntity: Carlos A. Lopez (former DOJ Trial Attorney/federal prosecutor); Barrett R. Howell (Dallas-based criminal defense attorney)
State_County: Texas - Dallas County (Dallas); Texas - Tarrant County (Fort Worth)
SchemeSummary: A bill of information charges a former DOJ prosecutor with unauthorized disposal of government records for deleting text messages with a defense attorney from his government-issued phone in April 2023, after a district judge in an underlying health care fraud prosecution ordered production of their communications; the defense attorney is charged with aiding and abetting by deleting the same messages from his own phone. The conduct concerns obstruction/record destruction, not billing fraud.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, as the conduct is destruction of government records. Detection belongs to the agency's mobile device management and retention system, where message backups and deletion events are logged. Court-ordered production compliance can be tested by comparing carrier metadata records against the messages actually produced.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Retention deletion audit: on government device ID x custodian, compute the count of message deletion events occurring after a litigation hold date recorded in the case management system; fires when that count exceeds zero; action internal affairs referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Anna Elperin (osteopathic physician, owner of Awake Health, PLLC)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges the physician improperly performed DOT commercial driver's license physicals and certified applicants as physically qualified when they were not, failing to transmit required certification data to DOT; separately she kept a pre-signed prescription pad at her clinic allowing staff to write themselves controlled-substance prescriptions and signed prescriptions for staff and others that she then took for her own personal use.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, controlled-substance prescriptions carry a prescriber DEA number whose dispensing dates fall on days with no clinic encounter claim by that NPI. PDMP records show the same prescriber writing scheduled drugs to persons sharing the clinic's employer address in payroll or NPPES practice-location files. The National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners shows DOT examination certificates issued without matching electronic transmission of CMV driver exam results. Pharmacy claims show identical drug, strength and quantity across multiple patients on one prescription date, consistent with pre-signed blanks. Prescriber's PDMP scheduled-drug patient count exceeds peers of the same specialty with no corresponding office-visit claim volume.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescription-without-encounter rate: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the share of PDMP controlled-substance prescriptions with no paid E/M claim for that patient within the lookback window; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit on that prescriber's pharmacy claims. 2) Staff-to-prescriber prescribing loop: on prescriber NPI, compute the count of distinct controlled-substance recipients whose address or employer matches the practice location in NPPES or payroll files; fires when the count exceeds zero; action postpay audit. 3) Same-day script clustering: on prescriber NPI x date of service, compute the count of controlled-substance prescriptions sharing identical NDC, strength and quantity; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Stephanie L. Roberts (executive director of Cancer Services of Gaston County)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: As executive director of a non-profit providing support and resources to cancer patients, Roberts embezzled more than $136,000 from the organization between January 2016 and January 2022, failed to remit over $200,000 in payroll taxes withheld from employees' paychecks to the IRS, and filed false personal income tax returns overstating tax withheld and paid. She pleaded guilty to theft in connection with health care, failure to pay over trust fund taxes, and filing a false return, and was ordered to pay $157,722.69 restitution to the non-profit and $62,612 to the IRS.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim and no adjudication point; the loss is embezzlement from a nonprofit plus unremitted trust-fund payroll tax. The nearest detection route is IRS matching of employee Forms W-2 withholding totals against the employer's filed Forms 941 deposits. A second route is the nonprofit's Form 990 showing officer-controlled disbursements without independent board or dual-signature approval. Bank records showing entity checks payable to the executive director are visible to the organization's auditor, not to a payer.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) W-2 to 941 reconciliation: on employer TIN x quarter, compute the difference between aggregate employee withholding reported on W-2s and trust-fund tax deposited per Form 941; fires when the gap exceeds zero for consecutive quarters; action postpay audit referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California
FraudEntity: Rafael Castro (VA benefits recipient, former Veterans Health Administration and IRS employee); Miriam Castro (wife, designated primary caregiver)
PayerName: Department of Veterans Affairs (Caregiver Support Program)
SchemeSummary: Rafael Castro falsely told the VA at least six times that he was unemployed and needed high-level assistance with daily activities such as dressing and grooming, qualifying his wife Miriam for Caregiver Support Program payments equivalent to a full-time 40-hour-per-week home health aide, while he actually worked full time for the Veterans Health Administration and later the IRS; the couple collected more than $130,000 in caregiver benefits over roughly six years.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the veteran's self-reported unemployment contradicts federal payroll and SSA wage records showing full-time employment. Caregiver stipend tiers assume full-time aide hours that overlap the veteran's own recorded work hours on the same days. The veteran's other medical claims show no encounters documenting dependence in dressing, grooming or other activities of daily living. Caregiver and veteran share a residential address and household bank account in the benefit application file. Reassessment records repeat identical functional scores across years with no clinical claim supporting decline.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Employment-versus-dependency contradiction: on beneficiary, compute the overlap in hours between employer-reported paid work hours and the stipend-assumed caregiver assistance hours per day; fires when overlap exceeds zero hours on the same calendar day; action payment suspension. 2) Clinical corroboration gap: on beneficiary x benefit year, compute the count of paid claims containing ADL-dependency diagnoses or functional assessments; fires when the count is zero while a high-tier caregiver stipend is paid; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Household relationship linkage: on beneficiary x caregiver, compute the count of shared address and shared deposit-account matches across application and payment files; fires when both match and no independent reassessment exists; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Irene Oluwatoyin Oshiyoye (operator); Dr. Adekunle Oshiyoye (deceased, operator); Advance Visiting Physicians, P.C.
State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (Farmington Hills); Southeast Michigan
SchemeSummary: Operator of Advance Visiting Physicians allegedly billed Medicare and Michigan Medicaid for home health visits that were actually performed by unlicensed and unsupervised foreign doctors, contrary to program rules; resolved via a $250,000 False Claims Act settlement based on ability to pay, following a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the rendering NPI on home visit claims has no active state medical licence on the licence board file for the date of service. Rendering NPIs appear in NPPES with foreign medical school credentials but no state licence or residency training record. Visit volume attributed to a single supervising physician NPI exceeds feasible hours per day across dispersed home addresses. Payroll and timesheet records list clinicians who never appear as rendering NPIs on submitted claims. CMS-855 enrolment lists no supervising physician relationship for the unlicensed personnel performing the visits.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence-on-date-of-service match: on claim line, compute an exact match of the rendering NPI to an active, unexpired state licence in the board file covering the date of service; fires on any registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Supervision hour feasibility: on supervising physician NPI x date of service, compute total attributed home-visit minutes plus estimated travel minutes between beneficiary addresses; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Payroll-to-claim identity reconciliation: on provider NPI x month, compute the count of rendering NPIs on claims absent from the agency's payroll and timesheet files; fires when the count exceeds zero; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Oleg Beretsky (owner of Obest, Inc.); Obest, Inc.
State_County: New York - Nassau County (Plainview); New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Beretsky, through Obest Inc., cultivated control over elderly Russian-speaking Medicare beneficiaries identified via a nonprofit senior services employee, then steered them only to doctors, social workers, pain specialists and diagnostic companies who paid him kickbacks based on patient volume or Medicare reimbursement; he also pushed providers to bill Medicare for unnecessary or never-rendered services, generating over $22 million in claims and $12.4 million in payments, which he laundered through cash payments to relatives and family-name accounts.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a tight closed set of unrelated provider NPIs shares an unusually high proportion of the same beneficiary panel. Beneficiaries in that panel share a common recruiter-linked address or phone number captured in enrolment and claim demographic fields. Referral graph degree shows one non-clinical entity's associated NPIs directing beneficiaries only to a fixed group of billing providers. Beneficiaries receive duplicate diagnostic and behavioural services from multiple NPIs within days without any documented ordering encounter. Provider bank deposits and CMS-855 ownership disclosures show payments to a common management entity tied to per-patient volume.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Closed referral clique: on beneficiary cohort, compute the Jaccard overlap of beneficiary panels across provider NPI pairs and the graph degree of shared beneficiaries; fires when overlap is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 2) Shared contact-detail cluster: on address or phone value, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries sharing it across enrolment and claim demographics; fires when the count exceeds a household-plausible level versus the calibrated percentile; action site visit. 3) Duplicative service saturation: on beneficiary x 30 days, compute the count of distinct NPIs billing the same CPT service category; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented ordering encounter; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Florence Ndubizu (co-owner and pharmacist-in-charge, Healthcare Pharmacy); Healthcare Pharmacy
SchemeSummary: Pharmacist-in-charge and co-owner of a single-location Trenton pharmacy, with employee conspirators at her direction, filled fraudulent oxycodone prescriptions outside the usual course of professional practice, diverting millions of dosage units (including over 800,000 pills in 2014) to street-level dealers, and manipulated pharmacy records to evade state and federal reporting requirements; a DEA inventory audit found more than 64,000 oxycodone pills diverted between April 2015 and August 2017. Her husband and co-owner was separately convicted of tax evasion.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the pharmacy's oxycodone NDC dispensed units far exceed same-volume peer pharmacies in ARCOS and wholesaler pedigree data. Dispensing claims cluster on a handful of prescriber DEA numbers writing high-dose immediate-release oxycodone to cash-adjacent patients. Beneficiary residence ZIPs on claims lie far outside the pharmacy's normal service radius on its enrolment file. PDMP records show early refills and identical quantity-per-fill patterns across unrelated patients at one store. DEA closing inventory reconciliation against acquisition and dispensing records leaves an unexplained pill shortfall.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Opioid acquisition-dispensing reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute wholesaler-acquired oxycodone dosage units minus units dispensed on claims and PDMP records plus inventory change; fires when the unexplained difference exceeds zero units; action payment suspension. 2) Controlled-substance mix concentration: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the ratio of Schedule II opioid units to total dispensed units and the share from the top three prescriber DEA numbers; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-size peers; action prepay edit. 3) Patient travel radius: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of opioid claims where beneficiary ZIP distance exceeds the pharmacy's trailing median service radius; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Kevin Aguilar
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Aguilar conspired to submit seven fraudulent PPP loan applications and three fraudulent EIDL applications on behalf of four businesses, obtaining approximately $3.3 million in PPP funds and $450,000 in EIDL funds, then laundered the proceeds through other businesses he created to appear legitimate and spent them on Texas residential properties, a $100,000 truck, and personal expenses.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim and no adjudication point; this is pandemic loan fraud against SBA programs. The nearest route is matching the payroll figures on loan applications against IRS Forms 941 and state unemployment wage filings for the same employer TIN. A second route is deduplicating applications by TIN, bank account and applicant identity across PPP and EIDL portals before disbursement. Post-disbursement, tracing loan proceeds to real-property and vehicle purchases shows no payroll use.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll attestation reconciliation: on employer TIN, compute the difference between application-claimed monthly payroll and IRS 941 plus state wage-file reported wages; fires when the claimed amount exceeds filed wages; action prepay edit at loan disbursement. 2) Deposit-account concentration: on bank account number, compute the count of distinct borrower entities receiving disbursements; fires when the count exceeds one; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Vishnudat Seodat (internist/physician)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Seodat, a Long Island internist, ordered hundreds of medically unnecessary transcranial doppler brain scans using false diagnoses for a mobile medical diagnostics company, receiving approximately $100 in cash per test; a co-conspirator billed Medicare and private insurers roughly $1 million for the scans. He was sentenced to two years of supervised release (one year home confinement) plus a $50,000 fine, $52,100 forfeiture and $342,876 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one ordering NPI accounts for nearly all transcranial doppler CPT volume billed by a single mobile diagnostic supplier. Ordering diagnoses on the claims are boilerplate cerebrovascular codes absent from the beneficiary's prior claim history. Place of service on the scan claims is a physician office rather than a facility with vascular ultrasound accreditation. Scan volume per beneficiary repeats at fixed intervals with no follow-up neurology or treatment claim after abnormal findings. The ordering physician's TCD ordering rate per 100 beneficiaries far exceeds internal medicine peers in the same state.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Orderer-supplier dependency: on ordering NPI x supplier NPI, compute the share of that supplier's TCD CPT volume attributable to one orderer and the orderer's share of ordered tests going to that supplier; fires when both shares are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Diagnosis-history mismatch: on claim line, compute whether the ordering diagnosis appears in the beneficiary's prior 12 months of paid claims; fires when it is absent for all listed diagnoses; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Post-test action gap: on beneficiary x TCD test, compute days to any subsequent neurology, imaging or treatment claim; fires when no such claim exists within the clinical follow-up window; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Dr. Kenneth Fishberger (internist)
State_County: New York - Suffolk County (East Setauket, Long Island)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Fishberger, a Long Island internist, used false diagnoses to order hundreds of medically unnecessary transcranial doppler brain scans for a mobile medical diagnostics company, which billed Medicare and private insurers approximately $891,978; he received cash kickbacks of about $100 per test. Sentenced to two years supervised release (one year home confinement), $50,000 fine, $48,000 forfeiture and $342,876 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one internist's ordering NPI supplies a disproportionate share of a mobile diagnostic company's transcranial doppler claims. The ordering diagnosis codes on scan claims do not appear anywhere in the beneficiary's prior claim history. Scan CPT volume per ordering NPI exceeds same-specialty peers per 100 attributed beneficiaries. Beneficiaries receive repeat scans at fixed intervals with no subsequent treatment or specialist claim. The supplier's CMS-855 enrolment lists mobile units serving locations far from the ordering physician's practice address.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Single-orderer concentration: on supplier NPI x quarter, compute the share of TCD CPT lines originating from the top ordering NPI; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-service peers; action claim suspension. 2) Unsupported ordering diagnosis: on claim line, compute the presence of the ordering diagnosis in the beneficiary's 12-month claim history; fires on absence; action prepay edit. 3) Repeat-test cadence: on beneficiary x CPT, compute the count of paid scans in a rolling 12 months and days between them; fires when the count exceeds the coverage-policy frequency limit; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Jordona Ndon (former nurse practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner digitally signed hundreds of orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces for Delaware Medicare beneficiaries she never physically examined, after telemedicine calls often under two minutes, with order information pre-populated by unqualified telemarketers, enabling Medicare billing for the braces.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on L-code brace claims has no prior in-person or evaluation-and-management encounter with the beneficiary. Telehealth encounter records tied to the order show call durations far below any plausible examination time. One ordering NPI signs brace orders for beneficiaries across many states within a single week. Multiple distinct supplier NPIs bill the same beneficiary for overlapping orthotic HCPCS within one month. Order documents share identical templated text and diagnosis codes across hundreds of unrelated beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the brace date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Telehealth duration feasibility: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute total billed or logged telehealth minutes divided by count of signed DMEPOS orders; fires when minutes per order fall below the minimum documented examination time; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Orderer geographic dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Montana
FraudEntity: Tristan Ashley Svejkovsky (nurse practitioner)
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Montana
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner billed Blue Cross Blue Shield of Montana for 158 vitamin B-12 injections that never occurred, inflating units from 1 to 1,000 per injection (raising payment from ~$4.88 to $4,880) and later claiming $15 million per injection, and backdated claims to appear before her license suspension; she also wrote at least 28 controlled-substance prescriptions using a friend's DEA registration number after surrendering her own. Total billed $62,310,000 with $613,108 paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claim lines report unit counts for an injection HCPCS thousands of times the maximum medically unlikely edit value. Submitted charge per line exceeds the fee-schedule allowance by orders of magnitude with no pricing modifier. Dates of service on newly submitted claims precede the submission date and fall after the licence suspension date on the state board file. The rendering NPI's licence status in the board file and PECOS is suspended for the billed service dates. Controlled-substance prescriptions carry a DEA registration number registered to a different prescriber NPI in the DEA file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Unit ceiling edit: on claim line, compute billed units against the medically unlikely edit maximum for the HCPCS; fires when units exceed the MUE value; action prepay edit. 2) Licence-effective-date check: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute whether the service date falls inside an active licence period in the state board and PECOS files; fires on any registry mismatch, including backdated service dates; action claim suspension. 3) DEA-to-prescriber binding: on prescription record, compute an exact match between the DEA registration number and the prescriber NPI in the DEA registrant file; fires on mismatch; action prepay edit on the associated pharmacy claim.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Joseph Schwartz (owner/operator of Skyline Management Group LLC); Skyline Management Group LLC
State_County: New Jersey - Essex County (Newark); nursing/rehabilitation facilities in 11 states
SchemeSummary: Schwartz, owner/operator of Skyline Management Group, withheld trust fund employment taxes from the pay of employees at nursing and rehabilitation facilities in 11 states but failed to pay over more than $38 million to the IRS, and also failed to file the required annual Form 5500 report for the company's 401K plan for 2018.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim and no adjudication point; the loss is unremitted trust-fund employment tax across facilities. The nearest route is IRS matching of aggregate employee W-2 withholding to Form 941 deposits for each facility employer TIN under common ownership. A second route is DOL matching of Form 5500 filings against the plan sponsor list for 401K plans. Common ownership across states is visible in CMS-855A ownership disclosures, which links delinquent TINs to one operator.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Common-owner tax delinquency linkage: on owning entity from CMS-855A ownership fields, compute the count of subsidiary employer TINs with W-2 withholding exceeding Form 941 deposits; fires when the count exceeds zero; action postpay audit and change-of-ownership scrutiny at re-enrolment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Rodney L. Yentzer (former owner of Pain Medicine of York/All Better Wellness); John H. Johnson (physician, 'Physician 1'); Paula Z. Johnson (physician, 'Physician 2'); Florentina Mayko (former CEO of PMY); Pain Medicine of York (PMY, a/k/a All Better Wellness)
PayerName: Medicare; Pennsylvania Medicaid; private insurance companies; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (COVID-19 provider relief funds)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Yentzer, who controlled the Pain Medicine of York pain clinics, agreed with physician John H. Johnson to order multiple urine drug tests for every chronic opioid patient at every office visit regardless of individualized need; the specimens were routed to PMY's in-house lab so PMY collected the payments, billing Medicare over $10 million from mid-2017 through 2019 (Medicare paid over $4 million), plus Pennsylvania Medicaid and private insurers. Proceeds funded luxury goods and were funneled to the incarcerated Johnson and his wife, who was put on the PMY payroll as a no-work employee to shield income from his restitution obligation; Yentzer also kept over $191,000 in HHS COVID-19 provider stimulus funds after PMY had closed. Figures span four sentenced defendants (Yentzer 42 months, Johnson 97 months, Mayko 30 months, Paula Johnson probation), and the settlement total aggregates their restitution, fines and civil settlement payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, definitive urine drug testing CPT codes are billed at every office visit for essentially all chronic opioid patients of one clinic. The ordering NPI and the performing laboratory NPI share ownership in the CMS-855B disclosure, indicating in-house self-referral. Tests per beneficiary per year far exceed the calibrated percentile for pain-management peers. Panel breadth in billed drug classes is identical across all patients regardless of prescribed medication or risk level. Provider relief fund attestation records conflict with the clinic's claim history showing no services after closure.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Reflex testing rate: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of definitive urine drug test claims to office-visit claims for chronic opioid patients; fires when the ratio approaches one-to-one and is above the calibrated percentile versus pain-management peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Panel-uniformity index: on ordering NPI, compute the distinct-value count of drug-class code combinations billed across its beneficiaries; fires when a single combination covers a share above the calibrated percentile of tests; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Relief-fund activity check: on provider TIN, compute the count of paid claims with dates of service after the last relief-fund attestation period; fires when the count is zero while funds remain retained; action postpay audit and recoupment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Martin Elling (former senior partner, McKinsey & Company); McKinsey & Company
SchemeSummary: Elling, who directed McKinsey's consulting engagements advising Purdue Pharma on how to 'turbocharge' OxyContin sales by targeting high-value prescribers, learned of investigations into Purdue and deliberately deleted a 'Purdue' folder, documents and Outlook emails from his McKinsey laptop between April and September 2018 to impede the DOJ investigation. He pled guilty to obstruction; McKinsey had separately agreed the prior month to pay $650 million to resolve criminal and civil investigations.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim and no adjudication point; the conduct is obstruction by deleting consulting records. The nearest detection route is forensic preservation and audit-log review of custodian devices once a litigation hold issues. A related non-claims signal is manufacturer-sponsored prescriber targeting data reported under Open Payments and marketing-spend disclosures.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) High-value-prescriber targeting linkage: on prescriber NPI, compute the correlation between Open Payments manufacturer marketing contacts and growth in that drug's dispensed units; fires when growth is above the prescriber's own trailing baseline; action postpay audit of the associated pharmacy claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Martin Elling (former senior partner, McKinsey & Company); McKinsey & Company (consulting firm to Purdue Pharma)
SchemeSummary: Elling, who directed McKinsey's client-service team on roughly 30 Purdue Pharma engagements (including the 2013 'Evolve to Excellence' project to boost OxyContin sales by targeting High Value Prescribers), deleted a 'Purdue' folder with over 100 documents and a Purdue Outlook email folder from his McKinsey laptop between April and September 2018 while aware of investigations into Purdue's opioid conduct; he pleaded guilty to obstruction and was sentenced to six months' prison, two years' supervised release with 1,000 hours community service, and a $40,000 fine (McKinsey separately paid $650 million in 2024 to resolve related criminal and civil investigations).
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim and no adjudication point; the offence is destruction of consulting documents to impede an investigation. The nearest route is litigation-hold enforcement with device audit logs and mailbox retention records held by the employer. A second non-claims route is monitoring manufacturer targeting of high-volume opioid prescribers through Open Payments and dispensing data.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Opioid prescriber growth surveillance: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the change in dispensed morphine-milligram-equivalents relative to the prescriber's own trailing baseline; fires when growth is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Miranda Rachel Briggs, a/k/a Miranda Rachel Fisher (former spouse of deceased veteran)
State_County: Georgia - Chatham County (Savannah); Georgia - Effingham County (Rincon)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA Dependency and Indemnity Compensation; CHAMPVA)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: After divorcing an Army veteran and being removed from his VA benefits, Briggs falsely claimed to be his surviving spouse following his 2018 death, submitting paperwork asserting they were married until death and legally changing her surname to his, thereby obtaining approximately $80,000 in VA Dependency and Indemnity Compensation and about $49,000 in CHAMPVA medical care benefits.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the claimed surviving-spouse status conflicts with the state vital records divorce decree on file. The applicant's name change postdates the veteran's death recorded in the Death Master File and state death index. The applicant had previously been removed as a dependent in the veteran's own benefit record, showing a prior status change. CHAMPVA medical claims are paid under a beneficiary identifier whose marital-status field was never re-verified against court records. Application signature dates cluster immediately after the veteran's date of death in the benefits file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Marital-status registry match: on claimant, compute an exact match of claimed marriage-until-death status against state vital records marriage and divorce filings; fires on any registry mismatch; action prepay edit on survivor benefit payments. 2) Prior-dependent removal contradiction: on veteran file x claimant identity, compute whether the claimant was previously removed as a dependent before the date of death; fires when removal exists without documented remarriage; action payment suspension. 3) Name-change timing: on claimant SSN, compute days between the surname change record and the veteran's date of death in the Death Master File; fires when the change follows death; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Craig A. Spiegel (pediatrician); April Bingham (co-defendant)
SchemeSummary: Pediatrician issued prescriptions for opioids, benzodiazepines and stimulants with no legitimate medical purpose to adult women (many former patients) in exchange for sex acts, nude photos or cash, and prescribed to co-defendant Bingham using the names of her ex-husband, mother and friends to exploit their insurance benefits; Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and Illinois Medicaid lost $114,480. Bingham was separately sentenced to 21 months; Spiegel awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a pediatric-specialty NPI writes controlled-substance prescriptions dispensed to adult beneficiaries far outside the specialty's age profile. Pharmacy claims list beneficiaries whose PDMP fill histories show identical prescriber, drug and quantity across ostensibly unrelated persons. Prescription fills occur for beneficiaries with no corresponding office-visit claim to that prescriber. Concurrent opioid, benzodiazepine and stimulant combinations appear across the prescriber's panel in PDMP records. Fill pickups are made by one common individual across several beneficiary identities per pharmacy signature logs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Specialty-age mismatch: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the share of controlled-substance fills for beneficiaries outside the specialty's expected age band from NPPES taxonomy; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-taxonomy peers; action prepay edit. 2) Prescription-without-visit rate: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary, compute days between each controlled-substance fill and the nearest paid E/M claim with that prescriber; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action claim suspension. 3) Shared-pickup identity: on pharmacy NPI x pickup signatory, compute the distinct count of beneficiaries whose controlled-substance fills that person collected; fires when the count exceeds household-plausible levels versus the calibrated percentile; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Konstantinos "Kosta" Diamantis (Deputy Secretary, Connecticut Office of Policy and Management); Christopher Ziogas (State Representative, attorney); Helen Zervas (optometrist and owner of Family Eye Care, charged separately)
State_County: Connecticut - Hartford County (Farmington); Connecticut - Hartford County (Bristol)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: An optometrist who had fraudulently overbilled Connecticut Medicaid for services not provided or not medically necessary paid $95,000 in bribes, routed through her fiance (a state representative), to a state OPM deputy secretary who pressured DSS officials to cancel the pending Medicaid billing audit and accept a favorable $599,810 settlement; the officials also lied to the FBI and one omitted the bribe income from his 2020 tax return.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the optometry NPI bills eye examination and testing CPT volumes per beneficiary above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers. Beneficiaries appear on claims with recurring diagnostic tests but no corresponding refraction or treatment progression in their claim history. Rendering hours implied by billed procedure times exceed the practice's staffed clinic hours on given dates of service. An open audit case in the payer's integrity system is closed by administrative direction without documented sampling results. Settlement amount recorded in the remittance history is far below the extrapolated overpayment computed by the auditor.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Service-time feasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed typical procedure minutes for billed CPT lines; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or the posted clinic hours; action claim suspension. 2) Audit-closure integrity: on audit case ID, compute the difference between the auditor's extrapolated overpayment and the final settled amount, together with the count of non-audit staff approvals; fires when the settlement discount is above the calibrated percentile of closed audits; action postpay audit re-opening. 3) Testing intensity ratio: on provider NPI x quarter, compute diagnostic test CPT lines per distinct beneficiary; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Christopher Ziogas (former Connecticut State Representative); Helen Zervas (optometrist and owner of Family Eye Care); Konstantinos Diamantis (senior official, CT Office of Policy and Management - charged by indictment)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Optometrist Helen Zervas fraudulently overbilled Connecticut Medicaid for eye care services she did not provide or that were not medically necessary; when DSS noticed an audit of Family Eye Care's billing in January 2020, she and her fiance, State Representative Christopher Ziogas, paid bribes totaling $95,000 (payments of $20,000, $10,000 and $65,000, reimbursed by Family Eye Care checks) to OPM official Konstantinos Diamantis, who pressured DSS officials to cancel the audit and accept a $599,810 settlement. Ziogas also committed bank fraud by negotiating a $5,500 check from a client trust to Diamantis and lied to federal agents; Zervas has pleaded guilty and Diamantis is awaiting trial.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the practice bills eye examinations and diagnostic tests per beneficiary at rates above same-specialty peers in the state. Claim lines exist for dates of service when the beneficiary has other claims placing them elsewhere. Billed procedure minutes per rendering NPI per day exceed feasible clinic hours. Practice checks reimburse third-party payments to a public official, visible in the entity's bank records during an open audit. An open billing audit is administratively cancelled and settled far below the auditor's extrapolated exposure recorded in the case file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Phantom-visit conflict: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of claims from other providers whose service location conflicts with the optometry visit; fires when conflicting same-day claims exceed zero; action prepay edit. 2) Daily service-minute ceiling: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed typical minutes for all billed CPT lines; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Settlement discount outlier: on audit case ID, compute the ratio of settled amount to auditor-extrapolated overpayment; fires when the ratio is below the calibrated percentile of comparable closed audits; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Stephen D. Meis, M.D. (Medical Director, Golden Sunrise Pharmaceutical Inc. and Golden Sunrise Nutraceutical Inc.); Huu Tieu (Chief Executive Officer); Golden Sunrise Pharmaceutical Inc.; Golden Sunrise Nutraceutical Inc.
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Meis, medical director of Golden Sunrise, and CEO Huu Tieu sold and mailed boxes of herbal drug vials (including 'Imunstem') marketed as an 'Emergency D-Virus Plan of Care' COVID-19 treatment, with labeling falsely claiming FDA approval as a prescription medicine and efficacy against the virus; no Golden Sunrise product was ever FDA approved. Meis pleaded guilty to introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce; co-defendant Tieu was previously sentenced to 18 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health-care claim and no adjudication point; unapproved herbal vials were sold directly to consumers. The nearest route is FDA labeling surveillance matching product claims of prescription status against the NDC directory and approved drug listings. A second route is payer detection if any such product is ever submitted with an NDC absent from the FDA listing file.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) NDC validity check: on claim line, compute an exact match of the billed NDC to an active FDA-listed approved product with matching prescription status; fires on any registry mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Richard E. Moore (executive vice president and part owner of Nexus Services Inc.); Nexus Services Inc.
SchemeSummary: Moore, who controlled the finances of Nexus Services Inc., withheld Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from employees' wages but failed to pay those funds over to the IRS and failed to file quarterly employment tax returns for many quarters from Q1 2015 through Q1 2024, causing a tax loss of about $3.1 million.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim here and no payer adjudication point, so no prepay edit can apply. The decisive signal is an IRS filing-versus-deposit mismatch: W-2 wage totals reported to SSA with no matching Form 941 for those quarters. Federal Tax Deposit records showing zero EFTPS deposits from an EIN whose payroll provider files continue is the nearest non-claims route. A registered agent or officer appearing on multiple EINs with the same 941 delinquency pattern extends the review.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll withholding reconciliation: on EIN x quarter, compute the difference between SSA W-2/W-3 reported withholding and total EFTPS federal tax deposits plus filed Form 941 liability; fires when the gap is non-zero for consecutive quarters; action postpay audit (IRS trust fund recovery assessment).

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia; Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs
FraudEntity: Richard Moore (executive vice president and part owner of Nexus Services Inc.); Nexus Services Inc.
SchemeSummary: Moore, part owner and EVP of Nexus Services Inc., withheld Social Security, Medicare and income taxes from employees' wages for many quarters from Q1 2015 through Q1 2024 but failed to pay them to the IRS or file employment tax returns, causing about $3.1 million in tax loss while spending company funds on luxury cars, his wedding, and publishing his spouse's book.
WaysToIdentify: No claim is submitted and there is no adjudication point, so a payer-side prepay control cannot reach this conduct. The nearest route is IRS matching of SSA-reported W-2 withholding against Form 941 filings and EFTPS deposits for the same EIN. Officer-level exposure is visible where the same responsible person appears on CMS-855 ownership fields or state corporate filings for multiple delinquent EINs. Large owner distributions from business accounts while trust fund deposits are zero is the corroborating bank-records signal.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Trust fund gap by responsible officer: on EIN x responsible officer, compute the sum of W-2 withheld tax minus EFTPS deposits across quarters; fires when the cumulative gap is positive for two or more consecutive quarters; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Marlenin Vito (Medicaid Coordinator at a Stamford assisted living facility; later bookkeeper at an alarm company and a law firm)
State_County: Connecticut - Fairfield County (Stamford); Connecticut - Hartford County (Hartford); New York - Westchester County (White Plains)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: As Medicaid coordinator at a Stamford assisted living facility, Vito generated roughly 500 checks from the facility's system, forged a coworker's signature, cashed them purportedly to give cash to residents, kept the money (~$310,820), and covered it up with false debits to residents' patient trust account ledgers and fabricated account statements; she also pocketed residents' COVID-19 Economic Impact Payments and continued deducting for cancelled supplemental insurance. After termination she stole approximately $23,558 from a White Plains alarm company (false overtime and company-funded product orders) and about $27,179 from a Hartford law firm via forged 'Petty Cash' checks; figures span all three victim companies.
WaysToIdentify: At facility audit, resident patient trust account ledger debits have no matching signed resident receipt or countersignature in the facility disbursement file. Check images from the facility bank account show a single employee as maker with a forged second signature on hundreds of sequential checks. Resident trust balances decline while the resident has no discharge, no personal spending pattern, and MDS shows immobility. IRS Economic Impact Payment deposits credited to resident trust accounts are withdrawn in cash within days. Continued payroll or trust deductions for a supplemental insurance policy already terminated in the carrier's cancellation file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Trust ledger disbursement concentration: on facility TIN x employee, compute the count and dollar sum of patient trust account checks where that employee is maker within a quarter; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer facilities of similar bed count; action postpay audit. 2) Unsupported cash debit: on resident x month, compute the sum of trust ledger debits lacking a scanned signed receipt; fires when that sum is above zero for consecutive months; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Dead-policy deduction: on resident x insurance policy number, compute the days between the carrier cancellation date and the latest deduction posted; fires when that gap is positive; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Michael W. Luehrsen
SchemeSummary: Luehrsen pleaded guilty to perjury for falsely testifying at his prior trial that he was out of town when an altered compound prescription form was faxed from his father's Buffalo-area home; the underlying trial involved conspiracy to commit health care fraud tied to altered compounded-drug prescriptions. He agreed to pay approximately $2 million in restitution and forfeit approximately $2 million in assets.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the compounded-drug claim's prescription image shows ingredient or quantity fields in different handwriting or font from the prescriber block. Fax header transmitting station ID and timestamp on the received prescription do not match the prescriber's registered practice fax on NPPES. The prescriber NPI's compound prescribing volume for that pharmacy is far above the same-specialty peer baseline. The same beneficiary receives high-margin compound kits with no prior E/M encounter with the ordering NPI. Prescriber attestation letters returned on ADR contradict the pharmacy's retained hardcopy for the same Rx number.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber-source mismatch: on claim line, compute an exact match test between the originating fax number or e-prescribe origin ID and the prescriber's NPPES and DEA registered practice location; fires on registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Compound concentration by prescriber: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI x month, compute the count of high-cost compound claims and its ratio to that prescriber's total prescriptions; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Alteration audit: on pharmacy NPI, compute the share of sampled compound Rx images whose quantity or ingredient field differs from the prescriber-confirmed original; fires when that share exceeds zero; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Timothy Craig Jolloff; Lisa Ann Jolloff
PayerName: Small Business Administration (SBA); PPP approved lenders
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Married couple submitted false EIDL and PPP applications to the SBA and PPP lenders, misstating employee counts, average monthly payroll, gross revenue and cost of goods sold, and falsely certifying how proceeds would be used, obtaining eleven EIDLs, eight PPP loans and EIDL advances totaling about $3.4 million that they spent on boats, real estate, vehicles, jewelry and unrelated businesses; both defendants were sentenced (97 months and 36 months) and ordered to pay $3.4 million restitution plus $3.4 million forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point; the payer is a loan program, not a claims system. The decisive route is SBA cross-matching applicant IRS Form 941 and W-2 payroll data against the stated average monthly payroll on the PPP application. Duplicate EIDL and PPP awards to related applicants sharing a bank account, address, or phone across applications are visible in the loan intake file. Post-disbursement bank monitoring showing proceeds moved to boat, vehicle, and real estate purchases rather than payroll is the nearest downstream control.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll attestation mismatch: on applicant EIN, compute the ratio of claimed average monthly payroll to IRS Form 941 reported wages for the same period; fires when the ratio exceeds one by more than rounding; action claim suspension before disbursement. 2) Applicant clustering: on bank account number x address, compute the distinct count of EIDL and PPP applications submitted; fires when that count exceeds one without documented affiliation disclosure; action documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Marcus Asay (founder and chairman); Antonio Gastelum (COO, CFO and Compliance Officer); Agricultural Contracting Services Association dba American Labor Alliance (ALA) (company)
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Through ALA, the defendants sold three sham products to workers and businesses: a purported 401(k) retirement plan whose contributions (over $620,000 in losses to more than 3,000 people) were spent on personal and business expenses and covered up with premiums from other schemes; workers' compensation coverage falsely certified on certificates of insurance and policy declarations as backed by national insurers, generating $2.25 million in premiums; and bogus Affordable Care Act hardship exemptions sold for a few hundred dollars although only government agencies can issue them. Asay also laundered pension funds through multiple bank accounts; figures and penalties span both individuals and the corporate defendant (corporate fine $2.5 million plus $69,250 restitution each from Asay and ALA).
WaysToIdentify: There is no adjudicated health care claim; the products sold were unlicensed insurance and a sham retirement plan. The nearest route is state department of insurance verification that the certificate of insurance's named carrier and policy number exist in the carrier's own policy file. DOL Form 5500 filings absent for a plan collecting employee 401(k) deferrals is the second registry check. Any entity marketing ACA hardship exemptions can be matched against the CMS exemption issuance file, which contains only government-issued certificate numbers.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Certificate registry verification: on certificate of insurance, compute an exact match of the named carrier NAIC code and policy number against that carrier's in-force policy file; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension and referral to the state insurance regulator. 2) Deferral-without-plan check: on employer EIN x plan year, compute the sum of employee 401(k) deferrals withheld per payroll records minus deposits reported on Form 5500; fires when the gap is positive; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Ruthia He (founder and CEO of Done); David Brody (clinical president of Done); Done (California-based digital health company)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Through the telehealth company Done, He and Brody used over $40 million of deceptive social-media and keyword advertising to recruit drug seekers into a monthly subscription, capped initial appointments at under half a typical psychiatric exam, refused to pay for follow-up care, paid nurse practitioners up to $60,000/month to refill prescriptions without clinical interaction, and used an 'auto-refill' feature that issued Adderall prescriptions for years (including for deceased patients), distributing over 40 million stimulant pills. To keep subscribers paying, they submitted false prior authorization requests to insurers falsely claiming DSM-5 diagnosis practices, urine drug screens, and prior failed non-stimulant trials, causing Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers to pay over roughly $14 million; He also moved operations to China, used disappearing-message apps, deleted documents and wired over $1 million to a Chinese shell company to obstruct the investigation.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Schedule II stimulant fills continue for beneficiaries whose date of death appears in the Death Master File. Prior-authorisation records assert prior non-stimulant trials and urine drug screens with no corresponding pharmacy NDC history or CPT 80305-80307 claims for that beneficiary. Rendering NPIs bill initial psychiatric evaluations (CPT 90792) at durations implying more encounters than fit in 24 hours. The same telehealth TIN shows near-universal stimulant prescribing with no follow-up E/M claim after the initial visit. Refills issue on exact monthly cadence with no interval telehealth encounter claim from any rendering NPI.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Decedent dispensing: on claim line, compute the gap in days between the fill date and the Death Master File date of death; fires when the fill date is after the death date; action prepay edit. 2) Prior-auth assertion verification: on prior-authorisation request, compute the count of beneficiary claims matching the asserted urine drug screen CPT and prior non-stimulant NDC in the lookback; fires when that count is zero while the request asserts them; action prior-authorisation requirement with documentation request (ADR). 3) Prescriber stimulant throughput: on rendering NPI x day, compute total billed encounter minutes and the count of distinct beneficiaries receiving Schedule II stimulants; fires when billed minutes exceed 24 hours or the count is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Alan Redmond (principal architect/controller of the businesses); Arthur Walsh (senior executive); Jesus Barrera (senior executive); Albert Groff (head sales agent and manager); Bene Market LLC (company); Seguro Medico LLC d/b/a Quick Health, Q Health, Benefits Now, Express Benefits, YourBenefits4U (company)

SchemeSummary: Defendants ran a boiler-room call center near Reading, PA that bought live transferred calls from lead generators and used bait-and-switch pitches - falsely claiming to be the 'national enrollment center for health insurance' working with 30+ A-rated carriers - to sell consumers limited benefit discount health/dental plans misrepresented as comprehensive major medical insurance, collecting tens of millions in commissions; tactics included unlicensed sales staff, churning/policy-flipping, double-billing, altering recorded sales calls to deceive regulators, and nominee ownership to conceal Redmond's control. Redmond also allegedly withheld over $1.2 million in trust fund taxes from employee wages between 2019 and 2022 without paying the IRS.

The nearest route is state insurance department producer licence file matching of the selling agent name against the National Insurance Producer Registry. Repeat cancellations and rewrites of the same consumer within months are visible in the plan administrator's enrolment and billing file. Duplicate monthly ACH debits to one consumer from two plan IDs appear in the merchant processor chargeback record. Payroll withholding versus Form 941 deposit mismatch on the call centre EIN is the separate IRS route.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Unlicensed seller check: on enrolment record x selling agent, compute an exact match of the agent name and NPN against the state producer licence file for the consumer's state; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension of commission payment. 2) Churn and double-bill: on consumer x plan administrator, compute the count of distinct policy IDs billed within a rolling 12 months and the count of overlapping active billing periods; fires when overlap exceeds zero; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Central District of California
FraudEntity: Juan Carlos Esparza (owner of House of Angels Hospice); Petros Fichidzhyan; Karpis Srapyan; Susanna Harutyunyan; Mihran Panosyan; House of Angels Hospice
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Valley Village, Winnetka, Granada Hills)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Defendants operated four sham hospice companies that billed Medicare roughly $16 million for hospice services that were medically unnecessary and never provided, using foreign nationals' identities as straw owners to enroll with Medicare, open bank accounts and sign leases, then laundered the proceeds through shell company accounts and assets. Restitution totals span five defendants ($1,825,012; $2,822,963; $3,203,574; $4,680,146; $17,129,060), plus $2,920,383 seized and forfeiture of two homes; longest sentence was 12 years (Fichidzhyan).
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855A owner listed holds a recent visa or foreign passport identity that appears as owner on several unrelated hospice applications sharing an address. At adjudication, hospice election periods exist for beneficiaries whose other Part B claims show active curative treatment from unrelated physicians. Attending physician NPI on the hospice certification has no prior claim history with the beneficiary in the payer's remittance file. Hospice routine home care days are billed with no corresponding nurse or aide visit line for weeks at a time. Payments from multiple hospice PTANs route to bank accounts sharing one EFT routing and account number on CMS-588.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Straw-owner graph: on owner SSN or ITIN from CMS-855A, compute the count of distinct enrolled provider PTANs sharing that owner, address, or CMS-588 bank account; fires when that count exceeds one; action site visit before enrolment approval. 2) Election-versus-curative conflict: on beneficiary x hospice election period, compute the count of paid curative or aggressive-treatment claims from unrelated NPIs during the period; fires when that count is above zero; action prepay edit. 3) Service-absent hospice days: on beneficiary x hospice NPI x month, compute the ratio of billed routine home care days to documented nurse or aide visit lines; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus peer hospices; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Edward Cannatelli; Robbyn Cannatelli; Thomas Farese; Virginia Lockett; Patsy Truglia (co-conspirator, previously pleaded guilty); LouTricia Morgan (co-conspirator, previously pleaded guilty)
State_County: Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa); Florida - Broward County (Parkland, Fort Lauderdale, Margate, Sunrise)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants ran a telemarketing operation that harvested Medicare beneficiaries' names, dates of birth and Medicare ID numbers to generate medically unnecessary orthotic brace orders, then sent them to purported telemedicine vendors that paid kickbacks to physicians who signed the orders without contacting beneficiaries; the signed orders supported bogus DME claims spread across three DME storefronts controlled by the conspirators to avoid Medicare scrutiny. Two co-conspirators (Truglia and Morgan) previously pleaded guilty in separate cases.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on the L-code brace claim has no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary in the payer's claim history. One telemedicine ordering NPI signs brace orders for beneficiaries across many states within a single week. Three supplier PTANs share a common CMS-855S contact person, address, or CMS-588 bank account while billing the same L-codes. Beneficiary residence ZIPs sit far outside each supplier's declared service area on its enrolment record. Beneficiaries deny contact when surveyed, and no delivery proof of delivery exists on ADR response.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Supplier common-control graph: on CMS-588 bank account x address, compute the count of distinct DMEPOS PTANs billing overlapping L-codes; fires when that count exceeds one; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Demitrious Gilmore (owner of WM Wellness, LLC and Gilmorehands, Inc. d/b/a Work-Med); Gary Martin (owner of medical clinics); Damon Heath Roberts (co-defendant, pleaded guilty); Khadeer Khan Mohammed (owner of American Premier Labs LLC); Olatunbosun Osukoya (owner of Ayo Biometrics, LLC d/b/a Cambridge Diagnostics)
State_County: Texas - Lubbock County (Lubbock); Texas - Collin County (McKinney, Plano); Texas - Dallas County (Richardson)
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; Department of Labor Office of Workers Compensation Program (DOL-OWCP); other private insurers
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Four separately indicted Northern District of Texas defendants collectively billed roughly $210 million: Gilmore billed DOL-OWCP about $19 million ($17 million paid) for custom knee braces, physical therapy (including hours billed while the claimant was in surgery), PRP treatments and at-home ultrasonic devices that were unnecessary or never provided; Martin allegedly funneled Medicare beneficiary information (including deceased beneficiaries) to co-conspirators who billed over $73 million for over-the-counter COVID-19 tests and paid him kickbacks off the reimbursements; Mohammed used stolen physician identifiers to submit about $93 million ($65 million paid) in Medicare claims for genetic testing never ordered or performed; and Osukoya billed over $25 million to Medicare, TRICARE and other insurers for EEG testing, paying over $450,000 in kickbacks disguised as loans, medical directorships and consulting fees and falsifying diagnoses. Over $1 million was seized from Gilmore's accounts and nearly $6 million from Mohammed's.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claims carry an ordering physician NPI whose own claim history shows no beneficiary contact and whose specialty never orders that test. Beneficiary date of death in the Death Master File precedes the date of service on OTC COVID test and lab claims. Physical therapy units are billed for minutes overlapping the same claimant's surgical anesthesia time on another claim. Genetic testing panels bill for beneficiaries with no cancer diagnosis code and no prior oncology encounter. Payments described as loans, medical directorships, or consulting fees flow from the lab TIN to referring NPIs on the same providers' 1099 and bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible concurrency: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping billed minutes across all rendering NPIs including anesthesia and facility times; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero or total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Decedent service: on claim line, compute the gap in days between date of service and the Death Master File date of death; fires when service date follows death; action prepay edit. 3) Orderer-specialty implausibility: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute the count of ordered genetic or DME claims and the share with no prior E/M between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when that share is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Dr. Shakeeb Chinoy (physician); Dr. Sunil Manjila-Varghese (physician); Rommel Harvey (clinic owner/operator); Gregory Sparks (patient recruiter)
State_County: Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit); Michigan - Oakland County (Bloomfield Hills); Michigan - Washtenaw County (Ann Arbor)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges two doctors, a clinic owner/operator and a patient recruiter conspired to issue thousands of opioid prescriptions (over 400,000 dosage units of Schedule II opioids, street value over $7 million) to purported patients with no legitimate medical need, and that Medicare and Medicaid were billed over $1 million for medically unnecessary prescription and maintenance medications.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Schedule II opioid dosage units per prescriber NPI per month sit far above same-specialty peers in PDMP and Part D data. Beneficiaries travel long distances from residence ZIP to the clinic and then to one dispensing pharmacy, visible in claim addresses. Office visit E/M claims supporting the prescriptions are billed at a per-day count exceeding a plausible clinic day. Patients share a common recruiter-linked address or phone across enrolment records at the same clinic. Cash-pay visit fees precede insured claims for maintenance drugs with no diagnostic imaging or urine screening history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Opioid MME concentration: on prescriber NPI x month, compute total Schedule II morphine milligram equivalents dispensed and the ratio of opioid to non-opioid prescriptions; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Prescriber-pharmacy-beneficiary triangle: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI, compute the count of shared beneficiaries and the median beneficiary-to-clinic distance; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Visit-day throughput: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with E/M claims and implied total minutes; fires when implied minutes exceed 24 hours; action prepay edit.
