SchemeSummary: Seven defendants allegedly billed Medicare and Medicaid more than $110 million for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill; UPHC marketers told beneficiaries they qualified for hospice, the owner paid kickbacks to group home owners and a hospital discharge coordinator for patient referrals and bribed a physician to falsely certify and re-certify terminal illness. After a search of UPHC, the operators opened new hospice companies under straw owners and laundered Medicare reimbursements through controlled accounts to conceal ownership.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one certifying physician NPI signs terminal-illness certifications for a share of a hospice's admissions far above same-specialty peers. Beneficiaries remain on hospice past two benefit periods with live-discharge rates above peer hospices in the payer's remittance history. Referral source addresses cluster on a handful of group home addresses in the beneficiary enrolment file. Hospice patients simultaneously receive curative Part B services from unrelated NPIs during the election period. After a payer action, new hospice PTANs enrol at the same address or bank account with different CMS-855A straw owners.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Certifier concentration: on certifying physician NPI x hospice PTAN, compute the count of terminal-illness certifications and its share of that hospice's admissions; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Non-terminal indicator: on beneficiary x election period, compute the count of live discharges plus paid curative claims from unrelated NPIs during the period; fires when that count is above zero; action prepay edit. 3) Successor-entity linkage: on address x CMS-588 bank account x phone, compute the count of distinct hospice PTANs enrolled within 24 months; fires when that count exceeds one; action site visit and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lindsay N. McCray (also known as Lindsay Rogers) (employee of a medical practice); Alexandra M. Christensen; Heather T. Bradley (also known as Heather Thomas); Jennifer E. Purves
SchemeSummary: While employed by a medical practice, McCray allegedly forged controlled substance prescriptions using the names, signatures, and DEA registration numbers of the practice's two physicians without their knowledge, causing over 300,000 hydrocodone and over 30,000 oxycodone pills to be unlawfully dispensed; she also allegedly distributed amphetamine with Bradley and Purves, and conspired with Christensen.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, controlled substance claims carry a prescriber DEA number whose dispensed volume in PDMP far exceeds that physician's own trailing baseline. Prescriptions are written for individuals with no prior encounter claim at the prescriber's practice TIN. Prescription pad serial numbers or signature images differ from the prescriber's file exemplars held by the pharmacy. Multiple beneficiaries share a pickup address, phone, or cash payment pattern across pharmacies for the same DEA number. Prescriber attestation on ADR shows the physician did not authorise the prescriptions for those names.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber baseline break: on prescriber DEA x month, compute hydrocodone and oxycodone dosage units dispensed and the ratio to that prescriber's trailing twelve-month mean; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit and prescriber alert. 2) No-encounter dispensing: on prescription x prescriber NPI, compute the count of prior E/M encounters between that NPI and the named patient; fires when that count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Pickup clustering: on address or phone x pharmacy NPI, compute the count of distinct patient names filling Schedule II prescriptions from one DEA number; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lindsay N. McCray (also known as Lindsay Rogers) (medical practice employee); Alexandra M. Christensen; Heather T. Bradley (also known as Heather Thomas); Jennifer E. Purves
SchemeSummary: While employed at a medical practice, McCray forged controlled substance prescriptions using the names, signatures and DEA registration numbers of the practice's two physicians, issuing them in the names of non-patients or fictitious persons; area pharmacies dispensed over 300,000 hydrocodone and over 30,000 oxycodone pills, which Christensen and others picked up and resold for shared profit, while Bradley and Purves filled Adderall/amphetamine prescriptions in their own and others' names for resale with payments passing through McCray.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Schedule II volume attributed to one DEA registration jumps far above that prescriber's own trailing baseline in PDMP data. Named patients have no encounter history with the prescriber's practice TIN and some do not exist in the payer's eligibility file. One person picks up prescriptions for many unrelated patients, recorded in pharmacy pickup logs and signature files. Adderall prescriptions issue to persons sharing the practice's staff addresses in NPPES and payroll records. Cash payment with no insurance adjudication dominates fills tied to that DEA number.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) DEA volume break: on prescriber DEA x month, compute dispensed Schedule II dosage units versus that prescriber's trailing twelve-month mean; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit and prescriber verification. 2) Phantom-patient check: on prescription, compute an exact match of the patient name and date of birth against the practice's encounter roster and the payer eligibility file; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Pickup agent degree: on pickup signer x pharmacy NPI, compute the distinct count of patients whose controlled substances that signer collected in 90 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit.

FraudEntity: Raef Hamaed (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Tarek Fakhuri (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Ali Abdelrazzaq (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Kindy Ghussin (pharmacist/pharmacy owner); Eastside Pharmacy; Harper Drugs; Wayne Campus Pharmacy; Heartland Pharmacy; Heartland Pharmacy 2

Beneficiaries show refills on exact schedule with no corresponding prescriber encounter or diagnosis in their other claims. Refill claims continue after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File. High-cost NDC mix at these PTANs is far above same-specialty peer pharmacies of similar script count. Common ownership across five pharmacy PTANs is visible in CMS-855B ownership fields and shared CMS-588 bank accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler acquisition units from pedigree and ARCOS data; fires when billed exceeds purchased; action payment suspension. 2) Unclaimed-refill check: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the count of paid fills with no matching prescriber encounter claim or prescription record in the lookback; fires when that count is above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Common-ownership aggregation: on owner TIN or bank account, compute summed high-cost NDC billing across linked pharmacy PTANs and its growth versus trailing baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: John Ageudo Rodriguez (pharmacist, owner of Pharr Family Pharmacy); Mohammad Imtiaz Chowdhury (marketer); Hector de la Cruz Jr. (marketer); Alex Flores Jr. (marketer)

SchemeSummary: Pharmacist-owner of Pharr Family Pharmacy paid kickbacks, via marketers, to medical providers who referred compounded drug prescriptions to his pharmacy, then billed more than $110 million in compound drug claims to the Department of Labor, TRICARE and Medicare. Four defendants pleaded guilty; sentences ranged from 30 to 60 months.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compound claim dollars concentrate in a small set of referring NPIs whose compound share far exceeds same-specialty peers. Average paid amount per compound claim at this pharmacy is far above peer pharmacies for the same J- and NDC-level ingredients. Referring providers receive marketer payments recorded as commissions on the pharmacy's 1099s and bank transfers. Beneficiaries have no prior E/M encounter with the referring NPI before the compound prescription date. Claims cluster in DOL-OWCP and TRICARE lines with no comparable commercial volume for the same drugs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referrer compound concentration: on referring NPI x pharmacy NPI x month, compute compound claim dollars and their share of that prescriber's total prescribing; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Ingredient cost outlier: on claim line, compute paid amount per compound claim against the peer median for the same ingredient NDC set; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies; action prepay edit. 3) Marketer payment linkage: on pharmacy TIN x payee NPI, compute the dollar sum of outbound payments to entities whose principals also appear as referring NPIs; fires when that sum is above zero; action payment suspension.

FraudEntity: Joseph Huff (pharmacist); Jenifer Huff (spouse)

FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims; Upcoding; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: A pharmacist and his wife diverted oxycodone and hydrocodone from their pharmacy (the wife trading pills for cocaine, meth and marijuana), billed Kentucky Medicaid for prescriptions never ordered by a prescriber, billed insurers for brand-name Adderall while dispensing generic, billed for medication never dispensed, falsely reported a pharmacy robbery to DEA, and used another provider's name and NPI to issue prescriptions. Restitution totaled $17,518.19 (Joseph) plus $5,730.43 (Jenifer); sentences were 3 years and 2 years respectively.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed brand Adderall NDCs are not present in the pharmacy's wholesaler purchase pedigree for the same period. Dispensed Schedule II units in ARCOS exceed the sum of units supported by valid prescriber-originated prescriptions. Claims carry a prescriber NPI who has no PDMP record of writing for that beneficiary. Refill claims exist for beneficiaries with no encounter or eligibility activity in their other claims. A reported theft or robbery filed with DEA on Form 106 coincides with a purchase-to-dispense shortfall in the same NDCs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Brand-versus-stock mismatch: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x month, compute billed brand units minus wholesaler-acquired brand units from pedigree data; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit. 2) Prescriber origin verification: on claim line, compute an exact match of the prescriber NPI and DEA against the state PDMP record for that prescription number; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Diversion shortfall: on pharmacy NPI x controlled NDC x quarter, compute ARCOS receipts minus billed dispensed units minus reported losses on DEA Form 106; fires when the unexplained gap is above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Herline Lochard (registered agent/manager, Center for Professional Training and Development Inc., Center for Professional Training Inc., Wheatland Institute Inc.); Carleen Noreus (president, Carleen Home Health School, Inc.; VP, Carleen Home Health School II, Inc.); Patrick Buchanan (owner, Sigma Institute of Health Careers, Inc.); Gilbert Hyppolite (owner, Techni-Pro Institute LLC); Irene Matthews (registered agent/manager, Agape Academy of Sciences, LLC); Lemuel Pierre (owner, Med-Life Enterprise, Inc./founder of Med-Life Institute locations); Joel Lubin (registered agent and administrator, Ideal Professional Institute, Inc.); Jose Napoleon (director of admissions, Azure College, Inc.); Victor Escalante Zerpa (incorporator, Academus University Corp); Cleophat Tanis (co-owner/operator, Med-Life Institute Naples); Lonnette Blair (Chief Academic Officer, Carleen Home Health School II, Inc.); Stephanie Dorisca (Head of Nursing, Techni-Pro Institute LLC)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami, North Miami, Miami Gardens, Coral Gables); Florida - Broward County (Plantation, Lauderhill, Fort Lauderdale, Lauderdale Lakes); Florida - Palm Beach County (West Palm Beach, Boca Raton, Delray Beach); Florida - Orange County (Orlando); Florida - Osceola County (Kissimmee); Florida - Collier County (Naples)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of now-closed Florida for-profit nursing schools sold fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts (approximately 7,300 fake diplomas) falsely showing that purchasers had completed required coursework and clinical training; buyers used the documents to qualify for the NCLEX exam, obtain RN/LPN licenses in states including Florida, California and Pennsylvania (including multi-state compact licenses), and then obtain nursing jobs, salaries and benefits from unwitting health care employers nationwide. Figures span 12 defendants; only Herline Lochard has been sentenced (13 months) after pleading guilty, Patrick Buchanan pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing, and the remaining defendants are charged by indictment or information.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, the applicant's nursing programme appears on a state board list of closed or sanctioned schools with disputed transcripts. Transcript-issuing institution and clinical hour records fail to match the school's registrar file held by the state education agency. Licence lookup shows NCLEX eligibility approved on a diploma issued within an implausibly short enrolment span. Clusters of licensees from one school share consecutive certificate numbers and identical clinical rotation sites and dates. Employer credentialing files show no verifiable clinical preceptor contact for those rotations.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) School-source cluster: on nursing school code x graduation cohort, compute the count of licensees whose transcripts list identical clinical sites and dates; fires when duplicate site-date tuples exceed one per preceptor capacity; action claim suspension of credentialing approval. 2) Enrolment-duration impossibility: on licensee, compute the gap in days between programme start date and diploma date against the board-required minimum programme length; fires when the gap is shorter than the regulatory minimum; action documentation request to the state board. 3) Registry verification: on rendering NPI, compute an exact match of licence number and status against the state licence board file and OIG LEIE at each claim; fires on registry mismatch or revocation; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Shontavia Riddick
PayerName: North Carolina Department of Commerce, Division of Employment Security (NCDES)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Riddick submitted more than 65 fraudulent pandemic unemployment benefit claims to the North Carolina Division of Employment Security, requesting over $340,000 by making false representations about the applicants' employment and supplying fraudulent supporting documents.
WaysToIdentify: No health care claim exists; the payer is a state unemployment agency, so the control point is benefit claim intake, not adjudication of a medical claim. The decisive signal is claimant wage records absent from the state's quarterly UI wage base for the named employer. Many claims filed from one IP address, device fingerprint, email domain, or routed to one bank account are visible in the NCDES intake log. Employer identity on the claim can be exact-matched against the state's registered employer account file.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Wage-record verification: on claimant SSN x employer account, compute the difference between claimed wages and state quarterly UI wage records; fires when no wage record exists for the named employer; action claim suspension before first payment. 2) Filer clustering: on IP address or bank account number, compute the distinct count of unemployment claims filed within 90 days; fires when that count exceeds one household plausibility threshold; action payment suspension and identity documentation request.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Absolute Physical & Aquatic Therapy, LLC (physical therapy billing company); Chipley Physical Therapy, LLC (outpatient physical/aquatic therapy provider); Ruben Laurel (owner/operator of both entities); Lorrie Laurel (physical therapist, co-owner of CPT)
State_County: Florida - Chipley, Marianna and Bonifay (Florida panhandle)
SchemeSummary: Government's False Claims Act complaint alleges the defendants submitted 613 claims to the United States for physical therapy services purportedly rendered by physical therapist Lorrie Laurel at Chipley Physical Therapy while she was actually out of the country, including on cruises to Mexico, Jamaica, Aruba and the Bahamas, between July 2019 and March 2024; a later related release notes the defendants collectively agreed to pay $754,722.88 to resolve the litigation.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare rendering NPI dates of service against that clinician's absence from any other claim activity nationwide during the same span. Count timed-therapy units billed under one rendering NPI per date of service and convert to treatment hours. Cross-check CPT 97110, 97140 and 97530 units against the clinic's staff roster and licence file for a second qualified renderer. Test whether every claim in the period carries the same single rendering NPI despite multi-therapist appointment volume. Match dates of service to passport or vessel manifest records obtained during investigation of clinician-absence tips.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible therapy day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total timed units for CPT 97110, 97112, 97140 and 97530 multiplied by 15 minutes; fires when the total exceeds a physically workable day of 24 hours or the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Sole-renderer concentration: on billing TIN x month, compute the share of therapy lines carrying one rendering NPI divided by all therapy lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Renderer continuity gap: on rendering NPI x week, compute the count of consecutive service days billed with zero corroborating co-signature or supervising NPI on the claim; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Community Health System (hospital system operating Community Regional Medical Center and Clovis Community Medical Center); Physician Network Advantage Inc. (affiliate health care technology business)
PayerName: Medicare; other governmental health care programs
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged Community Health System and its affiliate PNA induced Fresno-area physicians to refer patients to Community facilities by providing extravagant perks (expensive wine, liquor, cigars and meals in a custom-built lounge called HQ2), subsidies for electronic health records technology and equipment in physicians' private offices, and bonuses ostensibly for clinical integration activities that actually rewarded referrals; the resulting referred hospital services were billed to Medicare and other federal programs in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law. Settled for $31.5 million, with qui tam relator Michael Terpening receiving about $5 million.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment and credentialing, compare hospital CMS-855A ownership and financial-relationship disclosures against Stark exception documentation for EHR subsidies to referring physicians. Compute each referring physician's share of admissions to one hospital system from Medicare Part A and Part B claim linkage. Compare physician bonus payments reported in the system's clinical-integration ledger against that physician's referral volume. Check whether subsidised EHR and equipment recipients are precisely the top-referring NPIs in the claims file. Review Open Payments and the hospital's vendor expense records for meals and entertainment concentrated on referring NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral-payment correlation: on referring NPI x hospital TIN x year, compute the correlation between dollars paid to the physician and the paid amount of that physician's referred inpatient and outpatient claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 2) Subsidy-referral concentration: on referring NPI, compute the share of total Medicare admissions directed to the subsidising system; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline after the subsidy start date; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Disclosure mismatch: on hospital TIN, compute the count of physicians receiving in-kind support who are absent from CMS-855A financial-relationship disclosures; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Felipe Ruiz (podiatrist at West Coast Podiatry Inc.); Jose Gabriel Aguirre (skin graft sales representative); West Coast Podiatry Inc.
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Madera County; California - Stanislaus County
SchemeSummary: Podiatrist Ruiz bought skin grafts from sales representative Aguirre and let Aguirre - an unlicensed person who patients called 'Dr. Gabe' - apply the grafts to Medicare and Medi-Cal beneficiaries without Ruiz present; claims were then submitted falsely representing that Ruiz performed the applications, and Ruiz paid Aguirre a share of the millions in resulting payments. Both defendants were charged (indicted April 2025), pleaded guilty in September 2025, and each was sentenced to 63 months in a scheme described as $3.2 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count skin-substitute application CPT 15271-15278 lines per rendering NPI per date of service and convert to clinician hours. Compare graft square-centimetre units billed against wholesaler purchase pedigree invoices for that product's Q-code. Test whether the rendering NPI appears on other claims at a different place of service during the same application dates. Check the state licence board file and NPPES for the individual physically documented as performing the application in the chart. Compare the supplier's Q-code acquisition volume against paid application volume for the same beneficiary panel.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Graft day impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of CPT 15271-15278 applications multiplied by typical procedure minutes; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Product-to-claim reconciliation: on billing NPI x Q-code x quarter, compute billed square centimetres minus wholesaler-invoiced square centimetres; fires when billed exceeds purchased; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension. 3) Unlicensed applier exposure: on claim line, compute a match of the documented performing individual's name against the state licence board file and NPPES; fires on exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Felipe Ruiz (podiatrist, West Coast Podiatry Inc.); Jose Gabriel Aguirre (skin graft sales representative); West Coast Podiatry Inc. (podiatric medical practice)
State_County: California - Fresno County; California - Madera County; California - Stanislaus County
SchemeSummary: Podiatrist Ruiz bought skin grafts from sales representative Aguirre and let Aguirre, who was not a licensed health care provider, apply the grafts to Medicare and Medi-Cal beneficiaries; claims were then submitted falsely representing that Ruiz performed the graft applications, and after Medicare/Medi-Cal paid Ruiz he passed payments to Aguirre. Both defendants pleaded guilty and each was later sentenced to 63 months in a scheme described as involving $3.2 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count skin-substitute application CPT 15271-15278 lines under one rendering NPI per date of service across all places of service. Compare billed graft units against the practice's wholesaler pedigree and Q-code purchase invoices. Verify the individual named in the operative note against the state licence board file and NPPES at the credentialing stage. Test whether payments received by the billing TIN are promptly transferred to a supplier bank account matching the graft vendor. Compare per-beneficiary graft reapplication frequency to same-specialty peers for the same wound diagnosis.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Renderer capacity ceiling: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total skin-substitute applications and multiply by minimum documented procedure minutes; fires when the total exceeds a 24-hour day; action prepay edit. 2) Purchase-versus-bill gap: on billing TIN x Q-code x quarter, compute billed units divided by invoiced units from wholesaler pedigree data; fires when the ratio exceeds one; action postpay audit. 3) Payment passthrough: on bank account x month, compute the share of payer remittances forwarded to a single vendor account within seven days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Kelo White; Donald Ray Pierre; Ifeanyi Vincent Ntukogu (pharmacist)
State_County: California - Fresno County (Fresno); California - Madera County (Madera)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: White and Pierre obtained more than 450,000 oxycodone and hydrocodone pills using prescriptions bearing forged signatures of more than 10 doctors; pharmacist Ntukogu vetted and filled the prescriptions to avoid regulatory red flags in exchange for cash, and the pills were resold for profit. Sentences span three defendants: White 90 months, Ntukogu 87 months, Pierre 112 months.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare the prescriber NPI on oxycodone and hydrocodone NDC fills against that prescriber's own claim history for the beneficiary. Count controlled-substance fills per prescriber NPI at one pharmacy NPI and compare to PDMP prescriber totals. Compute the pharmacy's ratio of Schedule II opioid dispensed dosage units to all dispensing using ARCOS purchase data. Check beneficiary travel distance between residence ZIP and pharmacy ZIP on high-dose opioid fills. Test for repeated identical quantity, day-supply and directions across prescriptions from multiple unrelated prescriber NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber attribution mismatch: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI x month, compute opioid fills at that pharmacy minus opioid prescriptions recorded for the prescriber in the state PDMP; fires on any positive difference; action prepay edit. 2) Opioid concentration: on pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute Schedule II dosage units dispensed divided by total dosage units, using ARCOS receipts as denominator control; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Template prescription clustering: on pharmacy NPI x week, compute the count of distinct prescriber NPIs sharing an identical NDC, quantity and day-supply string; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Lilit Gagikovna Baltaian (physician)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Porter Ranch/Los Angeles)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: A licensed California physician falsely certified Medicare beneficiaries as needing home health care - including pre-signing blank, undated certification forms that four Los Angeles-area home health agencies then falsified to show she had examined patients and made supporting clinical findings - enabling the agencies to bill Medicare about $1.5 million; she took cash payments for the referrals and separately billed Medicare for signing the certifications.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check whether the certifying NPI on the home health face-to-face certification has any prior E/M claim with that beneficiary. Count distinct home health agency billing NPIs relying on one certifying physician NPI within a quarter. Compare certification dates on the plan of care against the physician's own claim calendar for patient-contact activity. Test OASIS assessment homebound findings against the beneficiary's concurrent outpatient and therapy claims showing mobility. Compare the certifying physician's G-code certification billings to same-specialty peers at claim adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Certifier-encounter gap: on beneficiary x certifying NPI, compute days between the certification date and the nearest E/M claim between them; fires when no encounter exists within the required face-to-face window; action prepay edit. 2) Certifier fan-out: on certifying NPI x quarter, compute the count of distinct home health agency NPIs and beneficiaries certified; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Homebound contradiction: on beneficiary x episode, compute the count of outpatient or ambulatory claims inconsistent with the OASIS homebound field; fires when the count exceeds zero; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Prescriptions Plus (pharmacy, Gastonia, N.C.)
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy agreed to pay $204,000 in civil penalties for failing to maintain complete and accurate Controlled Substances Act records of oxycodone and alprazolam received and distributed and failing to monitor its staff pharmacist, which the government alleged negligently enabled illegal distribution of those drugs; the pharmacy also entered a Memorandum of Agreement with DEA.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim and no adjudication point here because the failure is a DEA recordkeeping and inventory obligation, not a billing act. The nearest detection route is reconciling ARCOS and wholesaler pedigree receipts of oxycodone and alprazolam against the pharmacy's dispensing records and biennial inventory. A second route is DEA registrant inspection of the perpetual controlled-substance log against staff pharmacist dispensing under each pharmacist licence number.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on pharmacy DEA registration x quarter, compute ARCOS-reported receipts of a given NDC minus dispensed dosage units plus inventory, and refer any unexplained shortage to DEA for inspection.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Genexe, LLC (d/b/a Genexe Health, marketing company); Immerge, Inc. (parent company); Jason Green (CEO); Jason Gross (COO)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Philadelphia County (Eastern District of Pennsylvania); Colorado - Arapahoe County (Greenwood Village)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Marketing company Genexe and parent Immerge, with executives Green and Gross, paid independent contractors with no medical training to collect cheek-swab DNA samples from Medicare beneficiaries at malls, churches, retirement homes and nursing facilities, then paid kickbacks to telemedicine providers/physicians for orders for medically unnecessary CGx and PGx genetic tests; labs billed Medicare (often over $6,000 per test) and kicked back $800-$2,000 per swab to Genexe. Settled for $6 million under the False Claims Act, with about $1.3 million going to four whistleblower relators.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check whether the ordering NPI on CGx and PGx CPT codes had any treating relationship claim with the beneficiary before the order date. Count distinct beneficiary states and distinct laboratory NPIs tied to one telemedicine ordering NPI per week. Compare beneficiary residence ZIPs to clusters at nursing facilities, malls and churches sharing identical collection dates. Test whether test results are followed by any therapy change in the beneficiary's subsequent Part B or Part D claims. Compare per-beneficiary genetic panel dollars against same-specialty peer laboratories at claim adjudication.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order without treating relationship: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days since the last E/M encounter between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Telehealth orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states and distinct billing lab NPIs on genetic-test orders; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Collection-site clustering: on laboratory NPI x collection date, compute the count of beneficiaries sharing an identical address or facility identifier; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Patrick C. Moore Jr. (kickback broker/recruiter network organizer)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Moore directed a network of recruiters to induce Medicare beneficiaries to accept medically unnecessary genetic tests, receiving about $4.3 million in kickbacks from co-conspirators for supplying beneficiary insurance information, DNA specimens and doctors' orders, and paying kickbacks down to recruiters. Associated laboratories billed Medicare about $24 million and were paid about $7.2 million; Moore created sham invoices showing fabricated hours worked to disguise per-referral payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, verify that the ordering NPI on CGx claims has prior evaluation-and-management claims with the same beneficiary. Compute the number of distinct laboratory NPIs billing the same beneficiary for overlapping genetic panels within 90 days. Compare marketing-entity payments described as hourly consulting against the count of specimens delivered in the same period. Test whether a small set of ordering NPIs accounts for most of a lab's genetic-test revenue. Check bank-account linkage between the laboratory TIN and recruiter entities during enrolment ownership review.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Duplicate panel saturation: on beneficiary x CPT panel, compute the count of distinct laboratory NPIs paid within a rolling 90 days; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented repeat indication; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer concentration: on laboratory NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid genetic-test dollars attributable to the top ordering NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Per-specimen payment pattern: on laboratory TIN x month, compute vendor payments divided by specimens received; fires when the quotient is near-constant across months despite varying invoiced hours; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Kenneth Terrell Harrison (owner); Aurtism, LLC (outpatient behavioral health counseling service)
PayerName: Medicaid (Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System - AHCCCS, American Indian Health Plan)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Harrison concealed his ownership of Aurtism, LLC when it enrolled as an AHCCCS provider in 2019 because his criminal history would have disqualified it, then obtained AHCCCS ID numbers for enrollees (mostly American Indian Health Plan members), some obtained fraudulently, and billed AHCCCS $6,538,485 for behavioral health counseling services that were never provided.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, compare disclosed owners and managing employees on the provider application against criminal-history and OIG LEIE screening for undisclosed controlling parties. Check whether beneficiaries billed for counseling have any corroborating claim history with other providers in the plan file. Count encounters billed per rendering NPI per date of service and convert to clinician hours. Compare beneficiary enrolment records for AHCCCS ID numbers issued near the provider's first billing date at shared addresses. Test whether the new provider's paid dollars ramp from zero to peer-top-decile within months of enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Hidden-owner screen: on provider TIN, compute the count of controlling individuals found in bank signatory or corporate registry records but absent from the enrolment ownership disclosure; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension and site visit. 2) Counselor capacity ceiling: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute billed therapy units multiplied by code-defined minutes; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) New-enrollee ramp: on billing NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by the provider's first-quarter trailing baseline; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Nita Almuete Paddit Palma (concealed owner of Magnolia Gardens Hospice and C@A Hospice); Percy Dean Abrams (marketer); Magnolia Gardens Hospice; C@A Hospice
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Palma, excluded from Medicare due to prior kickback convictions, secretly bought two hospices through her daughter and husband and concealed her ownership, then paid marketers including Abrams up to $1,000 per month per referred patient; marketers falsely told non-terminal patients they did not need to be dying to enroll and forwarded their identifying information, allowing Palma to bill Medicare roughly $6,000 per patient month for a total of about $10.6 million in hospice claims, and fake patient charts were created and submitted when Medicare requested supporting documentation. Palma received 108 months and $8,270,032 restitution; Abrams received three years probation with two years home confinement.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, screen every CMS-855A disclosed owner, spouse and family member against OIG LEIE and prior exclusion records for straw-owner patterns. Compare hospice length of stay and live-discharge rate against same-specialty peers using paid claim history. Check whether certifying physician NPIs have any prior encounter claim with the enrolled beneficiary. Count beneficiaries whose terminal diagnosis lacks supporting hospital, imaging or oncology claims in the beneficiary's other claims. Test marketer payments recorded in the hospice's ledger against per-patient enrolment counts.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Excluded-party ownership link: on provider TIN, compute the count of disclosed owners sharing an address, surname or bank account with an OIG LEIE-excluded individual; fires on any exact registry match; action claim suspension. 2) Live-discharge and long-stay rate: on hospice NPI x quarter, compute live discharges plus beneficiaries exceeding 180 days divided by total beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Terminality corroboration: on beneficiary x election period, compute the count of supporting diagnostic or hospital claims in the twelve months before election; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Bayonne Drydock and Repair Corporation (government contractor); Bayonne Drydock's Risk Manager
SchemeSummary: Bayonne Drydock used subcontractors owned and/or controlled by its own Risk Manager to perform work on Navy ship government contracts, and those subcontractors employed approximately 52 individuals not authorized to work in the United States; the company paid $4,043,810.56 to resolve False Claims Act allegations, and the Risk Manager previously pleaded guilty to knowingly hiring and continuing to employ unauthorized aliens.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point because this is federal ship-repair contracting, not payer billing. The nearest detection route is comparing the prime contractor's subcontractor ownership disclosures against its own employee roster for conflicted insiders. A second route is matching subcontractor payroll against E-Verify and Form I-9 records for work authorisation on the government contract.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on prime contract x subcontractor TIN, compute a match of subcontractor principals against the prime's employee and officer roster, and refer any exact match to contracting-officer conflict review before invoice approval.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Mohammed Kazim Ali (co-owner, Noah Associates); Justin Hanson (co-owner, Noah Associates); Noah Associates (clinical laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Ali and Hanson, owners of Milwaukee-area lab Noah Associates, paid over $400,000 in kickbacks to the owner of a substance use treatment clinic for referrals of Medicaid and Medicare patients for urine drug testing; the tests were not physician-ordered or medically necessary and were billed using a physician's credentials without authorization (continuing even after the physician objected), yielding over $2.2 million in program payments. Ali was sentenced to 15 months, ordered to pay over $2.2 million restitution plus a $75,000 fine; Hanson pleaded guilty and awaited sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check whether the ordering NPI on urine drug testing claims has any encounter claim with the beneficiary near the specimen date. Contact-verify ordering physicians whose NPI appears on lab claims from an entity they have no contract with. Compute the share of one laboratory's testing volume referred by a single treatment-clinic owner or address. Compare definitive drug testing frequency per beneficiary per month against same-specialty peer laboratories. Trace payments from the laboratory TIN to the referring clinic's bank account during ownership and financial-relationship review.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Unauthorised orderer use: on ordering NPI x laboratory NPI x month, compute the count of ordered lines lacking any encounter claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when above zero for a majority of lines; action prepay edit. 2) Referral concentration: on laboratory NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid urine-drug-test dollars from one referring facility address; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Testing frequency: on beneficiary x month, compute the count of definitive drug test claims across all laboratory NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-diagnosis peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Substance Abuse Treatment Labs; Paul Fribush (owner)
SchemeSummary: The lab and its owner allegedly billed North Carolina Medicaid for the highest-reimbursing level of urine drug screening tests despite clear indications the tests were not medically necessary, collecting the top payment rate; they agreed to pay $850,000 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute the laboratory's share of definitive high-analyte-count drug testing codes versus presumptive screening codes. Check whether each definitive test claim follows a presumptive screen with an unexpected or inconsistent result in the beneficiary's claim history. Compare analyte classes billed against the ordering diagnosis on the claim for clinical relevance. Count identical definitive panels repeated per beneficiary per month regardless of treatment stage. Compare the lab's average paid amount per beneficiary encounter against same-specialty peer laboratories.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Definitive-tier skew: on laboratory NPI x quarter, compute definitive testing lines at the highest analyte tier divided by all drug-testing lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Reflex justification gap: on claim line, compute whether a paid presumptive screen with an abnormal result exists for the same beneficiary within the preceding days; fires when no such screen exists; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Panel repetition: on beneficiary x laboratory NPI x month, compute the count of identical highest-tier panels; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-diagnosis peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Jasmine Hoyle (owner of Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC and The Ultimate Sacrifice); Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC; The Ultimate Sacrifice
SchemeSummary: Hoyle, through two Winston-Salem companies she owned, billed North Carolina Medicaid for urine drug tests and office visits that were never performed - including 97 claims for a beneficiary who had never heard of the companies and provided no urine - collecting over $6 million that she laundered into personal purchases such as a Dodge Challenger.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, test whether billed beneficiaries have any other claim linking them to the billing entity's county or referring clinicians. Compare specimen and office-visit dates against the beneficiary's concurrent claims placing them elsewhere. Count claims per beneficiary from a newly enrolled billing NPI with no prior remittance history. Verify the ordering NPI's awareness by contacting prescribers whose identifiers appear on high-volume test claims. Compare paid dollars to enrolled staffing and site capacity recorded on the enrolment application and a site visit.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Orphan-beneficiary billing: on beneficiary x billing NPI, compute the count of paid lines where no other claim ties the beneficiary to that provider's referral network or geography; fires when the count is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 2) Startup revenue ramp: on billing NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by the provider's trailing three-month baseline since enrolment; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers of the same enrolment age; action payment suspension and site visit. 3) Beneficiary claim density: on beneficiary x billing NPI x year, compute the count of urine drug test and E/M lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Jasmine Hoyle (owner/operator of Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC and The Ultimate Sacrifice); LaTameria Davis (former business partner); Harvest Focused & Consulting Services, LLC; The Ultimate Sacrifice
State_County: North Carolina - Forsyth County (Winston-Salem); North Carolina - Guilford County (Greensboro)
SchemeSummary: Hoyle, through two Winston-Salem businesses she owned, billed North Carolina Medicaid for services never performed, largely urine drug testing screens - including 97 claims for a beneficiary who never received services or provided urine - collecting over $6 million that she spent on personal items such as a Dodge Challenger. She was sentenced to 44 months and $6,299,738.89 restitution; co-defendant LaTameria Davis pleaded guilty to conspiracy and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check for any prior encounter or referral claim tying each billed beneficiary to the billing entity. Compare paid urine drug screen volume to the enrolled site's equipment and CLIA certificate scope. Count repeat claims for the same beneficiary within short intervals lacking any treatment diagnosis in other claims. Compare the new billing NPI's payment ramp against its own trailing remittance history since enrolment. Verify physical laboratory operations and staffing against the CMS-855B enrolment address through a site visit.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) CLIA scope mismatch: on claim line, compute a match of the billed CPT to the laboratory's CLIA certificate-permitted test complexity; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Unlinked beneficiary rate: on billing NPI x month, compute the share of billed beneficiaries with no corroborating encounter claim from any provider in the same region; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 3) Revenue acceleration: on billing NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by the provider's trailing baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers of equal enrolment age; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Fred Beans Holdings, Inc.; Auto Express Enterprises, Inc.; Autorent of Doylestown Inc.; McCafferty Autorent Inc.; Noble Advertising, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Five affiliated Bucks County, PA car-related companies each applied for and received roughly $973,395 in PPP loans in April 2020, falsely certifying eligibility even though, counting affiliates, they had more than 500 employees; they then obtained forgiveness of the full loan amounts plus interest. The qui tam False Claims Act matter settled for $1,427,869 total across all defendants, with the relator receiving $142,786.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point because this is a pandemic business-loan certification, not a payer billing event. The nearest detection route is aggregating employee counts across commonly owned applicants using shared EIN officers, addresses and payroll filings before forgiveness. A second route is comparing certified employee headcount against state unemployment wage records for all affiliated entities.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on applicant group keyed by shared owner and address, compute the summed employee count from state payroll filings and block forgiveness when the affiliated total exceeds the programme size standard.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jamahl Rennelle Burch, aka Jarod or Jerrod Burch
PayerName: Virginia Medicaid; Virginia Employment Commission (state unemployment insurance and Federal Pandemic Unemployment Compensation)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Burch recruited Medicaid recipients into Virginia Medicaid's consumer directed care program, designated numerous individuals as personal care attendants, and used the recipients' and purported PCAs' personal identifying information to create accounts and submit and approve fraudulent timesheets for thousands of hours of personal and respite care that were never provided, causing at least $936,950.70 in Medicaid payments; he also used two purported PCAs' identities to file fraudulent unemployment claims yielding $15,720 in UI/FPUC benefits.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare submitted attendant timesheet hours against EVV visit records with matching telephony or GPS check-in and check-out. Count total paid attendant hours per attendant identifier per day across all consumers. Test whether the same submitter account created, approved and edited both the consumer and attendant portal records. Check attendant identities against the state licence or registry file, the Death Master File and duplicate Social Security numbers. Compare the consumer's authorised service plan units in the prior-authorisation record against billed units.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Attendant day impossibility: on attendant identifier x date of service, compute total paid personal-care and respite hours summed across all consumers; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) EVV corroboration gap: on claim line, compute paid units minus units supported by a matching EVV visit record; fires when the difference is above zero; action claim suspension. 3) Self-approval concentration: on portal user account x month, compute the count of distinct consumers and attendants whose timesheets that account both submitted and approved; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-programme peers; action postpay audit and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Jeremiah Yzaguirre (operator, Southwest Medical Homepatient); Maria Luisa Yzaguirre (operator, Southwest Medical Homepatient); Southwest Medical Homepatient (DME company)
SchemeSummary: The husband-and-wife operators of DME provider Southwest Medical Homepatient billed Medicare approximately $14 million for power wheelchairs, parts and repairs for only 37 beneficiaries between 2019 and 2023, including about $736,072 for one beneficiary by falsely claiming to have replaced expensive parts hundreds of times; the parts and repairs were never provided and proceeds bought cryptocurrency, a vehicle, electronics, collectibles and purses.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count power wheelchair repair and replacement-part HCPCS lines per beneficiary per year against the base K-code delivery date. Compute paid dollars per beneficiary for the supplier and compare to same-specialty DMEPOS peers. Test whether replacement claims for the same part exceed the device's expected lifetime service intervals. Check for prior-authorisation records and physician orders supporting each repair episode. Compare the supplier's distinct beneficiary count against total billed dollars on its remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Repair frequency ceiling: on beneficiary x supplier NPI x part HCPCS x year, compute the count of paid replacement lines; fires when the count exceeds the manufacturer-supported replacement interval for that item; action prepay edit. 2) Revenue per beneficiary: on supplier NPI x quarter, compute paid dollars divided by distinct beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Order corroboration: on claim line, compute the presence of an ordering NPI encounter and a signed repair order within the lookback window; fires when absent; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Ester N. Mbaya (president of Cool Waters, LLC, home health care agency)
SchemeSummary: As president of home health agency Cool Waters, LLC, Mbaya submitted Medicaid claims for home health services that were never provided or were inflated, obtaining over $1 million; she also submitted altered bank statements and falsified paychecks to four financial institutions to obtain loans and lines of credit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare billed home health visit units against EVV records and payroll timesheets for the named field staff. Count visits per rendering aide or nurse identifier per date of service and convert to hours. Compare the agency's visits per episode against the plan of care units in the prior-authorisation record. Test whether beneficiaries billed have concurrent inpatient or nursing facility claims on the same dates. Compare the agency's paid dollars per beneficiary against its own trailing baseline and same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staff day impossibility: on rendering staff identifier x date of service, compute billed visit minutes summed across beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) EVV and payroll reconciliation: on agency NPI x week, compute billed visit hours minus payroll hours paid to field staff; fires when billed exceeds payroll; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension. 3) Overlapping institutional stay: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of home health lines coinciding with an inpatient or SNF claim; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Thelma "Wendy" Epps (Licensed Alcohol and Drug Abuse Counselor, owner of Miracles to Destiny LLC); Miracles to Destiny LLC; Dennis Tomczak (LADC, Medicaid provider); Shawn Tyson (LADC, Medicaid provider)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: After Connecticut Medicaid suspended Epps as a provider for a credible fraud allegation, she arranged for two other licensed counselors (Tomczak and Tyson) to bill Medicaid under their own provider numbers for psychotherapy counseling she purportedly performed, paying Tomczak 25% of Medicaid receipts; Epps also used Tyson's portal login to submit claims, and many of the billed psychotherapy sessions (including some dated on holidays) were never provided at all. Medicaid paid $330,547.71 through Tomczak's number, $7,879.40 for Tyson-attributed services billed under Tomczak, and $663,081.32 through Tyson's number; Epps was sentenced to 27 months and ordered to pay $1,001,058.43 restitution, while Tomczak and Tyson pleaded guilty and await sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, psychotherapy CPT 90834/90837 claims carry rendering NPIs whose portal submission IP and device fingerprint match a provider suspended in the payer's enrolment file. The suspended individual appears as an owner or managing employee on the billing entity's CMS-855 ownership fields shared with the billing NPIs. Claim dates of service fall on federal holidays and weekends at rates far above same-specialty peers in remittance history. Summed session minutes for a rendering NPI on one date of service exceed 24 hours. Two billing NPIs submit identical beneficiary panels and identical session times, indicating one person performing under borrowed numbers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Suspended-party submission linkage: on billing NPI x submitter credential, compute the count of claims whose submitter login, IP, or 855 associated-person matches an NPI under payment suspension or LEIE exclusion; fires on exact registry match; action claim suspension. 2) Impossible therapy day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed timed-unit minutes from CPT 90832/90834/90837 modifiers; fires when total exceeds 24 hours or documented clinic hours; action prepay edit. 3) Holiday and panel-overlap pattern: on rendering NPI x month, compute the share of sessions dated on federal holidays plus the Jaccard overlap of beneficiary panels with any other rendering NPI; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Commonwealth Care Alliance, Inc. (acquirer/successor); Reliance HMO, Inc. (Medicare Advantage plan operator)
SchemeSummary: Reliance HMO paid cash to healthcare professionals and administrative staff at physician practices for contact information of patients who signed 'permission to contact' cards, and paid four physicians/practices $2,500 each characterized as advances on 'coordination of care' services, allegedly to induce enrollment of Medicare beneficiaries in Reliance's Medicare Advantage plan, for which CMS pays monthly capitated payments. CCA, which acquired a 70% stake in Reliance in 2022, self-disclosed and paid $520,355.65.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment and plan oversight, the Medicare Advantage organization's vendor ledger shows per-lead payments to clinical or administrative staff at referring practices. Flat $2,500 'coordination of care' advances to physicians appear with no deliverable or encounter data supporting the service in claims. Enrollment files show beneficiary clusters where one practice TIN accounts for an outsized share of a plan's new enrollments in a month. Capitation payment records show new enrollees whose prior claims history is concentrated in practices receiving plan payments. Marketing 'permission to contact' card volumes reconcile poorly with CMS scope-of-appointment documentation retained by the plan.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Enrollment source concentration: on plan contract x referring practice TIN x month, compute the share of new MA enrollments whose prior-year claims history maps to that TIN; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer plans in the same county; action postpay audit. 2) Payment-to-referrer linkage: on physician NPI, compute the sum of plan vendor payments coded as care coordination divided by the count of coordination encounters submitted; fires when encounters are zero while payments are positive; action payment suspension. 3) Lead-purchase ledger match: on plan x payee bank account, compute the count of payees whose tax ID matches staff at practices sending enrollments; fires on exact registry match; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Gerald Congdon, M.D.; Coastal Urgent Care LLC; Coastal Wellness Center LLC; Gbenga Aluko, M.D.; Eagle Medical Center PC; Anup Banerjee, M.D.; Gastonia Medical Specialty Clinic P.A.; Omar Hussain (laboratory marketer); Curis Healthcare Inc. (marketing company); Saeed Medical Group Ltd. d/b/a Alliance Immediate and Primary Care
State_County: South Carolina - Georgetown County (Pawleys Island); South Carolina - Horry County (Myrtle Beach); South Carolina - Anderson County (Anderson); North Carolina - Mecklenburg County (Charlotte); North Carolina - Gaston County (Gastonia); Illinois - Cook County (Chicago)
SchemeSummary: Physicians and their practices allegedly received remuneration disguised as office space rent, phlebotomy and toxicology payments from an Anderson, S.C. laboratory in exchange for ordering lab tests, while a marketer and his company took volume-based commissions from that lab and paid cash to a clinic for test orders, resulting in false Medicare and TRICARE lab claims; the $1,913,808 total spans all settling defendants (Congdon $400,000, Aluko $250,000, Banerjee $206,000, Hussain/Curis $817,808, and Saeed Medical Group with Hussain/Curis $240,000).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, ordering-NPI concentration shows one laboratory receiving nearly all toxicology and blood panel orders from a small set of practices. The laboratory's ledgers show rent, phlebotomy, and processing payments to those same ordering physicians' TINs, tracked against fair-market-value benchmarks. Per-beneficiary toxicology panel breadth from those ordering NPIs exceeds same-specialty peers on definitive drug testing G-codes. Marketer commission payments in lab records scale with the dollar value of Medicare and TRICARE claims generated. Ordering physicians show no corresponding E/M encounter or documented medical-necessity indication before the panel dates of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral-source exclusivity: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the share of lab claims routed to a single laboratory NPI plus the count of distinct labs used; fires when exclusivity is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Payment-linked ordering: on laboratory TIN x ordering NPI, compute the ratio of lab-to-physician payments (rent, phlebotomy, processing) to allowed charges from that orderer; fires when the ratio is nonzero and volume rose above the orderer's trailing baseline; action payment suspension. 3) Panel breadth without encounter: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute the mean count of definitive drug test analytes per beneficiary and the days to the nearest E/M claim; fires when analytes exceed the peer percentile with no E/M in the lookback; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Health Net Federal Services, LLC (TRICARE managed care support contractor); Centene Corporation (corporate parent)
State_County: California - Sacramento County (Rancho Cordova); Missouri - St. Louis
PayerName: TRICARE (Defense Health Agency, U.S. Department of Defense)
SchemeSummary: HNFS allegedly falsely certified in required annual reports to the Defense Health Agency that it complied with cybersecurity controls in its contract to administer the TRICARE program, when it had failed to timely scan for and remediate known vulnerabilities and ignored third-party and internal audit findings on access controls, firewalls, patch management and password policies; HNFS and parent Centene agreed to pay $11,253,400 to resolve False Claims Act liability.
WaysToIdentify: There is no clinical claim here and no adjudication point; the false statement sits in an annual contractor compliance certification to the Defense Health Agency. The nearest detection route is contract administration: reconcile certified vulnerability-scan and patch cadence against the contractor's own scanner logs and third-party audit reports. Independent IV&V or DCAA-style audits of access control, firewall, and password policy artifacts would surface the gap before the next certification payment.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on contractor contract x reporting period, require submission of raw scanner and patch-remediation export files and compare the count of open critical vulnerabilities past the contractual remediation window against the certified figure, withholding contract payment on mismatch.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Gerald Congdon, M.D.; Coastal Urgent Care, LLC; Coastal Wellness Center, LLC; Gbenga Aluko, M.D.; Eagle Medical Center, PC; Anup Banerjee, M.D.; Gastonia Medical Specialty Clinic P.A.; Omar Hussain (laboratory marketer); Curis Healthcare Inc. (marketing company); Saeed Medical Group Ltd. d/b/a Alliance Immediate and Primary Care
State_County: South Carolina - Pawleys Island; South Carolina - Myrtle Beach; South Carolina - Anderson; North Carolina - Charlotte; North Carolina - Gastonia; Illinois - Chicago
SchemeSummary: Physicians and their practices allegedly received remuneration from an Anderson, S.C. laboratory disguised as office space rental, phlebotomy, and toxicology payments in exchange for ordering lab tests, while marketer Omar Hussain and Curis Healthcare received volume-based commissions from the lab and paid cash to Saeed Medical Group for test orders; resulting lab claims were billed to Medicare and TRICARE. Settlements total $1,913,808 across all defendants ($400,000 Congdon, $250,000 Aluko, $206,000 Banerjee, $817,808 Hussain/Curis, $240,000 Saeed/Hussain/Curis).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a handful of ordering NPIs send nearly all their toxicology and clinical chemistry orders to one out-of-area laboratory NPI. Laboratory financial records show space rental, phlebotomy, and processing fees flowing to those same ordering practices' TINs. Marketer entities receive commissions proportional to billed lab dollars, visible in lab ledgers requested at credentialing or audit. Beneficiary distance from the laboratory's CMS-855B service area exceeds the norm for same-specialty peers. Ordered panels lack any preceding E/M encounter between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary in claims history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Single-lab funnel: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the share of ordered lab allowed dollars going to one laboratory NPI; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Remuneration-to-volume ratio: on laboratory TIN x ordering practice TIN, compute the sum of lease, phlebotomy, and commission payments divided by allowed charges generated; fires when nonzero and the orderer's volume is above its trailing baseline; action payment suspension. 3) Geographic implausibility: on laboratory NPI x beneficiary, compute the distance from beneficiary ZIP to the 855B enrolled service area; fires when the distance is above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Amstrong Chapajong (personal care aide and community support worker)
SchemeSummary: Chapajong, working as a personal care aide and community support worker, submitted false timesheets to his employers claiming to have provided in-person personal care and telephonic behavioral health services to multiple D.C. Medicaid beneficiaries at the same time from different locations, causing D.C. Medicaid to pay $113,243 for duplicative services never rendered.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one aide's rendering NPI or employee ID shows overlapping service minutes for different beneficiaries at different addresses on the same date. EVV visit records show clock-in GPS coordinates inconsistent with travel time between consecutive beneficiary addresses. Summed timesheet hours submitted across multiple employer agencies for one aide exceed 24 hours in a day. Telephonic community-support claims and in-person personal care claims for the same worker occupy identical clock intervals. Aide-submitted timesheets lack matching EVV telephony call-origin numbers for the beneficiary's registered phone.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cross-employer overlap: on aide identifier x date of service, compute overlapping service minutes across all employing agency claims using start and end times; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero or total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Travel infeasibility: on aide identifier x consecutive visit pair, compute the gap in minutes between visits minus the driving time between EVV-captured addresses; fires when the gap is negative; action claim suspension. 3) EVV-to-timesheet reconciliation: on beneficiary x aide x date, compute the count of billed units without a matching EVV check-in or telephony origin record; fires when unmatched units exceed zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: David Ralph Webber (owner/operator of Passion Plus Enterprises Inc. and Whole Science Health); Passion Plus Enterprises Inc.; Whole Science Health
SchemeSummary: Webber allegedly imported hundreds of thousands of capsules containing sildenafil and tadalafil from Indian manufacturers without FDA registration or a wholesale/prescription license, had packaging falsely labeled '100% Natural' with false ingredients and no prescription requirement, and sold them under brand names such as 'Kinky Kong' and 'Stif' to smoke shops, convenience stores, adult novelty stores and directly to consumers via his website, generating over $2.5 million in revenue.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point; the products were sold cash-and-carry to retail shops and consumers outside any payer network. The nearest detection route is FDA import screening: entry lines from unregistered foreign drug establishments declared as dietary supplements but containing PDE5 inhibitors. State board of pharmacy wholesale-distributor licensure files and DSCSA pedigree records would show no licensed distributor behind these shipments.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on importer of record x entry line, compare the declared foreign manufacturer against the FDA drug establishment registration file and the consignee against state wholesale distributor licences, detaining entries with no registry match.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Xuhan Zhang a/k/a "Shelia Zhang" a/k/a "Xuhan Mei" (medical doctor); Jing Qi Mei (office manager, billing)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a physician and her office-manager husband billed Medicare and Blue Cross Blue Shield roughly $20 million (about $6.5 million paid) for inpatient hospital physician services never rendered - including after the hospital closed, for patients actually residing in nursing homes, for deceased patients, and for more than 24 hours of services in a single day; charges include aggravated identity theft and money laundering, and about $6 million in bank funds plus a Tesla Cybertruck were seized.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, inpatient E/M claims (99221-99233) carry a facility CCN and place of service 21 for dates after that facility's Medicare certification was terminated. Summed typical-time minutes for the rendering NPI on a single date of service exceed 24 hours. Beneficiaries on the inpatient claims have concurrent skilled nursing facility or long-term care claims covering the same dates. Dates of service fall after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File and CMS enrollment records. No corresponding facility inpatient stay exists for the beneficiary in Part A claims for those dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Facility-status mismatch: on claim line, compare the date of service against the billed facility CCN's termination or closure date in the CMS provider-of-service file; fires on any date after closure; action prepay edit. 2) Impossible provider day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed CPT typical-time minutes across all professional claims; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Setting and vitality conflict: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of inpatient professional claims with no matching Part A inpatient stay, or with a date after the Death Master File date of death, or overlapping an SNF stay; fires when the count exceeds zero; action prepay edit and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Wendy Gibson-Fitzgerald
State_County: North Carolina - Guilford County (High Point); North Carolina - Forsyth County (Winston-Salem)
SchemeSummary: Gibson-Fitzgerald used a victim's personal identifying information to take out loans and obtain credit cards in the victim's name, secured high-interest loans against the victim company's equipment and accounts receivable, and made hundreds of unauthorized money transfers from the victim's personal and business accounts into her own accounts, spending the $466,776.79 on trips and retail shopping; no health care payer was involved (she had a prior 2012 health care fraud/kickback conviction).
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point; this is identity-based bank and consumer credit fraud against an individual and a company. The nearest detection route is financial institution monitoring: repeated transfers from personal and business accounts into an accounts-payable clerk's own accounts. Credit bureau new-account alerts and lender identity verification against SSA and issuing-authority records would surface the impersonation at loan origination.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on originating business account x beneficiary bank account, compute the count and sum of transfers to accounts titled to an authorized signer or bookkeeper and hold when the count is above the account's trailing baseline.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Casey Mahoney (owner/operator of Healing Path Detox LLC and Get Real Recovery Inc.)
State_County: California - Orange County (Huntington Beach, San Juan Capistrano)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Mahoney paid nearly $2.9 million in kickbacks to 'body brokers' who recruited patients with lucrative insurance policies to his two Orange County addiction treatment facilities, concealing the payments through sham fixed-fee contracts while actually negotiating amounts based on patients' insurance reimbursements and billable treatment days; brokers paid patients cash and even supplied drugs so patients would qualify for higher-paying levels of care.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, admitted patients cluster from out-of-state ZIPs far from the facility, all holding recently issued individual PPO policies. Facility vendor ledgers show fixed-fee 'marketing' contracts whose actual payments track billable treatment days per admitted patient. Definitive urine drug testing claims per patient per week exceed same-specialty peers, and positive results follow admission timing suspiciously. Level-of-care billing (H0010/H0018 residential vs outpatient) shifts upward immediately after admission with no matching ASAM assessment documentation. The same patient identifiers recycle through multiple admissions across affiliated facility TINs within short intervals.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Broker payment per admission: on facility TIN x marketing vendor, compute vendor payments divided by the count of new admissions attributable to that vendor; fires when the per-admission amount varies with billed treatment days rather than a fixed contract rate; action payment suspension. 2) Patient-origin dispersion: on facility NPI x month, compute the count of distinct out-of-state beneficiary ZIPs and the mean policy age in days at admission; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Level-of-care and testing intensity: on beneficiary x admission, compute definitive drug-test claims per week and days billed at the highest level of care without a dated ASAM assessment; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Paul Njoku (owner and CEO of Opnet Health Care Services Inc., d/b/a P & P Health Care Services); Opnet Health Care Services Inc. d/b/a P & P Health Care Services
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
