SchemeSummary: Njoku, owner/CEO of a Houston home health agency, billed Medicare over $400,000 (receiving over $360,000) for home health services without maintaining required documentation, then fabricated records in response to a Medicare records request by cutting out old doctor and nurse signatures and taping them onto newly created physician orders, nursing notes and assessments - including continued use of a registered nurse's signature after she left in 2017. A witness also testified he bribed a doctor to approve home health services.
WaysToIdentify: On ADR response, physician and nurse signatures on plans of care are pixel-identical images reused across different beneficiaries and dates. Signing nurse NPIs remain on submitted 485s and visit notes after their state licence board file shows separation or lapsed licence. Certifying physician NPIs show no face-to-face encounter claim with the beneficiary within the required window before episode start. One certifying physician NPI signs an outsized share of a single agency's episodes relative to same-specialty peers. Documents produced in response to records requests bear creation metadata dated after the payer's request.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Signature-image reuse: on agency NPI, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries whose submitted plan-of-care signature images hash-match another document; fires when the count exceeds one for any hash; action claim suspension and postpay audit. 2) Signer licence validity: on rendering or signing clinician NPI x date of service, compare the date against state licence board effective and end dates plus the agency's payroll roster; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 3) Certifier concentration and face-to-face gap: on certifying NPI x agency NPI, compute the share of the agency's episodes certified and the days between the face-to-face E/M claim and episode start; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile versus peers or no encounter exists; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Sally Njume-Tatsing (owner/operator of three Labelle Home Health agencies)
State_County: Ohio - Franklin County (Reynoldsburg); Ohio - Knox County (Mt. Vernon); Ohio - Cuyahoga County (Parma)
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Owner of three Labelle Home Health agencies personally did all Medicaid billing for nursing services while living out of state, inflating hours of home health aide services, billing registered-nurse rates for care actually provided by licensed practical nurses, and billing for patients who were deceased or ineligible for Medicaid, resulting in $5.7 million in losses.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed RN-rate procedure codes are paired with rendering staff whose state licence board record shows LPN licensure only. Dates of service fall after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File or after Medicaid eligibility termination in the state eligibility file. Aide hours billed per beneficiary per week exceed the units authorized on the prior-authorisation and plan of care. Summed staff hours across the owner's three agency NPIs exceed 24 hours per day per worker. All claims for three agency TINs are submitted from a single out-of-state IP address tied to the common owner in CMS-855A ownership fields.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence-tier mismatch: on claim line, compare the skill level implied by the billed HCPCS (RN vs LPN vs aide) against the rendering clinician's licence class in the state board file; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Eligibility and vitality screen: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of billed units dated after the Death Master File date of death or outside the Medicaid eligibility span; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Authorization overage across commonly owned agencies: on beneficiary x week, compute billed hours summed across all agency NPIs sharing an 855A owner minus prior-authorised hours; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: M&Y Care, LLC (home health care provider)
SchemeSummary: M&Y Care allegedly billed Medicare and Michigan Medicaid under CPT code G0156 (home health aide services under a home health plan of care) for services actually rendered by insufficiently trained staff, when it should have billed the non-skilled care rate that was about 74% lower; resolved via a $334,807.20 FCA settlement arising from a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, G0156 home health aide units are billed by staff whose training certificates are absent from the agency's personnel file at credentialing. The rendering worker identifier on G0156 lines does not appear on the state home health aide certification registry. The agency's ratio of G0156 units to non-skilled personal care units is far above same-specialty peers in the same state. Beneficiaries on G0156 claims lack a matching skilled nursing or therapy visit establishing a home health plan of care. OASIS assessments do not document any aide-level skilled need corresponding to the billed G0156 units.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Aide certification match: on rendering worker identifier x claim line for G0156, compare the worker against the state home health aide certification registry and agency training file; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Skilled-rate mix outlier: on agency NPI x quarter, compute G0156 units divided by total aide-and-personal-care units; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Plan-of-care anchor: on beneficiary x episode, compute the count of G0156 units with no skilled nursing or therapy visit and no OASIS assessment in the episode window; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Desert Imaging Services, L.P.; In Tandem Solutions Group, LLC; Leroy Candelaria; Donald Burris; Vox Intus, LLC; East El Paso Physician's Medical Center, LLC d/b/a Foundation Surgical Hospital of El Paso
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Desert Imaging billed medical imaging services under Foundation Surgical Hospital's NPI as hospital outpatient services, even though the patients had no connection to the hospital, to obtain higher federal health care program reimbursement rates; the hospital kept 17% of the payments in exchange for the use of its NPI. Settlement amounts span multiple defendants: $693,913 (Desert Imaging/In Tandem/Candelaria), $325,000 forfeiture (Burris/Vox Intus), and a $2,081,739 consent judgment against the hospital.  Resolved a qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, imaging claims billed under a hospital NPI with place of service 22 originate from equipment and addresses on a separate freestanding imaging center's 855B enrolment. Service facility address on the claim does not match any provider-based department listed on the hospital's CCN attachment in PECOS. Beneficiaries billed as hospital outpatients have no other claims from that hospital before or after the imaging date. Technical-component volume under the hospital NPI jumps above its trailing baseline right after a management or lease agreement date. Revenue-share ledgers show a fixed percentage of imaging collections retained by the hospital for NPI use.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Service-address to provider-based match: on claim line, compare the service facility address and NPI against the hospital CCN's registered provider-based department list in PECOS; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Orphan hospital outpatient: on beneficiary x hospital CCN, compute the count of imaging claims where the beneficiary has no other encounter with that CCN within the lookback window; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Technical-component surge: on hospital NPI x month x imaging CPT family, compute technical-component units versus the facility's trailing twelve-month baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-size hospital peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Ajay Aggarwal (anesthesiologist and pain medicine physician); Ajay Aggarwal (sole proprietorship); PRWCSWTX LLC (The Pain Relief & Wellness Center)
State_County: Texas - Harris County (Houston/Bellaire); Texas - Brazoria County (Lake Jackson); Texas - Matagorda County (Van Vleck)
PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs
SchemeSummary: Aggarwal allegedly billed Medicare and DOL workers' compensation programs for surgical implantation of neurostimulator electrodes - invasive operating-room procedures paying thousands of dollars each - when patients actually received electro-acupuncture devices placed in his clinic by inserting monofilament wire a few millimeters into the ear and taping the device behind the ear with no incision. He agreed to pay $2,053,515 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, CPT 64553/64555 neurostimulator electrode implantation is billed with place of service 11 rather than an operating room or ASC. No matching facility claim, anesthesia claim, or implantable-device HCPCS appears for the same beneficiary and date of service. The same rendering NPI reports implantation volumes per day above the calibrated percentile versus neurosurgery and pain-medicine peers. Device invoices and DSCSA-style supplier records show purchases of auricular electro-acupuncture kits, not implantable pulse generators or leads. No subsequent programming or pulse-generator insertion claims follow the alleged implants in beneficiary claims history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Setting-and-device coherence: on claim line for neurostimulator implantation CPT codes, compute the count of same-beneficiary same-date facility, anesthesia, and implantable-device claims; fires when that count is zero or place of service is office; action prepay edit. 2) Implant volume implausibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of implantation procedures and derived operative minutes; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers or exceeding available clinic hours; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Absent follow-through: on beneficiary x implant date, compute the days to any subsequent generator insertion or electronic analysis claim; fires when none exists within the expected window; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Dr. Benjamin Tiongson (pain management physician); Pain Reduction Center P.A. (his medical practice entity)
State_County: Texas - Harris County (Houston), Fort Bend County (Sugar Land), Katy
SchemeSummary: Physician allegedly billed Medicare for surgical implantation of neurostimulator electrodes (an invasive operating-room procedure paying thousands of dollars each) when in fact patients only received electro-acupuncture devices inserted a few millimeters into the ear and taped behind the ear in his clinic, with no incision made.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, neurostimulator electrode implantation CPT codes appear with place of service 11 and no facility or anesthesia claim for the same beneficiary date. Device acquisition records show auricular electro-acupuncture units rather than implantable leads for the billed HCPCS. The rendering NPI's implantation counts per week far exceed same-specialty peers in the same locality. No pulse-generator insertion or device programming claim ever follows the alleged electrode implants in beneficiary claim history. The specialty on the rendering NPI's PECOS enrolment does not include surgical privileges consistent with implantation.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Implant-without-operative-context: on claim line, compute the count of matching same-date facility, anesthesia, or device HCPCS claims for the beneficiary; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Peer volume outlier: on rendering NPI x week, compute the count of neurostimulator implantation procedures per enrolled specialty; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Downstream device silence: on beneficiary x implantation claim, compute the gap in days to any generator insertion or analysis-programming claim; fires when no such claim exists in the expected window; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division / U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Christopher Obaze (owner and pharmacist-in-charge, Chrisco Pharmacy); Chrisco Pharmacy; co-conspirators including a pharmacy technician
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Obaze ran Chrisco Pharmacy as a 'ghosting pharmacy,' buying hydrocodone and oxycodone from wholesalers and reselling at least 2,268,700 pills in bulk to drug traffickers with no physicians, patients, or prescriptions involved; he hid the activity by reporting no dispensing to the Texas prescription monitoring program, structuring cash deposits with false bank documents, and aiding false tax returns understating pharmacy gross receipts.
WaysToIdentify: The pills were sold for cash to traffickers, so no claim reaches a payer and there is no adjudication point. The decisive non-claims route is ARCOS and wholesaler pedigree data: controlled-substance purchases far exceeding the pharmacy's dispensing volume. State prescription drug monitoring program filings showing near-zero dispensed schedule II opioids against large wholesale acquisitions expose the gap directly. Bank structuring patterns in cash deposits and Suspicious Activity Reports provide a second, financial route.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on pharmacy DEA number x month, compute ARCOS-reported hydrocodone and oxycodone dosage units acquired minus PDMP-reported dispensed units plus payer-claimed units, and refer for DEA administrative action when the unexplained difference is above the calibrated percentile versus same-size pharmacy peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Dorian Farmer (owner of several businesses, including Titleist Technologies, Inc. d/b/a Summit Joint Performance)
SchemeSummary: Farmer, owner of several businesses, withheld employment trust fund taxes (Social Security/Medicare) from employees' pay but, instead of remitting them to the IRS, embezzled the funds for personal use, took large unreported cash distributions from one business, and failed to file tax returns for himself and Titleist Technologies for tax year 2000, causing a total tax loss of $806,653.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point; this is employment tax withholding theft and unfiled returns. The nearest detection route is IRS matching of Forms W-2 and W-3 wage withholding totals against Forms 941 filed and trust fund deposits actually made. Repeated nonfiling by a business with active payroll registration and state unemployment wage filings is visible without any payer involvement.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on employer EIN x quarter, compute reported W-2 withheld Social Security and Medicare tax minus Form 941 deposits received, and open a trust fund recovery examination when the difference is positive and recurs across quarters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Christina Ann Mobley, also known as Kris Mobley (business manager/bookkeeper of a Fortuna construction company)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: As business manager who assumed bookkeeping duties at a Fortuna, Calif. construction company, Mobley allegedly diverted company funds to herself by directing company checks and electronic payments to her personal credit card accounts, using the company credit card for casino cash advances and personal travel, writing company checks to herself, and inflating her vacation time, hours and bonuses plus issuing duplicate payroll checks in the company payroll system, embezzling more than $500,000 between January 2022 and November 2024. No health care payer was involved.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point; this is employee embezzlement from a private construction company. The nearest detection route is bank and card monitoring: company payments routed to a personal credit card account held by the bookkeeper. Payroll system audit logs showing duplicate payroll checks and self-approved hour and bonus edits would surface it internally.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on employee ID x pay period, compute the count of payroll disbursements and the sum of hour, bonus, and accrual adjustments made by the same user who approves them, and require dual authorization when the count exceeds one per period.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Javier Alfonso Nunez Suarez (beneficiary)
SchemeSummary: Defendant, a Colombian national illegally residing in Houston, allegedly impersonated a U.S. citizen to fraudulently apply for and obtain SSA disability benefits in February 2016, then used that status to qualify for Medicaid, continuing to collect both until his arrest for a total theft of government funds exceeding $588,000.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the applicant's name, SSN, and date of birth combination fails SSA Enumeration Verification System matching in the state Medicaid eligibility file. Citizenship and immigration status returns no match in the SAVE system despite an attested U.S. citizen declaration. The same SSN shows concurrent wage or identity activity inconsistent with the claimed disability status in SSA records. Address and contact data on the Medicaid application match records already tied to a different identity in the state's master person index. Long benefit tenure with no verified employment history or immigration record persists across annual redetermination files.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Identity verification gate: on applicant record at eligibility determination, compute the SSA EVS and SAVE match result across name, SSN, date of birth, and status fields; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension pending verification. 2) Duplicate-identity linkage: on SSN x master person index, compute the count of distinct beneficiary identities sharing SSN, address, or phone; fires when the count exceeds one; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Redetermination drift: on beneficiary x annual redetermination, compute the gap in days since the last successful SSA and SAVE re-verification; fires when the gap exceeds the redetermination cycle; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Ana Juanita Andrade-Reyes (owner of shell construction company)
State_County: Florida - Duval County (Jacksonville); various Florida counties
PayerName: Internal Revenue Service (IRS); workers' compensation insurance carrier
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Defendant set up a shell construction company and bought a minimal workers' compensation policy (payroll of $169,400, premium ~$11,352), then 'rented' certificates of insurance to dozens of work crews so contractors would believe the crews were insured and employed by the shell company. Contractors issued payroll checks (~$8 million total) to the shell company; she cashed them, kept about 6%, and distributed cash to workers without withholding or reporting payroll taxes, evading $2,048,182 in Social Security, Medicare and income tax withholding, and depriving the insurer of about $591,978 in proper premiums.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the loss is unremitted payroll tax and understated workers' compensation premium. The nearest detection route is the carrier's premium audit comparing declared payroll on the policy application against certificates of insurance issued to unrelated contractors. State workers' compensation certificate-verification registries can be matched to check-cashing volume reported by the depository bank under BSA reporting. IRS Form 941 wage totals filed by the insured entity can be reconciled against 1099/bank deposit inflows for the same EIN.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Premium-to-deposit divergence: on policy EIN x quarter, compute the ratio of bank deposits credited to the entity over declared payroll on the workers' compensation application and Form 941; fires when the ratio exceeds the calibrated percentile versus same-class-code policyholders; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Krishnaswami Sriram (medical doctor)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Doctor evaded roughly $1.6 million in taxes, penalties and interest by transferring rental properties in name only to his children, moving about $600,000 to accounts in India, and omitting accounts and property from IRS submissions; he also admitted falsifying medical records to bill Medicare $136,980.36 for in-home physician visits purportedly provided to beneficiaries who were actually inpatients elsewhere or deceased.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, home visit E/M codes 99341-99350 carry dates of service after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File. Home visit place of service 12 overlaps an inpatient or SNF stay on the same beneficiary's Part A claims. The rendering NPI's daily home visit count implies travel and face-to-face time exceeding 24 hours. Beneficiary residence addresses in the enrolment file lie far outside the practice's service radius on CMS-855I. Home visit volume for the NPI jumps sharply above its own trailing monthly baseline without new staff on the enrolment record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Death and inpatient overlap: on claim line, compute whether the date of service falls after the Death Master File date or inside a paid Part A inpatient or SNF stay for the same beneficiary; fires on any overlap day; action prepay edit. 2) Home visit day capacity: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of typical times for billed home visit codes plus inter-address travel minutes; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Baseline break: on rendering NPI x month, compute home visit line count divided by the provider's trailing twelve-month mean; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California
FraudEntity: Krishnaswami Sriram (doctor)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Doctor billed Medicare $136,980.36 for in-home physician visits that never occurred, claiming to treat beneficiaries on dates when they were dead or residing in inpatient facilities, supported by false statements in medical records; he separately evaded roughly $1.6 million in taxes by transferring rental properties to his children in name only, moving about $700,000 to accounts in India, and omitting assets from an IRS offer-in-compromise.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, home visit CPT lines bear dates of service after the beneficiary's date of death recorded in the Death Master File. The same beneficiary has a concurrent paid inpatient or nursing facility Part A claim covering the home visit date. The rendering NPI bills more home visits per calendar day than travel between beneficiary addresses physically allows. No prior encounter history exists between the rendering NPI and the beneficiary in the payer's remittance history. Documentation returned on ADR shows identical narrative text across unrelated beneficiaries and dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Decedent service edit: on claim line, compute the gap in days between date of service and the Death Master File date for the beneficiary; fires when the date of service is later; action prepay edit. 2) Concurrent institutional stay: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of paid Part A institutional days overlapping a place-of-service 12 professional line; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Visit-day impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total billed home visit minutes plus geocoded travel minutes between service addresses; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Kartik Bhatia (DME company owner/operator); Raju Sharma (co-conspirator)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Bhatia and co-conspirators operated DME companies that paid telemarketing firms for orthotic brace orders (ankle, wrist, knee, back) and billed Medicare over $2 million for braces beneficiaries did not need or want, with doctors' signatures on orders from physicians who never treated or prescribed for the beneficiaries; after CMS suspended payments to his company, he opened a new DME company to continue the same billing. He also made false statements to law enforcement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on L-code brace claims has no prior E/M encounter with the beneficiary in claims history. A single ordering NPI signs brace orders for beneficiaries spread across many states within one week. The same beneficiary receives multiple distinct brace HCPCS from unrelated supplier NPIs within thirty days. At enrolment, the new supplier's CMS-855S owners, address or bank account match an entity already under payment suspension. Beneficiary telephone contact records show no request for the device before the order date.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days since the last E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Suspended-entity re-enrolment link: on applicant NPI, compute the count of exact matches on CMS-855S owner SSN, practice address or bank routing/account against suppliers with active payment suspension; fires when the count exceeds zero; action site visit and prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Brace saturation: on beneficiary x brace HCPCS family, compute distinct paid supplier NPIs in a rolling 30 days; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented replacement reason; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Minhaj Feroz Muhammad (owner/controller of clinical laboratories); Sufyan Feroze (owner/controller of clinical laboratories)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two brothers allegedly owned and controlled, sometimes through straw owners, four clinical laboratories in Illinois and California that submitted over $293 million in claims to Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for COVID-19 laboratory testing never performed, collecting about $65 million, then moved proceeds between their labs and businesses to buy overseas real estate, gold bars, luxury watches and vehicles.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, COVID-19 test claims under U0003/U0004/87635 exceed the lab's CLIA certificate instrument capacity for that date of service. Ordering NPIs on the claims have no other claim relationship with the tested beneficiaries in payer history. Beneficiary residence ZIPs cluster in states thousands of miles from the lab's CMS-855B service address. At enrolment, the listed owner on CMS-855B is a straw with no prior PECOS or NPPES laboratory history. Multiple lab NPIs share the same bank account, mailing address or authorised official across enrolment records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Capacity ceiling: on lab NPI x date of service, compute billed test line count divided by validated daily throughput for the analysers on the CLIA certificate; fires when the ratio exceeds one; action claim suspension. 2) Common-control graph: on TIN and bank account, compute the distinct count of enrolled lab NPIs sharing that account, address or authorised official in CMS-855B; fires when the count exceeds one; action site visit and prepay edit. 3) Orderer-beneficiary linkage: on claim line, compute the count of prior claims between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary in the lookback window; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Cassandra Marie Strube (administrator at nursing and senior living facilities)
SchemeSummary: While employed as an administrator at at least five nursing and senior living facilities, Strube stole fentanyl patches, hydrocodone, morphine, and oxycodone from the facilities' narcotics emergency kits and locked medication carts and rooms; she was sentenced to three years' probation and ordered to pay $1,975.61 restitution, a $5,000 fine, and a $200 special assessment.
WaysToIdentify: There is no billed claim and no adjudication point, because controlled substances were removed from facility emergency kits rather than billed. The nearest detection route is reconciliation of the facility's narcotic count sheets and e-kit pharmacy replenishment invoices against MAR administration entries. State PDMP and ARCOS distributor shipment data for the facility DEA number can be compared to documented resident administrations. Automated dispensing cabinet override and access logs identify one badge repeatedly opening carts outside administration windows.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Kit reconciliation variance: on facility DEA number x drug NDC x month, compute wholesaler units received minus units documented on the MAR plus waste witnessed; fires when the unexplained variance exceeds zero units; action postpay audit and referral to the state board.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Mohammed Asif (owner and director of American Labworks LLC); American Labworks LLC (diagnostic testing laboratory)
SchemeSummary: Asif, listed as owner/director of American Labworks LLC in Everett, WA, allegedly conspired to bill Medicare more than $8.7 million (over $1.1 million paid) for COVID-19 and respiratory illness lab tests that were never ordered or performed, using referring-physician names without authorization, including dates of service after the beneficiary or the referring physician had died; he withdrew $260,000 from the lab's account and returned to India.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, respiratory panel and COVID test lines carry dates of service after the beneficiary's Death Master File date. The referring NPI on the claim is deceased or retired per NPPES deactivation and PECOS status on the service date. No ordering physician encounter with the beneficiary exists anywhere in the payer's claim history. The lab's state test-site licence and CLIA certificate expiry date precede the billed dates of service. Payments deposited to the lab account are withdrawn in near-total lump sums within days of remittance.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dead-party edit: on claim line, compute whether the date of service postdates the beneficiary Death Master File date or the referring NPI's NPPES deactivation date; fires on either mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Licence validity: on lab NPI x date of service, compute the gap in days between the service date and the CLIA or state test-site licence expiry in the registry; fires when the service date is after expiry; action claim suspension. 3) Cash-out velocity: on provider bank account x week, compute withdrawals divided by Medicare remittances deposited in the trailing 30 days; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Mohammed Asif (owner and director of American Labworks LLC); American Labworks LLC (diagnostic testing laboratory)
SchemeSummary: Asif, owner/director of American Labworks LLC in Everett, WA, conspired to bill Medicare more than $8.7 million for COVID-19 and other respiratory illness lab tests that were never ordered or performed, using referring-physician names without authorization (some physicians and beneficiaries were deceased on the claimed service dates) and continuing after the lab's test-site license expired; Medicare paid over $1.1 million, which Asif withdrew from the lab's bank account, including a $260,000 withdrawal before fleeing to India.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed test dates of service fall after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File. The referring NPI listed on the claim was deceased or deactivated in NPPES on the service date. The lab's state test-site licence in the health department registry had expired before the billed dates. No prior encounter links the referring NPI to the beneficiary anywhere in claims history. Enrolment records show a foreign-resident authorised official with sole signature authority over the payment bank account.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Registry mismatch edit: on claim line, compute exact matches of date of service against beneficiary and referring-provider death or deactivation dates in the Death Master File and NPPES; fires on any service date later; action prepay edit. 2) Licence lapse hold: on lab NPI, compute days between date of service and the state test-site or CLIA expiry date; fires when the gap is positive; action payment suspension. 3) Referral concentration: on lab NPI x referring NPI, compute the share of the lab's billed lines attributable to referrers with zero other claims for those beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
FraudEntity: Patients Choice Laboratories (PCL) (diagnostic laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: PCL allegedly used a $5,000/month sham 'Marketing Services Agreement' with an infection prevention company (paying it about $1.86 million total) and paid 1099 sales reps commissions of at least $372,000 based on referral volume, to obtain referrals for respiratory pathogen panels; the company swabbed long-term care residents for COVID-19 and PCL used the same specimens to bill Medicare for medically unnecessary RPPs at 43 facilities (sometimes billing RPPs with no COVID test performed), collecting over $6 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, respiratory pathogen panel CPT 0202U/87631-87633 lines appear for nearly every resident at a facility on the same collection date. The same specimen collection date shows an RPP billed without any corresponding COVID-19 test line. Ordering NPIs are facility physicians with no documented order in the lab requisition or the beneficiary's other claims. The lab's vendor ledger shows fixed monthly marketing payments to an entity that also controls specimen access at the referring facilities. Sales representative 1099 payments scale linearly with referred test volume, visible in the lab's own commission records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Facility-wide panel sweep: on referring facility CCN x collection date, compute the share of residents with an RPP line billed; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile versus same-setting peers; action claim suspension. 2) Reflex mismatch: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of RPP lines with no COVID-19 test line on the same specimen date; fires when the count exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 3) Referral-source concentration: on lab NPI x referral-source entity, compute the share of billed lines originating from facilities served by one contracted marketing counterparty; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Timothy Mark Anderson (Iowa licensed attorney providing Medicaid eligibility planning services)
SchemeSummary: Attorney assisting elderly clients with Iowa Medicaid nursing home eligibility took a $186,000 check from a client and transferred her a wrecked, inoperable 1961 Rolls Royce, then submitted documents to Iowa Medicaid falsely valuing the car at $194,000 so the couple's over $400,000 in assets would be sheltered under the one-automobile exclusion and Father-1 would qualify for Medicaid-funded nursing home care.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the declared value of the excluded automobile on the Medicaid asset schedule far exceeds NADA or Kelley Blue Book valuation for that year and model. State DMV title records show the vehicle transferred to the applicant's representative within the five-year lookback. Bank records disclosed on the application show a large check to the same attorney contemporaneous with the vehicle transfer. The vehicle registration record shows non-operable or salvage status inconsistent with the claimed appraisal. The submitted appraisal lacks an independent licensed appraiser identifier verifiable in state registry files.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Vehicle valuation mismatch: on Medicaid application x excluded automobile, compute declared value minus published guide value for the VIN year, make and model; fires when the difference exceeds the guide value; action documentation request (ADR) before eligibility approval. 2) Transfer-window check: on applicant x asset, compute days between the DMV title transfer date and the application date; fires when inside the statutory lookback period; action claim suspension of eligibility pending review. 3) Representative concentration: on filing attorney or representative ID, compute the count of applications claiming a high-value automobile exclusion; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer filers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Kevin M. Whitman (individual falsely claiming to be a physician)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Whitman, not a licensed physician and without a DEA registration, allegedly posed as a medical doctor and used a DEA Registration Number belonging to Strong Memorial Hospital to issue 177 Schedule II prescriptions (173 for oxycodone, 38,067 dosage units) to nine individuals; a fake University of Rochester Medical School diploma was recovered from his residence.
WaysToIdentify: At pharmacy adjudication, the prescriber DEA number on Schedule II claims belongs to a hospital institutional registration rather than an individual practitioner. The prescriber name transmitted on the NCPDP claim does not match any individual in NPPES or the state licence board file. PDMP records show one DEA number writing oxycodone for a small closed set of patients at high dosage units. The prescribing address on the script does not match the DEA registrant's registered location in the DEA database. The prescriber has no NPI on any other medical claim for those same patients.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber identity validation: on claim line, compute exact match of prescriber DEA number, name and NPI against the DEA registration file, NPPES and the state licence board file; fires on any mismatch or institutional-only registration; action prepay edit. 2) Institutional DEA misuse: on DEA number x month, compute the count of outpatient Schedule II claims written under a hospital registrant number by non-affiliated pharmacies; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Concentrated opioid writer: on prescriber DEA x quarter, compute oxycodone dosage units divided by distinct patients; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension and board referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Charmaine Gatlin (former Chief Operating Officer of Jackson Health Foundation)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami); Florida - Broward County (Weston)
SchemeSummary: As COO of the Jackson Health Foundation, the nonprofit fundraising arm of Miami's Jackson Health System, Gatlin allegedly approved and submitted at least $3.6 million in false vendor invoices for goods and services never provided to the Foundation, including roughly $2 million to a Georgia audiovisual vendor that kicked back $1 million to her, plus invoices used to buy designer goods from Louis Vuitton, Gucci and Apple and a rose gold golf cart delivered to her home; charged as wire fraud conspiracy, wire fraud and money laundering.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, since the loss is nonprofit foundation funds paid on vendor invoices. The nearest detection route is accounts-payable matching of invoices to purchase orders, receiving records and contracts in the foundation's ERP. Vendor master file screening detects new payees whose bank account or address matches an employee record. Kickback flow is visible as vendor disbursements followed by deposits to the approving officer's personal account in bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Three-way match and payee-employee overlap: on vendor ID x invoice, compute the count of invoices approved by one officer with no purchase order or receiving record, plus exact matches of vendor bank account or address to employee HR records; fires when either count exceeds zero; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: personnel announcement that John P. Heekin was sworn in as U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.
WaysToIdentify: This is a personnel announcement, not a fraud case, so there is no claim and no adjudication point. No payer data, provider NPI or service line is implicated anywhere in the item. JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Lino Mallari Gutierrez a/k/a 'Joe Gutierrez' (owner/operator of two DME companies); unnamed co-conspirators (straw owners)
State_County: Florida - Martin County (Palm City); Florida - Middle District of Florida
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gutierrez and co-conspirators operated two DME companies held in the names of straw owners and billed Medicare more than $10.9 million (over $5 million paid) for medically unnecessary orthotic braces. They paid kickbacks to marketing companies that used call centers to solicit Medicare beneficiaries and telemedicine companies to obtain signed doctors' orders, and Gutierrez filed false records with his employer and a regulatory organization and moved Medicare proceeds between accounts after learning of law enforcement action.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, brace L-code claims cite ordering NPIs whose only contact with the beneficiary is a brief telehealth code on the same day. Beneficiary states on the supplier's claims span far beyond its CMS-855S service area. Enrolment records list owners with no DMEPOS history whose identity documents match those on other suspended supplier applications. Multiple supplier NPIs share a payment bank account or authorised official in CMS-855S. Marketing vendor payments in the supplier's ledger track referral counts rather than fixed fees.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Telehealth-only order: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the count of prior in-person or longitudinal encounters between orderer and beneficiary excluding a same-day brief telehealth code; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Straw-owner and account linkage: on bank account and authorised official ID in CMS-855S, compute the distinct count of enrolled DMEPOS NPIs sharing them; fires when the count exceeds one; action site visit and prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Geographic dispersion: on supplier NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states on paid brace lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Paul Njoku (owner and CEO of Opnet Health Care Services Inc., d/b/a P & P Health Care Services); Opnet Health Care Services Inc. d/b/a P & P Health Care Services
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Njoku's home health agency billed Medicare over $400,000 (receiving over $360,000) for home health services without maintaining required documentation; when Medicare requested records, he and others cut out and taped old physician/nurse signatures onto newly created doctors' orders, nursing notes and assessments, including using a departed nurse's signature without consent, and bribed a doctor to approve home health services.
WaysToIdentify: On ADR response, physician and nurse signatures on plans of care appear as pasted images identical in pixel form across different beneficiaries and dates. The certifying physician NPI has no face-to-face encounter claim with the beneficiary within the required window. A signing nurse's licence in the state board file shows employment terminated before the documented visit dates. OASIS assessments transmitted to the state repository are missing or their dates conflict with billed visit dates. The certifying physician certifies for one agency at a rate far above same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Face-to-face linkage: on episode x certifying NPI, compute days between the certification date and the nearest E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter falls inside the required window; action prepay edit. 2) Signature reuse detection: on submitted document image, compute the count of byte- or perceptual-hash matches of the signature block across distinct beneficiaries; fires when the count exceeds one; action claim suspension and postpay audit. 3) OASIS-to-claim reconciliation: on episode, compute the count of billed visit dates with no matching OASIS assessment or with staff credential lapsed in the state licence file; fires when the count exceeds zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Ndubuisi Joseph Okafor, M.D. (sole practitioner and owner of Okafor Medical Associates)
SchemeSummary: Okafor, sole owner of an internal medicine clinic in Northwest Washington D.C., prescribed oxycodone and promethazine with codeine for cash after minimal or no examination, including to undercover agents, confidential sources, and individuals using false identities whom he knew were diverting the drugs; the scheme spanned at least 45 states and hundreds of thousands of units. He also created backdated medical records for one patient after a complaint was filed with the D.C. Board of Health.
WaysToIdentify: In PDMP data, one prescriber writes oxycodone and promethazine-with-codeine for patients residing across dozens of distant states. The prescriber's practice has almost no billed E/M claims corresponding to the dated prescriptions, indicating cash-only visits. Patients filling those scripts show high early-refill rates and long pharmacy travel distances in dispensing records. Medical records produced after a complaint carry creation timestamps postdating the documented visit dates. The prescriber's morphine-milligram-equivalents per patient sit far above same-specialty peers in the state's PDMP report.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber geographic dispersion: on prescriber DEA x month, compute distinct patient states and mean patient-to-prescriber distance in PDMP fills; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit at the pharmacy and board referral. 2) Script-without-encounter: on prescriber NPI x patient, compute the count of controlled prescriptions with no billed or documented E/M encounter within the lookback; fires when the ratio exceeds the calibrated peer percentile; action postpay audit. 3) Record backdating: on chart document, compute the gap in days between electronic creation timestamp and the recorded visit date; fires when the gap exceeds the permitted late-entry window; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division (Fraud Section); U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
SchemeSummary: Not a specific fraud case: the Justice Department announced the expansion of its Health Care Fraud Unit's New England Strike Force into the District of Massachusetts, noting that in FY 2025 the U.S. Attorney's Office's Health Care Fraud and Affirmative Civil Enforcement Units recovered more than $450 million in fraudulently obtained funds.
WaysToIdentify: This is an enforcement-office expansion announcement rather than a single case, so there is no claim and no adjudication point. No provider NPI, service line or beneficiary is identified for any prepay edit. The nearest non-claims route is aligning payer data-sharing feeds with the strike force's regional analytics requests.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Data-sharing agreements can route payer claim extracts to the regional strike force for targeting outside the adjudication system.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois; Justice Department Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Offices for the Northern District of Illinois, Middle District of Florida, District of Maryland, Eastern District of New York and Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc.; Walgreen Co. and various subsidiaries (national pharmacy chain)
State_County: Nationwide (United States), including Illinois; Florida; Maryland; New York (Eastern District); Virginia
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other federal health care programs (TRICARE/Defense Health Agency, OPM, DOL programs referenced)
SchemeSummary: DOJ civil False Claims Act/Controlled Substances Act complaint alleging Walgreens pharmacists filled millions of controlled substance prescriptions (excessive opioid quantities, early refills, opioid/benzodiazepine/muscle relaxant 'trinity' combinations) despite clear red flags of illegitimacy, while corporate policies pressured pharmacists to fill quickly and withheld prescriber information, then billed Medicare, Medicaid and other federal health programs for those unlawful prescriptions. Case originated from four qui tam whistleblower suits, now consolidated with U.S. intervention; no liability determination yet.
WaysToIdentify: At pharmacy adjudication, claims for opioid, benzodiazepine and muscle relaxant NDCs overlap in days-supply for the same beneficiary. Refill claims arrive well before the prior fill's days supply is exhausted, visible in the payer's own remittance history. Single prescriptions exceed high morphine-milligram-equivalent daily thresholds computed from NDC strength and quantity. One prescriber DEA number accounts for an outsized share of a store's controlled dispensing in PDMP data. Beneficiaries fill controlled prescriptions at multiple pharmacies and prescribers within the same month.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Trinity concurrency: on beneficiary x date, compute overlapping days-supply across opioid, benzodiazepine and skeletal muscle relaxant NDCs; fires when all three overlap on the same day; action prepay edit. 2) Early refill: on beneficiary x NDC, compute days between fill date and prior fill date minus prior days supply; fires when the gap is negative beyond the plan's permitted tolerance; action claim suspension. 3) Store-level red-flag rate: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of controlled claims with an early refill, trinity overlap or high MME; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-volume peer pharmacies; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Vida Med Center LLC (purported DME company); Med-Union Medical Center, Inc. (purported DME company)
SchemeSummary: Two Medicare-enrolled DME companies allegedly submitted a combined $33 million in false claims for durable medical equipment that was medically unnecessary and not provided as represented (Vida Med billed $14.1M and was paid $8.76M; Med-Union billed $19.0M and was paid $14.2M, all paid claims resting on prescriptions from a single provider). The government filed two civil forfeiture complaints seeking $967,760.37 and $10,014,325.40 in fraud proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, essentially all of the supplier's paid claims cite a single ordering NPI. That ordering physician has no E/M encounter history with the beneficiaries receiving the equipment. Delivery documentation requested on ADR lacks beneficiary-signed proof of delivery matching the billed dates. Beneficiary residence ZIPs are far outside the supplier's CMS-855S service area. Payment inflows are swept from the supplier account to unrelated entities within days of remittance.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Single-orderer dependence: on supplier NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid dollars attributable to the top one ordering NPI; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Order-encounter gap: on claim line, compute days between date of service and the last E/M claim between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Proceeds sweep: on supplier bank account x week, compute outbound transfers to unrelated entities divided by Medicare deposits received; fires when the ratio exceeds the calibrated peer percentile; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Marieva Briceno (owner of three purported medical clinics)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Briceno owned three purported medical clinics in the Detroit area that paid Medicare beneficiaries to undergo unnecessary tests and procedures, then billed Medicare approximately $5,460,323 for those medically unnecessary services, of which Medicare paid about $2,998,322 (Briceno personally received about $513,200). She later concealed the fraud on her naturalization application; after a 2012 guilty plea and 60-month sentence, a court revoked her U.S. citizenship on Nov. 17, 2025.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a small closed set of beneficiaries receives the same diagnostic test panels repeatedly across the owner's several clinic NPIs. Those beneficiaries travel unusual distances past nearer providers to reach the clinics, visible in residence ZIP versus place of service. Test volume per beneficiary far exceeds same-specialty peer norms for the billed diagnosis codes. Multiple clinic NPIs share owners, address or bank account in CMS-855B enrolment records. Beneficiary cost-sharing is routinely waived or never collected, evident in absent secondary and patient-liability postings.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Beneficiary recycling: on beneficiary x owning TIN, compute the count of distinct clinic NPIs under common ownership billing the same test HCPCS in a rolling 90 days; fires when the count exceeds one; action prepay edit. 2) Tests per beneficiary: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute diagnostic test lines divided by distinct beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Patient travel and cost-share: on claim line, compute beneficiary-to-clinic distance plus the share of claims with zero collected coinsurance; fires when both are above the calibrated peer percentile; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida; Justice Department Civil Division, Office of Immigration Litigation
FraudEntity: Marieva Briceno (owner of three purported medical clinics)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Briceno owned three purported medical clinics in the Detroit area that paid Medicare beneficiaries to undergo medically unnecessary tests and procedures, and she and co-conspirators billed Medicare approximately $5.46 million for those services, of which Medicare paid about $3 million (Briceno personally received roughly $513,200). She pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud in 2012 and received 60 months; on Nov. 17, 2025 a court revoked her U.S. citizenship because she had concealed the fraud during naturalization.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, clinic NPIs bill diagnostic tests to a beneficiary cohort whose home ZIPs cluster far from the clinic address on CMS-855B. The same beneficiary IDs appear across three commonly-owned clinic TINs receiving identical test panels within weeks. Beneficiaries show no prior E/M encounter with the rendering NPI before the ordered test dates of service. PECOS ownership fields link the three clinic enrolments to one managing owner with recent enrolment dates and immediate high volume. Beneficiary sharing across unrelated clinic NPIs, measured on paid claim history, exceeds normal referral overlap for the specialty.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Shared-beneficiary ring: on beneficiary x owner entity from PECOS ownership fields, compute the count of distinct clinic NPIs billing the same CPT within 90 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Testing without evaluation: on claim line, compute days between the diagnostic CPT date of service and the most recent E/M claim for that beneficiary at any commonly owned TIN; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action documentation request (ADR). 3) New-enrolment ramp: on provider NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by the provider's trailing three-month baseline since PECOS enrolment date; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs / Criminal Division (Money Laundering and Asset Recovery Section)
FraudEntity: Bernard L. Madoff (chairman, Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC); The Western Union Company; Olalekan Jacob Ponle; Aydin Kalantarov, Zaur Kalantarli and Ali Kalantarli; Michael Little; Thuy Tien Luong (nail salon owner); Richard J. Sherwood and Thomas K. Lagan (attorneys)
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: General DOJ Asset Forfeiture Program announcement, not a single health care fraud case: it reports that over $12 billion in forfeited assets has been paid to crime victims (over $735.3 million in FY2024-early FY2025) and summarizes unrelated remission examples, including the Madoff Ponzi scheme, Western Union consumer fraud, business email compromise scams (one against a health care company that wired $1,652,254 to fraudulent malpractice-insurance wire instructions, of which $1,100,694 was recovered), fictitious-corporation EIDL loan fraud, bogus fuel tax credit refund fraud, forced labor, and estate embezzlement.
WaysToIdentify: There is no claim and no adjudication point here, since this is a forfeiture and victim-remission announcement rather than a billing scheme. The nearest detection route is bank-side payment controls, where a payee-name mismatch on a large outbound wire against the vendor master file stops the transfer. Corporate treasury callback verification against previously validated insurer banking details catches altered wire instructions before funds leave.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a treasury rule on outbound wire, computing whether the beneficiary bank account differs from the vendor master account of record, holding the payment until callback verification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Scott Taggart Roethle (telemedicine physician, anesthesiologist)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: A telemedicine doctor contracted with multiple health care companies and, via electronic portals, signed orders for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment, pain creams and genetic tests for thousands of patients he never evaluated or followed up with, receiving roughly $30 per order and $674,000 total from five companies; Medicare paid at least $1.5 million on his orders, with the government asserting total loss of $7 million to $9.5 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one ordering NPI signs DMEPOS, compounded cream and genetic test orders for beneficiaries spread across many states in a week. No E/M or telehealth encounter claim exists between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary before the order date of service. The same ordering NPI appears on claims from five unrelated supplier, pharmacy and lab TINs simultaneously. Ordered items span three unrelated benefit categories, which is implausible for one physician's specialty taxonomy in NPPES. Order counts per signing day exceed what a physician could evaluate within 24 hours.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states plus distinct billing supplier, lab and pharmacy TINs on ordered claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 2) Order-encounter gap: on claim line, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M or telehealth claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action prepay edit. 3) Signing-rate impossibility: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with orders divided by 24 hours; fires when implied minutes per patient fall below a clinically possible encounter length; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Jacqueline Brewster (travel nurse at Raleigh General Hospital)
SchemeSummary: A travel nurse used her own biometrics plus patients' individually identifiable health information to check out hydromorphone from automated dispensing cabinets at Raleigh General Hospital, siphoned off part of each vial and diluted the remainder to look full, then canceled/nulled the transactions to hide the diversion for her personal use.
WaysToIdentify: In the automated dispensing cabinet log, one nurse's biometric withdrawals of hydromorphone are followed by cancel or null transactions at a rate far above unit peers. Cabinet withdrawals lack a matching medication administration record entry for the named patient in the EHR. Withdrawals are recorded under patient identifiers whose care assignment roster does not include that nurse for the shift. Waste events lack the required second-witness signature in the cabinet record. Vial-level ARCOS and pharmacy inventory reconciliation shows dispensed volume exceeding documented administered plus wasted volume.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cancel-rate outlier: on nurse ID x week, compute cancelled or nulled controlled-substance cabinet transactions divided by total withdrawals; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-unit peers; action postpay audit. 2) Withdrawal-without-administration: on nurse ID x date, compute the count of hydromorphone withdrawals with no matching MAR administration or witnessed waste within the shift; fires when the count exceeds zero; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Unassigned-patient access: on nurse ID x patient, compute the count of cabinet withdrawals where the patient is absent from that shift's assignment roster; fires when the count exceeds zero; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Timothy Gaines Pollard (owner, Tim Pollard Construction)
SchemeSummary: Owner of a residential remodeling and fence installation business withheld federal income, Social Security and Medicare employment taxes from employees' paychecks from 2019 through 2021 but never remitted them to the United States, instead using the funds for personal expenses, causing a tax loss over $400,000.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, because this is unremitted employment tax on a construction payroll. The nearest detection route is IRS matching of Forms W-2 wage and withholding totals against Forms 941 filed and deposits actually received. State unemployment insurance wage reports showing active payroll with no federal deposit trail provide a second non-claims signal.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is an IRS reconciliation on employer EIN x quarter, computing withheld amounts reported on W-2 and 941 minus deposits received, escalating when the gap persists across consecutive quarters.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Seoul Medical Group Inc. (Medicare Advantage provider); Advanced Medical Management Inc. (wholly-owned subsidiary); Dr. Min Young Cha (founder and former president); Renaissance Imaging Medical Associates Inc. (radiology group)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles/Koreatown; Northridge)
SchemeSummary: Seoul Medical Group and Dr. Cha allegedly submitted diagnosis codes for two severe spinal conditions (spinal enthesopathy and sacroiliitis) for patients who did not have them, inflating risk scores so CMS paid Medicare Advantage plans more, a portion of which was passed to Seoul Medical Group; when an MA Plan questioned the enthesopathy diagnoses, Renaissance Imaging created radiology reports appearing to support them. Settlement totals $62.85 million across defendants ($58.74M Seoul/AMM, $1.76M Cha, $2.35M Renaissance).
WaysToIdentify: In risk-adjustment submissions, spinal enthesopathy and sacroiliitis ICD-10 codes appear at a rate far above same-region peers for the same provider group. Those diagnoses have no supporting treatment, imaging or specialist claim in the beneficiary's other encounter data. Retroactive additions of the codes arrive through supplemental chart-review submissions rather than the original encounter record. Radiology report creation timestamps postdate the MA plan's diagnosis query by weeks for the same beneficiary and date of service. The same two HCC-driving codes attach to a large share of one group's panel, with no deletions ever submitted.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) HCC code concentration: on provider group TIN x HCC diagnosis, compute the share of the attributed panel carrying that code in the encounter data submission; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty regional peers; action postpay audit. 2) Unsupported diagnosis: on beneficiary x HCC diagnosis year, compute the count of corroborating treatment, imaging or specialist claims within twelve months; fires when the count is zero; action documentation request (ADR) with medical record validation. 3) Late chart-review addition: on beneficiary x diagnosis, compute days between the encounter date of service and the supplemental submission or radiology report creation timestamp; fires when the report postdates the plan's query; action payment suspension of risk-adjusted amounts.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal jury in Detroit)
FraudEntity: Sherif Khalil (owner/operator of Spectra Clinical Labs); Spectra Clinical Labs
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Gardena; Redondo Beach)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Khalil, owner of Spectra Clinical Labs, paid marketers a percentage of Medicare reimbursements—concealed by routing payments through nominally independent marketing companies he secretly controlled—to induce orders for the highest-reimbursing urine drug testing panels; marketers trained doctors' office staff to send Spectra orders for medically unnecessary tests physicians never authorized, causing Medicare to pay over $4 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the lab bills the highest-tier definitive urine drug testing CPT for nearly every specimen, with presumptive screens rarely preceding them. Ordering NPIs attached to the lab's claims show no corresponding office E/M claim on or near the specimen collection date of service. A small set of ordering NPIs accounts for nearly all of the lab's volume, indicating marketer-driven funneling. The lab's Form 1099 and vendor payments to marketing entities are percentage-based, visible in CMS-855B ownership and contractor disclosures. Definitive analyte counts per specimen sit at the panel maximum regardless of patient diagnosis on the claim.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Panel-maximisation: on billing lab NPI x month, compute the share of definitive drug test claim lines billed at the top analyte tier, over total UDT lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Order concentration: on lab NPI, compute the Herfindahl concentration of paid volume across distinct ordering NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action documentation request (ADR) for signed physician orders. 3) Order without encounter: on claim line, compute days between specimen date of service and the nearest E/M claim linking that ordering NPI and beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Fadel Alshalabi (owner/CEO, Crestar Labs, LLC); Samuel Harris (owner, Flojo Recruiting d/b/a Secure Health); Benjamin Toh, M.D. (telemedicine doctor); Edward D. Klapp (former VP of Sales, Crestar Labs); Melissa L. Chastain (owner/CEO, Genetix LLC); Roger Allison (President, Genetix); Dakota White (former Director of Client Services/VP Operations, Crestar Labs); Robert Alan Richardson (principal, Freedom Medical Labs, LLC); Edward Burch (principal, Freedom Medical Labs, LLC); Elizabeth H. Turner (owner, Advanced Tele-Genetic Counseling)
State_County: Tennessee - Spring Hill (Maury/Williamson County); Texas; Maryland; Utah; South Carolina; Illinois - Chicago
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Marketing companies recruited elderly and low-income Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries at senior health fairs, door-to-door and in low-income neighborhoods to collect genetic samples; purported telemedicine doctors such as Dr. Toh were paid $20 per order to sign lab orders for patients they never contacted, and Crestar Labs billed Medicare and Medicaid often over $10,000 per genetic test, then paid over $12 million in kickbacks to the marketers. Across the conspiracy over $129 million was billed and over $35 million paid; Alshalabi got 5 years, Harris 30 months, Toh 13 months plus $495,000 restitution, with restitution for Alshalabi and Harris and sentences for seven other defendants pending.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, high-dollar CGx panels are billed with an ordering NPI having no prior claim history with the beneficiary. One telemedicine ordering NPI signs genetic test orders for beneficiaries across many states within a single week. Beneficiary cohorts share collection dates and ZIP clusters matching health-fair and door-to-door recruitment rather than clinical referral patterns. The ordered panel is billed with cancer screening CPT stacks that lack any oncology diagnosis in the beneficiary's other claims. Lab payments to marketing entities appear as percentage-based contractor arrangements in CMS-855B disclosure and bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line, compute days between the genetic test date of service and the most recent E/M or telehealth claim between the ordering NPI and beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action prepay edit. 2) Telemedicine orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct lab TINs on signed CGx orders; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Clinical-indication mismatch: on beneficiary x CGx CPT, compute the count of supporting oncology or hereditary-risk diagnoses in the prior twelve months of claims; fires when the count is zero; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Laboratory Corporation of America Holdings; Laboratory Corporation of America; Labcorp Tennessee, LLC; University Health System, Inc. (operator of University of Tennessee Medical Center)
SchemeSummary: UHS and Labcorp Tennessee allegedly held, or cancelled and resubmitted, physician orders for Caris laboratory tests until more than 14 days after a Medicare beneficiary's hospital discharge, circumventing Medicare's Date of Service/14-Day Rule so the lab could bill Medicare directly instead of billing the hospital; they paid $388,667.17 to resolve a qui tam suit (relator received $73,846.76), while Caris separately paid $2.8M in EDNY.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the lab's Part B claim date of service falls just past the 14-day window after the beneficiary's inpatient or outpatient discharge date on the hospital claim. The specimen collection date recorded on the lab claim precedes the billed date of service by more than two weeks. Order placement and cancel-resubmit timestamps in the lab information system cluster immediately before day fifteen. The same lab shows an unusual spike in claims with service dates on days 15 to 17 post-discharge relative to peers. The hospital's outpatient claim contains no corresponding pass-through charge for the same test.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Fourteen-day rule edit: on claim line, compute days between the beneficiary's hospital discharge date and the lab claim date of service using the specimen collection date; fires when collection falls inside 14 days but billing date falls outside; action prepay edit. 2) Post-discharge day clustering: on lab NPI x month, compute the share of Part B claims with service dates on days 15 through 21 after a discharge; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action postpay audit. 3) Order-timestamp lag: on ordering NPI x lab accession, compute days between physician order timestamp and reported date of service; fires when the gap exceeds the specimen stability window; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Christopher Grottenthaler (former CEO, True Health Diagnostics, LLC); Hong Davis, M.D. (physician); Elizabeth Seymour, M.D. (physician); Courtney Love (former True Health Account Executive/marketer); Stephen Kash (former True Health Director of Strategic Accounts/marketer); Laura Howard (former Boston Heart Area Sales Manager/marketer); Jeffrey Parnell (former Boston Heart sales representative/marketer); Stanley Jones (part-owner, LGRB Management Services LLC); Jordan Perkins (co-owner, Next Level Healthcare Consultants LLC); Ruben Marioni (co-owner, Next Level Healthcare Consultants LLC)
State_County: Texas - Collin County (Frisco, Plano); Texas - Denton County (Denton); Texas - Dallas County (Dallas); Texas - Milam County (Rockdale); Massachusetts - Middlesex County (Framingham)
SchemeSummary: Marketers, including employees of laboratory True Health Diagnostics and Boston Heart Diagnostics, paid physicians kickbacks disguised as investment distributions from purported management service organizations (Ascend MSO, Herculis MG, Eridanus MG) to induce referrals of lab tests to True Health, Boston Heart, and Little River Healthcare, which were then billed to Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE; the CEO also arranged kickbacks disguised as consulting fees, processing/handling fees, and copay/deductible waivers. Settlements total $6,068,462 across the CEO ($4.25M), two physicians ($358,842), and seven marketers ($1,459,620).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a small group of ordering physicians drives an outsized share of one lab's paid volume relative to their own patient panel size. Those same physicians appear as investors or members in MSO entities disclosed in CMS-855 ownership fields or state corporate registries. Beneficiary cost-sharing is systematically zero on the lab's remittance history, indicating routine copay and deductible waiver. Ordering physicians' test-per-patient counts exceed their specialty peers for cardiovascular and blood panels. Payments from the lab to physicians appear as consulting or processing fees in bank and 1099 records rather than fair-market service contracts.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral concentration with ownership overlap: on ordering NPI x lab TIN, compute paid dollars share plus an exact match between the ordering NPI and any owner listed in CMS-855 or MSO registry filings; fires on registry match with share above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action payment suspension. 2) Copay waiver pattern: on billing lab NPI x quarter, compute the share of claim lines with zero patient responsibility collected in remittance history; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action postpay audit. 3) Ordering intensity: on ordering NPI x panel CPT, compute tests per distinct beneficiary per year; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Munef Fadhel (owner, Great Lake Transportation, Inc.); Great Lake Transportation, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Fadhel, an owner of Great Lake Transportation, a company providing rides to Medicaid beneficiaries, submitted false records certifying shared rides as individual rides so as to obtain the higher per-trip reimbursement rate, causing a Medicaid loss over $95,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, multiple beneficiaries are billed individual-ride procedure codes with identical pickup and drop-off times on the same date of service.
