Trip records show the same vehicle and driver ID assigned to overlapping trips billed separately at the higher rate. GPS or trip-log mileage for the claimed individual rides matches a single shared route across beneficiaries. The broker's authorization record specifies shared-ride mode while the submitted claim carries the individual-ride modifier. The provider's share of individual-ride codes exceeds same-market NEMT peers serving comparable destinations.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Overlapping-trip detection: on vehicle ID x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between trips billed as individual rides; fires when any two individual-ride claims overlap in time; action prepay edit. 2) Mode mismatch: on claim line, compute an exact comparison between the billed ride-mode code and the mode on the transportation broker's prior-authorisation record; fires on mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Individual-ride share: on transportation provider NPI x month, compute individual-ride trips divided by total trips; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-market peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Munef Fadhel (owner, Great Lake Transportation, Inc.); Great Lake Transportation, Inc.
SchemeSummary: Fadhel, an owner of a non-emergency medical transportation company serving Medicaid beneficiaries, submitted false records certifying shared rides as individual rides to obtain a higher reimbursement rate, causing over $95,000 in Medicaid losses; he was sentenced to one year probation.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, two or more beneficiaries carry individual-ride codes with the same driver ID and overlapping pickup times on one date of service. Submitted trip mileage duplicates across beneficiaries, showing a single shared route billed multiple times at the solo rate. The claim's ride-mode code contradicts the mode recorded in the broker's trip authorization file. Signature logs or trip manifests list several riders for a trip billed as exclusive-use. The provider's individual-ride mix is far above same-market NEMT peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Manifest rider count: on trip ID, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries on the manifest for trips billed with an individual-ride code; fires when the count exceeds one; action prepay edit. 2) Driver overlap: on driver ID x date of service, compute overlapping minutes across separately billed individual-ride claims; fires when overlap exceeds zero minutes; action claim suspension. 3) Authorization mode match: on claim line, compute exact equality of billed mode code and broker prior-authorisation mode; fires on mismatch; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Henry Goolsby (physician); Patricia Lenae Goolsby (co-founder); Infinite Health Integrative Medical Center (clinic)
SchemeSummary: The physician, his wife and their clinic billed Medicare for surgically implanted neurostimulator electrodes (a procedure requiring a surgery center) when they had actually applied single-use, non-covered 'P-Stim' electro-acupuncture devices behind patients' ears in the office; they agreed to pay $450,000 under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the implanted neurostimulator electrode CPT is billed with office place of service 11 rather than a facility site. No facility, anesthesia or operating-room claim exists for the same beneficiary and date of service. The billing NPI's specialty in NPPES lacks surgical implantation privileges for the procedure billed. The same beneficiary receives repeated implantation codes at short intervals, inconsistent with a permanent implant's lifetime frequency. Supply and device invoices in the record match a single-use electro-acupuncture device with no covered HCPCS.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Place-of-service impossibility: on claim line, compute whether the implantation CPT is billed with place of service 11 and no matching facility or anesthesia claim on the same date of service; fires when both conditions hold; action prepay edit. 2) Implant repeat frequency: on beneficiary x implantation CPT, compute the count of paid implantation events in a rolling twelve months against the device's expected lifetime frequency; fires when the count exceeds one without an explant claim; action claim suspension. 3) Specialty-privilege mismatch: on rendering NPI x CPT, compute exact match between NPPES taxonomy and the surgical specialties eligible to bill the code; fires on mismatch; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Charles McKinley Griffin (owner/operator, Transformation Services); Tika Michelle Griffin (owner/operator and president, Transformation Services); Kirk Nathan Evans; Transformation Services
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Charles and Tika Griffin operated Transformation Services, which recruited Medicaid beneficiaries from disadvantaged backgrounds as clients and then submitted bills and records to South Carolina Medicaid for behavioral health services never rendered, and used unlicensed counselors; the entity was set up with Tika Griffin as president after Charles Griffin was barred as a Medicaid provider, concealing his role. All three defendants pleaded guilty; loss at least $246,335.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, an owner or officer listed on the CMS-855 and state Medicaid disclosure matches a name on the state exclusion list or OIG LEIE. Rendering staff NPIs on psychotherapy claim lines have no active credential in the state licensing board file for the date of service. Billed service hours per rendering clinician per day exceed 24 hours. Beneficiaries billed for weekly counseling show no corresponding transportation, pharmacy or physician claim activity consistent with engagement. Group session rosters in the record repeat identical progress-note text across unrelated beneficiaries.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Excluded-owner screen: on provider TIN, compute exact name and date-of-birth matches between CMS-855 owners and officers and OIG LEIE plus state exclusion files; fires on any match; action claim suspension and revalidation site visit. 2) Licence validity at service: on claim line, compute whether the rendering NPI held an active state licence spanning the date of service in the board file; fires on no active licence; action prepay edit. 3) Clinician hour impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed timed-unit minutes across all behavioral health CPTs; fires when total exceeds 24 hours; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Andrew Voegel-Podadera (anesthesiology resident); Pinnacle Health PC (Seattle-based healthcare provider)
SchemeSummary: Two matters: an anesthesiology resident at Seattle Children's, Harborview and UW Medical Center allegedly diverted fentanyl, hydromorphone and other narcotics for his own use over at least a year by obtaining controlled substances by fraud, sometimes using them while treating patients; separately, Pinnacle Health PC billed Medicare and TRICARE more than $500,000 for an injectable amniotic fluid product (FlowerAmnioFlo) that was experimental and not approved for any diagnosis, resolving False Claims Act liability for $1,115,976.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, an unclassified biologic HCPCS is billed with no FDA approval or covered indication tied to the submitted diagnosis. The product's NDC does not appear in the payer's covered-drug file or the FDA licensed biologics list. The billing practice's units and dollars for the product jump from zero to top-decile within a quarter. In the hospital setting, controlled-substance cabinet withdrawals by one clinician lack matching administration records for the named patient. Cancelled or wasted narcotic transactions by that clinician exceed unit peers without a second witness.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Non-covered biologic edit: on claim line, compute exact match of the billed NDC or HCPCS against the payer's covered-product file and FDA approval list; fires on no match; action prepay edit. 2) New-product ramp: on billing NPI x HCPCS x quarter, compute paid units divided by the provider's trailing baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Diversion reconciliation: on clinician ID x week, compute controlled-substance withdrawals minus documented administrations and witnessed wastes; fires when the unreconciled count exceeds zero; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Mindpath Care Centers, North Carolina, PLLC (behavioral health practice); Jeff Williams (former officer); Abigail Sheriff (former officer); Sarah Williams (former officer)
SchemeSummary: The government alleged that Mindpath, North Carolina's largest behavioral health practice, billed Medicare for psychotherapy and medication management sessions without documentation of separate and distinct psychotherapy treatments (separate time), ignoring repeated internal employee complaints about billing fraud; the practice and three former officers paid $1.9 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations arising from a whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, psychotherapy add-on CPTs 90833, 90836 or 90838 are billed with an E/M code on nearly every encounter for the practice. Documented psychotherapy minutes are absent or duplicate the E/M time in the submitted record. Summed E/M plus psychotherapy minutes per rendering NPI per date of service exceed a plausible workday. The practice's add-on ratio far exceeds same-specialty psychiatric peers in the payer's remittance history. Internal compliance complaints and repeat identical time statements appear across unrelated beneficiary notes.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Add-on ratio: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute psychotherapy add-on lines divided by total E/M lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Daily minute impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed E/M typical time plus billed psychotherapy minutes; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or the credentialed schedule; action claim suspension. 3) Distinct-time documentation: on claim line pairing E/M with an add-on, compute presence of a separately stated psychotherapy start and stop time in the record; fires when absent; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Magaly Travieso (advanced practitioner registered nurse, owner of ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.); Yudorki Ramirez (former spouse, money laundering); ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage Plans; Florida Medicaid; commercial insurance
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Travieso, an APRN who owned ProMed Healthcare clinic, billed over $20 million (receiving over $10 million) to commercial insurers, Medicare/Medicare Advantage and Medicaid for back and shoulder braces, physical therapy and psychosocial rehabilitation/mental health services that were medically unnecessary or never provided, paying patients kickbacks and fabricating progress notes with copied stock patient quotes (including typos) across dozens of elderly patients' records; her former spouse Ramirez laundered roughly $2.07 million of the proceeds into investment accounts and used funds for homes and a Range Rover, with over $6 million in assets forfeited across both defendants (9 years for Travieso, 3 years for Ramirez).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one clinic NPI bills orthotic L-codes, timed physical therapy units and psychosocial rehabilitation for the same beneficiaries in one week. Summed timed therapy and behavioral health units per rendering NPI per date of service exceed 24 hours. Progress notes across unrelated beneficiaries contain byte-identical narrative strings, detectable by text hashing of submitted documentation. Beneficiaries billed for braces have no orthopedic diagnosis or prior evaluation in their other claims. Clinic bank deposits from multiple payers move promptly into personal accounts and vehicle purchases, visible in financial records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cross-benefit stacking: on beneficiary x clinic NPI x week, compute the count of distinct benefit categories billed covering DMEPOS, therapy and behavioral health; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 2) Unit impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed timed units converted to minutes across all therapy and behavioral CPTs; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Duplicate-note detection: on provider TIN, compute the share of submitted progress notes whose normalized text hash matches another beneficiary's note; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR), then payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Magaly Travieso (advanced practitioner registered nurse, owner of ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.); Yudorki Ramirez (former spouse); ProMed Healthcare, L.L.C.
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage Plans; Medicaid (Florida); commercial insurance
SchemeSummary: Travieso, an APRN who owned ProMed Healthcare, allegedly submitted over $20 million in fraudulent claims to commercial insurers, Medicare/Medicare Advantage and Medicaid for back and shoulder braces, physical therapy, psychosocial rehabilitation and other mental health services, collecting over $10 million; she and her former spouse Ramirez then allegedly laundered the proceeds into a Range Rover, two Miami residences and investment accounts, leading to seizure of the vehicle and over $4 million from bank accounts.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the same beneficiaries receive brace L-codes, physical therapy and psychosocial rehabilitation from a single clinic NPI in one billing period. Timed units billed per rendering NPI per day exceed the hours available in a 24-hour day. Beneficiaries lack any prior evaluation or qualifying diagnosis supporting the ordered braces in their other claim history. Clinic payment volume rises sharply above its own trailing baseline across four payers simultaneously. Payer remittances flow into accounts that immediately disburse to personal asset purchases in bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Multi-payer volume ramp: on provider TIN x month, compute total paid dollars across payers divided by the provider's trailing six-month baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 2) Daily unit impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed timed-unit minutes across therapy and behavioral CPTs; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Brace without indication: on beneficiary x L-code, compute the count of qualifying musculoskeletal diagnoses and prior E/M encounters in the lookback; fires when the count is zero; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Nathan Mathews (owner, Emerald Lane Therapy Services and co-owner, Stars & Stripes Therapy); Jimmie Mathews (co-owner, Stars & Stripes Therapy); Amber Delger (subsequent co-owner, Emerald Lane Therapy Services); Emerald Lane Therapy Services; Stars & Stripes Therapy
SchemeSummary: Owners of two Lawton massage therapy businesses scheduled TRICARE beneficiaries for multiple appointments months in advance and continued billing the Defense Health Agency as if care was delivered even when beneficiaries missed appointments or stopped coming; Emerald Lane also billed under the NPI of an occupational therapist who no longer worked there. The two companies billed over $7 million and were reimbursed nearly $3 million; restitution figures ($1,410,255.66, $632,026.43 and $653,269.00) and sentences (87, 42 and 26 months) span the three defendants.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claims recur on a fixed weekly cadence for the same beneficiary with no gaps, matching a pre-booked schedule rather than delivered care. The rendering NPI on submitted lines shows no employment or credentialing record with the billing TIN for the date of service. Beneficiaries billed for ongoing visits have relocated or have no other claims in the region during the same period. Sign-in sheets or attendance records are absent for a large share of billed dates on ADR response. Billing continues under an NPI whose NPPES practice address no longer matches the billing site.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Perfect-cadence billing: on beneficiary x provider TIN, compute the count of consecutive billed visit dates matching the scheduled interval with zero no-show gaps; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Rendering-NPI affiliation: on claim line, compute exact match between the rendering NPI and the TIN's credentialed staff roster and NPPES affiliation on the date of service; fires on no active affiliation; action prepay edit. 3) Beneficiary presence check: on beneficiary x month, compute the count of other claims within the service area during billed treatment months; fires when zero while visits continue to be billed; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Junyi Liu a/k/a 'Jenny' (licensed acupuncturist, leader of scheme); Noemi Algodon; Mohamed Elmandouh; Gerard Estrella; Ramon Garcia III; Henler Datu Tahil; Jonathan Laqui; Mitzy Baldovino
State_County: New York - New York County (Manhattan); New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County (Queens)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Liu operated acupuncture/physical therapy offices in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens that billed Medicare and other insurers for services either not rendered or not as represented, using partner licensed therapists/acupuncturists' provider enrollments and fabricated medical documentation; cash kickbacks were paid to patients to supply insurance information (some never even visited the offices) and kickbacks of cash and wine were given to insurer employees. Liu separately obtained fraudulent COVID-19 unemployment benefits for herself and a family member; restitution of $23,855,425 to insurers, $40,075 to NY DOL, and $15,368,171 forfeiture relate to Liu, with seven co-defendants also pleading guilty.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, timed acupuncture and therapy units summed per licensed rendering NPI per date of service exceed 24 hours. Multiple clinic locations bill under the same borrowed licensed provider NPI on the same dates of service. Beneficiaries billed for repeated visits show no travel-consistent claim footprint and reside far from all three clinic addresses. Submitted treatment notes repeat identical text and identical measured findings across unrelated beneficiaries. Clinic enrolment records show licensed practitioners listed as supervising while payments flow to a non-licensed owner entity in bank records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Borrowed-licence detection: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct service locations billing under that NPI; fires when the count exceeds one at physically separated addresses; action claim suspension. 2) Timed-unit impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed acupuncture and therapy minutes from billed units; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Beneficiary-distance and duplication: on beneficiary x clinic TIN, compute distance from residence ZIP to service address plus the count of notes with matching text hashes; fires when distance exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peers with duplicate notes present; action documentation request (ADR), then payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Manishkumar Patel (leader of scheme, script seller)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; Device, DME; Drug_Prescriptions; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Patel and a coconspirator obtained DME, pharmaceutical and lab-test scripts by having call centers cold-call Medicare beneficiaries, then converting the call data into orders via cursory telemedicine visits, 'doctor chasing' (doctors signing without seeing patients), or outright forgery, and sold those scripts to DME suppliers, pharmacies and labs that billed Medicare; payments for the scripts were disguised as flat-rate marketing contracts to conceal kickbacks, causing about $48 million in Medicare losses. Patel was ordered to pay $48,150,692.49 restitution and forfeit $6,839,900.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on DMEPOS, pharmacy and lab claims has no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One telehealth ordering NPI appears on claims from unrelated supplier, pharmacy and laboratory NPIs across many beneficiary states weekly. Telehealth encounter claims show place-of-service 02 with unit times far below the billed CPT's required minutes. Beneficiaries receive braces, topical creams and cancer panels within days of each other from separate billing NPIs. Supplier remittance history shows volume jumping from near-zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of a marketing contract start date.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim linking that ordering NPI to the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Shared-orderer graph degree: on ordering NPI x month, compute the count of distinct billing NPIs and distinct beneficiary states across DMEPOS, Part D and lab claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Cross-silo bundle: on beneficiary x 30 days, compute the count of distinct service silos (DME L-code, compounded drug NDC, genetic test CPT) traced to one ordering NPI; fires when that count exceeds one; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Zakia Khan (owner of Happy Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., Family Social Adult Day Care Center Inc., Responsible Care Staffing Inc., and Tanwee Services Inc.); marketers employed by Khan; co-defendants
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Khan and marketers she employed paid cash kickbacks and bribes to Medicaid recipients to enroll at her two Brooklyn social adult day care centers, then billed Medicaid over $68 million for social adult day care services that were never provided or were induced by the kickbacks; multiple business entities, including a home health fiscal intermediary and a shell company, were used to launder proceeds and generate the cash for bribes. Khan agreed to forfeit $5 million including two properties, cash and gold jewelry.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed attendance days exceed signed daily sign-in-sheet records reconciled against the center's registration file. Enrolled recipients' residence addresses sit far outside the center's catchment on the Medicaid provider enrollment file. The same recipients simultaneously show personal care or home health visit claims overlapping the adult day care attendance hours. Enrollment surges cluster on marketer-linked recruitment dates rather than on assessment or care-plan dates. Ownership fields on the enrollment record link the day care TIN to a fiscal intermediary and a shell entity sharing one bank account.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Attendance-versus-roster: on provider NPI x date of service, compute billed attendance units minus signed sign-in-sheet entries; fires when billed units exceed documented entries; action prepay edit. 2) Concurrent-service overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between adult day care units and home health or personal care visit records including EVV timestamps; fires when overlap exceeds zero minutes; action claim suspension. 3) Common-account cluster: on bank account, compute the count of distinct billing TINs receiving remittance deposits; fires when that count exceeds one without disclosed common ownership in enrollment records; action site visit and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maine
FraudEntity: Joseph Dobie
SchemeSummary: Dobie allegedly used another person's identity to fraudulently obtain Medicaid and SNAP benefits, and was charged by complaint with aggravated identity theft, false statements relating to health care matters, and unlawful use of SNAP benefits as part of the 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the applicant SSN and name mismatch the Social Security Administration and state vital records identity verification file. The same SSN appears on active enrollment in another beneficiary's Medicaid identity record. Claims and SNAP redemptions post in a geography inconsistent with the enrollee's address of record. The enrollee identity matches a Death Master File entry or an identity flagged in a prior fraud referral. Enrollment application signature and contact phone match those already used on other member records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Identity verification mismatch: on applicant record, compute the count of mismatched fields (SSN, date of birth, legal name) against SSA and state vital records; fires when any field mismatches exactly; action claim suspension pending eligibility review. 2) SSN reuse: on SSN, compute the distinct count of active member IDs across Medicaid and SNAP files; fires when that count exceeds one; action prepay edit. 3) Contact-point sharing: on phone number or mailing address, compute the count of distinct enrollee IDs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-region enrollees; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case: this is a personnel announcement naming Lisa G. Johnston Acting United States Attorney for the Southern District of West Virginia.
WaysToIdentify: This is a personnel announcement, not a fraud matter, so no claim, no billing NPI and no adjudication point exists. There is nothing for a payer edit to evaluate at enrollment, prior authorisation or claim adjudication. The nearest non-claims route is routine tracking of Department of Justice press releases for later case linkage.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system is maintaining a case-intake feed that ingests only actual charging or settlement documents for provider watchlisting.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Arkansas
FraudEntity: Krameelah Banks (psychologist, owner and operator of Arkansas Behavioral Center)
PayerName: Medicare; Arkansas Blue Cross and Blue Shield
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Banks allegedly billed Medicare and Arkansas Blue Cross for thousands of hours of ongoing psychotherapy in the names of referral patients who were seen only once for pre-surgical psychological evaluations, including billing while vacationing in Florida and Mexico, more than 24 hours of services in a single day, and over 130 sessions for patients who had died, causing over $500,000 in losses; she allegedly created fictitious records to answer claim inquiries and misled the FBI by blaming her calendaring software.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, summed timed psychotherapy CPT units for the rendering NPI exceed 24 hours on a single date of service. Dates of service fall on days the rendering NPI has no local activity while claims post continuously without any covering NPI. Beneficiaries have dates of service after the date recorded in the Death Master File. Patients with only one prior pre-surgical evaluation CPT show long ongoing 90837 series with no interval diagnosis change. Records supplied in response to claim inquiries were created after the payer's ADR date, per document metadata.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed billed minutes from timed CPT codes 90832, 90834 and 90837; fires when total exceeds 24 hours or the provider's licensed practice hours; action prepay edit. 2) Post-mortem service: on claim line, compute days between date of service and the beneficiary's Death Master File date; fires when date of service is after date of death; action claim suspension. 3) Single-evaluation conversion: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the ratio of ongoing psychotherapy sessions to documented evaluation encounters; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR) then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: LiveCare Inc. (remote patient monitoring provider)
SchemeSummary: LiveCare Inc., which provides remote patient monitoring services to Type 2 diabetes patients, allegedly paid a marketing service for referrals of Medicare beneficiaries, causing claims tainted by kickbacks to be submitted to Medicare; resolved through a qui tam civil settlement of up to $4.9 million with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, remote patient monitoring CPT 99453/99454/99457 claims concentrate in beneficiary cohorts sourced from one marketing vendor rather than one clinic. Enrolled beneficiaries lack any prior treating-relationship E/M claim with the billing NPI. Device supply claims post monthly with transmission-day counts exactly at the minimum threshold for payment. The billing entity's cost data show flat per-referral marketing payments rather than fair-market fixed fees, visible in vendor contracts requested at audit. Enrollment growth spikes align with marketing campaign start dates rather than diabetes diagnosis incidence.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral-source concentration: on billing NPI x month, compute the share of new RPM beneficiaries with no prior E/M claim to that NPI; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Threshold clustering: on beneficiary x month, compute the count of device transmission days billed under 99454; fires when the distribution mass sits exactly at the minimum payable day count above the provider's trailing baseline; action prepay edit. 3) Marketer graph: on marketing vendor TIN, compute the count of distinct billing NPIs whose RPM volume rose after contract start; fires when that count exceeds one; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Dr. Eric Edward Haeger (physician, sleep clinic owner/supervisor)
SchemeSummary: Physician bought over 500 used, recalled Philips CPAP/BiPAP devices from online resellers, had staff pry out the recalled sound-abatement foam with screwdrivers and hooks outside any clean room, then dispensed the refurbished devices to Washington State Medicaid patients at his sleep clinic and billed Medicaid representing them as new devices in good working order.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, HCPCS E0601/E0470 claims are billed with new-equipment modifier NU while serial numbers match FDA recall listings for returned devices. Supplier acquisition records show purchases from online resellers rather than a manufacturer or authorized distributor pedigree. Device serial numbers on claims repeat across multiple beneficiaries over time. The supplier's CMS-855S enrollment lists no reprocessing or refurbishment capability at the site inspected. Beneficiary complaint and repair claim rates for the supplier exceed same-specialty peer rates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Recall serial match: on claim line, compare the reported device serial or model against the FDA recall registry for that HCPCS; fires on an exact registry match billed with modifier NU; action prepay edit. 2) Serial reuse: on device serial number, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries paid over the device lifetime; fires when that count exceeds one; action claim suspension. 3) Pedigree gap: on supplier NPI x HCPCS, compute paid units minus units traceable to authorized distributor invoices; fires when paid units exceed documented acquisitions; action site visit and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Eric Ndungu Mwangi (Kenyan national, owner of Linear Diagnostics); Linear Diagnostics (LD); Davendra Rampersaud (Guyanese national, owner of Caribbean Medical Supplies, Inc.); Caribbean Medical Supplies, Inc. (CMS)
PayerName: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) - KEMSA Medical Commodities Program
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Mwangi and his company Linear Diagnostics systematically stole USAID-funded HIV test kits and other health commodities intended for Kenya's government supply authority (KEMSA), selling them to Rampersaud and his Guyanese company CMS for over $177,000; Rampersaud fraudulently obtained a 'Letter of Authority' as an authorized distributor to win a sole-source contract with the Guyana Ministry of Health and resold the stolen USAID commodities to the Guyanese government. Rampersaud pleaded guilty, received credit for time served, three years supervised release and an $84,000 fine; Mwangi remains charged and is awaiting trial in Kenya.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim and no adjudication point here, since the loss is diverted grant-funded commodities, not billed services. Detection sits with grant commodity accounting, comparing shipped HIV test kit lot numbers against recipient warehouse receipt records. The nearest control is verifying distributor Letters of Authority directly with the manufacturer before sole-source award.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system is a lot-level reconciliation on donated-commodity shipment ID, computing shipped units minus units receipted at the designated national authority, with award suspension when the gap is nonzero.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Benjamin Tekippe (chiropractor, owner of Metairie Chiropractic & Rehab)
State_County: Louisiana - Orleans Parish (New Orleans); Louisiana - Jefferson Parish (Metairie)
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana; Louisiana unemployment insurance program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor recruited BCBSLA-insured patients at schools, public events and via social media with offers of 'free' chiropractic massages, then billed BCBSLA over $2.3 million (about $740,000 paid) for thousands of chiropractic services never performed, including on dates he was on vacation, out of the office or incarcerated; he fabricated patient records in staff handwriting to defeat an insurer audit. He also falsely certified weekly unemployment during COVID-19 while billing, collecting $12,952 in benefits.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, CPT 98940-98943 claims post on dates the rendering NPI was verifiably absent, evidenced by no other local activity and incarceration or travel records. Daily treatment counts for the solo rendering NPI exceed feasible hours given the timed service definitions. Members recruited at events show identical visit-frequency templates with no varying diagnosis or plan-of-care progression. Records produced during an insurer audit were written in a single hand across many patients and dated retroactively. Patients report no service when the payer sends explanation-of-benefit verification letters.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Provider-absent dates: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of billed encounters on dates matched to absence records such as incarceration or license-board and travel evidence; fires when count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 2) Daily capacity: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total encounters divided by feasible working hours using per-CPT service time; fires when implied hours exceed 24 or licensed practice hours; action prepay edit. 3) Member verification: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the rate of member survey denials of service among sampled paid claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Benjamin Tekippe (chiropractor and owner of Metairie Chiropractic & Rehab)
PayerName: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana; Louisiana unemployment insurance program
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor lured BCBSLA members with 'free' massages, then billed the insurer for non-covered full-body massages performed by massage therapists plus thousands of chiropractic services never performed - including on dates he was on vacation in Aruba or incarcerated - and fabricated/rewrote patient records to survive an insurer audit; he also filed false weekly COVID-era unemployment certifications claiming to be unemployed while billing for services, collecting $12,952.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, chiropractic manipulation CPT codes are billed where the rendering staff on the encounter record are licensed massage therapists, per the state licence board file. Claims post on dates the rendering NPI was out of the country or incarcerated with no covering provider on file. Nearly every new member's first visit follows a free-service promotion with identical coding patterns and no documented subluxation level. Audit-response records show uniform handwriting and creation dates after the ADR letter date. The same beneficiaries show high visit counts without any interim re-evaluation CPT.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence-scope mismatch: on claim line, compare the rendering individual's licence type in the state board file against the scope required by the billed CPT; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Absence-date billing: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of encounters billed on documented absence dates; fires when count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Promotion cohort intensity: on rendering NPI x member cohort, compute mean paid visits per member within 90 days of first visit; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana; Justice Department Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Adrian Dexter Talbot M.D. (owner/operator of Medex Clinical Consultants); Medex Clinical Consultants
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Louisiana); Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana
SchemeSummary: Talbot ran a cash-based clinic issuing prescriptions for Schedule II opioids; after taking a full-time job elsewhere in 2015 he pre-signed prescriptions (and directed a hired practitioner to do the same) for individuals he never examined, falsified patient records to make it appear exams occurred, and the prescriptions were then filled using patients' insurance, causing Medicare, Louisiana Medicaid, and BCBS of Louisiana to be billed over $5.4 million for over 1.8 million doses of controlled substances.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Schedule II NDC fills carry a prescriber NPI with no corresponding E/M claim for that beneficiary in the lookback window. The prescriber's written dates cluster in batches while the prescriber holds concurrent full-time employment claims elsewhere on the same dates. PDMP and ARCOS data show morphine milligram equivalents per prescriber far above same-specialty peers. Prescriptions written by a hired practitioner carry an identical signature image across many patients. Prescriber's clinic bills no office visits while pharmacy claims volume rises, visible in remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescription without encounter: on beneficiary x prescriber NPI, compute days between the Part D fill date and the nearest E/M claim by that prescriber; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Prescriber MME intensity: on prescriber NPI x month, compute total morphine milligram equivalents dispensed from NDC and days-supply fields; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Batch-signing pattern: on prescriber NPI x written date, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with controlled-substance prescriptions written that day; fires when implied minutes per patient fall below feasible visit length in a 24-hour day; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Michael L. Riggins (owner of Bluewater Healthcare); Bluewater Healthcare
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Riggins, owner of DME supplier Bluewater Healthcare, paid for doctors' orders for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment and tricked physicians into signing DME orders and certificates of medical necessity, then billed Medicare over $3.8 million and was reimbursed over $1.8 million despite hundreds of complaints about the fraudulent orders.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, DMEPOS claims cite ordering NPIs with no prior E/M encounter with the beneficiary. Ordering physicians disavow the certificates of medical necessity when the payer sends verification letters to the NPPES address of record. One supplier NPI concentrates orders from a narrow set of ordering NPIs recruited by a single marketer. Beneficiary complaint volume against the supplier exceeds same-specialty peer rates in the payer's grievance file. Supplier billing jumps from near-zero to top-decile within weeks of enrollment approval on the CMS-855S.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer concentration: on supplier NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid DMEPOS lines attributable to the top few ordering NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Complaint-adjusted ramp: on supplier NPI x month, compute paid amount growth versus the supplier's trailing baseline combined with the count of beneficiary complaints; fires when growth exceeds baseline while complaints exceed peer rate; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana; U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Scharmaine Lawson Baker (nurse practitioner, independent contractor for telehealth company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Nurse practitioner signed hundreds of orders for medically unnecessary cancer genetic tests after phone calls typically under 60 seconds, without exams, falsely diagnosing patients (e.g., male patients with cervical cancer) to justify testing; she took kickbacks from the telehealth company, causing over $12.1 million in Medicare claims with labs receiving over $1.5 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, hereditary cancer panel CPT and 81479 claims cite an ordering NPI whose telehealth encounter duration is under the billed code's minimum minutes. Ordered diagnosis codes are anatomically impossible for the beneficiary's sex recorded in the eligibility file. One nurse practitioner NPI orders panels for beneficiaries across many states within days. Ordering NPI has no oncology or genetics specialty taxonomy in NPPES for the tests ordered. Beneficiary has no prior cancer diagnosis or family-history counseling claim before the panel order.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Sex-diagnosis conflict: on claim line, compare the ordering diagnosis code against the beneficiary sex in the eligibility file; fires on exact edit mismatch such as cervical cancer for a male beneficiary; action prepay edit. 2) Encounter-duration floor: on ordering NPI x date of service, compute encounter minutes divided by the count of orders signed that day; fires when implied minutes per patient are below the billed code's minimum; action claim suspension. 3) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct laboratory NPIs on ordered genetic tests; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana; U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Shanone Chatman-Ashley (nurse practitioner, independent contractor for telehealth companies)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Working as a contractor for telehealth companies, the nurse practitioner signed more than 1,000 orders for medically unnecessary knee braces, suspension sleeves and other DME for Medicare beneficiaries she never examined, falsely certifying she had consulted with and assessed them, causing over $2 million in claims and over $1 million in reimbursements, in exchange for kickbacks from the telehealth companies.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, L-code brace claims cite an ordering NPI with no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One nurse practitioner NPI signs orders for beneficiaries in many states within a single week. Certifications state assessment occurred while no telehealth encounter claim exists for that date of service. The same beneficiary receives multiple brace HCPCS spanning unrelated joints within one month. Ordering NPI appears across several unrelated supplier NPIs sharing marketing contracts, visible in claim-level orderer-supplier pairings.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M or telehealth claim linking that NPI to the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action prepay edit. 2) Signer volume: on ordering NPI x day, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with signed DMEPOS orders; fires when implied assessment minutes exceed 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Multi-joint saturation: on beneficiary x 30 days, compute the count of distinct brace HCPCS across unrelated body regions; fires when that count exceeds clinically plausible one-per-region limits; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Dr. James Charasika (physician); Louisville Patient Centered Medical Home, P.S.C. (LPCMH) (practice)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that Dr. Charasika and his practice billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE as if the physician personally performed medical services when the services were actually rendered by nurse practitioners, without satisfying the conditions permitting billing at the higher physician rate. Resolved for $250,000 in a qui tam action, with relators receiving over $35,000 and the Kentucky Medicaid Fraud Control Unit over $68,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, E/M claims list the physician NPI as rendering while the practice's schedule and payroll show a nurse practitioner performed the visit. Physician rendering-NPI volume exceeds feasible daily encounters given the number of clinicians actually on site. Claims lack the incident-to conditions since no physician encounter for the same problem exists in the lookback. Physician is billing on dates with no on-site presence, unsupported by any concurrent supervision record. The practice bills almost no claims under its enrolled nurse practitioner NPIs despite their PECOS enrollment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Unused midlevel NPI: on TIN x quarter, compute the ratio of E/M lines billed under physician NPIs to the count of enrolled nurse practitioner NPIs with near-zero billing; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 2) Physician capacity: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total E/M encounters times typical code service time; fires when implied hours exceed 24 or documented on-site hours; action prepay edit. 3) Incident-to precondition: on beneficiary x TIN, compute days since the last physician-performed encounter for the same problem; fires when no qualifying physician encounter exists in the lookback; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Mississippi
FraudEntity: Reginald Fullwood, Jr. (owner of Jackson Medical Supply); Jackson Medical Supply (durable medical equipment company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Fullwood paid kickbacks to a marketer for completed doctors' orders so his DME company, Jackson Medical Supply, could bill Medicare and Medicare Advantage for medically unnecessary or ineligible orthotic braces; after Medicare began investigating, he opened a second entity under a nominee owner and continued the same kickback-for-orders billing, totaling about $12.4 million billed and $6.4 million reimbursed.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, orthotic brace claims cite ordering NPIs having no prior E/M encounter with the beneficiary. A single marketer-linked set of ordering NPIs supplies most of the supplier's paid volume. A new supplier NPI enrolls with a nominee owner while sharing address, phone or bank account with a supplier already under review, per CMS-855S fields. Beneficiaries already have a paid same-HCPCS brace within the reasonable-useful-lifetime window. Medicare Advantage and fee-for-service claims duplicate the same device for the same beneficiary.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Successor-entity link: on bank account or practice address, compute the count of distinct supplier NPIs enrolled, including those with prior payment suspension; fires when that count exceeds one across enrollment records; action site visit and prepay edit. 2) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim with the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists; action prepay edit. 3) Lifetime duplication: on beneficiary x HCPCS, compute months since the last paid same-code device across FFS and Advantage claims; fires when within the reasonable useful lifetime; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Mahlega Abdsharafat, aka "Mallie Sharafat"; Creative Hospice Care, Inc. and affiliated companies (Creative Hospice entities)
SchemeSummary: Creative Hospice and its owner allegedly paid medical directors monthly stipends and a signing bonus that rose or fell with the number of hospice patients each director referred, inducing referrals and causing false claims to federal health care programs; resolved for $9.2 million with over $1.5 million paid to three qui tam relators.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the certifying medical director NPI's monthly stipend tracks the count of patients that director referred, visible in cost report and contract records. A small set of medical director NPIs certifies most admissions for the agency. Certifying physicians also appear as referring NPIs on the same beneficiaries' prior claims, creating a closed referral loop. Live-discharge and long-length-of-stay rates exceed same-specialty peer rates in hospice claim history. Ownership and contractor disclosures on the CMS-855A do not list all compensated medical directors.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral-linked compensation: on medical director NPI x month, compute the correlation between stipend amount in contract records and the count of certified admissions; fires when payment varies with referral count; action postpay audit. 2) Certifier concentration: on hospice NPI x quarter, compute the share of admissions certified by compensated medical director NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Disclosure mismatch: on hospice TIN, compute the count of compensated physician NPIs absent from CMS-855A disclosure fields; fires when that count exceeds zero; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Petros Fichidzhyan (operator of sham hospice companies and owner of a home health care agency)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Fichidzhyan and co-schemers operated a series of sham hospice companies, using stolen identities of foreign nationals as nominee owners (to open bank accounts and sign leases) and misappropriating doctors' identifying information to certify that hospice care was needed, then billed Medicare for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill and never received care; Medicare paid nearly $16 million, of which he personally received nearly $7 million laundered through a dozen shell and third-party accounts. He also obtained over $1 million for his home health agency by fraudulently using a doctor's name to certify beneficiaries, paying the doctor $11,000 to cover it up.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, hospice election claims cite certifying physician NPIs with no other claim relationship to the beneficiary or the agency. Beneficiaries under the hospice benefit continue receiving curative and Part D claims inconsistent with terminal certification. Newly enrolled agencies list owners whose identity documents mismatch SSA and NPPES records on the CMS-855A. Multiple agency NPIs share one bank account and mailing address in enrollment and remittance data. Certifying physicians deny signing when the payer sends verification to the NPPES address of record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Certifier-relationship void: on beneficiary x certifying NPI, compute the count of prior claims linking that physician to the beneficiary before the hospice election date; fires when the count is zero; action claim suspension. 2) Non-terminal utilization: on beneficiary x hospice period, compute the count of curative treatment and Part D claims during election; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus hospice peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Shared-account cluster: on bank account, compute the count of distinct provider NPIs receiving Medicare deposits; fires when that count exceeds one without disclosed common ownership; action payment suspension and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Chaudhry Shabbir Ahmed (nominee owner of Dune Medical Supply, LLC and Prospect Health Solutions, Inc.); Dune Medical Supply, LLC; Prospect Health Solutions, Inc.
State_County: North Carolina - Guilford County (High Point); Florida - Broward County (Fort Lauderdale)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Ahmed used a sham purchase agreement to pose as sole owner of two DME companies (while a co-conspirator retained control), including on Medicare enrollment documents; the companies billed Medicare over $100 million for durable medical equipment beneficiaries never received, requested, needed, or that was never ordered, and Medicare deposited over $33 million into company accounts from which Ahmed withdrew large cash sums (e.g., $400,000 and $500,000).
WaysToIdentify: At enrollment, the CMS-855S ownership fields name a purchaser whose funding and control documents conflict with the seller's continuing signature authority on the bank account. Two supplier NPIs share address, phone and bank account across enrollment and remittance records. Billed DMEPOS lines cite ordering NPIs with no encounter or any order record at all. Beneficiaries deny receipt when the payer mails delivery verification against the claim's delivery date. Cash withdrawals in large round amounts follow Medicare deposits, visible in financial institution reporting.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Nominee-owner test: on supplier NPI, compute the count of mismatches between CMS-855S owners and bank account signatories plus prior-owner continuity; fires when any exact mismatch exists; action site visit before enrollment approval. 2) Delivery verification failure: on supplier NPI x month, compute the rate of beneficiary-denied deliveries among sampled paid claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Ramp anomaly: on supplier NPI x week, compute paid amount versus the supplier's trailing baseline and same-specialty peer median; fires when growth exceeds both thresholds; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Daniel Gonzalez-Munguia, aka "Alejandro Vasquez" (operator of online drug business)
SchemeSummary: Defendant operated an online drug business from Mexico from 2012 to 2021 selling bottles of Pentobarbital, a controlled substance sold in Mexico for euthanizing animals, to hundreds of buyers in the U.S. and worldwide for use in committing suicide; he shipped it disguised as a cosmetic product and used intermediaries to smuggle it into the U.S. Many buyers consumed the product and died.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim and no adjudication point, since the controlled substance was sold direct-to-consumer across borders for cash. No NDC, prescriber NPI or pharmacy billing record enters any payer system. The nearest detection route is customs parcel screening and payment-processor monitoring of recurring foreign merchant transactions mislabeled as cosmetics.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system is import-manifest and payment-processor screening on merchant account, computing counts of small international parcels declared as cosmetics from repeat shippers, with referral to DEA and CBP.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nebraska
FraudEntity: Paul M. Hughes; The Hughes and Company Foundation USA Coalition Company; The Hughes and Company Foundation USA Coalition- Virtual Infirmary
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Hughes submitted a false NPI application to CMS falsely claiming to be a physician and Advanced Registered Nurse Practitioner, obtained an NPI number, and then used it to submit fake prescriptions to pharmacies, including a fraudulent electronic prescription for a Schedule III controlled substance listing a real doctor as the prescriber.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855I and NPPES taxonomy claim a physician or ARNP credential absent from the state licence board file. The NPI was issued with no matching state licence number verifiable in the primary-source licensure registry. E-prescribing traffic shows a Schedule III prescription whose prescriber NPI conflicts with the DEA registrant name on the transaction. The new NPI writes controlled-substance prescriptions with no associated E/M claim history in payer remittance data. Prescriber address on the pharmacy claim matches no PECOS practice location for that NPI.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence-registry mismatch at enrolment: on provider NPI, compute an exact match test between NPPES taxonomy plus licence number and the state board file record; fires when no active licence record exists for that name and taxonomy; action prepay edit on all claims citing that NPI as prescriber. 2) Prescriber-DEA identity conflict: on claim line, compute whether the prescriber NPI, DEA registrant name and pharmacy-reported prescriber name agree exactly across NPPES, the DEA registration file and the NCPDP claim; fires on any mismatch for a scheduled drug; action claim suspension. 3) Zero-encounter prescriber: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of controlled-substance prescriptions dispensed to E/M claims billed by that NPI; fires when the denominator is zero or the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (sentenced in Tampa, Florida)
FraudEntity: Robert Desselle (marketer)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Desselle paid non-medical marketers to recruit Medicare beneficiaries at grocery stores, pharmacies and car dealerships into medically unnecessary genetic tests, then bribed a telemedicine company to generate doctors' orders; clinical laboratories paid him kickbacks for the referrals and billed Medicare $11.5 million, of which Medicare paid $4.5 million and Desselle personally received over $2.1 million. Restitution of $4.5 million plus $2.1 million forfeiture were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on cancer-panel CPT lines has no prior E/M claim with that beneficiary. One telemedicine ordering NPI signs genetic-test orders for beneficiaries across many distant states weekly. Beneficiary residence ZIPs on the claim sit far outside the laboratory's CLIA and CMS-855B service area. The same beneficiary receives duplicate hereditary-cancer panels from unrelated laboratory NPIs within months. Laboratory volume for these CPTs jumps from near-zero to peer-top-decile after a new marketing contract or PECOS ownership change.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Telehealth orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the distinct count of beneficiary states and distinct laboratory NPIs on ordered genetic-test claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Panel duplication: on beneficiary x CPT family, compute the count of distinct laboratory NPIs paid within a rolling 180 days for hereditary-cancer panels; fires when that count exceeds one; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Shahram Naghshbandi (laboratory marketer); John Bello (laboratory marketer); RiteRx4U LLC (marketing company); Dr. Abbesalom Ghermay (physician); Dr. James Cook (physician); Family Medical Centers, P.C. (medical practice); Dr. Daniel Theesfeld (physician); H8 Pain Management Center of Texas PLLC (medical practice); Troy Belton (medical practice owner); Advantage Medical Group (outpatient clinic)
State_County: Texas - Tarrant County (Fort Worth); Texas - Collin County (Plano); Texas - Gregg County (Longview); Texas - Harris County (Houston); Texas - Dallas County (Dallas); Texas - Denton County (Denton); Virginia - Chesterfield County (Chesterfield/Chester); Virginia - Richmond; South Carolina - Richland County (Columbia); New Jersey - Union County (Kenilworth); Florida - Orange County (Orlando)
SchemeSummary: Lab marketers and their companies paid physicians and clinic owners kickbacks disguised as investment distributions/returns from purported management service organizations (MSOs) in exchange for ordering clinical laboratory testing from labs in New Jersey, Texas, Virginia and Florida; the labs paid the marketers commissions based on reimbursement, and the tainted referrals produced false Medicare lab-testing claims. Six settling parties and associated entities agreed to pay a combined $1,137,914 (Naghshbandi $400,000 plus 10-year exclusion, Bello/RiteRx4U $140,000, Ghermay $228,482, Cook/Family Medical Centers $206,987, Theesfeld/H8 Pain Management $99,125, Belton/Advantage Medical Group $63,320).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, ordering physicians who hold MSO investment interests show lab-order volume far above same-specialty peers. Ownership and contract disclosures on the laboratory's CMS-855B omit the marketer entities collecting percentage-of-reimbursement commissions. A small set of ordering NPIs supplies most of a distant out-of-state laboratory's referral volume. Ordered test panels repeat the identical CPT bundle across unrelated beneficiaries of one clinic TIN. OIG LEIE and prior settlement lists tie marketer principals to multiple laboratory NPIs at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral concentration graph: on laboratory NPI, compute the share of paid lab claims attributable to the top ordering NPIs plus each orderer's distance in miles to the lab; fires when concentration and distance are both above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action postpay audit. 2) Orderer-versus-peer intensity: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute lab CPT claims per distinct beneficiary with an E/M encounter; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement for those panels. 3) Ownership-disclosure mismatch: on TIN, compute the count of common principals or addresses shared between marketer/MSO entities and enrolled laboratory NPIs in CMS-855 ownership fields; fires when any undisclosed shared principal exists; action claim suspension pending enrolment revalidation.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Amanda Nicole Manatt (registered nurse)
State_County: Iowa - Marshall County (Marshalltown); Iowa - Story County
SchemeSummary: A registered nurse working at two Iowa hospitals obtained controlled substances, including fentanyl and hydromorphone (Dilaudid), that were intended for patients and took them for her own use, and falsely documented in a patient record that a controlled substance had been administered.
WaysToIdentify: In the hospital's automated dispensing cabinet log, one nurse's fentanyl and hydromorphone withdrawals exceed unit peers per shift. Cabinet withdrawal events lack matching administration entries or waste witnesses in the eMAR record. Pain scores and reassessment documentation are missing for patients recorded as receiving the diverted doses. Discrepancy and override counts for that employee ID rise above the nurse's own trailing baseline. Pharmacy inventory reconciliation shows unresolved variances on the units and shifts that nurse worked.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dispense-to-administer gap: on rendering nurse ID x shift, compute the count of controlled-substance cabinet withdrawals minus matched eMAR administrations plus witnessed wastes; fires when the unmatched count exceeds zero repeatedly above the employee's trailing baseline; action postpay audit of associated claims. 2) Peer-shift opioid intensity: on nurse ID x unit x shift, compute milligram morphine equivalents withdrawn per assigned patient; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-unit peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Override rate: on nurse ID x week, compute cabinet override withdrawals divided by total withdrawals; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action site visit by pharmacy compliance.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Amanda Nicole Manatt (registered nurse)
State_County: Iowa - Marshall County (Marshalltown); Iowa - Story County (Ames)
SchemeSummary: An ER registered nurse obtained controlled substances (fentanyl, hydromorphone, morphine) in patients' names at two Iowa hospitals, documented them in medical records as administered to patients, and diverted them for her own use; the false records caused health care benefit programs to be billed for drugs never administered. Restitution of $5,258.20 plus a $5,500 fine and $300 assessment were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: Charge lines for fentanyl, hydromorphone and morphine post without corresponding eMAR administration timestamps in the patient record. One emergency-department nurse ID accounts for cabinet withdrawals per patient above same-unit peers. Billed drug units exceed dispensing-cabinet withdrawal quantities reconciled to the same encounter. Waste documentation lacks a second-witness signature on a large share of that nurse's controlled-substance events. The same nurse appears on diversion-relevant discrepancy logs at two facilities sharing the payer's remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Billed-versus-administered reconciliation: on claim line x encounter, compute billed controlled-substance units minus eMAR-documented administered units; fires when the difference is greater than zero; action prepay edit. 2) Unwitnessed waste rate: on nurse ID x week, compute controlled-substance waste events without a second witness divided by total waste events; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-unit peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Cross-facility diversion linkage: on employee identity x quarter, compute the distinct count of facilities with unmatched withdrawal events for that person; fires when that count exceeds one; action postpay audit of drug charges.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Joel Smithers (physician)
SchemeSummary: Smithers ran a Martinsville medical office where he prescribed Schedule II controlled substances (oxymorphone, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl) to every patient, distributing over 500,000 pills to patients who traveled hundreds of miles; he accepted no insurance and collected over $700,000 in cash and credit card payments. Convicted at retrial of 466 counts of illegal prescribing plus maintaining a drug-involved premises and sentenced to 40 years.
WaysToIdentify: In PDMP data, essentially every patient of one prescriber NPI receives a Schedule II opioid at each visit. Pharmacy claims show beneficiaries travelling hundreds of miles between home ZIP and the prescriber's PECOS practice address. Prescribed morphine milligram equivalents per patient per day exceed same-specialty peer distributions in dispensing records. The practice bills no insurer, so opioid volume appears only in PDMP and ARCOS pharmacy-level dispensing data. Multiple patients of that prescriber share identical drug, dose and quantity combinations on the same dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Universal-opioid prescribing rate: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute distinct patients receiving a Schedule II opioid divided by distinct patients in PDMP records; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement for opioid fills from that prescriber. 2) Patient travel radius: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the median miles between patient residence ZIP and the prescriber practice ZIP on dispensed controlled-substance prescriptions; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit plus referral to the licence board. 3) MME intensity: on prescriber NPI x patient, compute average daily morphine milligram equivalents dispensed; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit on pharmacy claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Benjamin Jamal Washington (scheme leader)
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Los Angeles); Maryland - Prince George's County (Hyattsville)
SchemeSummary: Washington and co-conspirators stole doctors' personal identifiers (NPI, DEA numbers), obtained fake driver's licenses and paid telecom employees for SIM swaps to hijack physicians' phone numbers, then opened fraudulent e-prescribing accounts in the doctors' names and issued at least 5,600 fraudulent prescriptions for oxycodone and promethazine with codeine, which they picked up at pharmacies nationwide and resold for profit.
WaysToIdentify: E-prescribing enrolment records show a new account for an existing prescriber NPI opened from an unrecognised device and address. Pharmacy claims list a prescriber DEA number whose dispensing pattern jumps far above that prescriber's trailing baseline within days. Oxycodone and promethazine-with-codeine fills cluster at pharmacies far from the prescriber's NPPES practice location. Contact phone number on the prescriber account changed shortly before the surge, per credentialing and identity-verification logs. The same beneficiary identifiers appear at many unrelated pharmacy NPIs within a short window in dispensing history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber baseline break: on prescriber DEA/NPI x week, compute controlled-substance prescription counts versus that prescriber's trailing 26-week mean; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile of within-prescriber change; action claim suspension pending prescriber confirmation. 2) Geographic dispersion of fills: on prescriber NPI x week, compute the distinct count of pharmacy NPIs and states dispensing that prescriber's controlled-substance scripts; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 3) Credential-change velocity: on prescriber e-prescribing account, compute days between a change to phone number, address or device fingerprint and the next controlled-substance transmission; fires when that gap is short and volume exceeds baseline; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Jariatu Jalloh (community support worker employed by a District Mental Health Rehabilitation Service provider)
SchemeSummary: While working as a community support worker for a D.C. Mental Health Rehabilitation Service provider, Jalloh allegedly submitted encounter notes for community support services she never provided and overbilled for services she claimed to provide, causing the D.C. Medicaid program to pay over $234,500.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one community-support worker's billed service minutes per date of service exceed twenty-four hours. Encounter notes are submitted with identical narrative text across many beneficiaries and dates in the provider record. Billed units per beneficiary per month exceed the authorised amount on the Medicaid prior-authorisation record. Service dates fall on days the worker was not scheduled per agency timesheets and payroll files. Beneficiaries show no other claims or contact activity on the dates community support was billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible service day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of billed community-support units converted to minutes plus travel time; fires when total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Authorisation overrun: on beneficiary x rendering NPI x month, compute billed units minus units authorised on the prior-authorisation record; fires when the difference is above zero; action claim suspension. 3) Note-template duplication: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the share of encounter notes with text similarity above the calibrated duplicate threshold across distinct beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer workers; action documentation request (ADR) then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Carolyn Bryant-Taylor (former director and corporate officer/owner-operator); Kafomdi "Josephine" Okocha (owner-operator); Samuel Okocha (owner-operator); Shekita Gore a.k.a. Shekita Steele (director of nursing); Elizabeth Ilome (nurse/personal care employee); Eno Utuk (nurse/personal care employee); 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service (Medicaid-enrolled home health agency)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Upcoding; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of a Medicaid-enrolled home health agency billed Virginia Medicaid for private duty nursing, personal care and respite services that were never provided or were billed in excess of what was delivered; Bryant-Taylor and Josephine Okocha paid patients' parents/guardians for blank, pre-signed nursing notes that employees then filled out to support the false claims. Bryant-Taylor is the first of six charged co-conspirators to plead guilty.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, private duty nursing claim hours have no matching EVV clock-in and clock-out visit record. Aggregate billed hours per employee per day across beneficiaries exceed twenty-four hours in payroll-linked claim data. Nursing notes carry guardian signatures dated identically across many blank pre-signed forms in the medical record. Payments from the agency's bank account to beneficiary guardians appear alongside claims for those beneficiaries. Billed personal care and respite hours exceed the plan-of-care hours on the Medicaid service authorisation.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) EVV-to-claim reconciliation: on claim line, compute billed hours minus EVV-verified visit minutes for the same beneficiary, worker and date; fires when billed hours exceed verified minutes; action prepay edit. 2) Worker day impossibility: on rendering staff ID x date of service, compute summed billed hours across all beneficiaries; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Authorisation overrun: on beneficiary x agency NPI x month, compute billed private duty nursing, personal care and respite hours minus authorised plan-of-care hours; fires when positive; action documentation request (ADR) then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Le Thu (doctor)
SchemeSummary: A Boston doctor signed, or had untrained individuals sign, false medical documentation and orders for Medicare beneficiaries' genetic testing, falsely certifying she had consulted with and examined patients and would use results for treatment, when she never communicated with them; third-party laboratories then billed Medicare approximately $35.3 million on these orders, of which Medicare paid about $25.3 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one certifying physician NPI signs genetic-test orders for beneficiaries with whom she has no E/M claim. The signing NPI's ordered-test volume is far above same-specialty peers per week in claim data. Beneficiary residence states on ordered tests span the country while the physician has one PECOS practice location.
