SchemeSummary: Osteopathic physician illegally prescribed opioids from his home, continuing to prescribe to a patient he knew had a substance-abuse disorder without any medical evaluation or testing and after the patient moved out of New England, and directed the patient to a distant pharmacy because local pharmacies refused to fill his prescriptions.
WaysToIdentify: In PDMP records, the prescriber NPI issues Schedule II opioid prescriptions on dates with no corresponding E/M claim for that patient. The patient's residence ZIP in eligibility files lies hundreds of miles from both the prescriber and the dispensing pharmacy. The prescriber's practice location on the CMS-855 and NPPES record is a residential address without a registered clinical site. Multiple local pharmacies have refused fills, visible as reversed or rejected claims in switch and remittance history. No urine drug screen or treatment-plan claim accompanies chronic opioid prescribing for a patient with an opioid use disorder diagnosis.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescription without encounter: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary x fill date, compute days since the last paid E/M claim between them; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Geographic implausibility: on claim line, compute the mileage between beneficiary residence ZIP, prescriber practice ZIP, and dispensing pharmacy ZIP; fires when all three distances exceed the calibrated peer travel percentile; action claim suspension. 3) Rejection-shopping: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the count of distinct pharmacies with rejected or reversed opioid claims preceding a successful fill elsewhere; fires when above the provider's trailing baseline; action postpay audit.

FraudEntity: Aaron Neil Williamsky (owner of more than twenty durable medical equipment supply companies)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Williamsky opened or purchased more than twenty New Jersey DME companies using nominee/straw owners to hide his ownership, submitted fraudulent doctors' orders and claims to Medicare for orthotic braces, and closed companies one-by-one to evade Medicare audits and recoupment. Orders were generated by marketing companies cold-calling elderly beneficiaries offering free braces, with per-patient kickbacks disguised in sham contracts as 'business process outsourcing' and 'marketing expenses,' and proceeds laundered through overseas shell corporations and foreign real estate.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, CMS-855S records for many supplier NPIs share addresses, bank accounts, phones, or authorised officials pointing to one hidden principal. New supplier NPIs begin billing brace L-codes at peer-top-decile volume within weeks of activation, then cease abruptly after an ADR. Ordering NPIs on the brace claims have no prior E/M encounter with the beneficiary in claim history. Beneficiary residence ZIPs lie far outside the supplier's declared service area on the enrolment record. The same beneficiary receives duplicate L-code braces from multiple unrelated supplier NPIs within a rolling month.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Common-principal graph: on bank account and enrolment address, compute the distinct count of supplier NPIs sharing that identifier in PECOS and payment files; fires when the count exceeds one without disclosed common ownership; action site visit before privileges activate. 2) Ramp-then-stop pattern: on supplier NPI x week, compute weekly allowed amount divided by the provider's trailing baseline and the days between activation and peak billing; fires when peak occurs above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Order-encounter gap and duplication: on beneficiary x L-code, compute days since the ordering NPI's last E/M claim and the count of distinct paying supplier NPIs in thirty days; fires when no encounter exists or supplier count exceeds one; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Ritesh Kalra (internist/physician, owner of medical practice)
SchemeSummary: Doctor allegedly ran a pill mill out of his Fair Lawn office, issuing over 31,000 oxycodone prescriptions (plus promethazine with codeine) without legitimate medical purpose, including to an incarcerated patient, and demanding sexual favors from female patients in exchange for prescriptions. He also allegedly billed New Jersey Medicaid for in-person visits and counseling sessions that never occurred, supported by false progress notes with fabricated dates of service and boilerplate exam notes lacking vital signs.
WaysToIdentify: In PDMP data, the prescriber NPI's oxycodone prescription count per month far exceeds same-specialty peers in the state. Prescription and E/M dates of service fall on days when the beneficiary was incarcerated or hospitalised per other claims and correctional rosters. Progress notes returned on ADR lack vital signs and repeat identical boilerplate text across different beneficiaries. Billed E/M and counseling units per rendering NPI per date imply more than twenty-four hours of patient contact. Promethazine with codeine NDC fills accompany oxycodone fills for the same beneficiaries at abnormal frequency.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Contact-hour impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed time-based minutes from billed E/M and counseling CPT codes; fires when the total exceeds twenty-four hours; action prepay edit. 2) Incompatible-location visit: on claim line, compute an exact match of the date of service against inpatient, incarceration, or institutional-stay spans in the beneficiary's other records; fires on any overlap; action claim suspension. 3) Opioid prescribing outlier: on prescriber NPI x month, compute oxycodone prescription counts and total morphine milligram equivalents per patient from PDMP and pharmacy claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Pain Specialists, P.A. (pain clinic with locations in Northfield, Vineland, and Cape May Courthouse, NJ)
State_County: New Jersey - Atlantic County (Northfield); New Jersey - Cumberland County (Vineland); New Jersey - Cape May County (Cape May Courthouse)
PayerName: Medicare; New Jersey Medicaid; private insurance plans
SchemeSummary: The clinic billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers using its owner-physician's NPI for services and procedures requiring his in-person consultation or direct supervision on dates when he was traveling and not present, collecting about $58,365; the related civil settlement covered listing a physician as rendering provider for services actually performed by non-physician practitioners with no physician in the office, contrary to Medicare incident-to and Medicaid own-NPI billing rules. Corporate defendant agreed to $58,365.26 restitution, an $81,711.36 fine and a $240,000 civil settlement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claims carry the owner-physician's rendering NPI on dates his airline or hotel records place him out of state. Rendering-NPI claim volume for supervision-required CPT codes continues unbroken across weeks with zero of that physician's own personal encounters elsewhere. The practice employs enrolled nurse practitioners and physician assistants in PECOS whose own NPIs never appear as rendering on any claim. Daily service minutes summed across all CPT codes under one rendering NPI exceed a feasible workday at that place of service. The same TIN bills incident-to codes at place of service 11 on dates payroll timesheets show no physician on site.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Solo-NPI saturation: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total time-typical minutes implied by billed CPT codes and units; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Absent-supervisor detection: on TIN x date of service, compute the count of supervision-required CPT lines divided by the count of distinct mid-level rendering NPIs billing that day; fires when mid-level count is zero while supervision-required lines are positive; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Enrolled-but-silent staff: on TIN x quarter, compute the count of PECOS-affiliated non-physician practitioner NPIs with zero rendering lines; fires when that count is above zero while incident-to volume is above the provider's trailing baseline; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division and U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Medsinbox Pharmacy LTC LLC, d/b/a Farmacia San Antonio (pharmacy)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; New Jersey Medicaid
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy submitted claims to Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; inventory records showed it had not purchased enough medication from wholesalers to fill the prescriptions billed. Resolved for $625,000 under the False Claims Act with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, NDC-level units billed exceed units the pharmacy purchased per wholesaler pedigree and 340B/ASP acquisition files. Dispensing counts for high-cost NDCs rise sharply above the pharmacy's own trailing baseline without matching invoice records. Beneficiaries on the paid claims have no prior encounter with the prescriber NPI listed on the Part D record. Fill records show refills with no beneficiary copay collection or signature log entry at the point of sale. Prescriber NPIs on the claims are geographically distant from the pharmacy's CMS-855S service area.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Inventory reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler-invoiced acquired units; fires when billed exceeds acquired; action payment suspension. 2) Prescriber-encounter gap: on claim line, compute days between fill date and the most recent Part B encounter between listed prescriber NPI and beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 3) High-cost surge: on pharmacy NPI x week, compute paid dollars for top-decile-cost NDCs divided by the pharmacy's trailing 26-week mean; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-region pharmacy peers; action documentation request (ADR).

FraudEntity: NUWAY Alliance, Inc. (substance use disorder treatment provider)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Unbundling
SchemeSummary: NUWAY Alliance paid Medicaid patients (in the form of compensation, e.g. housing/other value) to seek reimbursable intensive outpatient substance use disorder treatment, violating the Anti-Kickback Statute, and also double-billed Medicaid for the same period of treatment time as distinct billable units, billing for IOP services not actually provided. Resolved by an $18.5 million civil FCA settlement plus a 5-year Corporate Integrity Agreement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, IOP session time units billed for one beneficiary on one date overlap with other billed treatment units for the same clock hours. Facility bills the maximum daily IOP units for nearly all attending beneficiaries, above same-specialty peers. Beneficiary attendance logs and EVV or sign-in records do not support the units submitted. Beneficiaries receive housing or stipends from an affiliated entity that shares ownership on the CMS-855A and state enrollment disclosures. Enrollment surges follow recruitment into agency-controlled sober housing rather than clinical referral.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Same-clock double billing: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping minutes across all billed behavioral health and IOP time units at the same or affiliated TINs; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero; action prepay edit. 2) Max-unit saturation: on facility NPI x month, compute the share of beneficiary-days billed at the maximum allowable IOP units; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Housing-linked referral: on beneficiary x facility NPI, compute the count of beneficiaries whose address matches a property owned by a disclosed affiliate in state ownership filings; fires when that count is above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Michelle Forsythe (licensed mental health counselor)
PayerName: Two unnamed commercial health insurance companies
SchemeSummary: Licensed mental health counselor allegedly used the names and insurance policy information of 22 individuals, without their knowledge, to bill two health insurance companies for counseling sessions she never provided, including for a person she had never treated; the insurers electronically transferred payments to her, and the government seeks forfeiture of $483,511.44 in proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, psychotherapy claims name members with no prior encounter or referral history with this rendering NPI. Summed session minutes under one rendering NPI exceed feasible daily hours across the member panel. Members generate no cost-share payment, no copay collection and no explanation-of-benefits contact response. Members' addresses and other claims cluster outside any plausible catchment for a solo counselor. Claim submission timestamps cluster in bulk batches rather than following individual session dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Hours-per-day impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed time-typical minutes for billed psychotherapy CPT codes and units; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 2) No-relationship members: on rendering NPI x member, compute the count of prior encounters, referrals or authorizations before the first billed session; fires when zero for a share of the panel above the calibrated peer percentile; action documentation request (ADR) to the member. 3) Batch-submission pattern: on rendering NPI x submission timestamp, compute the count of distinct members and distinct dates of service in a single batch; fires when above the provider's trailing baseline; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania)
FraudEntity: American Health Foundation Inc. (nonprofit owner); AHF Management Corporation (managing entity); AHF Montgomery Inc. d/b/a Cheltenham Nursing and Rehabilitation Center (nursing home); AHF Ohio Inc. d/b/a The Sanctuary at Wilmington Place (nursing home); AHF Ohio Inc. d/b/a Samaritan Care Center and Villa (nursing home)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Philadelphia County (Philadelphia); Ohio - Montgomery County (Dayton); Ohio - Medina County (Medina); Ohio - Franklin County (Dublin)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that three AHF-affiliated skilled nursing facilities billed Medicare and Medicaid for skilled nursing services that were grossly substandard - inadequate staffing and infection control, unsanitary/pest-infested buildings, unnecessary antibiotic, antipsychotic, antianxiety and hypnotic medications, and missing resident care plans and assessments - thereby obtaining federal payments for care that failed to meet required standards. The AHF entities collectively agreed to pay $3.61 million and enter a five-year chain-wide quality-of-care Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, per-resident-day RUG/PDPM billing continues while payroll-based journal (PBJ) nurse staffing hours per resident day sit far below case-mix expected levels. State survey files show repeat immediate-jeopardy and infection-control deficiencies at the same CCNs still billing full skilled days. MDS assessments and care plans are missing or submitted late for residents whose SNF claims were paid for those covered days. Part D and facility drug records show antipsychotic, anxiolytic and hypnotic starts without a matching MDS diagnosis of a qualifying condition. Antibiotic dispensing per resident-day runs above the calibrated percentile versus same-size peers with no culture or laboratory claim.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staffing-to-billed-days gap: on facility CCN x quarter, compute PBJ nurse hours per resident day divided by case-mix expected hours using billed RUG/PDPM days; fires when the ratio falls below the calibrated percentile versus same-size peers; action payment suspension pending site visit. 2) Missing assessment on paid days: on beneficiary x SNF stay, compute the count of billed covered days lacking a transmitted MDS assessment or care plan within required timeframes; fires when the count exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 3) Psychotropic saturation: on facility CCN x month, compute the share of residents with paid antipsychotic, anxiolytic or hypnotic NDC fills lacking a qualifying MDS diagnosis; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-size peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Ronald F. Ambrosia (physician)
SchemeSummary: Physician allegedly billed Medicare for application of single-use percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation devices (P-Stim) taped behind patients' ears in an office setting as if they were surgically implanted neurostimulators, using higher-paying surgical codes despite no surgery, anesthesia, or operating room, contrary to CMS guidance.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, implanted-neurostimulator CPT codes appear with place of service 11 rather than a facility setting. No anesthesia claim or facility claim exists for the same beneficiary on the same date of service. No implantable pulse generator or lead HCPCS device code is billed or supplied with the surgical implantation code. The rendering NPI's specialty on PECOS lacks surgical privileges consistent with implantation procedures. Device purchase invoices requested on ADR show single-use auricular electro-acupuncture kits rather than implantable generators.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Implant code in office setting: on claim line, compute the presence of an implanted-neurostimulator CPT with place of service equal to office; fires on exact mismatch with the code's approved settings; action prepay edit. 2) Missing device pairing: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of implantable generator or lead HCPCS lines accompanying the implantation CPT; fires when that count equals zero; action claim suspension with documentation request (ADR). 3) Surgical code without facility or anesthesia: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the share of implantation CPT claims with no matching facility or anesthesia claim; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Mohammed Ahmad (licensed physician/telemedicine contractor); Lifeline Recruiting Inc. (Florida-based DME/telemedicine company); Alicia Hiller (owner of Lifeline Recruiting)
SchemeSummary: Lifeline Recruiting bought leads of Medicare beneficiaries and used call centers to target those eligible for orthotic braces and other DME, then sent pre-completed orders to physician Ahmad, who signed them certifying the DME as medically necessary and falsely indicating he had examined patients and performed tests; the signed orders generated approximately $267,402 in claims to Medicare, of which about $126,643 was paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on L-code brace claims has no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI signs DME orders for beneficiaries spread across many states within one week. The certifying physician's NPPES practice address lies far from beneficiary residence ZIPs on the claims. Orders certify physical testing while no diagnostic or testing CPT was ever billed for those beneficiaries. Multiple unrelated supplier NPIs submit claims citing the same single ordering NPI in a short window.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer geographic dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Certification without testing: on ordering NPI x HCPCS, compute the share of certified brace orders with no diagnostic CPT billed for the beneficiary in the prior 90 days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Sidney L. Glover, Jr. (sole owner of Teaching Excellence, LLC)
PayerName: Medicaid (Ohio Medicaid, via Ohio Department of Disabilities)
SchemeSummary: Glover, sole owner of a home healthcare business serving individuals with disabilities that was funded largely through the Ohio Department of Disabilities/Ohio Medicaid, failed to report more than $1 million in gross business receipts for 2015-2017 on his federal income tax returns and spent some of the unreported earnings on personal expenses, causing about $155,000 in unpaid taxes.
WaysToIdentify: There is no false claim and no adjudication point here, because the billed services were rendered and the loss is unreported income tax. The nearest detection route compares Medicaid remittance totals paid to the provider TIN against gross receipts reported on the owner's federal returns. A second route flags owner-account withdrawals from the provider's bank account paying personal expenses while payroll filings show minimal wages.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Remittance-to-return reconciliation: on provider TIN x tax year, compute the difference between total Medicaid remittances paid and gross receipts reported on filed returns; fires when the difference exceeds zero materially; action referral for postpay audit and IRS data-share.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Daniel R. Hitlan (owner of small businesses)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Hitlan obtained three fraudulent Paycheck Protection Program loans for small businesses he owned by creating fictitious payroll documents and forms; IRS records showed no payroll, withholdings, or return filings for the entities. He spent the proceeds on Rolex watches, a Cadillac Escalade, a vintage Corvette, and real estate.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, since the loss is a federally guaranteed small-business loan. The nearest detection route matches payroll figures on the loan application against IRS Forms 941 and W-2 filings for the same EIN. A second route checks whether the applicant EIN has any wage-withholding deposit history or state unemployment registration before disbursement. A third route counts distinct loan applications sharing one owner SSN, bank account or address.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll attestation mismatch: on applicant EIN, compute the ratio of application-claimed annual payroll to IRS Form 941 reported wages; fires when no 941 exists or the ratio exceeds one materially; action prepay edit on disbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Richard Swenson, M.D. (physician at Accident Care and Treatment Center, Inc.)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleged that Dr. Swenson failed to maintain DEA Forms 222 for certain purchases of Hydrocodone/Acetaminophen (Schedule II) and failed to keep required purchase records for Schedule III and IV controlled substances at his Oklahoma City practice; he paid $130,000 in civil penalties without admitting liability and agreed to permanently stop dispensing and administering controlled substances.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim at issue, because the violation is missing DEA Form 222 and Schedule III-IV purchase records. The nearest detection route reconciles ARCOS distributor reports of Schedule II shipments to the registrant DEA number against the registrant's on-hand order-form inventory. A second route compares controlled-substance purchase volumes to administered or dispensed units documented in the practice's own records. A third route flags registrants purchasing Schedule II product with no corresponding in-office administration billing history.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) ARCOS-to-dispensing reconciliation: on DEA registrant number x quarter, compute ARCOS-reported units received minus units dispensed or administered per practice records and claims; fires when the unexplained gap exceeds zero materially; action site visit by the regulator.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Alexander Frank
SchemeSummary: Frank was indicted on 25 counts of health care fraud for billing Medicare approximately $3.2 million for face-to-face visits with beneficiaries in skilled nursing facilities that he never performed or performed only in part.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the rendering NPI's billed SNF visit codes imply service minutes exceeding 24 hours on a single date of service. The physician bills visits at multiple facility addresses on the same day beyond feasible travel time between them. Billed visit dates fall outside the beneficiary's covered SNF stay dates on the facility's own institutional claims. Visit claims occur on dates after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File. Subsequent-visit code 99310 dominates the provider's mix versus same-specialty peers billing in SNFs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible service day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total typical minutes implied by billed E/M codes; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Facility travel infeasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct facility addresses billed and the minimum driving time between them; fires when required travel plus service minutes exceed 24 hours; action claim suspension with documentation request (ADR). 3) Visit outside covered stay: on beneficiary x date of service, compute whether a matching SNF institutional claim covers that date; fires on exact mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Natasha Allmon (behavioral health counselor)
SchemeSummary: A behavioral health counselor submitted thousands of false claims to Blue Cross Blue Shield for 60-minute psychiatric counseling sessions purportedly provided to her own family members nearly every day of the year, including claims totaling more than 24 hours of treatment in a single day, billing about $1.4 million and collecting roughly $1.1 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, summed timed psychotherapy units for one rendering NPI on one date of service exceed 24 hours. Beneficiary surname and address on the claim match the rendering NPI's NPPES and licence-board address, indicating self-referral to family. Session counts per beneficiary run near-daily for a full calendar year without any treatment-plan or diagnosis change. The rendering NPI bills only a handful of distinct beneficiaries yet ranks top-decile in paid dollars. No facility, pharmacy or other provider claims corroborate the intensity of the billed psychiatric treatment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Hours-per-day impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of timed minutes implied by billed psychotherapy CPT units; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Household concentration: on rendering NPI, compute the share of paid claims for beneficiaries sharing the provider's address or surname per NPPES and enrolment records; fires when that share exceeds zero materially; action claim suspension and postpay audit. 3) Session frequency outlier: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute paid 60-minute session days per 365-day window; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Dr. Naveed Aslam (licensed oncologist); Somerset Hematology and Oncology, P.C. (his medical practice)
State_County: Michigan - Oakland County (West Bloomfield); Michigan - Wayne County (Detroit)
SchemeSummary: An oncologist used his medical practice's access to purchase expensive prescription cancer drugs from his supplier, then diverted and resold more than $17 million of those drugs outside the FDA-regulated supply chain through co-conspirators' company to end customers who could not otherwise obtain them, personally profiting over $2.6 million.
WaysToIdentify: There is no fraudulent claim adjudicated here, since the loss is diversion of legitimately purchased oncology drugs outside the supply chain. The nearest detection route reconciles wholesaler pedigree purchase records by NDC against units administered on the practice's J-code claims. A second route compares the practice's buy-and-bill purchase volume to its distinct chemotherapy patient count in claims. A third route checks whether purchased lot numbers later surface at unlicensed downstream sellers under DSCSA tracing.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Purchase-to-administration reconciliation: on practice TIN x NDC x quarter, compute wholesaler-reported units purchased minus units billed on J-code claim lines; fires when the unexplained surplus exceeds zero materially; action postpay audit and licensure referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Timothy Doyle (operations manager)
State_County: Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); New York - Suffolk County (Selden)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Doyle and managers of a mobile medical diagnostics company paid doctors cash and checks per transcranial doppler (TCD) brain scan ordered, disguising the per-test payments as sham space rental and administrative service agreements at purported fair market value; the medically unnecessary TCD scans generated about $70.6 million in Medicare billings, of which Medicare paid roughly $27.2 million to the TCD company.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, ordering physicians' transcranial doppler volumes track exactly with monthly payments recorded as rent or administrative fees from the testing company. The ordering NPI orders TCD scans for beneficiaries lacking any stroke, TIA or cerebrovascular diagnosis on prior claims. Scan claims cluster on single days at one practice address, indicating mobile sweep days rather than clinical indication. Rented space square footage and hours on the lease cannot support the number of tests billed there. Ordering physicians' TCD ordering rates exceed same-specialty peers by a wide margin at enrolment-linked addresses.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Payment-to-referral correlation: on ordering NPI x month, compute the correlation between vendor payments recorded in Open Payments or vendor ledgers and count of TCD scans ordered; fires when the ordering rate is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers with any vendor payment present; action payment suspension. 2) Indication absent: on claim line, compute whether a cerebrovascular or syncope diagnosis appears on the beneficiary's claims within the prior 12 months; fires when no qualifying diagnosis exists; action prepay edit. 3) Sweep-day density: on testing NPI x service address x date, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries scanned divided by feasible scan minutes; fires when required minutes exceed 24 hours; action claim suspension with documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Faith Newton (operator of Arbor Homecare Services LLC); Winnie Waruru (co-defendant); Arbor Homecare Services LLC
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Newton used Arbor Homecare Services to bill MassHealth at least $100 million for home health nursing visits and home health aide services that never occurred, directing staff to create copy-and-paste falsified nursing notes, paying kickbacks for patient referrals, creating sham employment of patients' family members as aides, pressuring doctors to sign unnecessary Plans of Care, and forging training documents for uncertified aides; she also wrote herself and her husband backdated $2 million checks from the payroll account. Newton was sentenced to 12 years, a $250,000 fine and $99,734,517 restitution; co-defendant Waruru pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed home health visit units have no matching EVV check-in and check-out record for the beneficiary and aide. Aide NPIs or employee IDs on timesheets accumulate visit minutes exceeding 24 hours on a single date of service. Nursing notes submitted on ADR are byte-identical across beneficiaries and dates, indicating copy-and-paste templates. Aides listed on paid visits do not appear in the state home health aide certification registry on the service date. Aide surnames and addresses match the beneficiaries they serve, indicating sham family employment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) EVV-to-claim reconciliation: on claim line, compute billed visit minutes minus matched EVV verified minutes for the same beneficiary, aide and date; fires when unmatched minutes exceed zero; action prepay edit. 2) Caregiver hour impossibility: on aide ID x date of service, compute total billed visit minutes across all beneficiaries; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Registry mismatch: on aide ID x date of service, compute whether an active state aide certification exists on that date; fires on exact registry mismatch; action payment suspension and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Eric Karlewicz a/k/a 'Anthony Mazza' (operator of marketing company Empire Pain Center Holdings LLC); Nicco Romanowski (operator of Empire Pain Center Holdings LLC); Empire Pain Center Holdings LLC (marketing company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Operators of a New Jersey marketing company cold-called Medicare and TRICARE beneficiaries to pressure them into accepting back, shoulder and knee braces, then paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies which paid doctors to sign DME prescriptions without medical necessity and often without speaking to patients; the orders were sold to DME suppliers nationwide who billed Medicare and TRICARE over $127 million and kicked back a share (over $63 million) to Empire. Both defendants were ordered to pay $127.6 million restitution jointly, plus forfeitures of over $63 million (Karlewicz) and over $5.5 million (Romanowski), and Karlewicz/Empire consented to a $63.8 million False Claims Act judgment.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on brace L-codes has no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with the beneficiary. One telemedicine ordering NPI writes DME orders for beneficiaries across dozens of states within a single week. The same beneficiary receives back, knee and shoulder braces from several unrelated supplier NPIs within thirty days. Supplier NPIs sharing one marketing vendor show synchronized volume ramps just after PECOS enrolment or ownership change. Payment flows show suppliers remitting per-order fees to a common marketing TIN and bank account.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the last E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Shared-orderer supplier graph: on ordering NPI, compute the graph degree of distinct billing supplier NPIs and distinct beneficiary states per week; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Multi-brace saturation: on beneficiary x 30 days, compute the count of distinct brace L-codes and distinct supplier NPIs paid; fires when distinct suppliers exceed one without documented replacement reason; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Paul Richard Randall; Kyrollos Mekail; Patricia Anderson; Monte Vista Pharmacy
State_County: California - Orange County (Orange); California - Riverside County (Moreno Valley); California - Los Angeles County (West Hills)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants exploited Medi-Cal's temporary suspension of prior-authorization requirements to bill, through Monte Vista Pharmacy, more than $269 million (paid over $178 million) from May 2022 to April 2023 for 19 high-reimbursement, non-contracted generic drugs (including an over-the-counter vitamin, Folite) that were medically unnecessary and often never dispensed to patients; prescriptions were procured by kickbacks and proceeds were laundered through a third party to pay co-schemer Anderson. Randall charged by complaint; Anderson charged by information; Mekail pleaded guilty in August 2024 and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the pharmacy NPI's paid dollars concentrate in a handful of high-reimbursement non-contracted generic NDCs far above peer mix. Claim volume for those NDCs surges immediately after the prior-authorisation suspension effective date in the plan rule file. Dispensed NDC quantities exceed the pharmacy's wholesaler acquisition units in DSCSA pedigree data for the same period. Prescribing NPIs on the fills show no prior encounter claims with those beneficiaries. Beneficiaries have no refill continuity or matching diagnosis for an over-the-counter vitamin billed at high cost.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Acquisition-to-dispensing reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x month, compute units billed minus units purchased per wholesaler pedigree records; fires when billed units exceed purchased units; action payment suspension. 2) Post-policy surge on narrow NDC set: on pharmacy NPI x week, compute the share of paid dollars from the top five NDCs versus the provider's trailing baseline; fires when the share rises above the trailing baseline and above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Prescriber-encounter gap: on claim line, compute days between fill date and last encounter claim between the prescribing NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Marielys Feliciano Rodriguez (owner of shell construction company)
State_County: Florida - Orange County (Orlando); various Florida counties
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Rodriguez set up a shell construction company, bought a minimal workers' compensation policy in its name, and 'rented' certificates of insurance to dozens of subcontractor work crews, falsely representing to contractors that the crews were her employees. Contractors issued payroll checks to the shell company (about $13 million cashed); she cashed them and paid crews in cash minus a ~6% fee, with no wages reported and over $3 million in payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare, income tax) unpaid, and defrauding the workers' comp carrier of premium.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, because the loss is unpaid payroll tax and workers' compensation premium. The nearest detection route compares certificate-of-insurance payroll exposure filed with the carrier against check volume deposited to the policyholder's bank account. A second route matches state unemployment wage filings for the EIN against gross contractor payments made to that EIN. A third route flags one policy's certificates issued to dozens of unrelated contractors within a year.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Premium-to-cashflow mismatch: on policy EIN x year, compute deposited contractor payments divided by payroll exposure declared on the workers' compensation policy; fires when the ratio exceeds one materially; action carrier premium audit and state referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Michael Brier (owner); Recovery Connections Centers of America, Inc. (RCCA)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; other private health insurers
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Brier and his addiction-treatment chain RCCA billed Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for 45-minute counseling sessions when patients actually received sessions of 5-15 minutes or none at all, with staff directed to move patients through quickly; they also submitted a Medicare enrollment application concealing Brier's role and his prior federal tax conviction. Brier got 98 months and $3,515,100 restitution plus roughly $1 million forfeiture; RCCA received probation and the same $3,515,100 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the facility's mix is dominated by the 45-minute psychotherapy CPT with near-absent shorter-duration codes versus same-specialty peers. Summed session minutes per counselor per date of service exceed the counselor's feasible working hours. Beneficiary throughput per rendering NPI per day exceeds what 45-minute sessions physically allow in 24 hours. The CMS-855B enrolment omits an owner or managing employee identified in state corporate registry and bank signatory records. Disclosed ownership fields conflict with an existing federal conviction record checked against OIG LEIE and court data at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Session minutes impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total minutes implied by billed timed counseling CPT units; fires when the sum exceeds available hours in 24; action prepay edit. 2) Duration code skew: on provider NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of 45-minute session claims to all timed counseling claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR) then postpay audit. 3) Undisclosed principal: on enrolling TIN, compute the count of officers, signatories or registry principals absent from CMS-855 ownership and managing-employee fields; fires when the count exceeds zero; action enrolment site visit and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Armen Muradyan (owner/operator of Genex Laboratories); Genex Laboratories
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Muradyan secretly owned and controlled Genex Laboratories, a blood testing lab, using a paid nominee to pose as owner and hold bank accounts that received more than $23 million in Medicare reimbursements; he gave the nominee false financial summaries so Genex income went unreported, omitted Genex activity from his own returns (tax loss over $8.5 million federal and $2.7 million California), and obtained nearly $100,000 in COVID EIDL funds via an application for a fictitious company with fabricated employees and income.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855B owner listed has no verifiable industry history and appears as sole signatory on the receiving bank account. Remittance payments for one laboratory NPI route to a bank account whose signatory differs from the disclosed owner in enrolment records. The nominal owner appears as owner on multiple unrelated enrolments within a short window across payers. Laboratory test volume ramps from zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of PECOS approval. Ordering NPIs on the lab's claims are geographically distant from the lab's enrolled service address.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Nominee-owner detection: on enrolling NPI, compute the count of distinct provider enrolments sharing the same disclosed owner SSN, address or phone in PECOS; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action enrolment site visit. 2) Payee-owner mismatch: on bank account, compute the count of distinct provider NPIs receiving remittances and whether the account signatory matches the CMS-855 disclosed owner; fires on exact mismatch; action payment suspension. 3) Post-enrolment volume ramp: on provider NPI x month, compute paid dollars versus the provider's trailing baseline since enrolment; fires when growth exceeds the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty new enrollees; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Hassan Abdellatif, aka 'Eric' (owner/operator of El Milagro Mini Market, Supermercado El Grande, Star Mini Market, In & Out Grocery, and Harding Grocery); eight unnamed co-defendant store owners/workers
PayerName: USDA Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Convenience-store owner and eight co-defendants let customers use federally funded WIC checks to pay for items not eligible under the program, often at inflated prices, then redeemed the vouchers for cash reimbursement; ten stores redeemed over $19 million in WIC checks over eight years, with more than $6.5 million at two of Abdellatif's stores alone. He was also convicted of willfully failing to file corporate tax returns.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no clinical adjudication, because the instrument is a WIC food voucher redeemed by a retail vendor. The nearest detection route compares each vendor's redeemed voucher dollars against wholesale purchase invoices for WIC-eligible foods stocked. A second route compares average redemption per voucher across vendors of the same size and peer group. A third route matches redemption spikes to store inventory capacity observed at authorization site visits.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Redemption-to-inventory ratio: on vendor ID x quarter, compute redeemed WIC dollars divided by documented wholesale purchases of WIC-eligible items; fires when the ratio exceeds one or is above the calibrated percentile versus peer vendors; action redemption hold and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Raju Sharma (owner of Pharmagears, LLC and RR Medco, LLC); Pharmagears, LLC; RR Medco, LLC
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sharma contracted with telemarketing companies that generated DME orders (back and knee braces) by targeting Medicare beneficiaries, paying the marketers on a per-lead/per-order basis while nominally contracting for a flat fee; he then billed Medicare through Pharmagears, RR Medco and related companies for medically unnecessary equipment that beneficiaries did not want or could not use, ordered by practitioners who never examined them or through unauthorized use of practitioners' NPIs, billing about $29.6 million and collecting about $15.8 million used to buy Ferraris, a Mercedes and Rolex watches.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, ordering NPIs on brace L-codes have no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with the beneficiaries. Ordering NPIs appear on claims from supplier NPIs in states where those practitioners have never billed any other service. The same practitioner NPI is used across suppliers under common ownership per CMS-855S disclosure fields. Beneficiaries receive multiple brace L-codes within thirty days from suppliers sharing one bank account. Supplier marketing payments are structured as flat fees but scale linearly with monthly order counts in ledgers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days since the last E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) NPI misuse detection: on ordering NPI x supplier NPI, compute the count of ordered claims where the ordering NPI has no other billing activity in that beneficiary's state; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension with documentation request (ADR). 3) Common-ownership supplier cluster: on bank account or TIN, compute the count of distinct supplier NPIs paid and their shared ordering-NPI overlap; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Raju Sharma (owner of Pharmagears, LLC and RR Medco, LLC); Pharmagears, LLC; RR Medco, LLC
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Sharma allegedly contracted with telemarketing companies that generated DME orders (back and knee braces) by targeting Medicare beneficiaries, paying the marketers per lead/order rather than the flat fee stated in contracts, then billed Medicare approximately $29.6 million (paid ~$15.8 million) for medically unnecessary DME ordered by practitioners who never examined the beneficiaries or through unauthorized use of practitioners' NPIs; proceeds bought two Ferraris, a Mercedes-Benz and Rolex watches, which were subject to seizure warrants.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, brace L-code claims carry ordering NPIs with no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with the beneficiary. Marketing contracts obtained on ADR show flat fees while payment ledgers scale with order counts month over month. Practitioner NPIs used on orders show no telehealth or office claim for those beneficiaries on any date. Beneficiary residence ZIPs fall far outside the supplier's service area declared on the CMS-855S. Several supplier NPIs sharing one owner submit claims citing the same small pool of ordering NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the date of service and the most recent encounter claim linking that ordering NPI to the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer concentration: on supplier NPI x month, compute the share of paid brace claims attributable to the top three ordering NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Service-area breach: on claim line, compute the distance between the beneficiary residence ZIP and the supplier's enrolled service area on CMS-855S; fires when outside the declared area; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Kelley Oliver-Hollis (owner, Serenitycare LLC)
PayerName: Medicaid (Pennsylvania Home and Community-Based Services Waiver Program); Social Security Administration
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Oliver-Hollis, an enrolled Medicaid provider operating group homes for intellectually disabled adults under Pennsylvania's HCBS Waiver Program, submitted weekly claims for HCBS benefits that falsely represented the homes were staffed with adequate workers as the program required, while the homes were understaffed and fell into unsanitary, unsafe disrepair. She also acknowledged 39 additional counts including false statements on health care matters, money laundering, and misuse of Social Security benefits as a representative payee.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, weekly HCBS residential claims attest required staffing ratios while payroll and timesheet records show fewer staff hours than residents billed. EVV or shift records show no staff clock-ins covering hours billed as staffed residential support. State licensing inspection files record unsanitary or unsafe conditions at addresses still billing full waiver units. The same staff member's hours across group home addresses exceed 24 hours on a single date. The representative-payee provider receives beneficiary Social Security funds while also billing waiver units for the same residents.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staffing-ratio attestation test: on group home site x week, compute total paid staff hours from payroll or EVV divided by billed resident-days times the waiver-required ratio; fires when the computed ratio falls below the program-required minimum; action payment suspension. 2) Staff hour impossibility: on staff ID x date of service, compute total hours claimed across all sites; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Licensing-deficiency crosswalk: on provider NPI x site address, compute the count of open state health or safety citations during the billed service week; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension with site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio; U.S. District Court, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Sharon Romaine Ward (owner of Halo Home Healthcare); Halo Home Healthcare
State_County: Ohio - Butler County (West Chester); Ohio - Hamilton County (Cincinnati)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Ohio Department of Medicaid); Department of Veterans Affairs health care programs
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Ward founded Halo Home Healthcare in 2015 while excluded from federal health care programs due to a prior felony prescription-forgery conviction, concealing her ownership, and the company submitted at least 92,770 Medicaid claims totaling $8,556,776.58 for home health services not performed - including continuing to bill Medicaid while a patient was hospitalized - and employed over 50 workers with disqualifying criminal histories; she also gave false information to her business tax preparer causing false returns. Restitution figures span Ohio Medicaid ($8,403,299.24), the VA, and the IRS ($81,617).
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, cross-match every CMS-855A owner, officer and managing-employee SSN against the OIG LEIE and state exclusion list. Compare the disclosed owners in PECOS against state corporate filings to expose a concealed principal behind a nominee. At adjudication, overlap home health visit dates against the beneficiary's inpatient claims for the same dates of service. Compare billed visit units to EVV check-in and check-out records for the same aide, date and beneficiary. Screen every employee NPI or payroll record against the state criminal-background-check registry required for direct-care staff.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Excluded-principal match: on provider NPI x disclosed owner SSN, compute exact-match count against OIG LEIE and state exclusion files at CMS-855 screening and revalidation; fires when any exact registry match exists; action claim suspension. 2) Inpatient overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of home health visit lines whose service date falls inside a paid inpatient admission span; fires when that count exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 3) EVV-to-claim gap: on rendering aide NPI x date of service, compute billed units minus EVV-verified visit minutes divided by 15; fires when billed units exceed EVV minutes; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Kansas
FraudEntity: Daniel Reif, Inc., d/b/a The Medicine Shoppe (retail pharmacy); Daniel Reif (owner and Pharmacist-in-Charge)
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy allegedly failed to maintain complete and accurate records and inventories of controlled substances and failed to keep certification records for retail sales required by the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act, in violation of the civil recordkeeping provisions of the Controlled Substances Act; it agreed to pay $200,000 to resolve the allegations.
WaysToIdentify: There is no claim and no adjudication point here, since the violation is controlled-substance recordkeeping rather than billing. The nearest detection route is DEA inspection comparing ARCOS purchase data against the pharmacy's biennial inventory and dispensing logs. A second route is auditing the electronic pseudoephedrine logbook required by the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act for missing purchaser certifications.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy DEA number x NDC x quarter, compute ARCOS-reported units received minus units dispensed in the pharmacy dispensing file; fires when the unexplained gap exceeds the pharmacy's trailing baseline; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Adnan Arshad, aka 'Eddie' (owner of MTK Taxi LLC and part owner of All-Star Taxi LLC); five unnamed co-conspirators who previously pleaded guilty
State_County: New York - Suffolk County (Montauk, Ronkonkoma, Mount Sinai, Long Island); New York - New York City
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Arshad, owner/part-owner of Long Island ambulette/taxi companies, paid kickbacks to Medicaid beneficiaries to order medical transportation (largely to methadone/addiction treatment centers) from his companies, then billed Medicaid roughly $20 million for rides that generally were never provided - including claims for at least two deceased beneficiaries and for hospitalized or incarcerated individuals. He also inflated claims by directing beneficiaries to request rides to New York City clinics and list false addresses to obtain higher long-distance reimbursement rates (over $16 million billed for trips to three NYC treatment centers), and laundered proceeds into homes, luxury cars, and more transport vehicles; five co-conspirators also pleaded guilty.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, match every trip date of service against the Death Master File date of death for the beneficiary. Compare trip dates against the beneficiary's inpatient and incarceration eligibility spans in the Medicaid eligibility file. Check whether the beneficiary has any same-day treatment claim from the destination clinic NPI on the trip date. Compare the pickup address on the claim to the address of record in the eligibility file to detect mileage inflation. Count distinct beneficiaries whose trips all originate from one carrier and terminate at the same three clinic NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Decedent and custody trips: on claim line, compute whether the date of service falls after the Death Master File date of death or inside an inpatient or incarceration eligibility span; fires when either condition is true; action prepay edit. 2) Destination-encounter match: on beneficiary x trip date, compute the count of treatment claims from the destination provider NPI within the trip date; fires when that count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Address-mileage mismatch: on claim line, compute the mileage implied by the eligibility-file residence ZIP minus billed loaded mileage; fires when billed mileage exceeds the geocoded distance; action prepay edit and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Andrew Do (owner and operator of three mail-order pharmacies); Family Care Investments d/b/a Value Pharmacy
SchemeSummary: Do, who owned three mail-order pharmacies in Orange County, California, allegedly paid kickbacks to induce referrals of prescriptions for compounded topical creams, filled those prescriptions, and billed Medicare for reimbursement; the resulting claims were alleged to be false under the False Claims Act. He agreed to pay $600,000 based on inability to pay, with the qui tam relator receiving up to $100,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute the share of the pharmacy's Part D dollars concentrated in compounded topical cream NDCs and high-cost bulk ingredient codes. Measure the road distance between beneficiary residence ZIP in eligibility data and the mail-order pharmacy's CMS-855S practice location. Check whether prescribing NPIs on those creams have any prior evaluation-and-management claim with the same beneficiary. Count how many prescribers concentrate a majority of their compound scripts in this one pharmacy chain's NPIs. Compare marketing or consulting payments disclosed in Open Payments against prescriber referral volume into the pharmacy.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Compound concentration: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the ratio of compounded topical cream NDC paid dollars to total paid dollars; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Prescriber-pharmacy exclusivity: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the share of compound claims routed to a single pharmacy TIN; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Orderer-encounter gap: on claim line x prescriber NPI, compute days since the last E/M claim between prescriber and beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Raheel Naviwala (owner of marketing companies and a DME supply company)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Naviwala bought lists of Medicare beneficiaries and used telemarketers to pitch orthotic braces, pre-filling prescriptions for the highest-paying braces; he paid telemedicine doctors to sign the prescriptions without speaking to patients, then sold the signed orders to DME suppliers (disguised as marketing/consulting fees via sham contracts and invoices) that billed Medicare, TRICARE and other insurers. He also owned a DME supplier that billed Medicare for up to nine braces per patient and hid his ownership behind nominee owners; insurers paid at least ~$100 million tied to his companies and he pocketed over $10 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count distinct L-code braces billed to one beneficiary across all supplier NPIs within a rolling period. Check whether the ordering telemedicine NPI has any prior evaluation-and-management or telehealth encounter claim with that beneficiary. Count distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs served by one ordering NPI in a week. Compare CMS-855S disclosed owners across suppliers for shared addresses, bank accounts and nominee officers indicating common control. Compare supplier volume after a PECOS ownership change against its own trailing baseline.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Brace saturation: on beneficiary x rolling 90 days, compute the count of distinct orthotic L-codes and distinct supplier NPIs paid; fires when multiple braces are paid without a documented replacement reason; action prepay edit. 2) Telehealth orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS claims plus the count with no prior E/M; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Common-control cluster: on bank account and remittance address across CMS-855S records, compute the graph degree of linked supplier NPIs; fires when degree exceeds one undisclosed link; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Daniel Dadoun (owner of several New Jersey businesses)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Dadoun submitted false PPP loan applications for his New Jersey businesses to obtain over $3.2 million, then filed fraudulent loan forgiveness applications misrepresenting payroll expenses and employee counts, supported by falsified tax documents and altered bank statements; he pleaded guilty to bank fraud and money laundering.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, because the loss is a forgiven SBA loan rather than a paid claim. The nearest detection route is matching payroll figures on the loan application against IRS Forms 941 and state wage filings for the same quarters. A second route is comparing bank statements submitted with forgiveness applications against lender-held originals for altered balances.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll attestation match: on borrower EIN x quarter, compute claimed payroll dollars on the loan and forgiveness applications minus IRS Form 941 reported wages; fires when the difference exceeds the filed amount; action postpay audit by the lender and SBA.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Daniel Dadoun (owner of several New Jersey businesses)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Dadoun submitted false PPP loan applications for his New Jersey businesses, obtaining over $3.2 million, then filed fraudulent loan forgiveness applications misrepresenting payroll expenses and employee counts, supported by falsified tax documents and altered bank statements; he pleaded guilty to bank fraud and money laundering and was ordered to pay $3,239,773 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, since the funds were SBA-guaranteed loan proceeds rather than payer reimbursements. The nearest detection route is cross-matching application payroll and headcount against IRS Form 941 and state unemployment insurance wage records. A further route is checking whether multiple loans were issued to related entities sharing one owner, address or bank account.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Related-borrower cluster: on bank account and owner SSN across loan applications, compute the count of distinct borrower EINs sharing the identifier; fires when the count exceeds one undisclosed affiliate; action postpay audit before forgiveness.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Hawaii
FraudEntity: Stephen Timothy Wells (owner of Oahu Spine and Rehab)
State_County: Hawaii - Honolulu County (Oahu: Kailua and Aiea)
SchemeSummary: Wells, owner of a physical therapy clinic with Kailua and Aiea locations, used unqualified personnel (massage therapists, athletic trainers, personal trainers, and one person with no license or certification) to deliver physical therapy, then billed TRICARE and Medicare as though licensed practitioners had provided the services; he was ordered to pay $392,157.20 in restitution and 9 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, verify each rendering NPI on therapy claims against the state physical therapy licence board file for an active licence. At adjudication, compare the rendering NPI on 97110 and 97140 lines against the clinic's roster of licensed therapists on file. Compute total timed therapy units billed per rendering NPI per day and convert to hours to test physical possibility. Check whether the same licensed therapist NPI appears as renderer at two clinic locations during overlapping treatment minutes. Compare the clinic's paid therapy minutes to its licensed full-time-equivalent staffing reported at enrolment.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence verification: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute whether the NPPES taxonomy and state licence board file show an active therapy licence covering that date; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Impossible therapy day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of timed CPT units multiplied by 15 minutes; fires when total exceeds a physically possible workday; action claim suspension. 3) Capacity ratio: on provider NPI x week, compute paid therapy minutes divided by licensed therapist full-time-equivalents on the enrolment roster; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Nosson Sklar, a/k/a "Nathan Sklar" (owner and CEO of physical rehabilitation company)
PayerName: Three unnamed health benefit programs (federal health care programs referenced by HHS-OIG)
SchemeSummary: Sklar, owner/CEO of a company operating physical rehabilitation facilities around New York City, submitted or caused submission of more than $20 million in claims to three health benefit programs listing a physician (Victim-1) as the rendering provider, using forged/unauthorized physician signatures, though that doctor did not provide the services or work with the company; roughly $12.4 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare the rendering physician NPI on claims against that physician's own reassignment records in PECOS for the billing TIN. Contact-verify billed rendering NPIs against NPPES practice address and the physician's other claim footprint in a different market. Compute the share of one clinic group's total claim dollars attributed to a single rendering NPI. Compute daily service counts and units under that rendering NPI to test physical possibility of one physician's workday. Check whether the physician's signature-bearing documentation matches a signature log or attestation on file at credentialing.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Reassignment mismatch: on claim line, compute whether an active CMS-855R reassignment links the rendering NPI to the billing TIN on the date of service; fires on any exact PECOS mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Single-renderer concentration: on billing TIN x month, compute the share of paid dollars carried by the top rendering NPI plus that NPI's daily encounter count; fires when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension. 3) Physician workday: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed service time implied by billed CPT codes; fires when it exceeds 24 hours or a physically possible day; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: John Drivas (owner and operator of Red's Sandwich Shop, Red's Kitchen and Tavern, and Red's Seabrook)
State_County: Massachusetts - Salem; Massachusetts - Peabody; New Hampshire - Seabrook
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Restaurant owner paid $1,496,417 in under-the-table wages to employees without reporting them or paying over federal employment taxes (causing over $439,000 in IRS losses), and collected Massachusetts state and local meals taxes from customers but intentionally omitted $1,596,775 of those taxes from monthly reports and payments to the Massachusetts Department of Revenue.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, because the loss is unremitted employment and meals taxes. The nearest detection route is comparing IRS Form 941 reported wages against point-of-sale gross receipts and bank cash deposits for the same period. A second route is matching state meals tax collected on register data against monthly returns filed with the state revenue department.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Receipts-to-return gap: on business EIN x month, compute point-of-sale taxable sales multiplied by the meals tax rate minus tax remitted on the filed return; fires when the shortfall exceeds zero; action state revenue audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Patrick Boyd (co-owner, Safe Chain Solutions); Charles Boyd (co-owner, Safe Chain Solutions); Adam Brosius (co-owner/CEO, pleaded guilty); Safe Chain Solutions (pharmaceutical wholesaler); Peter Khaim (owner, Boulevard 9229 - supplier); Gentek (supplier)
State_County: Maryland - Talbot County (Easton); Florida - Broward County (Fort Lauderdale) and South Florida; nationwide distribution
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: The Boyd brothers, through their wholesale company Safe Chain Solutions, bought more than $92 million in black-market HIV medications from at least five suppliers (over $35 million from Boulevard 9229 and over $42 million from Gentek) that had been acquired from patients on the street through 'buyback' schemes, had prescription labels stripped and were repackaged in scavenged cardboard boxes; they resold the misbranded, sometimes tampered or wrong-drug bottles to thousands of pharmacies nationwide using falsified pedigree paperwork to make them appear sourced from legitimate distributors, and failed to report pharmacy complaints to the FDA. Two owners were convicted at trial; co-owner Adam Brosius previously pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, match the dispensed NDC and serial number against DSCSA transaction history to confirm an unbroken pedigree from the labeler. Check whether the upstream wholesaler on the pedigree holds an active state wholesale distributor licence for the shipping period. Compare a pharmacy's high-cost HIV NDC acquisition volumes against its dispensing claim volume for the same NDCs. Detect beneficiaries with repeated early refills of high-value antiretrovirals that never appear in adherence or lab monitoring claims. Count complaint reports of wrong-drug or tampered bottles tied to one wholesaler across pharmacy NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Pedigree break: on claim line x NDC serial number, compute whether a continuous DSCSA transaction chain exists back to the labeler; fires on any missing or unlicensed upstream node; action prepay edit. 2) Buy-back refill pattern: on beneficiary x antiretroviral NDC, compute days between fills divided by days supply; fires when refills occur before the prior supply is exhausted repeatedly; action claim suspension and postpay audit. 3) Supply-dispense imbalance: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute dispensed units minus units acquired from licensed distributors per pedigree data; fires when dispensed exceeds documented acquisitions; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Kafomdi "Josephine" Okocha (co-owner, 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service); Samuel Okocha (co-owner); Carolyn Bryant-Taylor (co-owner/operator); Shekita Gore a.k.a. Shekita Steele (director of nursing); Elizabeth Ilome (nurse/personal care employee); Eno Utuk (nurse/personal care employee); 1st Adult N Pediatric Healthcare Service (Medicaid-enrolled home health agency)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Upcoding; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Owners and staff of a Medicaid-enrolled home health agency providing private duty nursing, personal care and respite care billed Virginia Medicaid for nursing services never provided or in excess of what was provided, supporting the claims with falsified records; owners paid parents/guardians of patients for blank, pre-signed nursing notes that were then filled out to document the fraudulent billing. Two owners pled guilty on this date, a third pled guilty the prior week, and three other charged defendants have pending charges; the $10 million figure is the total attributed to the scheme.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare billed private duty nursing units against EVV check-in and check-out records for the same nurse, beneficiary and date. Compute nursing hours billed per rendering NPI per day to test physical possibility across concurrent beneficiaries. Compare billed hours against the hours authorised on the prior-authorisation and plan-of-care record for that beneficiary. Verify each rendering nurse NPI against the state nursing board licence file for an active licence on the service date. Detect nursing notes with identical signature dates or template text across different beneficiaries in ADR-returned documentation.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) EVV shortfall: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute billed nursing units minus EVV-verified minutes divided by the unit length; fires when billed exceeds verified; action prepay edit. 2) Authorisation overage: on beneficiary x authorisation period, compute paid hours minus prior-authorised hours; fires when paid exceeds authorised; action claim suspension. 3) Impossible caregiver day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed billed hours across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or overlapping visit minutes occur; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Brandon Nowak (officer/operator, Alternative Integrative Medicine, LLC d/b/a AIM Health); Jason Simmons (officer/operator, Alternative Integrative Medicine, LLC d/b/a AIM Health); Alternative Integrative Medicine, LLC d/b/a AIM Health
PayerName: Medicare; Medicare Advantage; Medicaid Managed Care; four unnamed private insurers
SchemeSummary: Owners of a Warwick pain management clinic allegedly told patients massage therapy was insured and then billed Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid Managed Care and four private insurers for covered services never provided - acupuncture, physical therapy, and evaluation and management office visits - as well as infrared therapy, hot/cold therapy, therapeutic activity and self-care training that the clinic had no qualified providers to deliver.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare CPT codes billed against the licensed disciplines on the clinic's credentialing roster and rendering NPI taxonomies. Check whether acupuncture and therapy lines carry a rendering NPI with the corresponding state licence in the board file. Compute the ratio of therapy and E/M lines billed per beneficiary visit day against same-specialty peers. Detect identical daily CPT bundles repeated for every beneficiary regardless of diagnosis in remittance history. Compare beneficiary-reported service via post-payment questionnaires against E/M visits with no supporting chart entry.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Taxonomy-service mismatch: on claim line, compute whether the rendering NPI taxonomy and state licence permit the billed CPT on that date; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Cloned visit bundle: on provider NPI x beneficiary x date, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries receiving the identical CPT combination that day divided by total beneficiaries seen; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Unstaffed modality volume: on provider NPI x month, compute paid units of therapy codes with no correspondingly licensed staff on the credentialing roster; fires when units exceed zero; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Dr. Kamal Kabakibou (pain-management physician); Kamal Kabakibou, M.D., P.C. d/b/a The Center for Pain Management (medical practice)
State_County: Georgia - Atlanta (Fulton County); Georgia - Blue Ridge (Fannin County)
