PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; U.S. Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs
SchemeSummary: The government alleged the doctor's pain clinics used an in-house lab to perform medically unnecessary and duplicative urine drug tests billed to Medicare, TRICARE and the Department of Labor, and that he pre-signed Schedule II opioid prescriptions left for nurse practitioners to dispense while he was out of the country. The practice and doctor jointly pay $3.5 million, with 5 years of DEA monitoring reports and a 3-year HHS-OIG integrity agreement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute the count of definitive urine drug test panels per beneficiary per month billed by an in-house lab under the same TIN. Compare presumptive and definitive test pairs on the same specimen date for duplicative billing. Compute the share of the clinic's lab claims referred by ordering NPIs within its own ownership group per PECOS. Compare Schedule II prescription dispensing dates against the prescriber's documented presence, using absence of any same-day E/M claim. Check whether nurse practitioners issued opioid prescriptions under the physician's DEA number outside supervision records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) UDT frequency: on beneficiary x ordering NPI x month, compute the count of definitive drug test HCPCS units and analyte counts; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Duplicative confirmation: on specimen date x beneficiary, compute the count of presumptive plus definitive tests billed for the same analytes; fires when confirmation occurs without a discordant presumptive result; action prepay edit. 3) Prescriber-presence gap: on prescribing NPI x date of service, compute the count of Schedule II prescriptions attributed on days with zero claims or encounters by that prescriber; fires when the count exceeds zero; action documentation request (ADR) and postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Office of Foreign Litigation (in coordination with the Public Ministry of Panama)
FraudEntity: Dr. Rolando Chin (surgeon residing in Panama); nearly 40 other Panamanian defendants including doctors, pharmacies, corporations and a hospital
PayerName: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs - Foreign Medical Program
SchemeSummary: Panamanian doctors and pharmacies submitted false and inflated claims to the VA's Foreign Medical Program, which pays for care of U.S. veterans living abroad, including claims for services never rendered and medicines never received as well as deceptive billing for services performed; Dr. Chin pleaded guilty in Panama to fraud charges and entered a restitution agreement with the United States, and VA's suspension of the roughly 40 defendants is projected to save almost $25 million in FY2025 FMP expenditures.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication of Foreign Medical Program claims, verify the billing provider's foreign licence and registration against the host country regulator file. Compare submitted invoices for the same veteran across providers for duplicate dates of service and identical line items. Compute per-veteran annual paid dollars and encounter counts against the FMP peer distribution in that country. Compare dispensed medication quantities to the veteran's documented diagnoses and prior FMP pharmacy history. Detect clusters of unrelated provider claims sharing one bank account or remittance address in the payment file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Foreign licence verification: on billing provider ID, compute whether an active host-country licence and registration exist for each date of service; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 2) Veteran utilisation outlier: on veteran x year, compute paid FMP dollars and distinct encounter count; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus in-country peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Shared payee cluster: on bank account in the FMP payment file, compute the count of distinct provider IDs receiving deposits; fires when the count exceeds one undisclosed affiliate; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Matthew Brown (owner/operator of Elite Payroll and other businesses); Elite Payroll
State_County: Florida - Martin County; Florida - St. Lucie County; Florida - Palm Beach County
SchemeSummary: Brown's payroll services company collected the full amount of Social Security, Medicare and federal income taxes withheld from client companies' employees' wages, then filed false employment tax returns with the IRS that substantially underreported the liabilities, paying only the underreported amount and pocketing the difference (e.g., collecting $219,000 for one 2021 quarter but reporting and paying only about $32,000). More than $20 million in withheld taxes was diverted to buy real estate, a yacht, an aircraft and luxury cars including 27 Ferraris.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, because the loss is withheld employment taxes diverted by a payroll agent. The nearest detection route is reconciling client employees' Forms W-2 withholding totals against Forms 941 filed by the agent for the same EINs. A second route is IRS notice matching of EFTPS deposits against reported liabilities per quarter per client EIN.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) W-2 to 941 reconciliation: on client EIN x quarter, compute summed W-2 federal withholding minus withholding reported and deposited on Form 941; fires when the shortfall exceeds zero; action IRS examination of the third-party payroll agent.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Amstrong Chapajong (personal care aide and community support worker)
SchemeSummary: Chapajong, working as both a personal care aide and community support worker, billed D.C. Medicaid for overlapping shifts, claiming to provide in-home personal care and behavioral health services to multiple clients in different locations at the same time; Electronic Visit Verification data showed he was usually not near the clients' homes. He was paid $461,369 for the overlapping-hours shifts.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compute overlapping service minutes for one rendering aide NPI across different beneficiaries on the same date. Compare EVV geolocation stamps against the beneficiary's address of record in the eligibility file. Sum all billed units per rendering worker per day across both personal care and behavioral health programs to test the 24-hour limit. Measure travel time implied between consecutive visit locations versus the gap between claimed shift end and start. Detect one worker billing under two different program provider NPIs for the same hours.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Overlapping shift detector: on rendering worker NPI x date of service, compute overlapping minutes across all beneficiary visit spans including other program lines; fires when overlap exceeds zero minutes; action prepay edit. 2) EVV geofence mismatch: on visit record, compute distance between the EVV check-in coordinates and the beneficiary's eligibility-file address; fires when distance exceeds the geofence radius; action claim suspension. 3) Daily hour ceiling: on rendering worker NPI x date of service, compute summed billed units converted to hours across all payer programs; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or an impossible shift; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Pfizer Inc. (parent/acquirer); Biohaven Pharmaceutical Holding Company Ltd. (subsidiary, drug manufacturer)
State_County: New York - Erie County (Buffalo); New York - Monroe County (Rochester)
SchemeSummary: Biohaven allegedly paid health care providers speaker-bureau honoraria and high-end restaurant meals to induce them to prescribe the migraine drug Nurtec ODT, including repeat programs with no educational value and programs attended by speakers' spouses, relatives, friends and practice colleagues; resulting prescriptions were billed to Medicare and other federal health care programs. Pfizer, which acquired Biohaven in October 2022 and ended the programs, paid $59,746,277 (about $50.2 million federal, $9.5 million state Medicaid) to resolve the qui tam action, with the whistleblower receiving about $8.4 million.
WaysToIdentify: Match Open Payments speaker fee and meal records to each prescriber's Part D claim volume for the promoted NDC. Compute the prescriber's share of the drug written before and after the first speaker payment date. Detect repeat programs where the same speaker NPI and same attendee NPIs recur across sessions in the manufacturer's transparency file. Identify attendees who are the speaker's practice colleagues under the same TIN in NPPES and PECOS. Compare per-attendee meal spend against fair-market-value thresholds in the payments file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Payment-to-prescribing lift: on prescriber NPI x NDC, compute paid Part D claim counts in the 12 months after the first Open Payments speaker fee minus the 12 months before; fires when the lift is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 2) Repeat-attendee graph: on speaker NPI x program series, compute the count of repeat attendee NPIs and attendees sharing the speaker's TIN; fires when repeats exceed the calibrated percentile versus peer programs; action postpay audit. 3) Brand concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the promoted NDC's share of that prescriber's claims in its therapeutic class; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Pfizer Inc. (parent/acquirer); Biohaven Pharmaceutical Holding Company Ltd. (wholly-owned subsidiary, drug manufacturer)
SchemeSummary: Biohaven allegedly paid health care providers speaker-bureau honoraria and high-end restaurant meals to induce them to prescribe the migraine drug Nurtec ODT, including sham repeat programs on the same topic and programs attended by speakers' spouses, family and practice colleagues with no educational need; resulting prescriptions were billed to Medicare and other federal health care programs. Resolved by a $59,746,277 FCA settlement (approx. $50.2M federal, $9.5M state Medicaid) from a qui tam suit by a former sales representative who receives ~$8.4M.
WaysToIdentify: Link Open Payments speaker honoraria and meal transactions to each recipient prescriber's subsequent Part D claims for the promoted NDC. Compute the change in that prescriber's brand share before and after the first honorarium date. Count sessions with an identical program topic and speaker NPI repeated within the manufacturer's transparency reporting. Identify attendee NPIs sharing a group practice TIN or surname with the paid speaker in NPPES records. Compare per-head meal spend on program records against documented educational content and attendance need.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Honorarium-prescribing correlation: on prescriber NPI x NDC, compute the ratio of post-payment to pre-payment paid claim counts using Open Payments dates; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 2) Sham-program detector: on speaker NPI x program topic, compute the count of repeat sessions and the count of attendees under the speaker's TIN; fires when both exceed peer program norms; action postpay audit. 3) High-cost brand share: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute promoted NDC paid dollars divided by class dollars; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Assertio Therapeutics Inc., f/k/a Depomed Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer)
State_County: Illinois - Lake Forest (company headquarters); District of Columbia
SchemeSummary: Assertio (then Depomed) allegedly marketed its fentanyl nasal spray Lazanda to high-volume TIRF prescribers - including some flagged for diversion or later indicted - placing them on speakers' bureaus and advisory boards, and ran a 'Signature Support Program' to secure insurer/Medicare Part D approval, causing 13 prescribers to write Lazanda prescriptions for Medicare and TRICARE beneficiaries without breakthrough cancer pain (the only FDA-approved indication). Resolved for $3.6 million under the FCA, with $657,000 to the qui tam relators.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check every TIRF fentanyl NDC claim for a cancer diagnosis on the beneficiary's other claims within the lookback period. Verify prescriber and beneficiary enrolment in the TIRF REMS registry before payment of the Part D claim. Link Open Payments speaker and advisory board payments to each prescriber's TIRF volume. Compare the prescriber against DEA action lists and state board discipline files for diversion findings. Detect prior-authorisation submissions routed through a manufacturer-funded reimbursement hub rather than the prescriber's office.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Off-label TIRF edit: on claim line, compute whether the beneficiary has any malignancy diagnosis code on claims within the lookback window; fires when no cancer diagnosis exists; action prepay edit. 2) REMS registry match: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary, compute enrolment status in the TIRF REMS registry at the fill date; fires on any exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Sponsored-prescriber concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute TIRF claim counts alongside Open Payments dollars from the manufacturer; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Assertio Therapeutics, Inc., formerly known as Depomed, Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Assertio (f/k/a Depomed) allegedly marketed its transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl nasal spray Lazanda to high-volume TIRF prescribers, including some flagged for diversion or later indicted, placed them on its speakers' bureau and advisory boards, and ran a 'Signature Support Program' to secure insurance/Medicare Part D approval, causing false claims to Medicare and TRICARE for patients without breakthrough cancer pain; resolved via $3.6 million FCA settlement of a 2017 qui tam suit.
WaysToIdentify: At Part D adjudication, TIRF fentanyl NDCs appear for beneficiaries with no cancer diagnosis on any prior medical claim. The prescribing NPI's TIRF volume sits far above same-specialty peers in the payer's prescriber profile file. Open Payments records show speaker and advisory payments from the labeling manufacturer to the same prescribing NPIs. Prior-authorisation packets for these NDCs are submitted by a manufacturer-funded hub rather than the prescriber's own office fax or portal. Some prescribing NPIs carry state board sanctions or DEA registration actions visible at credentialing.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Off-label TIRF indication check: on claim line x beneficiary, compute the count of oncology diagnosis codes on that beneficiary's medical claims in the prior 12 months for TIRF NDCs; fires when the count is zero; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Prescriber TIRF concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute TIRF NDC claim count and its share of that prescriber's total Part D opioid claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Sponsored-prescriber overlay: on prescriber NPI x NDC, compute the sum of Open Payments speaker and consulting dollars from the NDC's labeler in the prior year; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers and TIRF volume also exceeds peer baseline; action prepay edit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Raad Kouza (pharmacist, pharmacy owner); Ramis Kouza (pharmacy manager)
State_County: Michigan - Wayne County; Michigan - Oakland County
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
SchemeSummary: Two brothers operating Michigan pharmacies billed Medicare, Medicaid and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan for expensive prescription drugs (antipsychotics, inhalers) that were never dispensed, concealing resulting inventory shortages from multiple auditors, causing over $15 million in losses. Both were ordered to pay approximately $15.5 million in restitution plus the same amount in forfeiture; sentences were 8 years (Raad) and 5 years (Ramis).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed NDC units exceed the pharmacy's documented wholesaler acquisition units for the same NDC in the invoice and pedigree file. Dispensed quantities of high-cost antipsychotics and inhalers exceed peer pharmacies of the same script volume in the payer's remittance history. Beneficiaries billed for these NDCs have no matching office-visit or diagnosis claims supporting the therapy. Refill intervals are shorter than days-supply on the prior fill, indicating fills never taken. Audit responses across two related pharmacy NPIs share identical inventory documents and common ownership on CMS-855B filings.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler-invoiced units acquired; fires when billed units exceed acquired units; action claim suspension then postpay audit. 2) High-cost NDC concentration: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the ratio of paid dollars for the top five NDCs to total paid dollars; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-region peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Common-owner aggregation: on TIN x owner SSN from CMS-855B, compute the sum of purchase-to-dispense shortfall units across all linked pharmacy NPIs; fires when any linked NPI shows a shortfall; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: John Ageudo Rodriguez (licensed pharmacist, owner of Pharr Family Pharmacy)
SchemeSummary: Rodriguez, a pharmacist who owned Pharr Family Pharmacy, paid over $24 million in kickbacks to marketers who had relationships with physicians and clinics to steer prescriptions for expensive compounded drugs to his pharmacy, which then billed more than $110 million to federal health care programs.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a small set of prescriber NPIs accounts for nearly all of the pharmacy's compounded-drug claims despite being far from the pharmacy. Compound claims carry high-cost bulk ingredient NDCs with per-claim paid amounts above same-state pharmacy peers. Beneficiary residence ZIPs are hundreds of miles from the dispensing pharmacy's 855B practice location. The pharmacy's general ledger and 1099 filings show large payments to marketing entities not enrolled as providers. Refill counts continue after the beneficiary has no further contact claims with the prescriber.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber concentration graph: on pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute the share of compounded-drug paid dollars from the top ten prescriber NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state pharmacy peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Distance anomaly: on claim line, compute miles between beneficiary ZIP and pharmacy 855B service address for compound HCPCS/NDC claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies; action prepay edit. 3) Compound cost outlier: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute mean paid dollars per compound claim; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers or above the pharmacy's trailing twelve-month baseline; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Cynthia Ann Herrera (pharmacist)
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a pharmacist submitted or caused submission of fraudulent Medicaid claims for prescriptions that doctors had never prescribed, using doctors' personal identifying information without consent, resulting in more than $2 million in Medicaid payments between 2018 and 2024.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the prescriber NPI on the claim has no other prescribing activity for that beneficiary in any payer claim history. Prescriber NPIs used are inactive, retired, or in NPPES specialties that never prescribe the billed drug class. A single pharmacy NPI accounts for an outsized share of one prescriber's total Medicaid scripts. Prescriber-attested outreach letters go unanswered or are disclaimed by the physician's office. Fill dates fall outside the prescriber's licensed practice dates on the state board file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber-beneficiary linkage: on claim line, compute the count of medical encounter claims between the listed prescriber NPI and the beneficiary in the prior 12 months; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Single-pharmacy prescriber capture: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute the pharmacy's share of that prescriber's total dispensed claims; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR) to the prescriber. 3) Registry status mismatch: on claim line, compare prescriber licence status and DEA registration on the state board file at the date of service; fires on exact mismatch such as expired, retired, or deceased; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Eastern District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Isaiah Okoh (pharmacist); unnamed co-conspirator
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
SchemeSummary: Okoh, a pharmacist at three Michigan pharmacies, and a co-conspirator submitted claims to Medicare, Medicaid and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan for prescription drugs that were never dispensed and never ordered by any doctor, using forged physician prescriptions to conceal the scheme, causing over $6 million in losses; he was sentenced to 80 months and ordered to pay $3,889,760 restitution plus $3,230,147 forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed NDC units exceed the pharmacy's wholesaler acquisition units in invoice and pedigree data. Prescriber NPIs on the claims have no encounter claims with the billed beneficiaries. Prescription images produced in audit share identical handwriting or signature bitmaps across different prescriber NPIs. Three pharmacy NPIs with common ownership on CMS-855B show the same NDC mix and the same top prescribers. Beneficiaries have no diagnosis on file supporting the dispensed drug class.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler-invoiced units; fires when billed exceeds acquired; action claim suspension. 2) Orphan-prescriber rate: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of claims whose prescriber NPI has no encounter claim with the beneficiary in 12 months; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-region pharmacy peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Common-ownership cluster: on owner identifier from CMS-855B, compute the count of linked pharmacy NPIs sharing the same top-five prescriber NPIs; fires when overlap exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peers; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Justin Bell (pharmacist, owner and operator of Georgetown Pharmacy); Georgetown Pharmacy
SchemeSummary: Pharmacist owner of Georgetown Pharmacy solicited unwitting Kentucky Medicaid patients to accept expensive medicated scar pads (reimbursed over $14,000 per box of twelve) that they had no medical need for and in some cases never used or discussed with their providers, then submitted eight claims causing Kentucky Medicaid to pay $118,621.28 for medically unnecessary prescriptions.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, high-cost medicated scar-pad NDCs are billed for beneficiaries with no surgical, burn, or wound diagnosis in prior claims. Paid amount per unit is extreme relative to the state's average pharmacy claim, visible in remittance history. All such claims trace to one pharmacy NPI and a handful of prescriber NPIs. Beneficiaries have no encounter claim with the listed prescriber near the fill date. There are no refills or follow-up wound-care claims, which is inconsistent with genuine therapy.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Indication gap for high-cost topical NDCs: on claim line, compute the count of wound, burn, or post-surgical diagnosis codes on the beneficiary's claims in the prior 180 days; fires when zero; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Per-claim cost outlier: on pharmacy NPI x NDC, compute mean paid dollars per claim against the state pharmacy distribution; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action claim suspension. 3) Prescriber-contact check: on claim line, compute days since the beneficiary's most recent encounter with the listed prescriber NPI; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Medsinbox Pharmacy LTC LLC d/b/a Farmacia San Antonio (pharmacy)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; Medicaid (New Jersey Medicaid Program)
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy allegedly submitted claims to Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed it had not purchased enough medication to fill the prescriptions billed. Settled for $625,000 with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed NDC units exceed units the pharmacy purchased per wholesaler invoices and drug pedigree records. The pharmacy's paid dollars per prescription exceed same-state peers in the payer's remittance history. Beneficiaries billed for chronic-therapy NDCs show no supporting diagnosis or prescriber encounter claims. Refill timing is inconsistent with days-supply on the prior fill for the same NDC. The pharmacy's dispensing volume rose sharply above its own trailing baseline without any enrolment change in PECOS.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Inventory reconciliation edit: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler-acquired units; fires when the difference is positive; action claim suspension then postpay audit. 2) Early-refill density: on beneficiary x NDC x pharmacy NPI, compute the count of fills whose gap from the prior fill is less than the prior days-supply; fires when the count exceeds the pharmacy's trailing baseline percentile versus peers; action prepay edit. 3) Volume step change: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by the trailing twelve-month mean; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: A Plus Pharmacy LLC (former owner of A Plus Pharmacy, Manalapan, New Jersey)
SchemeSummary: A Plus Pharmacy LLC allegedly submitted claims to Medicare Part D for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed the pharmacy had not purchased enough of the medications to fill the prescriptions billed. It agreed to pay $350,000 with no admission of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Part D billed units for specific NDCs exceed wholesaler-invoiced acquisition units for the same pharmacy NPI. The pharmacy's high-cost NDC mix diverges sharply from same-state pharmacies of similar script count. Beneficiaries lack diagnosis or prescriber encounter claims supporting the dispensed drugs. Fill patterns show automatic monthly refills with no beneficiary cost-share collection recorded. Rapid growth in paid dollars occurs against the pharmacy's own trailing baseline in remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler-invoiced units; fires when billed exceeds acquired; action claim suspension. 2) High-cost mix divergence: on pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid dollars from NDCs above the state cost-per-claim median; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Auto-refill without contact: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the count of consecutive fills with no intervening prescriber encounter claim; fires when the count exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peers; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (sentencing in Houston, Southern District of Texas)
FraudEntity: Arthur Billings (owner, operator and pharmacist-in-charge of Health Fit Pharmacy); Deanna Winfield-Gates (relief pharmacist); Jeremy Branch (pharmacist-in-charge, 2017); Frank Cooper (relief pharmacist); Health Fit Pharmacy
State_County: Texas - Harris County (Houston); Texas - Fort Bend County (Missouri City)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Health Fit Pharmacy operated as a cash-only pill mill: for hundreds of dollars per prescription it dispensed hydrocodone, oxycodone and other abused drugs to straw 'patients' sent and funded by black-market drug traffickers, who resold the pills; the prescriptions were often fraudulent, written in the names of physicians whose identities had been stolen. More than half a million opioid pills were distributed; owner Billings also made false statements on a disability benefits application. Forfeiture figures ($2.6M, $60,000, $68,931.44, $5,000) and sentences (12 years, 6 years, 22 months, 20 months) span four defendants.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication and in PDMP data, the pharmacy dispenses Schedule II opioids almost entirely as cash transactions with no insurance adjudication record. ARCOS and wholesaler pedigree data show opioid purchase volumes far above same-size pharmacy peers. Prescriptions carry prescriber NPIs whose PDMP history shows no other activity in that state. Patient cohorts share long travel distances, identical drug cocktails, and same-day fills at one pharmacy. The owner's disability benefit application conflicts with payroll and business income records held by the agency.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Controlled-substance acquisition outlier: on pharmacy DEA number x quarter, compute morphine-milligram-equivalent units purchased from ARCOS divided by total prescriptions dispensed; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-size peers; action site visit. 2) Cash-fill share: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of Schedule II fills in PDMP with no corresponding payer adjudication record; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus state peers; action prepay edit on that pharmacy's remaining claims plus referral. 3) Prescriber-identity validation: on prescription record x prescriber NPI, compute whether the prescriber's DEA registration, state licence, and NPPES address match the prescription face; fires on exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Samuel "Sam" Khaimov (co-owner of Prime Aid Union City, lead pharmacist of Prime Aid Bronx); Yana Shtindler (administrator of Prime Aid Union City); Ruben Sevumyants (operations manager); Alex Fleyshmakher (employee and on-paper owner of Prime Aid Bronx); Prime Aid Pharmacies
State_County: New Jersey - Hudson County (Union City); New York - Bronx County (Bronx)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; private health benefit providers; pharmacy benefit managers
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Drug_Prescriptions
SchemeSummary: Prime Aid specialty pharmacies billed PBMs, Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers for at least $65 million in refills of expensive specialty medications (Hepatitis C, Crohn's, rheumatoid arthritis) that were never dispensed and never even ordered or stocked, and paid bribes (cash, checks, wires, meals, and an employee placed inside a doctor's office) to doctors and their staff to steer prescriptions to the pharmacies; when PBMs audited, employees falsified records and forged shipping records. Khaimov received 87 months and Shtindler 72 months; two co-defendants pleaded guilty and await sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, specialty NDC billed units exceed the pharmacy's wholesaler acquisition and cold-chain purchase records for those products. Refill claims continue with no shipment tracking numbers matching the carrier manifest supplied at PBM audit. A handful of prescriber NPIs generate nearly all high-cost specialty scripts routed to two commonly owned pharmacy NPIs. Beneficiaries lack hepatitis C, Crohn's, or rheumatoid arthritis diagnoses and lab monitoring claims consistent with therapy. Pharmacy payroll records show staff placed inside a referring physician's office, visible in 1099 and payment ledgers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Specialty inventory reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus wholesaler-invoiced units for specialty NDCs; fires when billed exceeds acquired; action payment suspension. 2) Refill without clinical footprint: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the count of paid refills with zero supporting diagnosis or monitoring lab claims in the prior 180 days; fires when the count exceeds one; action prepay edit. 3) Referral concentration: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute the pharmacy's share of that prescriber's specialty scripts and the prescriber's share of the pharmacy's specialty dollars; fires when both exceed the calibrated percentile versus peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Randy Yost (owner of Randy's Gateway Drug)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Virginia Medicaid); TRICARE; other insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Upcoding; Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment
SchemeSummary: Pharmacy owner dispensed cheaper generic Schedule II medications (e.g., in place of OxyContin) while billing Medicare, Virginia Medicaid, TRICARE and private insurers for more expensive brand-name drugs; also billed for prescriptions never dispensed, and re-billed medications that patients returned without reversing the original charge. Adjusted government loss of $1,309,515; ordered to pay restitution of $1,035,279.44 to Medicare, $271,274.03 to Virginia Medicaid and $2,961.75 to TRICARE, plus 18 months imprisonment.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed brand NDC units exceed brand units the pharmacy purchased, while generic purchases of the same molecule dominate wholesaler invoices. Brand-versus-generic dispensing ratio for Schedule II opioids sits far above same-state pharmacy peers. Returned-to-stock inventory entries have no corresponding reversal transaction in the payer's remittance history. Some billed prescriptions have no matching PDMP dispensing record for the beneficiary. Beneficiaries show gaps between claimed days-supply and next-fill dates inconsistent with actual pickup logs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Brand-billed versus brand-purchased: on pharmacy NPI x molecule x quarter, compute billed brand NDC units minus wholesaler-invoiced brand units; fires when billed exceeds acquired; action claim suspension. 2) Unreversed return detection: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the count of fills with a return-to-stock inventory entry but no claim reversal in remittance history; fires when the count is above zero; action postpay audit. 3) PDMP-to-claim match: on claim line for Schedule II NDCs, compute whether a PDMP dispensing record exists with matching beneficiary, NDC, and fill date; fires on exact mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Nyesha D. Paris, aka Nyesha D. Henderson and Nyesha D. Jackson (business owner)
PayerName: Medicaid; Paycheck Protection Program (SBA); Lowe's Home Improvement
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: Paris ran more than a dozen fraud schemes causing over $600,000 in losses to 15 victims: she billed Pennsylvania Medicaid nearly $150,000 for home health services purportedly provided by her business but never rendered; obtained over $120,000 in PPP pandemic loans by inflating payroll, submitting fake documents and falsely certifying her companies were operating in February 2020; and stole over $40,000 in merchandise and gift cards from Lowe's using a shell company and fraudulent business accounts. Restitution of $545,993 and a forfeiture judgment of $84,008 were ordered.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, home health visit claims have no matching EVV check-in and check-out record for the beneficiary and caregiver. Billed aide hours exceed the payroll and timesheet hours the agency reports to the state wage system. Rendering caregiver identifiers are absent from the state registry or duplicated across simultaneous visits. The agency's Medicaid billing volume grew from near zero with no plan-of-care or supervisory visit claims. Provider bank account and TIN match those used in unrelated benefit applications flagged in fraud-file cross-checks.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) EVV-to-claim reconciliation: on claim line, compute billed service minutes minus matched EVV verified minutes for that beneficiary, caregiver, and date; fires when unmatched minutes are above zero; action prepay edit. 2) Payroll capacity ratio: on provider NPI x quarter, compute billed aide hours divided by hours reported on state payroll filings; fires when the ratio exceeds one; action payment suspension. 3) New-agency ramp: on provider NPI x month, compute paid dollars divided by trailing three-month mean for agencies enrolled under two years; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: James Sessoms
PayerName: Medicaid (Pennsylvania Department of Human Services / HHS); SNAP (USDA)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sessoms used stolen and fabricated identities, valid SSNs assigned to others, fake driver's licenses bearing his photo, and fraudulent birth certificates for fictitious spouses and children to file false SNAP and Medicaid benefit applications with the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, obtaining $1,063,633 in benefits and selling the fraudulently obtained SNAP cards for cash at a local supermarket.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the applicant's SSN does not match the name and date of birth in the SSA numident verification response. Multiple approved cases share one mailing address, one phone number, and one bank account across different applicant identities. Submitted birth certificates for dependents have no corresponding record in the state vital records file. The photograph on the driver's licence submitted matches images on other applications under different names. Issued SNAP EBT cards are redeemed almost entirely at a single retailer in high-value even-dollar transactions.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Identity verification mismatch: on benefit application, compute the SSA numident match result across name, SSN, and date of birth; fires on any exact mismatch; action claim suspension of the eligibility determination pending documentation request. 2) Household collision graph: on address, phone, or bank account, compute the count of distinct approved case identifiers sharing that value; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-county caseload; action site visit. 3) Dependent vital-records match: on each listed dependent, compute whether a state vital records birth entry matches name and date of birth; fires on exact mismatch; action prepay edit on benefit issuance.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Aboudramane Karamoko; Sekou Fofanah; Shamaire Brown; Quamaire Brown
State_County: New Jersey; New York; Pennsylvania; Indiana; Rhode Island
SchemeSummary: Four Philadelphia defendants conspired to break into approximately 55 UPS warehouses across multiple states, prying open or breaking loading bay doors and targeting parcels labeled 'lithium-ion battery' that contained high-value electronics such as cell phones, stealing about $1,600,157 in merchandise; all four were ordered to pay that amount in restitution and received sentences of 24 to 39 months (longest imposed on Karamoko). Not a health care fraud scheme, though prosecuted by an AUSA of the Health Care Fraud Unit.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim here and no payer adjudication point, so no prepay or postpay control applies. The theft involves parcel cargo and is detected through carrier facility access logs, door-forcing alarms, and parcel scan gaps. The nearest detection route is reconciling last-scan location against delivery exceptions for high-value electronics shipments.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a carrier-side check on facility x night that counts high-value parcels with a terminal scan but no outbound scan and escalates when the count exceeds the facility's trailing baseline.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: James Sessoms
PayerName: Medicaid (Pennsylvania Department of Human Services / HHS); SNAP (USDA)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sessoms used stolen and fabricated identities, valid SSNs assigned to others, fake driver's licenses bearing his photo, and fraudulent birth certificates for fictitious spouses and children to submit false SNAP and Medicaid benefit applications to the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, obtaining $1,063,633 in benefits and selling the fraudulently obtained SNAP cards for cash at a local supermarket.
WaysToIdentify: At eligibility determination, the SSN on the application fails the SSA numident match against submitted name and date of birth. One residential address, phone number, or payee bank account appears across several approved cases with different identities. Dependent birth certificates submitted have no matching entry in the state vital records registry. The same facial image appears on identity documents filed under multiple applicant names. EBT redemptions concentrate at one retailer in round-dollar amounts inconsistent with household size.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Numident mismatch edit: on benefit application, compute the SSA verification result across SSN, name, and date of birth; fires on exact mismatch; action claim suspension pending documentation request. 2) Shared-attribute degree: on address, phone, or bank account, compute the distinct count of approved case identifiers linked to that value; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-county caseload; action site visit. 3) Retailer concentration: on EBT card x month, compute the share of redemption dollars at a single retailer FNS number; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-county households; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Ghodrat Pirooz Sholevar, M.D. (psychiatrist owner); Nueva Vida Multicultural/Multilingual Behavioral Health, Inc. (mental health clinic company)
PayerName: Medicaid (Community Behavioral Health, Philadelphia Medicaid program administrator)
SchemeSummary: Psychiatrist and his three Northeast Philadelphia clinics billed Medicaid for whole 15-minute 'units' of medication management ('med checks') for children and adults when the appointments were substantially shorter, and falsified start/end clock times in patient records - including overlapping times showing two or three patients seen in the same 15-minute window at two different clinic locations - and billed more med checks than could fit in a workday. Resolved by a $900,000 False Claims Act settlement with the doctor and his company.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the rendering NPI's billed time-based units for one date of service exceed the hours physically available in a workday. Documented start and end clock times overlap across different beneficiaries for the same rendering NPI. Claims for the same rendering NPI on one date carry two different service facility locations minutes apart. Nearly all med-check claims bill the same time-based CPT unit count, with no distribution across shorter codes. Encounter counts per provider day exceed same-specialty peers in the payer's remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible-day check: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of billed time-based CPT units multiplied by their code-defined minutes; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or the calibrated peer workday percentile; action prepay edit. 2) Overlapping-time detection: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of documented start-end intervals that overlap another beneficiary's interval; fires when overlapping minutes are above zero; action claim suspension. 3) Multi-site same-day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the distinct count of service facility addresses and the drive-time between them versus interval spacing; fires when travel time exceeds the documented gap; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Roman Berezhnoy (operator of ransomware affiliate group '8Base'/'Affiliate 2803'); Egor Nikolaevich Glebov (operator of ransomware affiliate group); Evgenii Ptitsyn (alleged Phobos ransomware administrator)
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly hacked into more than 1,000 victim networks worldwide - including a children's hospital, other health care providers, and schools - stole and encrypted data with Phobos ransomware, then extorted ransom payments (over $16 million received) in exchange for decryption keys, threatening to publish stolen files on a darknet site if victims did not pay.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point in this extortion scheme, so no prepay or postpay claims control applies. Detection sits with network telemetry: intrusion logs, ransomware note artefacts, and darknet leak-site monitoring. The nearest financial route is tracing ransom cryptocurrency wallet clusters through blockchain analytics and exchange KYC records.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. The nearest control outside the claims system is a security-operations check on provider network x day counting anomalous outbound data-transfer volume against the site's trailing baseline, with escalation to incident response.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Puerto Rico
FraudEntity: Raúl D. Villalobos-Meléndez (physician assistant posing as licensed physician)
SchemeSummary: Defendant, licensed only as a physician assistant and never having passed the USMLE, altered his PA license into forged provisional/permanent medical licenses and forged USMLE score reports and a JLDM certification to obtain a paid physician internship position at Hospital del Maestro (June 2023–May 2024), then submitted a CMS-855I enrollment form to CMS listing a false Puerto Rico medical license number and 'General Practitioner' specialty, reassigning his Medicare benefits to Physician HMO.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the medical licence number on the CMS-855I does not match any active record in the state licensing board file. NPPES taxonomy claimed as general practitioner conflicts with the physician assistant credential on the state registry. No ECFMG or USMLE verification record supports the submitted score reports at credentialing. Reassignment of benefits to a group is requested with no prior residency or hospital privileging verifiable at primary source. Enrolment application address and dates conflict with employment records at the named hospital.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Licence primary-source match: on CMS-855I application, compute an exact match of licence number, name, and issue date against the state board file; fires on any mismatch; action claim suspension of enrolment plus site visit. 2) Taxonomy-credential consistency: on provider NPI, compute whether the NPPES taxonomy requires a credential the applicant holds in the state registry; fires on exact mismatch such as physician assistant billing as physician; action prepay edit on all claims. 3) Post-enrolment claim block: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute whether the date falls within a verified active licence period; fires when the date lies outside it; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Neil K. Anand M.D. (physician, owner of in-house pharmacies)
PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Office of Personnel Management health plans; Independence Blue Cross; Anthem
SchemeSummary: Anand required patients seeking controlled-substance prescriptions to accept 'Goody Bags' of medically unnecessary medications dispensed by his own in-house pharmacies, billing Medicare, OPM plans, Independence Blue Cross and Anthem over $2.3 million; unlicensed medical interns wrote oxycodone prescriptions on blank forms pre-signed by Anand (20,850 tablets for nine patients), and he moved about $1.2 million of proceeds into a relative's account after learning of the investigation.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, controlled-substance prescriptions and same-day dispensing claims share one owner TIN across prescriber and pharmacy NPIs. Every opioid claim for a beneficiary is accompanied by additional non-controlled NDCs from the same in-house pharmacy on the same date. The prescription record shows an intern or unlicensed writer while the prescriber NPI is the supervising physician. Beneficiaries have no diagnosis supporting the bundled ancillary medications in their prior claim history. Opioid tablet quantities per beneficiary exceed same-specialty prescriber peers in PDMP and Part D data.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Self-referral bundle: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of NDCs dispensed by a pharmacy sharing the prescriber's owner TIN alongside a Schedule II fill; fires when the count exceeds one without a supporting diagnosis; action prepay edit. 2) Writer-prescriber mismatch: on prescription record, compute whether the individual documented as writing the order holds an active licence and DEA registration; fires on exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Opioid quantity outlier: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute total morphine-milligram-equivalents dispensed per beneficiary; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dr. Marion Lee (co-owner and medical advisor, Luminus Diagnostics); Luminus Diagnostics
State_County: Georgia - Tift County (Tifton); Louisiana - Orleans Parish (New Orleans)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Lee, co-owner and medical advisor of a Georgia diagnostic lab, paid and received kickbacks to obtain orders for medically unnecessary genetic tests, including through purported telemedicine, using 'dummy proof' order forms with prepopulated diagnosis codes and check-box panels; claims were routed through another Louisiana lab thought more likely to be paid and concealed by a sham contract, resulting in over $24 million billed to Medicare and about $4 million paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on high-cost genetic CPT claims has no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with the beneficiary. Requisition forms show identical prepopulated diagnosis codes across large numbers of unrelated beneficiaries. One telemedicine ordering NPI orders panels for beneficiaries spread across many distant states in a week. The same specimen and beneficiary are billed by two lab NPIs under a pass-through arrangement within days. Lab claim volume rises sharply against its own trailing baseline following an ownership change filed in PECOS.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the genetic test date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Diagnosis-template uniformity: on ordering NPI x CPT, compute the share of ordered claims carrying the single most frequent diagnosis code; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Pass-through duplication: on beneficiary x CPT x 30 days, compute the distinct count of billing lab NPIs paid for the same test; fires when the count exceeds one; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Neil K. Anand, M.D. (physician, owner of in-house pharmacies)
PayerName: Medicare; U.S. Office of Personnel Management (federal employee health plans); Independence Blue Cross; Anthem
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Anand billed Medicare, OPM, Independence Blue Cross and Anthem over $2.4 million for 'Goody Bags' of medically unnecessary prescription medications dispensed by pharmacies he owned, enticing patients to accept them by supplying oxycodone (20,850 tablets for nine patients) prescribed outside the usual course of practice; unlicensed medical interns wrote controlled-substance prescriptions on blank forms pre-signed by Anand, and he later moved about $1.2 million of proceeds into a relative's account. Ordered to pay over $2 million restitution and over $2 million forfeiture.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count NDC fills per beneficiary from pharmacies sharing a PECOS owner with the prescribing NPI on the claim. Oxycodone NDC quantities per prescriber on Part D PDE data sit far above same-specialty peers for nine beneficiaries. Prescription images show one pre-signed prescriber signature with different handwriting on drug and quantity fields. Ordering NPI on the claim belongs to a physician while the state licence board file shows the writer is an unlicensed intern. Beneficiary receives multiple high-cost non-controlled NDCs on the same date as each opioid fill, a bundled dispensing pattern.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Owner-linked pharmacy loop: on prescriber NPI x pharmacy NPI, compute the share of that pharmacy's paid claims written by prescribers listed in its CMS-855 or PECOS ownership records; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Opioid-plus-bundle co-fill: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of distinct non-controlled NDCs paid alongside a Schedule II opioid NDC from the same pharmacy; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Prescriber daily impossibility: on prescriber NPI x date of service, compute total controlled-substance dosage units plus the count of distinct patients; fires when patient count exceeds what 24 clinic hours permit; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia; U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Ndubuisi Joseph Okafor, M.D. (sole practitioner and owner of Okafor Medical Associates)
SchemeSummary: Okafor, sole owner of an internal medicine clinic in Northwest Washington D.C., sold prescriptions for oxycodone and promethazine with codeine for cash to walk-in 'patients' (including FBI undercover agents and confidential sources) after minimal or no examination, and prescribed opioids to individuals using false identities whom he knew were diverting the drugs; conduct spanned at least 45 states and hundreds of thousands of units. He also created backdated medical records for one patient to justify prescribing after a Board of Health complaint.
WaysToIdentify: In PDMP data, one prescriber NPI writes controlled-substance scripts for patients whose residence ZIPs span dozens of states. Pharmacy claims show the same prescriber NPI dominating oxycodone and promethazine-with-codeine NDC fills with no paid E/M claim for the patient. Cash-pay dispensing share for that prescriber's scripts is extreme in PBM and pharmacy remittance records versus peers. Patient identity fields on scripts fail SSN and date-of-birth matching against the payer's eligibility file and NPPES-verified demographics. Chart entries produced under ADR carry creation timestamps after the Board of Health complaint date but bear earlier service dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Opioid geographic dispersion: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the count of distinct patient states on filled oxycodone and promethazine-codeine NDCs in PDMP and pharmacy claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Script without encounter: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary, compute the days between the controlled-substance fill date and the nearest paid E/M claim by that NPI; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action claim suspension. 3) Backdating detector: on claim line, compute the gap in days between the electronic record creation timestamp supplied under ADR and the billed date of service; fires when the record postdates service beyond the documentation window; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Michigan
FraudEntity: Physicians Toxicology Laboratory, LLC (laboratory); Lund Capital Group, LLC (grandparent company); Matthew Ryan Lund (former president of PTL); Thomas C. Lund; Family Health Partners, P.C. (medical practice); Michael J. Septer, D.O. (owner of Family Health Partners); Advanced Pain Solutions, PLLC d/b/a Vitruvian Health (medical practice)
State_County: Michigan - Kent County (Grand Rapids); Michigan - Ionia County (Ionia); Florida - Hillsborough County (Tampa)
SchemeSummary: PTL created requisition forms allowing simultaneous 'blanket' orders of presumptive and definitive urine drug tests for all patients of Michigan medical practices, and placed its own in-office urine collectors who filled out the blanket orders without individualized medical-necessity determinations; PTL then ran and billed Medicare for these non-covered tests, and also billed for urine hormone tests used as specimen validity testing already bundled into UDT reimbursement. PTL and co-defendants pay $4,425,000; two ordering practices previously settled for a total of $188,633.18.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, presumptive and definitive UDT CPT codes appear on the same date of service for nearly every patient of an ordering NPI. The ordering practice's requisition forms obtained under ADR show pre-checked panels identical across all beneficiaries of that TIN. Urine hormone and specimen-validity CPT lines are billed separately alongside UDT codes already inclusive of validity testing. A single laboratory NPI receives orders from a handful of ordering NPIs whose UDT rate far exceeds same-specialty peers. Collection staff placed in the practice appear as the lab's employees in CMS-855B enrolment records while ordering under the practice's NPI.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Reflex-to-definitive ratio: on ordering NPI x month, compute the share of presumptive UDT claims followed by definitive UDT CPT lines on the same date of service; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Bundled validity unbundling: on claim line, compute the count of specimen-validity and urine hormone CPT codes billed with a UDT code on the same date of service for the same beneficiary; fires when that count exceeds zero against NCCI bundling rules; action prepay edit. 3) Order concentration: on laboratory NPI, compute the share of UDT revenue attributable to the top ordering NPIs and the distinct-beneficiary uniformity of ordered panels; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR), then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Comprehensive Healthcare Management Services, LLC, d/b/a Brighton Rehabilitation and Wellness Center (nursing home operator); Mt. Lebanon Operations, LLC, d/b/a Mount Lebanon Rehabilitation and Wellness Center (nursing home operator)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Allegheny County (Pittsburgh area, Mt. Lebanon); Pennsylvania - Beaver County (Brighton)
SchemeSummary: Two nursing home operating companies, acting through high-level personnel and employees, falsified staffing sheets and certifications submitted to the Pennsylvania Department of Health and CMS - adding names of people not working or not providing direct patient care - to appear compliant with minimum staffing ratios required as conditions of participation in Medicare and Medicaid, thereby avoiding penalties and continuing to receive federal funds. After a December 2023 jury conviction, Brighton was ordered to pay $12,629,257.46 restitution plus five years probation and Mt. Lebanon $2,721,312.10 plus one year probation.
WaysToIdentify: Payroll-Based Journal staffing hours reported to CMS exceed hours supported by the facility's payroll register and tax filings for the same quarter. Named staff on submitted staffing sheets hold no active licence in the state nurse aide registry or licence board file. Individuals counted as direct care appear in job-code fields as kitchen, laundry or administrative staff in payroll records. Reported nursing hours per resident day sit just above the state minimum ratio in every reporting period with implausibly low variance. Staffing spikes reported to the Pennsylvania Department of Health cluster on survey dates recorded in the state inspection file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) PBJ-payroll reconciliation: on facility CCN x quarter, compute the difference between direct-care hours reported in Payroll-Based Journal and paid hours in the payroll register by job code; fires when the reported hours exceed payroll hours; action postpay audit. 2) Ghost staff registry match: on facility CCN x reported staff name, compute the count of listed direct-care individuals with no active record in the state nurse aide or licence board file; fires when that count exceeds zero on an exact registry mismatch; action site visit. 3) Survey-day staffing spike: on facility CCN x date, compute the ratio of reported nursing hours per resident day on inspection dates to the facility's own trailing non-survey baseline; fires when above that baseline by the calibrated percentile versus state peers; action site visit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Toby Weatherbee (member of Plasterer's Local Union #9)
State_County: New York - Western District of New York (Pike, NY)
PayerName: Plaster's Local Union #9 health and welfare fund (union health care benefit program)
SchemeSummary: Weatherbee submitted 12 fraudulent invoices, including a fabricated $6,720 invoice from Dansville Dental Professionals, LLP, to his union's health and welfare fund for reimbursement of out-of-pocket medical expenses he never incurred, converting $44,012 of fund money to his own use. He received two years' probation and was ordered to pay $44,012 restitution.
WaysToIdentify: Member-submitted reimbursement invoices name a dental practice whose NPI and TIN do not match NPPES or the plan's provider file. No corresponding dental encounter claim exists from that practice for the member on the invoiced dates of service. Invoice numbers, fonts and totals repeat across multiple submissions from the same member in the fund's imaged claim records. Reimbursement payments route to a bank account already tied to the member in the fund's payment file rather than a provider account. The member's out-of-pocket reimbursement dollars far exceed same-plan peers within the benefit year.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Provider existence check: on member reimbursement claim line, compute the exact match of the invoiced provider name, NPI and TIN against NPPES and the state dental licence file; fires on registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Encounter corroboration: on member x invoiced date of service, compute the count of corroborating provider-submitted dental claims or eligibility-verified encounters; fires when that count is zero; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Member reimbursement velocity: on member x benefit year, compute the count and dollar sum of self-submitted out-of-pocket invoices; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-plan peers; action claim suspension, then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Cory Lloyd (president of insurance brokerage firm); Steven Strong (CEO of marketing company)
State_County: Florida - Martin County (Stuart); Texas - Tarrant County (Mansfield)
PayerName: Federal government (Affordable Care Act premium subsidies); insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly enrolled low-income and homeless individuals in fully subsidized ACA health plans by submitting false applications overstating projected income (and using mismatched addresses and Social Security numbers) so enrollees would appear eligible for federal premium subsidies; the brokerage collected commissions from insurers and paid Strong commissions for consumer referrals, with street marketers bribing consumers to enroll. Alleged federal subsidy payments totaled at least $161.9 million.
WaysToIdentify: Enrollment applications report projected household income sitting narrowly inside the fully-subsidized band while IRS and state wage data show far lower income. One broker NPN or agent ID appears on enrollments spanning thousands of consumers across unrelated addresses in the marketplace enrollment file. Applicant Social Security numbers and dates of birth fail SSA verification in the marketplace identity-proofing record. Enrollee mailing addresses resolve to shelters, mail drops or addresses reused across dozens of unrelated applications. Enrolled members generate no claims at all in the insurer's remittance history while premium subsidies pay monthly.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Income-band clustering: on broker NPN x month, compute the share of enrollments with attested income inside the fully-subsidized band and the mismatch rate against IRS and wage-data trusted sources; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer brokers; action payment suspension of commissions. 2) Address and identity reuse: on application, compute the distinct count of unrelated applicants sharing the same mailing address plus the count of SSA verification failures; fires when reuse exceeds a household-plausible count or verification fails; action prepay edit on subsidy payment. 3) Zero-utilization subsidy: on enrollee x plan year, compute the sum of advance premium tax credit dollars paid against the count of paid medical and pharmacy claims; fires when subsidy dollars accrue with zero claims beyond the calibrated percentile duration; action documentation request (ADR), then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section (federal jury in West Palm Beach, Florida)
FraudEntity: Cory Lloyd (president of insurance brokerage firm); Steven Strong (CEO of marketing company)
State_County: Florida - Palm Beach County (West Palm Beach); Florida - Martin County (Stuart); Texas - Tarrant County (Mansfield)
PayerName: Affordable Care Act federal premium subsidies (federal government); private insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Lloyd and Strong submitted false ACA marketplace enrollment applications for low-income, homeless, and substance-using individuals whose income did not meet the minimum eligibility threshold for fully subsidized plans, using coached answers, mismatched addresses and Social Security numbers, bribes to enrollees, and deliberately doomed Medicaid applications to enable off-cycle enrollment; the federal government paid at least $180 million of over $233 million in subsidies, and Lloyd earned insurer commissions and paid Strong for referrals.
WaysToIdentify: At marketplace application, attested household income sits just above the Medicaid floor for fully subsidized plans across an implausible share of one agent NPN's book. The Federal Data Services Hub returns an income data-matching inconsistency against IRS and SSA records for those same applications. Many applications from one agent NPN share a single mailing address, phone or bank routing detail in the enrollment record. Enrollees show zero paid medical or pharmacy claims after effectuation despite full-year APTC payments to the issuer. Special enrollment periods are claimed by loss-of-Medicaid attestation with no corresponding state Medicaid denial record on file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Income-floor clustering: on agent NPN x plan year, compute the share of submitted applications with attested household income within one FPL point above the subsidy minimum, over marketplace application income fields; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-market agent peers; action prepay edit on APTC effectuation plus documentation request (ADR). 2) Identity-element reuse: on agent NPN, compute the distinct-value count of enrollees divided by the distinct count of addresses, phones and SSN-prefix groups in the enrollment file; fires when the ratio exceeds one household per address beyond the agent's trailing baseline; action claim suspension of APTC and site visit. 3) Zero-utilization subsidy: on enrollee x issuer, compute the sum of APTC paid months minus months with any paid medical or pharmacy claim; fires when APTC months exceed zero and claim months equal zero for a full policy year; action postpay audit with agent commission recoupment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Liaquat Cheema (President of AFL Construction Co. Inc.); AFL Construction Co. Inc.
State_County: New York - Queens County; New York - New York County (Southern District of New York)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Cheema, president of a Queens construction company holding ~$12 million in New York City homeless-shelter contracts, submitted fraudulent invoices and supporting documents falsely claiming workers performed work and inflating material costs, using other people's identities (including a Social Security number) as purported workers. Separately, he and others obtained tens of thousands of dollars in Medicaid benefits by submitting false certifications and near-identical employment letters underreporting income and bearing the signature of a deceased 'project manager.'
WaysToIdentify: At Medicaid eligibility determination, the employment verification letters submitted by multiple applicants are near-identical in wording, layout and employer letterhead fields. The signer named on those letters matches a record in the Death Master File with a death date preceding the letter date. Attested wages on the Medicaid application contradict quarterly wage data for the same SSN in the state wage-match and IRS income file. Worker SSNs listed on city shelter-contract invoices belong to individuals with no state wage record for that employer or quarter. The contractor's invoiced material costs exceed vendor pedigree and purchase-order documentation held by the contracting agency.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Deceased signer check: on eligibility case, compute the match between the verification letter signer's name and SSN and the Death Master File death date versus the document date; fires on an exact registry match with death preceding the document; action claim suspension of eligibility and postpay audit. 2) Template letter reuse: on employer TIN x quarter, compute the count of distinct Medicaid applicants submitting employment letters with identical text hash and signature block; fires when that count exceeds one; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Wage-match gap: on applicant SSN, compute attested monthly income minus state quarterly wage-file income divided by wage-file income; fires when the negative gap exceeds the calibrated percentile versus same-program applicants; action prepay edit on benefit issuance.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Walter Stanzione (principal/leader of Fire Alarm Electrical Corp.); William Neogra (principal of Fire Alarm Electrical Corp.); Fire Alarm Electrical Corp.
PayerName: City of New York agencies (Department of Citywide Administrative Services, Department of Education, Department of Environmental Protection, Department of Sanitation)
SchemeSummary: The two principals of a fire alarm maintenance contractor holding New York City contracts submitted fraudulent invoices to four city agencies over an eleven-year period, buying supplies from legitimate retailers and re-invoicing them through secretly owned shell companies at three to five times the real cost, and altering genuine retailer invoices when city auditors grew suspicious; Stanzione siphoned off much of the proceeds for personal spending. Both defendants pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy; no health care payer was involved.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim here and no adjudication point, so no payer-side edit applies. The nearest detection route is municipal accounts-payable matching of subcontractor invoices to retailer receipts and pedigree documentation. Vendor beneficial-ownership disclosures compared against state corporate registries would expose shell intermediaries sharing the prime's bank account.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on vendor TIN x bank account, compute the count of distinct city vendors depositing to one account and the markup ratio of invoiced price to retailer receipt price, and refer accounts above the calibrated percentile to procurement audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Rhode Island
FraudEntity: Nicholas M. Ash
SchemeSummary: Ash allegedly falsely told a Providence VA Medical Center doctor that he had been on a combat deployment to Iraq/the Middle East and suffered PTSD and seizures from an IED blast, in order to obtain veterans' disability compensation and health care benefits; Defense Department records showed he never served outside the United States and was on non-deployable status.
WaysToIdentify: At benefit adjudication, the claimed combat deployment has no matching record in DMDC deployment files or the veteran's DD-214 foreign service block. The service treatment record contains no in-theater injury entry or line-of-duty determination for the asserted blast event. Personnel records show non-deployable status during the exact date range asserted in the compensation application. The PTSD stressor statement lacks any corroborating unit record, casualty report or award citation in the personnel file. The claimed diagnosis rests solely on self-report captured in a single VA clinician note with no prior treatment history in the health record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Deployment registry mismatch: on claimant file, compute the overlap in days between asserted deployment dates on the compensation application and DMDC deployment and DD-214 foreign service dates; fires when overlap equals zero; action claim suspension pending documentation request (ADR). 2) Stressor corroboration gap: on claimant x claimed stressor event, compute the count of independent corroborating records in personnel, casualty and line-of-duty files; fires when that count equals zero; action prepay edit before rating decision. 3) Self-report-only diagnosis: on rendering NPI x claimant, compute the count of prior encounters documenting the claimed condition before the compensation application date; fires when that count equals zero and the rating rests on one encounter; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Shawn R. Blankenship (licensed nurse practitioner, owner of Holistic Inc.); Holistic Inc. (medical clinic)
State_County: West Virginia - Putnam County (Winfield); West Virginia - Kanawha County (St. Albans)
PayerName: Medicaid (West Virginia Medicaid and its Managed Care Organizations)
SchemeSummary: Blankenship, a nurse practitioner who owned Holistic Inc. clinic (office-based opioid treatment, weight loss and smoking cessation counseling), caused false claims to be submitted to West Virginia Medicaid and its MCOs for services that were never provided and not medically necessary, including three smoking cessation counseling claims and a 15-minute office visit purportedly performed on October 29, 2020 when he and the clinic's other licensed nurse practitioners were in Hilton Head, South Carolina. Losses were approximately $600,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, dates of service fall on days when the rendering NPI's own claims cluster in a different state, evidenced by other payers' place-of-service and location data. Billed office visit and counseling units on a single date exceed the hours the rendering NPI could physically work in 24 hours. Smoking cessation counseling CPT codes are billed for beneficiaries whose claim history shows no tobacco-use diagnosis. Every licensed prescriber on the group TIN has zero prescription fills in state PDMP records on the billed treatment dates. Encounter volume for office-based opioid treatment is uniform day to day, unlike the provider's own trailing appointment pattern.
