FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible service day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of time-based CPT unit minutes across all payers and MCOs; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or exceeds clinic operating hours; action prepay edit and payment suspension. 2) Absent-provider day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of billed encounters on dates with no PDMP dispensing, no EVV record and no facility badge or travel corroboration; fires when the count is above zero on more than the provider's trailing baseline of such days; action documentation request (ADR) then postpay audit. 3) Unsupported counseling code: on claim line, compute whether a tobacco-use or opioid-use diagnosis appears on the beneficiary's claim history within the lookback; fires on an exact absence of any supporting diagnosis; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Clara Ann Mason (veterinarian, DEA-registered practitioner)
SchemeSummary: A licensed veterinarian ordered 14,200 dosage units of hydrocodone/acetaminophen and 1,400 dosage units of oxycodone HCL from a veterinary wholesaler between March 2018 and July 2023, failed to secure them or keep required DEA purchase, dispensing and inventory records, and after a 2023 administrative inspection warrant found at least 6,593 dosage units (9,796 total controlled substance units) unaccounted for, submitted apparently fabricated records claiming she dispensed large opioid quantities to pets before euthanasia; the court entered a $956,709 default judgment of maximum civil penalties.
WaysToIdentify: There is no insurance claim and no adjudication point here, since the controlled substances were bought from a wholesaler and never billed to a payer. The nearest detection route is ARCOS and wholesaler pedigree data showing hydrocodone and oxycodone purchases far above same-species veterinary practice norms for the DEA registration. A second route is the DEA registrant biennial inventory and dispensing log reconciliation, where purchased units minus documented dispensed and destroyed units leaves a large unaccounted balance.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Wholesaler purchase outlier: on DEA registrant number x quarter, compute the sum of Schedule II and III dosage units purchased from ARCOS and distributor pedigree files; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-registrant-class veterinary peers; action site visit by the state board and DEA inspection referral. 2) Inventory reconciliation gap: on DEA registrant number x audit period, compute purchased units minus dispensed, destroyed and on-hand inventory units from the required DEA records; fires when the unaccounted balance exceeds zero; action postpay audit of licensure and administrative inspection warrant.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
FraudEntity: PharmaLogic Holdings Corporation (radiopharmaceutical company) and nine of its acquired subsidiaries
SchemeSummary: Nine entities acquired by PharmaLogic Holdings filed NRC Form 526 certifications falsely claiming small-entity status under 10 C.F.R. 171.16(c), even though they exceeded the size limits, thereby obtaining reduced U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission annual licensing fees; the company agreed to pay $350,000 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point, so no payer-side prepay edit exists here. The nearest route is regulator-side verification of certified small-entity status against SAM.gov, IRS receipts data and corporate parent filings. Ownership change filings showing acquisition by a larger holding company should void prior small-entity fee certifications automatically.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on licensee entity EIN, compute the count of affiliated entities sharing a common parent in SAM.gov and Dun & Bradstreet, and refer certifications where the aggregated receipts exceed the regulatory size standard to fee recovery.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Ankita Singh, M.D. (physician who signed brace orders); Alfonso Bailey (leader) and Eric King and 19 others associated with Eye for Change Youth and Family Services, Inc.; Cleveland Clinic Foundation; Rite Aid Corporation and 10 subsidiaries/affiliates; Elixir Insurance Company, RX Options LLC and RX Solutions LLC (Rite Aid subsidiaries); Gregory Gerber, M.D.
State_County: Ohio - Northern District of Ohio (Cleveland, Akron, Toledo, Youngstown areas)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (Ohio); National Institutes of Health (grant funding)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Device, DME; Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; Retention of Overpayment; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Omnibus office round-up describing several separate health care fraud matters: Dr. Ankita Singh signed over 11,000 orthotic brace orders for ~3,000 Medicare beneficiaries she never examined, causing more than $8 million in fraudulent Medicare claims (26 months prison, $4,470,931.02 restitution); 21 people tied to Eye for Change Youth and Family Services manipulated billing, falsified records and used client identities to bill Ohio Medicaid (Bailey and King each 36 months, $4.5M restitution, $4.3M forfeited); Cleveland Clinic paid $7.6M over false NIH grant applications; Rite Aid entities paid $7.5M for medically unnecessary prescriptions and $101M for misreported Medicare drug rebates; and Dr. Gregory Gerber received 42 months plus $4.7M civil judgment and $861,892.13 restitution for medically unnecessary opioid prescribing.}
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, orthotic L-code claims carry an ordering NPI with no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI signs brace orders for thousands of distinct beneficiaries across many states in a quarter. Behavioral health claims list rendering staff whose NPI and state licence board file show no credential on the date of service. Beneficiary identifiers appear on counseling claims whose service dates conflict with the same beneficiary's inpatient or facility claims. Pharmacy claims show controlled-substance NDCs from one prescriber NPI at morphine-equivalent volumes above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim linking that NPI and beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Signer dispersion: on ordering NPI x month, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries and distinct beneficiary states on DMEPOS orders; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Rendering credential mismatch: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute an exact match of the NPI against the state licence board file and OIG LEIE effective dates; fires on any registry mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Recovery Centers of America (RCA) / TRC-OC, trading as Recovery Centers of America Holdings, LLC (drug and alcohol treatment provider)
State_County: Pennsylvania - Montgomery County (King of Prussia, corporate headquarters); Pennsylvania; Maryland
PayerName: Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; Medicaid
SchemeSummary: RCA allegedly billed the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and Medicaid from 2017 through 2019 for drug and alcohol treatment services at certain facilities that it failed to actually provide or document, and separately, DEA audits of its Pennsylvania and Maryland facilities from 2019 to 2024 found unlawful dispensing of controlled substances, missing controlled substances and recordkeeping failures. RCA paid $1 million to resolve the Controlled Substances Act allegations and $1 million for the False Claims Act allegations, with a qui tam whistleblower (a former Outcomes Supervisor) receiving $230,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, residential and IOP per-diem claims exceed the facility's licensed bed count on the same date of service. Group therapy HCPCS units billed per counselor NPI per day exceed feasible clinical hours in 24 hours. Dispensed buprenorphine or methadone NDC quantities exceed the facility DEA registrant's ARCOS purchase totals for the same period. Beneficiary attendance rosters requested by ADR are absent for a large share of billed session dates. Beneficiaries show billed treatment days overlapping paid inpatient or incarceration-period claims in the payer's own remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Bed-capacity overflow: on facility NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with paid per-diem residential lines divided by licensed beds on the state licence file; fires when the ratio exceeds one; action prepay edit. 2) Counselor hour impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of billed therapy units converted to minutes across all group and individual codes; fires when total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Dispense-versus-pedigree gap: on facility DEA registrant x quarter, compute dispensed controlled-substance units from claims minus ARCOS wholesaler acquisition units; fires when dispensed exceeds acquired; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Health Wealth Safe, Inc.; Dr. Subodh Agrawal (owner)
SchemeSummary: At the direction of owner Dr. Subodh Agrawal, Health Wealth Safe billed Medicare for remote physiologic monitoring services despite failing to supply patients with devices that automatically transmitted readings without human intervention, as Medicare coverage requires, making the claims non-reimbursable; resolved via a $1.29 million qui tam settlement with $238,650 to the relator.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, RPM CPT 99454 device-supply lines appear with no matching device supply or DME acquisition record for that beneficiary. Billed 99457 treatment-management minutes per rendering NPI per day exceed feasible staffed hours in 24 hours. The 99454 line is billed in a 30-day period without the required 16 days of transmitted readings documented on ADR. Beneficiaries have no prior E/M encounter with the billing NPI establishing the monitored chronic condition. The practice's RPM volume rises from near-zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of a PECOS ownership or specialty change.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Device-supply substantiation: on beneficiary x billing NPI x 30-day period, compute the count of documented transmission days supporting CPT 99454; fires when fewer than the 16 days the code requires; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Monitoring minute impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of 99457 and 99458 minutes across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) RPM volume ramp: on billing NPI x month, compute paid RPM line counts versus that NPI's trailing twelve-month baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: Dr. Samuel R. Chacon (OB-GYN, owner of Women's Health Center of Reno)
PayerName: Medicaid; Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield Healthcare Solutions; Health Plan of Nevada; Molina Healthcare of Nevada; Silversummit Healthplan; Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield of Nevada; Cigna Healthcare
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges an OB-GYN billed Medicaid and multiple commercial plans for medically unnecessary gynecologic tests and surgeries (hysterectomies, anterior/posterior and enterocele repairs, vaginal vault suspensions, bladder slings, urodynamic studies, physical therapy, ultrasounds), falsifying patient medical records to add symptoms patients never reported and misrepresenting diagnoses to patients; some procedures caused serious bodily injury.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the share of the surgeon's female patients receiving hysterectomy or sling CPT codes exceeds same-specialty peer rates. Urodynamic study CPT 51728 and pelvic ultrasound units per beneficiary per year exceed the provider's own trailing baseline. Diagnosis codes supporting incontinence surgery appear first on the claim dated the same day as the surgical booking. Prior-authorisation submissions repeat identical symptom narratives verbatim across unrelated beneficiaries. Post-operative complication and readmission claims for this rendering NPI's patients exceed peer rates in the payer's remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Surgical propensity outlier: on rendering NPI x year, compute the ratio of major gynecologic surgery claims to the count of distinct female patients with any E/M claim; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Diagnostic workup stacking: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the count of urodynamic and pelvic ultrasound units billed within 90 days before a surgical CPT; fires when above the provider's trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Harm signal rate: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the rate of post-surgical complication or readmission claims per 100 operated beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Hampshire
FraudEntity: Erik X. Alonso (psychotherapist, excluded provider)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Alonso, excluded from federal health care programs after a 2015 health care fraud conviction, began working in March 2022 for a New Hampshire-based telehealth mental health provider and provided psychotherapy services billed to New Hampshire Medicaid despite being on the HHS-OIG Exclusion List; he also caused claims for counseling sessions not provided as represented, including sessions in which a patient helped him with personal tasks such as preparing a presidential pardon application and medical licensure documents, causing NH Medicaid to pay about $173,998.83.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment and adjudication, the rendering NPI on psychotherapy claims matches an active entry on the OIG LEIE exclusion file. The individual appears as employed staff on the group's CMS-855B managing-employee fields despite exclusion. Billed psychotherapy CPT 90837 minutes per rendering NPI per day exceed feasible hours in 24 hours. Telehealth session claims lack corresponding platform connection logs when requested by documentation request. NPPES shows the rendering NPI enumerated in a state distant from all billed beneficiaries' residence ZIPs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Exclusion registry match: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute an exact match against OIG LEIE names, NPIs and exclusion effective dates; fires on any active exclusion covering the service date; action claim suspension. 2) Staff roster screen: on group TIN x quarter, compute the count of CMS-855B listed owners, managing employees and rendering NPIs matching LEIE or state licence-board sanction files; fires when the count exceeds zero; action payment suspension. 3) Therapy hour impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of psychotherapy CPT time-code minutes across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maine
FraudEntity: The Opportunity Alliance (residential treatment provider operating Morrison Place)
SchemeSummary: The Opportunity Alliance sent misleading urine drug requisition forms to Morrison Place clients' medical providers and treated individual test orders as standing orders for three presumptive and definitive urine drug tests per week for up to a year, directing a third-party lab to perform and bill Medicare and MaineCare directly for tests that were not medically necessary or validly ordered and instead served as residential monitoring.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, presumptive and definitive urine drug codes 80305-80307 and G0480-G0483 repeat on a fixed weekly cadence per beneficiary for months. The ordering NPI on the requisition has no corresponding office or telehealth encounter claim near most collection dates of service. Definitive testing is billed on the same date of service as a presumptive screen without a documented abnormal presumptive result. One residential treatment facility address supplies nearly all beneficiaries on a single lab NPI's toxicology claims. Ordering NPI signature dates on the lab's requisition and standing-order forms precede dates of service by up to a year.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Standing-order cadence: on beneficiary x lab NPI, compute the count of distinct toxicology dates of service per week for 80305-80307 and G0480-G0483 over a rolling 90 days; fires when the weekly count is constant and above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 2) Orderless requisition: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the days between the toxicology date of service and the nearest E/M or behavioral health encounter claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Reflex-without-trigger and facility concentration: on lab NPI x facility address, compute the ratio of definitive G0480-G0483 lines to presumptive lines with a documented abnormal result, plus the share of beneficiaries sharing one residential address; fires when either exceeds the provider's own trailing baseline and peer percentile; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Daniel Jacobsen (Licensed Clinical Social Worker/psychotherapist)
SchemeSummary: A licensed clinical social worker billed Virginia Medicaid and Medicare at least $335,824 for psychotherapy services never rendered, including days billed for more than 16 hours of services, and used higher-paying codes for more complex services than provided, supported by fabricated psychotherapy progress notes. He pled guilty, was sentenced to three months, paid restitution/forfeiture/fine, and then paid an additional $449,014.93 civil settlement (total $1,201,174.55).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, summed timed psychotherapy units for CPT 90832, 90834 and 90837 on one rendering NPI exceed 16 service hours in a day. The same rendering NPI bills 90837 for nearly every encounter, far above the 90834 share seen in peer remittance history. Claim dates of service fall on dates the beneficiary has inpatient or other facility claims that preclude an outpatient therapy session. Beneficiary rosters show identical session lengths and start times repeated across unrelated patients on the same date of service. Requested progress notes are near-verbatim duplicates across beneficiaries, with no signature or licence number matching the state board file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible clinician day: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total therapy minutes implied by CPT 90832, 90834, 90837 and 90853 units; fires when the total exceeds 16 hours in a 24-hour day; action prepay edit. 2) Highest-intensity code share: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of 90837 lines to all psychotherapy lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers and above the provider's trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Conflicting-location overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of outpatient psychotherapy lines overlapping an inpatient or facility stay on the beneficiary's other claims; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Wisconsin
FraudEntity: Justin Drew Hanson (co-owner, Noah Associates); Mohammed Kazim Ali (co-owner, Noah Associates); Noah Associates (clinical laboratory)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Hanson and co-owner Ali, of Milwaukee-area clinical lab Noah Associates, paid over $400,000 in kickbacks (concealed by sham agreements) to the owner of a substance use treatment clinic for referrals of Medicaid and Medicare patients for urine drug tests that no physician ordered and that were not medically necessary; the lab collected over $2.2 million. Hanson got 21 months and $2.2M restitution plus a $75,000 fine; Ali was sentenced to 15 months.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, definitive urine drug testing G-codes carry an ordering NPI that has no E/M or counseling claim with that beneficiary. A single substance use clinic NPI accounts for nearly all of one lab's presumptive and definitive UDT referral volume. Definitive testing panels bill the maximum drug-class tier on nearly every specimen with no presumptive screen first. Beneficiaries show weekly UDT claims far exceeding the frequency in their treatment plan documented on prior-authorisation records. The lab's CMS-855B ownership and PECOS records show payments or common addresses linking it to the referring clinic's owner.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referral concentration: on laboratory NPI x quarter, compute the share of UDT claim lines whose ordering NPI belongs to a single clinic TIN; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit and payment suspension. 2) Order without encounter: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between UDT date of service and the nearest E/M or SUD treatment claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 3) Definitive tier saturation: on laboratory NPI x month, compute the ratio of highest-tier definitive UDT lines to total UDT lines and the presumptive-to-definitive ratio; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Vicki Lynn Dowdy (home health attendant)
SchemeSummary: Dowdy, contracted as a home health attendant for two Medicaid recipients in the Roanoke area, submitted fraudulent timesheets and billed Virginia Medicaid for 1,970.5 hours of personal home health and respite care never rendered, receiving $24,760 in payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed personal care and respite units for the attendant NPI exceed 24 hours on given dates of service. EVV visit records show no check-in or check-out matching the billed units on those dates. Submitted timesheets carry signatures dated after the billing date on the payer's remittance history. Two beneficiaries are billed by the same attendant for overlapping minutes at different service addresses. Billed hours exceed the authorised hours on the Medicaid service plan and prior-authorisation record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Attendant hour ceiling: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of personal care and respite units converted to hours across all beneficiaries; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or overlapping visit minutes occur at distinct addresses; action prepay edit. 2) EVV reconciliation: on claim line, compute the difference between billed units and EVV-verified visit minutes for the same beneficiary, attendant and date; fires when no matching EVV record exists or the gap is nonzero; action claim suspension. 3) Authorisation overrun: on beneficiary x attendant NPI x week, compute billed hours minus prior-authorised hours; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Robert Burkich, M.D. (physician); Preventive Medicine Anti-Aging & Chelation, Inc. (his practice)
SchemeSummary: Burkich billed Medicare for chelation therapy using edetate calcium disodium (EDTA) - a drug reimbursable only for lead poisoning or lead encephalopathy - for patients who did not have lead poisoning, falsely representing to Medicare that patients suffered from lead poisoning or other heavy-metal diseases to evade coverage restrictions; he and his practice agreed to pay $700,000 under DOJ ability-to-pay guidelines.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, J0600 edetate calcium disodium claims carry no lead poisoning ICD-10 diagnosis, or carry one unsupported by any prior encounter. The billing NPI shows lead-poisoning diagnoses on a share of its panel far above same-specialty peers. Beneficiaries have no blood lead level laboratory claim preceding the chelation infusion date of service. The same beneficiary receives repeated chelation infusion lines across months without any interval lead testing claim. Infusion administration codes are billed in office place of service at volumes above the provider's own trailing baseline.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Lead diagnosis without test: on beneficiary x billing NPI, compute the count of J0600 chelation lines with a lead toxicity diagnosis but zero blood lead level laboratory claims in the lookback window; fires when the count is above zero; action prepay edit. 2) Diagnosis prevalence outlier: on billing NPI x year, compute the share of distinct beneficiaries carrying heavy-metal toxicity diagnoses; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Repeat infusion series: on beneficiary x HCPCS J0600, compute the count of infusion dates over twelve months without an intervening lead level result; fires when the count exceeds the labelled treatment course; action prior-authorisation requirement.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Daniel Iulian Teutoc (a/k/a "Simon Mikula"); Constantin Calin
State_County: Louisiana - Laplace, Slidell, Harvey, Boutte, Chalmette, and New Orleans (Eastern District of Louisiana)
SchemeSummary: Two Romanian nationals allegedly visited Walmart stores across southeastern Louisiana and used magnets to activate card skimming devices previously installed by co-conspirators at points of sale, electronically capturing customers' credit, debit and EBT card data on their cell phones and forwarding it to a co-conspirator so fraudulent charges could be made.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point here, since the theft is card data captured at retail point of sale. The nearest detection route is EBT processor monitoring for card-present transactions clustering at terminals previously used by other compromised cards. Card networks' common point of purchase analysis on settlement files identifies the specific store terminals where the compromised accounts overlap.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on merchant terminal ID x week, compute the count of distinct EBT accounts later reporting disputed transactions, and refer terminals above the calibrated threshold for physical inspection.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Tax Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: William Skaggs Jr. (owner of Nastar Roofing); Billie Adkison (office administrator/payroll manager); Nastar Roofing
SchemeSummary: Owner and payroll administrator of a roofing company withdrew over $21 million from company bank accounts to pay employees predominantly in cash without withholding Social Security, Medicare and federal income taxes, and filed or caused false employment tax returns that omitted the cash wages, causing a tax loss of nearly $2.5 million. Skaggs received 36 months and Adkison a year and a day.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the loss is unremitted employment tax on cash wages. The nearest detection route is IRS matching of Forms 941 wage totals against bank cash withdrawal volumes reported on currency transaction reports. State workers' compensation payroll filings compared with the same employer's federal wage returns show the same understatement.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on employer EIN x quarter, compute the ratio of aggregate cash withdrawals in CTR filings to wages reported on Form 941 and refer ratios above the calibrated percentile versus same-industry peers.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Anthony Delmaro (owner of Kings Roofing commercial roofing/paving business)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Delmaro concealed roughly $20.9 million in roofing/paving receipts (2012-2022) by cashing customer checks at check cashers, using UPS-mailbox addresses, an alias ('Sonny Rubino'), and false Forms 1099/W-9 in his father's or a relative's name, and never filed income or payroll returns; by hiding this income he also collected more than $500,000 in Connecticut Husky Health low-income Medicaid benefits from 2019 to April 2025. He agreed to pay $1,129,669 restitution to the IRS and $578,259 to Connecticut Medicaid.
WaysToIdentify: At Medicaid eligibility determination, the applicant's declared income has no matching wage or 1099 record in the state new hire and income verification files. Business registration and contractor licence records list the applicant as owner of an active roofing entity absent from the eligibility application. The mailing address on the eligibility file resolves to a commercial mailbox rather than a residence in the postal address file. Asset and check-casher currency transaction data show deposits far above the declared household income for the eligibility period. Names and Social Security numbers on associated Forms 1099 belong to relatives rather than the actual payee in IRS matching.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Income declaration mismatch: on beneficiary Medicaid case, compute declared annual household income minus the sum of IRS and state wage, 1099 and business receipt records for the same year; fires when the gap exceeds the eligibility threshold; action claim suspension and eligibility redetermination. 2) Hidden ownership screen: on applicant SSN, compute the count of active business entities listing that person as officer in the secretary of state and contractor licence files; fires when the count is above zero and unreported; action documentation request. 3) Commercial address flag: on eligibility case address, compute an exact match against the USPS commercial mail receiving agency file; fires on exact registry match; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Anthony Delmaro (owner/operator of Kings Roofing)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Delmaro concealed roughly $20.9 million in roofing/paving business receipts from the IRS by cashing customer checks at check cashers, using UPS mailbox addresses, aliases and false Forms 1099/W-9 in his father's and a family member's names, and never filing income or payroll returns; while concealing this income he also collected more than $500,000 in Connecticut Husky Health (Medicaid) low-income medical benefits, and was ordered to repay $1,129,669 to the IRS and $578,259 to Connecticut Medicaid.
WaysToIdentify: At Medicaid eligibility determination, declared income is contradicted by state and federal wage, 1099 and business receipt files for the same tax year. Secretary of state and contractor licence registries show the applicant owning an active paving business not disclosed on the application. The residence address on the eligibility record matches a commercial mail receiving agency in the USPS file. Check-casher currency transaction reports show deposit volumes incompatible with the declared low-income status. Forms 1099 tied to the business carry relatives' taxpayer identification numbers rather than the actual earner in IRS matching.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Income verification gap: on Medicaid case x benefit year, compute declared income minus summed IRS, state wage and 1099 amounts; fires when the difference exceeds the program income limit; action claim suspension and redetermination. 2) Undisclosed business ownership: on applicant SSN, compute the count of active entity registrations and contractor licences naming that individual; fires when that count is above zero with no disclosed self-employment income; action documentation request. 3) Address registry mismatch: on case mailing address, compute exact match to the commercial mail receiving agency file; fires on exact registry match; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Aaron Rossi (owner/operator of Reditus Labs); Reditus Labs
State_County: Illinois - Peoria County (Peoria); Illinois - Tazewell County (Morton)
PayerName: Medicare; State of Illinois; private health insurance companies
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Through his laboratory Reditus Labs, Rossi submitted COVID-19 test claims with codes for services that were never performed and collected payment from more than one source for the same test, defrauding Medicare, the State of Illinois and private insurers of a combined $525,520.61; he received an additional 37 months in prison and forfeiture of a $1 million recreational vehicle (separate prior fraud case carried 5 years and over $3 million in restitution/fines).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the same COVID-19 test CPT for the same beneficiary and specimen date appears on claims to Medicare, the state program and a commercial payer. Claim lines bill high-complexity or add-on test codes on specimens with no corresponding collection or accession record in the lab's submitted logs. Test volume per day at the lab NPI exceeds the instrument throughput declared on its CMS-855B enrolment. Beneficiaries on the claims have residence ZIPs with no other encounter linking them to that laboratory. Billed test counts exceed reagent and supply purchases in wholesaler pedigree data for the same period.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Cross-payer duplicate: on beneficiary x test CPT x date of service, compute the count of distinct payers billed by the same laboratory NPI; fires when that count exceeds one without a coordination-of-benefits indicator; action prepay edit. 2) Throughput impossibility: on laboratory NPI x date of service, compute total billed tests divided by declared instrument capacity and staffed hours; fires when the implied run rate exceeds physical capacity; action claim suspension. 3) Reagent-to-claim ratio: on laboratory NPI x month, compute billed test count minus test kits purchased in wholesaler pedigree data; fires when the difference is positive; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: RST-Sanexas, Inc. (manufacturer and marketer of electric stimulation devices); Richard Sorgnard (principal owner); Lisa Sorgnard (principal owner); Morhea Sorgnard (principal owner)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Sanexas and its owners marketed the neoGEN-Series electrical stimulation device for uses outside its FDA clearance (acute pain, nerve regrowth, combined with vitamin injections), causing provider customers to bill Medicare for non-covered, medically unnecessary electrical nerve stimulation, vitamin injections, and follow-up ENFD punch-biopsy testing; they also paid volume-based discounts/commissions to provider-owned distributorships and received commissions from a diagnostic lab for referring providers for ENFD testing, in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute. Settlement of $1.5 million, based on ability to pay, is joint across the company and the three owner defendants.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, electrical stimulation codes are billed with acute pain or neuropathy diagnoses outside the device's covered indications in the national coverage determination. The same beneficiary receives stimulation, vitamin injection and ENFD punch biopsy lines on the same date of service in a repeating bundle. Provider adoption clusters sharply by distributor territory, with new billers appearing in cohorts after a single marketing contact. Ownership fields on CMS-855 filings show treating providers holding equity in the distributorship supplying the device. One laboratory receives nearly all ENFD biopsy referrals from that same provider cohort.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Non-covered indication edit: on claim line, compute whether the electrical stimulation HCPCS and diagnosis pair matches an indication listed in the coverage determination; fires on exact registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 2) Bundled triad velocity: on rendering NPI x month, compute the share of beneficiaries receiving stimulation, vitamin injection and ENFD biopsy within seven days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Distributor-owner overlap: on rendering NPI, compute graph degree linking its CMS-855 owners to distributor and laboratory TINs receiving its referrals; fires when any shared owner exists; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Tina Marie Armstrong (owner, Safe at Home Medical Equipment and Supplies, LLC); Safe at Home Medical Equipment and Supplies, LLC; Dee Alice Moton (owner/licensed massage therapist, Flowing Hands Massage Clinical Therapy)
State_County: South Carolina - Florence; South Carolina - Aiken County (Aiken)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Device, DME; Unbundling; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Two South Carolina defendants charged in the 2025 national takedown: Armstrong allegedly billed Medicare and Medicaid $198,981.55 (of which $104,577.74 was paid) through her DME company for equipment no longer in service, never delivered, or not physician-authorized, and used patient identities; Moton allegedly billed the Veterans Administration $2,373,147.22 over two years through her massage therapy clinic for services never rendered, including mutually exclusive E&M codes, telehealth codes for in-person visits, unauthorized specialized services, and treatments for conditions veterans did not have (e.g., wheelchair therapy for a veteran with no wheelchair).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, DME claims carry no ordering physician NPI with a prior face-to-face encounter for that beneficiary in the lookback window. Rental line items continue after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File or after equipment pickup. Massage and therapy claims pair mutually exclusive E/M codes on the same date of service, tripping NCCI edits. Telehealth place-of-service and modifier combinations conflict with in-person therapy codes billed the same day. Wheelchair-related therapy codes appear for beneficiaries with no wheelchair HCPCS in their claim history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order authorisation check: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the count of face-to-face E/M claims between that NPI and the beneficiary before the DME date of service; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Mutually exclusive pairing: on rendering NPI x beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of code pairs violating NCCI mutually exclusive and telehealth place-of-service rules; fires when the count is above zero; action claim suspension. 3) Equipment-dependent therapy: on beneficiary, compute whether a device-specific therapy code is billed with zero prior claims for that device HCPCS; fires on exact absence; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Alabama
FraudEntity: Saad Enterprises Inc., d/b/a Saad Healthcare (hospice provider)
SchemeSummary: Saad Healthcare allegedly billed Medicare's hospice benefit for 21 patients in Alabama who were not terminally ill (life expectancy over six months) and thus ineligible, despite knowing they did not meet eligibility requirements; resolved for $3 million following a qui tam suit by two former employees who receive $540,000.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, hospice election periods extend far beyond six months with no documented decline in the certification of terminal illness. Live discharge rates at the hospice NPI are above the calibrated percentile versus peer hospices. Beneficiaries on the hospice benefit continue to have curative treatment or hospital claims from other providers. Face-to-face recertification encounters required at the third benefit period are missing from the attending NPI's claim history. The certifying physician's NPI signs terminal illness certifications for a share of the hospice's census far above peers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Long-stay concentration: on hospice NPI x quarter, compute the share of beneficiaries with cumulative hospice days beyond two benefit periods and no hospitalisation; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer hospices; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Live discharge rate: on hospice NPI x year, compute live discharges divided by total discharges from claim status codes; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit. 3) Recertification encounter gap: on beneficiary x benefit period, compute days between the recertification date and the nearest face-to-face encounter claim by the attending or hospice physician; fires when no encounter exists within the required window; action prepay edit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Michael Andrew Scott (owner/operator of Trusted Medical Partnership); Trusted Medical Partnership
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate; Device, DME
SchemeSummary: Scott told investors that he or his company Trusted Medical Partnership held purchase orders from health care providers for medical devices but lacked capital to fill them, soliciting loans with promises of quick, risk-free returns; the purchase orders were fabricated or doctored, the company conducted no legitimate business, and he spent the roughly $470,000 taken from at least 16 victims on casino gambling, personal expenses, and Ponzi-style payments to earlier investors.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the money came from private investors rather than a benefit program. The nearest detection route is verifying the claimed purchase orders directly with the named hospital or provider purchasers before funding. State securities regulators can match the promoter's promissory note offerings against bank records showing gambling and investor-to-investor transfers.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on lender or investor bank account, compute the share of incoming funds paid out to earlier investors within thirty days and refer accounts above the calibrated threshold to securities regulators.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Philip Yen, M.D. (radiologist; DEA registrant at Sutter Imaging Capitol Pavilion)
SchemeSummary: As the DEA registrant for Sutter Imaging Capitol Pavilion, Dr. Yen allegedly failed to keep the detailed receipt and dispensing records for controlled substances required by the Controlled Substances Act; a 2022 DEA inspection found multiple recordkeeping violations, and he agreed to pay $125,000 in civil penalties and complete CSA training.
WaysToIdentify: There is no benefit claim and no adjudication point, since the violation is controlled substance recordkeeping at a registered site. The nearest detection route is DEA comparison of ARCOS distributor shipment data to the registrant against the site's biennial inventory and dispensing logs. Registrant-level purchase volumes of contrast-sedation controlled substances can be compared with imaging procedure volumes billed under the site's NPI.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on DEA registration number x year, compute ARCOS units received minus units documented as dispensed, wasted or on hand, and schedule an inspection when the unexplained difference is above zero.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maine
FraudEntity: SVCMC Inc., formerly known as Saint Vincents Catholic Medical Centers of New York (health plan participating in the Uniformed Services Family Health Plan)
PayerName: TRICARE (Defense Health Agency, Department of Defense) - Uniformed Services Family Health Plan
SchemeSummary: Saint Vincent received capitated payments from the Defense Health Agency to provide care to military retirees and families under the USFHP program; after learning in 2012 that the capitation rates had been miscalculated, producing four years of overpayments, it allegedly concealed the overpayments, kept submitting invoices at the inflated rates, and conspired with the five other USFHP plans to avoid repaying the money. It agreed to pay $29 million, with the qui tam relators receiving $5.655 million.
WaysToIdentify: At payment reconciliation, the capitation rate on submitted invoices does not match the rate in the contracting agency's approved rate schedule. Per-member-per-month amounts paid diverge from the actuarially certified rate file for the same enrolment month. Enrolment counts on the invoice exceed the eligibility file's member months for that plan and period. Retained credit balances persist on the plan's ledger beyond the sixty-day overpayment return deadline. Identical rate variances appear simultaneously across all plans under the same program, indicating a shared rate error.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Rate schedule match: on plan TIN x month, compute invoiced per-member-per-month rate minus the contracted rate in the approved rate file; fires on any nonzero difference; action prepay edit. 2) Member month reconciliation: on plan TIN x month, compute invoiced member months minus eligibility file member months; fires when the difference is positive; action claim suspension. 3) Overpayment retention clock: on plan TIN, compute days since identification of a credit balance or rate variance; fires when days exceed the statutory sixty-day return deadline; action payment suspension and postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Terrance Owens Elliott, a.k.a. 'Tony Elliott' (church pastor, former San Bernardino City Council candidate, self-appointed trust co-trustee)
SchemeSummary: Elliott allegedly told a long-time friend she would lose her Medicare and Social Security benefits if she took an inheritance directly, set himself up as sole-signatory trustee of a trust holding her money using a fraudulently modified trust agreement, and diverted trust funds and her Social Security payments to his church and personal expenses; in related schemes he took a $65,000 'loan' from another victim's corporation via signed blank checks and caused a nonprofit to issue about 32 checks for fabricated litigation-related debts, totaling roughly $238,563 in losses.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the loss is diverted trust and Social Security funds. The nearest detection route is Social Security representative payee change monitoring when benefits redirect to a third-party account. Bank anti-money-laundering review can compare fiduciary account outflows to a church or personal accounts against the trust's stated purpose.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on beneficiary Social Security account, compute the count of payee or direct-deposit account changes within twelve months and require identity verification when above the calibrated threshold.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey; U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Frank Procopio (leader of '10th and O Crew'); Michael Procopio (co-leader)
SchemeSummary: Frank Procopio, a leader of South Philadelphia's '10th and O Crew,' obtained prescription oxycodone pills from area doctors' offices and, with co-conspirators working in shifts, sold them out of a 24-hour restaurant; law enforcement made a controlled buy and observed him splitting the proceeds. He received 57 months; his brother and co-leader Michael Procopio was convicted and sentenced to 72 months.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim for the street sales themselves, but the upstream office visits and fills are visible. At adjudication, oxycodone fills concentrate among a small set of prescriber NPIs with short-interval repeat visits from the same beneficiaries. Prescription drug monitoring program data show beneficiaries filling at multiple pharmacies with overlapping days supply. Cash-pay fills of the same prescriber's oxycodone appear alongside insured fills, hiding volume from the payer.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber opioid concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute total oxycodone morphine milligram equivalents dispensed per distinct patient from PDMP and pharmacy claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Overlapping fill days: on beneficiary x opioid NDC, compute overlapping days supply across distinct dispensing pharmacy NPIs; fires when overlap days are above zero; action prepay edit and pharmacy lock-in.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Fraud Section and U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Semler Scientific Inc. (device manufacturer); Bard Peripheral Vascular Inc. and related companies (distributor)
SchemeSummary: Semler manufactured and marketed the FloChec and QuantaFlo photoplethysmography devices for diagnosing peripheral arterial disease and, with distributor Bard, told providers that tests using the devices were reimbursable under CPT codes 93922/93923/93924, even though the devices do not perform an ankle brachial index test and Medicare does not cover photoplethysmography, causing providers to submit non-covered claims to Medicare. Semler paid $29.75 million and Bard $7.2 million (total ~$36.95 million) to resolve the qui tam FCA allegations, with relators receiving about $6.5 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, CPT 93922, 93923 and 93924 are billed by providers whose only vascular equipment is a photoplethysmography device not performing ankle brachial index measurement. Providers newly billing these codes cluster by device distributor territory and start dates. Non-invasive physiologic vascular study volume per provider is far above same-specialty peers with no vascular specialty on NPPES taxonomy. The same beneficiary receives repeat vascular studies at short intervals with no intervening abnormal finding or treatment claim. Submitted study reports lack segmental pressures and waveform documentation required by the coverage determination.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Specialty-code mismatch: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the count of 93922-93924 lines where the NPPES taxonomy is non-vascular and no vascular procedure claims exist; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Device-code eligibility: on claim line, compute whether the vascular study code is supported by a documented ankle brachial index measurement in the ADR response; fires when documentation shows photoplethysmography only; action prepay edit. 3) Repeat study interval: on beneficiary x CPT, compute days between successive vascular study claims; fires when the gap is below the coverage determination's minimum interval; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Indiana
FraudEntity: James Henley (organizer; claimed CEO of five fake businesses); Jameka Henley (wife, charged); Jimmie Bickers (associate, charged); OnTrack Real Estate Solutions; LDI Investments Corp; Lucario Investments; 317 Traffic; Henley Real Estate Solutions
State_County: Indiana - Marion County (Indianapolis); Indiana - Vanderburgh County (Evansville); Indiana - Johnson County (Greenwood); Indiana - Hendricks County (Plainfield); Kentucky
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Henley, his wife, and an associate used stolen personal information of 76 real people to file 120 pandemic unemployment insurance applications in ten states, collecting $1,119,426 via 65 benefit debit cards; Henley also filed fraudulent deeds with the Marion County Recorder to steal and resell five Indianapolis homes, faked a mortgage payoff to pocket $255,000 in sale proceeds, and drew $98,000 from an attorney's IOLTA trust account to pay his auto loans. Total loss $2,927,758.95; restitution $1,887,426.63 ordered against Henley, whose co-defendants remain charged but not convicted.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the losses are unemployment benefits, real property and trust funds. The nearest detection route is cross-state unemployment claim matching on Social Security number, bank routing and debit card mailing address. County recorder deed filings can be matched against the owner of record and require notarised identity verification before recording.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on unemployment claimant SSN, compute the count of distinct states with active claims and the count of claims sharing one mailing address, and suspend disbursement when either exceeds one.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Rotimi Iluyomade (Annandale-based doctor); Obioma Alozie Ndubuka a.k.a. 'Bankroll'; Raymono Alfonzo Russell II; Cameron Isaiah Lewis; Elhadj Malick Diallo; Zion Oluwademilade Adeduwon; Kenechukwu Brian Okwara a.k.a. 'Kene'; Yared Michael Tesfaye a.k.a. 'Yar'
State_County: Virginia - Fairfax County (Annandale); Virginia - Western District of Virginia
SchemeSummary: Co-conspirators visited a doctor's Annandale medical clinic with lists of fake 'patients' using fabricated names and false addresses to obtain fraudulent prescriptions for promethazine-codeine solution, oxycodone pills and hydrocodone-chlorpheniramine ('Tussionex'), which were transmitted to pharmacies across the country (at least 70 filled in the Western District of Virginia) and the drugs then distributed in multiple states; the doctor was convicted of distributing over 7,000 oxycodone pills, 34,000 mL of Tussionex and 107,000 mL of promethazine-codeine, while the seven arrested co-conspirators are charged.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, prescriptions from one clinic NPI dispense at pharmacies hundreds of miles away in multiple states within the same week. Patient identities on the prescriptions have no other claim history and addresses that fail USPS validation. Promethazine-codeine and Tussionex volumes per prescriber are far above same-specialty peers in PDMP dispensing data. Multiple patients on the same prescriber's controlled substance prescriptions share a single address or telephone number in the pharmacy record. Fills are predominantly cash-pay despite the patients holding coverage in the eligibility file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber geographic dispersion: on prescriber NPI x week, compute the count of distinct pharmacy states and the median miles from clinic to dispensing pharmacy; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Ghost patient screen: on patient record x prescriber NPI, compute the count of prior claims and the exact match of the address to USPS validated addresses; fires when zero prior claims and address validation fails; action claim suspension and site visit. 3) Shared identifier cluster: on prescriber NPI, compute the count of distinct controlled substance patients sharing one address or phone number in pharmacy records; fires when the count exceeds a household size; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee; United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee (Chattanooga)
FraudEntity: Rebekah Proctor (operator of Franklin Springs Academy, a daycare business)
FraudTypeAll: Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Proctor, who operated a daycare business, withheld income and FICA taxes from employees' paychecks but willfully failed to account for and pay them over to the IRS (first quarter 2022), and separately submitted PPP loan applications with false certifications (that she was current on federal taxes and would use funds for payroll/business expenses), spending the $105,800 (April 2020) and $118,000 (February 2021) in loan proceeds on personal expenses; she agreed to $893,232.26 restitution to the IRS and $223,800 to the SBA.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, since the losses are unpaid payroll taxes and an SBA loan. The nearest detection route is IRS matching of Forms W-2 withholding totals against Form 941 deposits for the same quarter. SBA underwriting can verify PPP payroll certifications against filed 941s and state unemployment wage reports before disbursement.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on employer EIN x quarter, compute withheld tax reported on W-2 and 941 filings minus deposits received, and hold loan disbursement when the difference is positive.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Minnesota
FraudEntity: Abdinajib Hassan Yussuf (President and CEO, Star Autism Center LLC); Asha Farhan Hassan; Anthony Waddell Jefferson (HSS provider owner); Lester Brown (HSS provider owner); Hassan Ahmed Hussein (co-owner, Pristine Health LLC); Ahmed Abdirashid Mohamed (co-owner, Pristine Health LLC); Kaamil Omar Sallah (owner, SafeLodgings, Inc.); Ultimate Home Health Services LLC
State_County: Minnesota - Hennepin County (Minneapolis); Minnesota - Ramsey County (St. Paul)
PayerName: Medicaid (Minnesota Medical Assistance / Minnesota Health Care Programs - DHS); UCare
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Multiple defendants billed Minnesota Medicaid programs for services not rendered: Yussuf's Star Autism Center used unqualified teenage relatives as 'behavioral technicians,' recruited Somali-community children into EIDBI autism services, paid monthly cash kickbacks to parents scaled to the DHS authorization amount, and submitted inflated claims billed without providers' knowledge, obtaining over $6 million (Hassan separately charged in a $14 million autism scheme plus $465,000 from Feeding Our Future and pleaded guilty). In the Housing Stabilization Services program, Jefferson and Brown flew from Philadelphia to recruit shelter and Section 8 residents as 'The Housing Guys' and fabricated client notes and fake employee signatures ($3.5 million in claims for ~230 beneficiaries); Hussein and Mohamed's Pristine Health worked with Foundation First to fabricate Housing Focused Plans and bill ~$750,000 for ~100 beneficiaries; Sallah's SafeLodgings double-billed overlapping service hours, claiming ~$1.4 million and receiving ~$1.3 million before he fled the country; and a search warrant alleges Ultimate Home Health Services billed over $1.1 million in Integrated Community Supports claims for 13 clients, including services purportedly delivered on nearly every day of a 447-day period and to a client who had died.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, compare EIDBI and Housing Stabilization service dates against the beneficiary's Death Master File and Medicaid eligibility span. Sum billed service units per rendering technician NPI per day to expose totals exceeding 24 hours across clients. Check each billed behavioral technician against the DHS provider registry and state EIDBI qualification roster for a credential on the date of service. Compare Housing Focused Plan signatures and staff signature blocks across agencies for identical fabricated names appearing at unrelated TINs. Compare billed units to the DHS prior-authorization amount, since billing exactly to the authorized ceiling every month signals fabricated encounters.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible staff day: on rendering staff ID x date of service, compute summed billed service minutes across all beneficiaries and agencies; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or overlapping visit minutes exist; action prepay edit. 2) Deceased or ineligible service date: on claim line, compute the gap in days between date of service and the beneficiary's Death Master File or eligibility termination date; fires when the service date is after that date; action claim suspension. 3) Authorization-ceiling saturation: on provider NPI x beneficiary x month, compute billed units divided by the DHS prior-authorized units; fires when the ratio equals one for a share of beneficiaries above the calibrated percentile versus same-program peers; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Providence Park, Inc., d/b/a Ascension Living Providence Village (skilled nursing facility owner/operator); Ascension Providence, f/k/a Providence Health Services of Waco (acute care hospital owner/operator)
SchemeSummary: A Waco skilled nursing facility allegedly billed federal health care programs for medically unnecessary Ultra-High Resource Utilization Group therapy, while the affiliated acute care hospital allegedly billed individual outpatient therapy when only group therapy was delivered and billed therapy services at three clinics without a physician-signed plan of care; resolved by a $6,526,851.64 payment to the United States and Texas following a qui tam suit and partial self-disclosure.
WaysToIdentify: On MDS assessments, compute the share of Medicare stays coded Ultra-High RUG and compare to same-state SNF peers. Check therapy minutes recorded on MDS against the therapy logs and staffing hours reported on the facility cost report. At adjudication, compare outpatient individual therapy CPT 97110 volume against group therapy CPT 97150 at the same site and hour. Verify a physician-signed plan of care exists in the medical record for each outpatient therapy episode before the certification period lapses. Look for therapy minutes clustering just above the Ultra-High RUG threshold in the payer's own remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) RUG concentration: on facility NPI x quarter, compute the fraction of Part A days billed at Ultra-High RUG over total days from MDS-linked claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state SNF peers; action documentation request (ADR) then postpay audit. 2) Individual-versus-group impossibility: on rendering therapist NPI x date of service, compute summed individual therapy minutes from timed CPT units plus concurrent group sessions; fires when the sum exceeds available clinical minutes in the shift; action prepay edit. 3) Missing plan-of-care certification: on claim line, compute presence of a signed plan of care with a physician NPI and signature date within the certification window; fires when no matching certification exists; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Dennis Michael Peyroux (chiropractor, clinic owner)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Peyroux purchased Medicare beneficiary identifiers and fabricated audio recordings of people posing as beneficiaries 'requesting' over-the-counter COVID-19 test kits, then billed Medicare through his chiropractic clinic for kits that were never requested or otherwise ineligible, misappropriating a former nurse practitioner's credentials as the referring provider on thousands of claims; ~$3.3M billed and ~$3.2M paid in about six months, with $3.2M restitution plus over $1M forfeited from bank accounts.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check whether the referring NPI on OTC COVID test kit claims has any other claim relationship with the beneficiary. Compare the billing chiropractic taxonomy in NPPES against the HCPCS billed, since test-kit supply is outside that scope. Count distinct beneficiary states per billing NPI per week on kit claims and compare to the enrolled service area. Query the referring NPI's own claim submissions, since a credential used only as referrer with zero rendering activity signals misappropriation. Compare per-beneficiary kit quantities against the program's per-month allowance in the payer's remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Referrer-without-relationship: on claim line x referring NPI, compute the count of prior encounters between that referring NPI and the beneficiary in the lookback; fires when the count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Taxonomy-scope mismatch: on billing NPI x HCPCS, compute an exact match between the NPPES primary taxonomy and the allowed specialty list for the code; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Kit quantity and dispersion: on billing NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiaries billed the kit HCPCS and distinct beneficiary states; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers or per-beneficiary allowance is exceeded; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Robert Tassin, M.D. (physician, independent contractor for telemedicine companies)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Tassin, working as an independent contractor for purported telemedicine companies, signed doctors' orders for cancer genetic (CGx) tests for Medicare beneficiaries he never saw or spoke with, falsely certifying in medical records that the tests were medically necessary; his orders generated over $6.6 million in claims to Medicare (over $2 million reimbursed) and he was paid roughly $30 per order, totaling $106,757.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check for any evaluation-and-management or telehealth claim by the ordering NPI for the beneficiary before the CGx date of service. Count distinct beneficiaries and distinct states on CGx orders per ordering NPI per week against same-specialty peers. Compare the ordering physician's state licences in the state board file to the beneficiary residence states on the claims. Compute the share of that ordering NPI's total Medicare activity that is CGx orders routed to a small set of lab TINs. Check the beneficiary's diagnosis history for a cancer or hereditary-risk diagnosis supporting the 81400-series codes billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between CGx date of service and the most recent E/M or telehealth claim between that NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct lab billing NPIs on CGx orders; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension. 3) Licence-state mismatch: on claim line, compute exact match between beneficiary residence state and the ordering NPI's active state board licences; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Robert Tassin, M.D. (physician working for purported telemedicine companies)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Through purported telemedicine companies, a physician signed doctors' orders for cancer genetic (CGx) tests for Medicare beneficiaries he never saw or spoke to, falsely certifying in medical records that the tests were medically necessary; he was paid roughly $30 per order, and the orders generated over $6.6 million in claims to Medicare, of which over $2 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, verify a prior E/M or telehealth encounter between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary before the CGx test date. Count distinct beneficiaries per ordering NPI per week on CGx orders versus same-specialty peers. Match beneficiary residence states to the ordering physician's licences in the state board file. Compute the concentration of one orderer's CGx volume into a handful of laboratory TINs. Check whether the beneficiary has any oncology or family-history diagnosis in prior claims supporting the panel billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the CGx date of service and the nearest prior E/M claim linking that NPI and beneficiary; fires when none exists in the lookback; action prepay edit. 2) Lab-orderer graph concentration: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the share of ordered CGx claims paid to the single top laboratory TIN and the count of distinct beneficiaries; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action payment suspension. 3) Diagnosis support: on claim line, compute the count of supporting oncology or hereditary-risk ICD-10 codes in the beneficiary's 12-month claim history; fires when zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Argosy Investment Partners V, L.P. (Small Business Investment Company); Argosy Investment Partners Parallel V, L.P. (affiliate); AIP-ECS Holdings LLC (portfolio company, PPP borrower)
PayerName: U.S. Small Business Administration (Paycheck Protection Program)
SchemeSummary: AIP-ECS Holdings LLC applied for, received and obtained forgiveness of a $1,205,352 second-draw PPP loan although other companies in its Argosy SBIC corporate group had already received PPP loans that pushed the group over the $4 million second-draw cap, making the loan ineligible. The Argosy entities and AIP-ECS collectively agreed to pay $1.5 million to resolve a qui tam False Claims Act suit, with the relator receiving $150,000.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point in this loan-eligibility case. The nearest detection route is cross-matching SBA second-draw applications to corporate affiliation, using EIN and common ownership recorded in SBIC portfolio filings. A second route is summing all PPP loans across affiliated borrowers sharing an ultimate parent before forgiveness is granted.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on ultimate parent entity, compute the sum of second-draw PPP loan amounts across all EINs linked by ownership filings and fire before forgiveness when the sum exceeds the statutory group cap.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Unified Care Services LLC (skilled nursing facilities chain); Emmanual David (owner); Casa Montana LLC; Geri-Care Inc.; Geri Care V LLC; Pacific Palms Healthcare LLC; Foothill Care Center Inc.; Mount Megiddo LLC; Canyon Properties III LLC; Cloverleaf Enterprises Inc.; Foothill Care Center LLC; Foothill Care Center II LLC; David Kleis III LLC; David Kleis II LLC; Miramonte Enterprises LLC; Washington Enterprises III LLC
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: A Torrance-based skilled nursing facility chain and its affiliates allegedly falsely certified on 2020 PPP loan and loan-forgiveness applications that each entity was a small business with fewer than 500 employees, concealing that they were part of a larger commonly owned and controlled chain that made them ineligible; they agreed to pay $18 million to resolve FCA allegations arising from a qui tam suit, with the whistleblower receiving $2,070,000.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim adjudication step in this PPP eligibility case. The nearest detection route is linking each borrower EIN to common owners disclosed on CMS-855A ownership and PECOS affiliation records for the facility chain. A further route is summing employee counts across commonly owned facility EINs from payroll tax filings before forgiveness of the loan.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on ultimate owner identified in CMS-855A ownership fields, compute total employees across all commonly owned facility EINs and fire when the total exceeds the 500-employee small-business certification made on the application.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of West Virginia
FraudEntity: Thompson Construction Group Inc. (contractor, Sumter, South Carolina)
State_County: West Virginia - central and southern West Virginia (2016 flood-affected region)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery funds)
FraudTypeAll: Falsify certificate; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
SchemeSummary: Thompson Construction Group was awarded contracts, funded by HUD CDBG-DR disaster recovery grants, to rebuild homes destroyed in the June 2016 West Virginia flooding; it submitted invoices falsely certifying that contractually required crawl space drainage systems and sump pumps had been installed in flood-plain homes and was paid federal funds, when the water management systems were never installed. It agreed to pay $95,535 restitution plus $95,535 in double damages under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point in this grant construction case.
