JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Tennessee
FraudEntity: Kossie Lamon Simmons (beneficial owner); Katina Marzie Simmons (listed 70% owner and manager); Tritia Margalizita Townsend (pharmacist in charge); SarJo Pharmacy, Inc.
SchemeSummary: SarJo Pharmacy billed the Federal Employees' Compensation Fund approximately $28.7 million (paid ~$16.3 million) for prescription medications supposedly dispensed to injured U.S. Postal Service claimants, when the drugs were not based on valid prescriptions, were not stocked by the pharmacy, and were never dispensed. Three defendants - the beneficial owner, the 70% owner/manager, and the pharmacist in charge - were charged by indictment.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, reconcile dispensed NDC units against the pharmacy's wholesaler pedigree and purchase invoices for the same drugs. Verify the prescriber NPI and DEA on each claim have a documented injury-claim relationship in the workers' compensation case file. Count distinct claimants per prescriber and per pharmacy relative to the size of the local injured-worker population. Compare average paid amount per prescription for compounded and high-cost NDCs against peer pharmacies in remittance history. Check refill intervals and quantities against the days-supply already paid on prior fills for the same claimant.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dispense-versus-acquisition gap: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute billed units minus units evidenced in wholesaler pedigree purchase records; fires when billed exceeds purchased; action payment suspension. 2) Prescription validity linkage: on claim line, compute whether the prescriber NPI appears as a treating provider on the claimant's accepted injury case file and has a paid encounter within the lookback; fires on registry mismatch; action prepay edit. 3) Cost-per-script outlier: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute mean paid amount per prescription and the share of top-cost NDCs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies serving the same program; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: William Stephan (medical doctor, family practice); Erik Berg; Scott Trapp; Michael Luehrsen
PayerName: Express Scripts, Inc.; unspecified health care benefit programs
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: A family practice doctor signed pre-filled compounded medication prescriptions presented to him by Erik Berg for 19 patients who were not his own, without a doctor-patient relationship or review of authorized refills; the prescriptions, averaging over $16,000 each and refilled more than 500 times, generated $8,750,315 in reimbursements from health care benefit programs, and Stephan later falsely told an Express Scripts audit that he had written the prescriptions himself. Stephan received one year probation and 100 hours community service; co-defendants Berg, Luehrsen and Trapp were separately convicted.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, check whether the prescriber has any prior paid encounter with the beneficiary before a high-cost compounded prescription. Compute the share of one prescriber's compounded scripts routed to a single pharmacy NPI. Compare average paid amount per compounded prescription against the prescriber's own trailing baseline and family-practice peers. Count authorized refills billed against the refill count on the original prescription record obtained at audit. Look for beneficiaries residing far outside the prescriber's NPPES practice service area.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) No-relationship compound script: on beneficiary x prescriber NPI, compute days since the last paid E/M encounter before the compounded drug fill; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Prescriber-pharmacy channel concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the share of compounded prescriptions dispensed by a single pharmacy NPI and the mean paid amount per script; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit. 3) Refill overrun: on prescription number, compute the count of paid refills minus refills authorized on the original order; fires when the difference exceeds zero; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Health First Urgent Care (urgent care clinic, Richland and Pasco, Washington)
State_County: Washington - Benton County (Richland); Washington - Franklin County (Pasco)
SchemeSummary: Health First Urgent Care billed Medicare and Washington Medicaid for PCR respiratory and urinary tract infection panel tests by 'unbundling' the predetermined panel and billing each individual component test separately, collecting more than the bundled panel rate; Washington also alleged the clinic billed for more expensive panel tests that were not medically necessary, such as for patients presenting with Covid-19 symptoms.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count component molecular CPT codes (87631 series and individual 87xxx targets) billed on the same specimen date where a panel code exists. Compute the summed allowed amount of component lines versus the bundled panel rate for the same date and beneficiary. Check whether the ordering diagnosis on respiratory or urinary panel claims supports multi-target testing rather than a single Covid-19 test. Compare each ordering NPI's panel-to-single-test ratio against urgent care peers in remittance history. Verify the laboratory's CLIA certificate covers high-complexity molecular testing for the codes billed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Panel unbundling detector: on beneficiary x specimen date x laboratory NPI, compute the count of component molecular CPT lines that map to an existing panel code and the summed allowed amount versus that panel rate; fires when component count exceeds the panel threshold or summed allowed exceeds the panel rate; action prepay edit. 2) Diagnosis-to-panel support: on claim line, compute whether the submitted ICD-10 codes match the payer's covered indication list for the multi-target panel; fires on exact policy mismatch; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Ordering intensity outlier: on ordering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of multi-target panel tests to single-target tests per patient encounter; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus urgent care peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Health First Urgent Care (urgent care clinic, Richland and Pasco, Washington)
State_County: Washington - Richland (Benton County); Washington - Pasco (Franklin County)
SchemeSummary: The urgent care clinic billed Medicare and Washington Medicaid for each individual component test of PCR respiratory and urinary tract infection panels rather than billing the single bundled panel code, inflating reimbursement; Washington also alleged the clinic billed for more expensive panel tests that were not medically necessary, such as for patients presenting with Covid-19 symptoms. Resolved by a $2,807,729 False Claims Act settlement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, count the component CPT codes on one claim that together match an existing NAAT respiratory or UTI panel code. Same beneficiary, same date of service, same rendering NPI shows multiple single-target PCR lines instead of one panel code. The clinic's paid-per-encounter amount for respiratory testing sits far above same-specialty urgent care peers in remittance history. Large panels are billed on encounters whose only diagnosis code is a COVID-19 symptom code with no other indication. Panel-to-single-test ratio for this NPI jumped sharply above its own trailing baseline after a fee schedule change.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Panel rebundling detector: on beneficiary x date of service x rendering NPI, compute the count of component PCR CPT lines that map to a single multiplex panel code; fires when that count meets the panel's component threshold without the panel code billed; action prepay edit. 2) Panel intensity outlier: on provider NPI x month, compute the ratio of paid dollars for respiratory or UTI molecular testing to total encounters; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Indication mismatch: on claim line, compute the share of large-panel claims whose diagnosis set contains only COVID-19 symptom codes; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Troy Health, Inc. (Medicare Advantage, Part D, and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan provider)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Troy admitted that its territory managers used proprietary software to unlawfully access pharmacy records and customer lists containing beneficiaries' names, dates of birth, Medicare ID numbers and insurance information, then used that stolen data to make deceptive sales calls and to enroll beneficiaries into Troy's Medicare Advantage plans without consent, including batch/automatic enrollments (over 300 in one day, over 2,700 during the Jan-Mar 2022 open enrollment) and manual fraudulent entries on the CMS website; Troy also paid kickbacks to pharmacies for enrollment referrals submitted through its Troy.ai platform. Resolved via non-prosecution agreement with a $1,430,008 criminal penalty adjusted for ability to pay.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment processing, count Medicare Advantage enrolment transactions submitted by one agent or plan NPI within a single day. Compare beneficiary-signed scope-of-appointment records against CMS online enrolment submissions for the same HICN or MBI. Cross-check enrolling beneficiary contact data against pharmacy dispensing records held by the same corporate TIN for common source of demographics. Track beneficiary-initiated disenrolment and rapid-disenrolment complaint rates per agent identifier in the plan's CTM file. Compare pharmacy payments in the plan's vendor ledger against the count of enrolments referred by those same pharmacy NPIs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Enrolment burst: on agent identifier x day, compute the count of distinct beneficiary enrolment transactions submitted to CMS; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer agents; action claim suspension of the enrolment batch pending beneficiary verification. 2) Consent-record gap: on enrolment record, compute the presence of a matching dated scope-of-appointment or recorded call before the submission timestamp; fires when no matching record exists; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Referral-payment coupling: on pharmacy NPI, compute the correlation between dollars paid from the plan's vendor ledger and the count of enrolments attributed to that NPI; fires when payment per enrolment exceeds zero for any referral-linked pharmacy; action payment suspension and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Alice F. Martin (owner/operator of Martin Logistics, TSA Transportation, A.F. Martin, Martin Global)
SchemeSummary: Trucking company owner phased out a tax-indebted company (Martin Logistics) while continuing operations through new entities, directing roughly $18 million in gross receipts from TSA Transportation into the bank account of another company she controlled (A.F. Martin) and moving trucks and trailers into Martin Global, thereby failing to report $3.6 million in taxable income and evading approximately $1.2 million in federal taxes.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim here and no adjudication point, so no payer edit applies. Detection sits with IRS revenue officers comparing Forms 1099-K and 1120 gross receipts against bank deposits for successor entities sharing an owner. State corporate registry and DOT operating-authority filings showing new entities at the same address with the same principal are the nearest lead.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest outside control: on taxpayer identification number, compute the count of successor entities sharing officer, address or vehicle title records while a prior entity carries unpaid trust-fund liability; fires on any match; action IRS collection referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Oklahoma
FraudEntity: Ladd Clayton Atkins (Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine)
SchemeSummary: Atkins, an osteopathic physician in Tulsa, was charged by information with conspiring with others to unlawfully prescribe Adderall, a Schedule II controlled substance, and with conspiracy to commit health care fraud, defrauding Medicare and Medicaid; the charge was announced as part of DOJ's 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown.
WaysToIdentify: In Part D PDE data, compute the share of this prescriber's fills that are Schedule II amphetamine NDCs versus same-specialty peers. Compare prescribed amphetamine days-supply against any office visit E/M claim between prescriber NPI and beneficiary in the lookback period. Check PDMP records for beneficiaries filling stimulants from multiple prescribers within overlapping days-supply windows. Compare beneficiary residence ZIP distance to the practice address on the CMS-855I enrolment record. Track the prescriber's stimulant volume growth against its own trailing baseline in remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Stimulant concentration: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of Schedule II stimulant claims to total prescription claims using NDC and days supply; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) No-encounter prescribing: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary, compute days between the controlled-substance fill date and the most recent E/M claim between the pair; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 3) Patient dispersion: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries receiving stimulants who live beyond the practice service radius on CMS-855I; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Jacqueline Espino (Arizona Department of Economic Security claims adjudicator); Brandilyn Lorenzen (Arizona Department of Economic Security claims adjudicator)
PayerName: Arizona Department of Economic Security (unemployment insurance and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance programs)
FraudTypeAll: Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
SchemeSummary: Two Arizona DES adjudicators accepted bribes to approve unemployment insurance and Pandemic Unemployment Assistance claims for individuals who were not eligible (Espino: 9 claims causing $140,298 in payments; Lorenzen: 24 claims causing $532,964), and each also embezzled DES funds for themselves and others (Espino $600,672; Lorenzen $2,461,520). Lorenzen was sentenced to 30 months and ordered to pay $2,994,484 restitution; Espino pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: There is no medical claim and no clinical adjudication point, but the state agency does adjudicate benefit claims and can control there. Adjudicator user IDs in the UI claims system can be grouped to show approvals concentrated in one examiner without wage-record support. Cross-matching claimant SSNs against state quarterly wage files and the National Directory of New Hires exposes ineligible approvals before payment. Bank routing and account numbers repeating across unrelated claimant records point to a single beneficiary of the payments.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Examiner override rate: on adjudicator user ID x week, compute the share of approved claims lacking matching quarterly wage records; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer adjudicators; action claim suspension pending second-level review. 2) Shared deposit account: on bank account number, compute the count of distinct claimant SSNs receiving benefit deposits; fires when that count exceeds one without a documented representative payee; action payment suspension. 3) Self-touch approvals: on adjudicator user ID, compute the count of approved claims whose address, phone or account matches the adjudicator's HR record; fires on any exact match; action payment suspension and referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Washington
FraudEntity: Avanish Kumar Jha; Rajnish Kumar Jha; Dhrishti Pharma International (company)
SchemeSummary: The Jha brothers, through their company Dhrishti Pharma International, advertised prescription drugs online and shipped counterfeit and adulterated medications from India to U.S. buyers, including fake 'Keytruda' containing none of the active cancer-fighting ingredient; payment was taken by wire transfer, direct money exchange, and cash picked up by U.S. intermediaries, with packaging designed to evade customs detection.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim in this scheme because buyers paid by wire and cash, so no adjudication edit fires. The nearest route is customs and import screening of parcels from India against FDA registered-importer lists and DSCSA pedigree requirements. Payment-processor and money-remitter reports showing repeated consumer wires to one foreign beneficiary for named drug products are the second route. Payers can still watch for oncology drug NDCs appearing in patient records with no matching specialty pharmacy dispensing claim.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest outside control: on shipper or consignee identifier, compute the count of inbound parcels declaring non-drug contents that test positive for pharmaceutical packaging in FDA-CBP screening; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer shippers; action import alert and seizure referral.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Zachary J. Lipman MD (physician); Michael Woo-Ming MD (physician, co-owner of Revive Medical of San Diego and Medical Wellness Group); Kevin Brown (Riverside County chiropractor, scheme orchestrator)
State_County: California - Butte County (Chico); California - Riverside County (Murrieta); California - San Diego County (San Diego)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Upcoding; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Chiropractor Kevin Brown used companies he owned to bill Medicare for surgically implanted neurostimulators when in fact staff merely taped disposable 'Stivax' electroacupuncture devices to patients' ears, a non-reimbursable item; Dr. Lipman received kickbacks from Brown for referring patients for Stivax devices ($290,000 settlement) and Dr. Woo-Ming's companies submitted the false neurostimulator implant claims ($85,000 settlement), for a combined $375,000 across the two defendants announced here.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, neurostimulator implant CPT and L-code lines appear with place of service office and no facility or anesthesia claim on the same date. The rendering or supervising NPI's taxonomy in NPPES is chiropractic, which cannot perform a surgical implant. No operative report or implant device serial number is present in the prior-authorisation or ADR record for the implant code. The same beneficiary has repeat implant claims within intervals shorter than any device lifetime, consistent with disposable auricular devices. Referring physician NPIs sending patients to this supplier receive payments recorded in Open Payments or the supplier's vendor ledger.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Implant without surgical footprint: on claim line, compute the count of same-date facility, anesthesia or operating-room claims for the beneficiary when a neurostimulator implant code is billed; fires when that count is zero with place of service office; action prepay edit. 2) Taxonomy-procedure mismatch: on rendering NPI x CPT, compute an exact match between NPPES taxonomy and the specialties permitted to bill implantation codes; fires on registry mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Implant frequency impossibility: on beneficiary x implant HCPCS, compute the gap in days between paid implant claims; fires when the gap is shorter than the device's expected lifetime without a documented revision; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; USAO - Central District of California
FraudEntity: Karpis Srapyan; Susanna Harutyunyan; Petros Fichidzhyan; Juan Carlos Esparza (sham hospice owner); Mihran Panosyan
State_County: California - Los Angeles County (Winnetka, greater Los Angeles area)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Defendants used four sham hospice companies - one owned by a co-defendant and three nominally owned by foreign nationals but controlled by the defendants - to bill Medicare nearly $16 million for hospice services that were never provided and not medically necessary, using foreign nationals' identities to open bank accounts, enroll with Medicare and sign leases, and misappropriating the identities of doctors (two deceased) to submit claims. Proceeds of roughly $3.2 million were laundered through accounts in the sham companies' and foreign nationals' names and spent on personal expenses including a BMW; figures span multiple co-defendants, with Fichidzhyan already sentenced to 12 years.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855A owner listed for the hospice shares an address, phone or bank account with other newly enrolled hospice NPIs. The attending or certifying physician NPI on the hospice election appears in the Death Master File or has no other Medicare billing activity. Beneficiaries on hospice claims continue receiving curative Part A and Part B services from unrelated providers during the election period. The hospice bills routine home care days with no NOE-consistent face-to-face encounter documentation and no OASIS or clinical record on ADR. Payment deposits route to a bank account opened weeks before enrolment under a foreign national's identity documents.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dead or dormant certifier: on certifying physician NPI, compute an exact match to the Death Master File date or a zero count of other paid claims in the prior year; fires on any match; action prepay edit and payment suspension. 2) Concurrent curative care: on beneficiary x hospice election period, compute the count of paid non-hospice acute or specialist claims during the election; fires when that count is above zero without a revocation record; action claim suspension. 3) Common-control cluster: on bank account and address in CMS-855A, compute the graph degree of distinct hospice NPIs sharing that node; fires when degree exceeds one; action site visit before first payment.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Syed Murtuza Kablazada (owner/operator of purported medical laboratories); Syed Mehdi Hussain (owner/operator of purported medical laboratories)
State_County: Illinois - Cook County (Arlington Heights); Illinois - DuPage County (Carol Stream)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Defendants operated purported medical laboratories that billed Medicare approximately $227 million (about $136 million paid) for over-the-counter COVID-19 test kits that were rarely provided, submitting claims for beneficiaries who never requested kits, including deceased individuals, using beneficiary names purchased from a marketing company. They installed foreign nationals as nominee/straw owners of the labs who were expected to flee the U.S. once investigations began.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, OTC COVID test kit HCPCS lines are billed for beneficiaries with a Death Master File date preceding the date of service. One lab NPI bills the kit code to a count of distinct beneficiaries spread nationwide far beyond its enrolled service area on CMS-855B. Beneficiaries have no ordering encounter and no prior claim relationship with the billing lab NPI. The billing NPI's volume rose from zero to peer-top-decile within weeks of a PECOS ownership change to a recently arrived owner. Beneficiary lists overlap heavily with other unrelated lab NPIs billing the same kit code in the same period, indicating a purchased list.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Deceased beneficiary edit: on claim line, compute the difference between date of service and the Death Master File date of death; fires when service date follows death; action prepay edit. 2) Kit saturation: on beneficiary x HCPCS, compute the count of distinct supplier or lab NPIs paid for the OTC test code in a rolling month plus total units against the per-month coverage limit; fires when units exceed the limit or suppliers exceed one; action prepay edit. 3) New-owner volume spike: on provider NPI x week, compute paid claim count divided by the provider's trailing 12-week baseline since the PECOS ownership change date; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Ramon Apellaniz (a/k/a "Kristopher Rockefeller," de facto operator, unlicensed); Suhail Aponte (manager and registered agent of Minds Cornerstone LLC, unlicensed); Minds Cornerstone LLC dba Minds Cornerstone Behavior Therapy Services
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Apellaniz, an unlicensed provider previously convicted in state court for Medicaid fraud through The Gemini Project, allegedly ran Minds Cornerstone LLC under a pseudonym (including while incarcerated) with nominal manager Aponte, and the two billed Connecticut Medicaid over $1.8 million for applied behavior analysis services to autistic children that were never rendered - including services on dates payroll showed no employee was paid, BCBA supervision billed without any corresponding behavioral technician service, and services for patients who were actually hospitalized inpatient. Some of the proceeds were allegedly used to pay restitution Apellaniz owed from his earlier state Medicaid fraud conviction.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, the individual controlling the billing entity is absent from the state licence board file for BCBA or behavior analysis. Cross-check owners and managers named on the Medicaid provider enrolment against the OIG LEIE and state exclusion list for prior program convictions. At adjudication, ABA service dates fall on days when the entity's payroll and EVV records show no technician clock-in. BCBA supervision codes are billed on dates with no corresponding behavior technician direct-service line for the same recipient. Recipients have concurrent inpatient hospital claims spanning the outpatient ABA service dates.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Exclusion and licence match: on enrolled TIN and each listed owner or manager, compute exact-name and SSN matches against OIG LEIE, state exclusion list and the licence board file; fires on any match or missing licence; action claim suspension and enrolment revocation. 2) Supervision without service: on recipient x date of service, compute the count of technician direct-service lines when a BCBA supervision code is billed; fires when that count is zero; action prepay edit. 3) Inpatient overlap: on recipient x date of service, compute overlapping minutes between paid outpatient ABA units and any inpatient admission span; fires when overlap is above zero; action prepay edit, then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Christopher Kyle Johnston (general counsel, Central Rexall Drugs); Trent Brockmeier (chief operating officer, Central Rexall Drugs); Central Rexall Drugs (compounding pharmacy)
PayerName: TRICARE; New Jersey State Health Benefits Program (state and local government and education employee health plans)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two executives took over a Louisiana compounding pharmacy and designed pain, scar, antifungal and vitamin compound formulas based solely on which ingredient combinations yielded the highest insurance reimbursement, testing formulas by submitting false claims using identifying and insurance information taken without consent from pre-existing pharmacy prescriptions. An outside sales force obtained prescriptions signed without patient visits or knowledge and paid patients and doctors, generating roughly $100 million in medically unnecessary claims to TRICARE and New Jersey public employee health plans; Johnston received about $34 million and Brockmeier about $5 million in profits, and 50 people have been convicted in the overarching conspiracy.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a small set of high-cost compound NDC ingredient combinations accounts for nearly all of the pharmacy's paid dollars. Average paid amount per compound claim for this pharmacy NPI is far above same-specialty peers in remittance history. Prescribing NPIs on the compound claims have no other claim relationship with the beneficiary and are clustered in distant states. Reversal-and-rebill patterns show repeated test submissions varying ingredient quantities for the same beneficiary within minutes. Beneficiary demographics on new compound claims exactly match records from older unrelated prescriptions at the same pharmacy, indicating reuse of stored data.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Reimbursement-tuned formula: on pharmacy NPI x compound ingredient set, compute the paid dollars share and the average paid per claim versus same-specialty peers; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Claim-probing behavior: on pharmacy NPI x beneficiary x day, compute the count of reversed then re-adjudicated compound claims with changed ingredient quantities; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action prepay edit. 3) No-encounter prescriptions: on prescriber NPI x beneficiary, compute days between compound fill date and the nearest E/M claim between the pair; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action documentation request (ADR) and payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Kenneth Charles Kessler III (owner/operator of DME supply companies); Michael Andrew Gomez (owner/operator of DME supply companies)
State_County: Florida - Miami-Dade County; Florida - Broward County
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two men who owned seven Florida DME supply companies allegedly paid kickbacks to marketing companies that used deceptive telemarketing to obtain Medicare beneficiaries' personal information, then had purported telemedicine companies generate doctors' orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces and continuous glucose monitors, which the defendants used to bill Medicare approximately $34.8 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering telehealth NPI on brace and CGM claims has no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI writes DMEPOS orders for beneficiaries across dozens of states within a single week. Beneficiary ZIPs fall far outside the supplier's declared service area on its CMS-855S enrolment record. Several supplier NPIs sharing owners, address or bank account on CMS-855S bill the same L-codes for overlapping beneficiary sets. CGM claims lack any diabetes diagnosis or insulin fill in the beneficiary's other claims history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim between ordering NPI and beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states and distinct supplier NPIs on ordered DMEPOS claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) CGM clinical support: on beneficiary x HCPCS, compute the count of diabetes diagnosis claims or insulin NDC fills in the prior year; fires when that count is zero; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Stephen Kash (laboratory sales executive, True Health Diagnostics); Courtney Love (laboratory sales executive, True Health Diagnostics); Christopher Grottenthaler; Blake Whitaker; Chrissy Alfaro; Charles Dickens; Marty Flores; Frederick Brown; Little River Healthcare (rural hospital); Stamford Memorial Hospital; True Health Diagnostics (clinical laboratory)
State_County: Texas - Milam County (Rockdale); Texas - Jones County (Stamford); Texas - Collin County (Frisco)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; Upcoding
SchemeSummary: Two rural Texas hospitals partnered with clinical lab True Health Diagnostics so that THD processed advanced cardiovascular lipid blood tests for a fee while the hospitals billed insurers for them as higher-paying hospital outpatient services; the hospitals paid a share of lab revenues to marketers who ran sham management services organizations offering 'investment returns' that were in fact disguised kickbacks to referring physicians, and THD sales executives leveraged those MSO kickbacks to boost referrals, revenues and commissions. Sentences and forfeitures span two defendants: Kash 18 months and $779,773.70 forfeiture, Love 12 months and one day and $217,268.75 forfeiture; Kash was also indicted for conspiring to launder the kickback proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, advanced lipid panel CPT codes are billed under a critical access hospital NPI while the specimen was collected far from the hospital service area. Referring physician ZIPs on hospital outpatient lab claims cluster in metropolitan areas hundreds of miles from the rural facility. The hospital's outpatient lab revenue share jumps above its own trailing baseline while inpatient volume stays flat. Referring physicians appear as investors in management services organizations disclosed in Open Payments or hospital vendor ledgers. Reference-lab pass-through arrangements are absent from the hospital's CMS-855A reported contractual and ownership fields.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Non-local reference testing: on hospital NPI x month, compute the share of outpatient lab lines whose referring NPI practice ZIP lies beyond the facility's service radius; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus rural hospital peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Lab revenue shift: on hospital NPI x quarter, compute outpatient lab paid dollars divided by total paid dollars against the facility's trailing four-quarter baseline; fires when the ratio rises above baseline while inpatient claim counts are flat; action postpay audit. 3) Investor-referrer link: on referring NPI, compute the count of paid lab lines routed to a facility whose MSO investor list or Open Payments record includes that NPI; fires when count is above zero; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Iowa
FraudEntity: Cori Lempiainen (nurse practitioner); Paul Baumert, M.D. (physician)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Device, DME; Falsify certificate; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Two practitioners billed Medicare for office visits and medical discussions they never provided (over 650 claims by Lempiainen, over 200 by Baumert) and signed thousands of orders for medically unnecessary orthotic braces based only on listening to recorded cold calls to beneficiaries, with whom they had no contact; they agreed to pay $150,000 and $14,325.96 respectively under the False Claims Act.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the practitioner bills telehealth E/M codes with no matching audio-video or interactive encounter record on ADR. One practitioner NPI signs DMEPOS orders for a count of distinct beneficiaries impossible within the E/M minutes billed that day. Ordered brace claims carry no prior treating-relationship claim between the ordering NPI and the beneficiary. Total billed E/M time for a rendering NPI on a date of service exceeds 24 hours. Beneficiary residences span dozens of states inconsistent with the practitioner's licence board file coverage.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Time impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute summed typical minutes for all billed E/M and telehealth codes; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Order-to-visit ratio: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of signed DMEPOS orders divided by the count of billed patient encounters; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Licence-state mismatch: on claim line, compute an exact match between beneficiary state and the states on the rendering NPI's licence board file; fires on mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee at Greeneville
FraudEntity: Monika D. Schorer (VA Medical Center employee); Teresa D. Schorer (VA Medical Center employee); Eric S. Smith (surgical sales representative); Landon Chester (surgical sales representative); Four Corners Medical Supply and Equipment LLC (VA vendor)
State_County: Tennessee - Mountain Home VA Medical Center (Washington County area, Jonesborough); Virginia - Bristol
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; Upcoding; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Two twin-sister VA Medical Center employees took cash-stuffed envelopes and a promised ownership stake in vendor Four Corners Medical Supply and Equipment LLC from surgical sales reps Eric Smith and Landon Chester, in exchange for allowing the reps to overbill the VA for surgical supplies, often medically unnecessary items; the employees set the vendor up in the VA payment system, filed false ethics disclosures, and tipped off the reps about supervisor scrutiny. Each sister received 8 months and a $10,000 fine plus $213,154.50 restitution; Smith received a year and a day and paid $120,433.45 restitution, and Smith and Chester forfeited $185,422.10, with total government recovery across all participants of $852,598 (Chester not yet sentenced).
WaysToIdentify: In the VA purchasing system, the count of purchase orders routed to one newly created vendor by a single contracting employee spikes above peers. Vendor registration records show an address, phone or bank account matching a VA employee's HR record. Unit prices paid for surgical supply SKUs exceed the Federal Supply Schedule or prevailing market benchmark on the same items. Employee financial disclosure filings omit an ownership interest in a vendor receiving payments. Quantities ordered exceed the surgical case volume recorded for the same period in facility case logs.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Buyer-vendor concentration: on employee user ID x vendor TIN, compute the share of that employee's approved purchase orders going to one vendor; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer buyers; action payment suspension pending contracting review. 2) Insider linkage: on vendor bank account and address, compute exact matches against employee HR and ethics disclosure records; fires on any match with no disclosed interest; action payment suspension and site visit. 3) Price and quantity variance: on purchase order line, compute unit price against the Federal Supply Schedule rate and quantity against recorded surgical case counts; fires when price exceeds schedule or quantity exceeds cases; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Josue Torres; Anthony Guerra
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Bronx County
PayerName: Private health insurance (unnamed commercial insurers); pharmaceutical manufacturer copay assistance programs
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Defendants allegedly accessed e-prescribing platforms using stolen identities of 18 physicians to issue approximately 693 fraudulent prescriptions (about 55,626 units, ~$2.64 million in value) for high-cost HIV and other medications in the names of 'sham patients' who did not need them, then used copay assistance cards in the sham patients' names (with private insurers paying part of the cost) to obtain the drugs cheaply at pharmacies and resell them on the black market.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, high-cost HIV NDC claims carry prescriber NPIs whose specialty in NPPES never prescribes those agents. Prescriptions originate from e-prescribing platform sessions whose IP address and device fingerprint differ from the prescriber's registered credentials. Patients receiving the antiretrovirals have no prior HIV diagnosis, lab claim or prior fill history with any payer. Copay assistance card enrolments cluster on beneficiaries sharing addresses, phone numbers or dates of birth. One prescriber's monthly high-cost specialty volume rises far above their own trailing baseline within days.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Credential-use anomaly: on prescriber NPI x e-prescribing session, compute the count of distinct IP addresses or device identifiers used against the prescriber's trailing baseline; fires when a new device issues prescriptions above baseline; action claim suspension. 2) Therapy-history gap: on beneficiary x NDC class, compute the count of prior HIV diagnosis claims, viral-load lab claims or prior fills; fires when that count is zero for a new antiretroviral fill; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Sham-patient clustering: on address and phone in member enrolment, compute the count of distinct patient identities using copay assistance for the same NDC; fires when count exceeds one household size; action prepay edit and postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Daniel Motha (co-owner and CEO of JDM Supply LLC); Jeffrey Motha (co-owner and head of sales of JDM Supply LLC); JDM Supply LLC; Jason Colantuoni (co-conspirator, pleaded guilty)
State_County: Massachusetts - Suffolk County (Boston); Florida - Miami-Dade County (Miami)
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Two brothers who co-owned JDM Supply LLC sold approximately 850,000 facemasks, manufactured by Advoque Safeguard, to a hospital for about $2.6 million by misrepresenting them as NIOSH-approved N95 respirators and supplying NIOSH-passing test results and approval documents belonging to a different mask; lab testing showed filtration efficiency of 83.94%-93.24%, below the 95% N95 requirement. They also sold scarce N95 masks to Massachusetts hospitals above prevailing market price in violation of the Defense Production Act. Both defendants received one year probation and a $9,500 fine each (totaling $19,000); a third conspirator awaited sentencing.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health insurance claim here, since a hospital bought supplies directly, so no adjudication edit applies. The nearest control is procurement verification of the NIOSH Certified Equipment List approval number against the exact model and manufacturer on the invoice. Supplier registration in FDA's establishment database and in GSA SAM exclusion records gives a second pre-purchase check. Independent filtration efficiency testing on a sampled lot compared to the 95 percent N95 requirement confirms misrepresentation before wide distribution.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest outside control: on purchase order line, compute an exact match between the model and approval number on submitted NIOSH documentation and the NIOSH Certified Equipment List entry for that manufacturer; fires on any mismatch; action hold payment and lot testing before acceptance.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Boris Arencibia (procured and sold diverted drugs); Jose Armando Rivera Garcia (owner of LDD Distributors); LDD Distributors
SchemeSummary: The two defendants bought high-priced prescription drugs (including HIV and cancer medications) from illicit street sources, including patients who sold their prescriptions and people who obtained prescriptions by fraud, then repackaged them without proper storage safeguards and falsified paperwork to make them appear to come from manufacturers or legitimate wholesalers. Through sham distribution companies (including Rivera Garcia's LDD Distributors) they sold roughly $28 million of diverted, misbranded drugs to pharmacies nationwide - some bottles containing wrong medications, vitamins or pebbles - and laundered the proceeds; figures and the 57-month sentence span both defendants across two related cases.
WaysToIdentify: DSCSA transaction history for high-cost NDCs traces back to distributors absent from the manufacturer's authorized trading partner list. Serial numbers and lot codes on received bottles repeat across multiple pharmacies or fail manufacturer verification requests. Wholesaler licence status in the state board of pharmacy file is expired or the entity is unregistered in ARCOS reporting. Purchase invoice prices for specialty drugs fall far below wholesale acquisition cost benchmarks. Pharmacy dispensing volume for these NDCs exceeds documented purchases from authorized wholesalers in the pedigree file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Pedigree authenticity: on NDC serial number, compute the count of verification failures or duplicate serials against manufacturer product identifiers; fires on any duplicate or unverifiable serial; action claim suspension for dispensed units. 2) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute dispensed units minus units purchased from authorized wholesalers per DSCSA records; fires when the difference is above zero; action prepay edit and postpay audit. 3) Unauthorized supplier: on distributor identifier, compute an exact match against state board of pharmacy licensure and the manufacturer's authorized distributor list; fires on registry mismatch; action payment suspension and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Yousef Ennab (licensed pharmacist, supervising pharmacist at Forest Care); Mohamed Hassan (licensed pharmacist, owner of more than a dozen pharmacies); Dr. Somsri Ratanaprasatporn (physician); Leticia Smith (medical receptionist); Bassam Amin (pharmacist); Omar Elsayed (pharmacist); Michael Kent (drug dealer); Anthony Mathis; Raymond Walker
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County; New York - Richmond County (Staten Island)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Prescriptions for 30-day supplies of oxycodone 30 mg were written out of a Brooklyn pill-mill medical practice (some by the doctor's receptionist, often for patients never examined and in some cases for stolen identities), then filled at pharmacies owned or supervised by the defendant pharmacists; the pills were handed to street drug dealers for cash payments, and the pharmacists also billed insurance companies for the medically unnecessary pills. Over 1.2 million pills worth more than $36 million in street value were distributed; two pharmacists were convicted at trial while seven co-defendants pleaded guilty (co-defendant Michael Kent received 9 years, and Hassan was later sentenced to 18 years).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one prescriber NPI writes oxycodone 30 mg 30-day supplies at a rate far above same-specialty peers in PDMP and claim data. Nearly all of that prescriber's fills route to a small set of pharmacy NPIs sharing owners on state licence records. Beneficiaries filling the oxycodone have no imaging, procedure or E/M claim supporting a chronic pain diagnosis. Prescriptions are signed on dates when the prescriber has no billed encounter for that beneficiary. Beneficiaries travel unusually long distances between residence ZIP, practice ZIP and dispensing pharmacy ZIP.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) High-dose opioid concentration: on prescriber NPI x month, compute the share of claims that are oxycodone 30 mg at 30-day supply and the average daily morphine milligram equivalents; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Prescriber-pharmacy channeling: on prescriber NPI, compute the share of opioid fills going to the top one or two pharmacy NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action prepay edit and payment suspension. 3) Distance triangle: on claim line, compute summed miles between beneficiary ZIP, prescriber practice ZIP and dispensing pharmacy ZIP; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer opioid claims; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York
FraudEntity: Mohamed Hassan (pharmacist, owner of approximately 20 pharmacies); Yousef Ennab (supervising pharmacist, Forest Care); Anthony Mathis (street narcotics dealer/patient recruiter); Michael Kent (co-defendant); Dr. Somsri Ratanaprasatporn (physician, pill mill); Leticia Smith (receptionist who forged prescriptions); Bassam Amin (pharmacist); Omar Elsayed (pharmacist); Raymond Walker (street dealer)
State_County: New York - Kings County (Brooklyn); New York - Queens County; New York - Richmond County (Staten Island)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Falsify certificate; IdentityFraud; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims
SchemeSummary: Prescriptions for 30-day supplies of oxycodone 30 mg were forged/illegally issued out of a Brooklyn pill-mill medical practice - often in the names of recruited nominal patients or people whose identities were stolen and who were never examined - then filled at roughly 20 pharmacies controlled by pharmacist Mohamed Hassan; the pills were handed to street dealers for cash while the pharmacists also billed insurers for the medically unnecessary pills, distributing more than 1.6 million oxycodone pills worth over $48 million in street value. Figures span multiple co-defendants: Hassan received 18 years, Kent 108 months, Walker 84 months, Mathis 36 months and Ennab 30 months, with forfeitures of $535,989.12 (Mathis) and $13,472.76 (Ennab) plus an undetermined amount for Hassan.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, one pharmacist licence number appears as pharmacist-in-charge across many pharmacy NPIs in the state board of pharmacy file. Those pharmacies' oxycodone 30 mg purchase volumes in ARCOS exceed peer pharmacies of similar prescription count. A single pill-mill practice NPI accounts for most controlled-substance fills across that pharmacy network. Beneficiaries on the prescriptions have no examination claim from the prescribing NPI on or before the written date. Patient identities on fills recur with mismatched dates of birth or addresses against payer eligibility files.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Common-control pharmacy network: on pharmacist licence number and bank account, compute the graph degree of distinct pharmacy NPIs sharing that node in board and enrolment records; fires when degree exceeds one without disclosed chain ownership; action site visit and payment suspension. 2) ARCOS-to-claims mismatch: on pharmacy NPI x quarter, compute oxycodone units purchased in ARCOS minus units dispensed on adjudicated claims; fires when the difference is above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies; action postpay audit. 3) Identity verification failure: on claim line, compute exact matches of member name, date of birth and address against the payer eligibility file and Death Master File; fires on any mismatch; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Asim Muhammad Ali (physician, owner of Central Diagnostic Laboratory and Institute for Pain Management LLC); Dr. Mohd Azfar Malik (psychiatrist, owner of Psych Care Consultants LLC)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; private health insurers
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Dr. Ali performed telephone-only 'annual wellness visits' for Medicare patients of Dr. Malik's Psych Care Consultants and billed them under Malik's name and Medicare billing number (Medicare paid $3,902), while Malik submitted claims to Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and private insurers for in-person services (including an inpatient hospital visit and a ketamine infusion) performed when he was out of state or out of the country, causing $19,442 in losses; Ali separately admitted paying kickbacks for urine specimens referred to his lab and pre-signing controlled-substance prescriptions without seeing patients. Figures span two defendants.}
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claims billed under one NPI carry dates of service when that physician's own travel and other-state claims place him elsewhere. Telephone-only contacts are billed as annual wellness visits G0438 and G0439 without the required in-person place of service or telehealth modifier. The rendering NPI on the claim differs from the clinician documented in the encounter note obtained through documentation request. Urine specimen volume from one referring practice NPI to one laboratory NPI rises sharply against the lab's trailing baseline. Controlled-substance prescriptions written under the prescriber NPI show no companion E/M claim for the beneficiary in the lookback window.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Provider-absence conflict: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of in-person place-of-service 11, 21 or 22 lines on dates where that NPI also has claims in a distant state or no local activity; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 2) Wellness-visit modality mismatch: on claim line, compute presence of G0438 or G0439 with place of service 11 alongside any telephone CPT 99441-99443 for the same beneficiary and date; fires on exact code-modality mismatch; action prepay edit. 3) Referral-concentration surge: on referring NPI x laboratory NPI x month, compute the count of urine drug test specimens and its ratio to that referrer's total lab orders; fires when above the referrer's trailing baseline and peer percentile; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Jared Wheat (founder, owner and CEO of Hi-Tech Pharmaceuticals, Inc.); Hi-Tech Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (dietary supplement manufacturer)
SchemeSummary: After a legitimate third-party audit found 75 GMP deficiencies at Hi-Tech's supplement plant, Wheat and Hi-Tech fabricated a GMP compliance certificate from 'PharmaTech Consulting' (secretly owned by Wheat), forged a Belize attorney's signature, altered the audit report's 'Not Acceptable' entries to 'Acceptable,' and also faked FDA Certificates of Free Sale; these documents were sent to customers (some of whom passed them to foreign regulators), and customers paid at least $4,763,292 to Hi-Tech, with the company also convicted of laundering the proceeds.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim here and no adjudication point, because the product is a dietary supplement sold to commercial customers rather than billed to a payer. The nearest detection route is verifying GMP certificates and FDA Certificates of Free Sale directly with the issuing auditor and FDA export-certification system. Ownership overlap between the certifying consultancy and the manufacturer is visible in state corporate registry and beneficial-ownership filings.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on certificate issuer entity, compute the count of certificates naming clients whose corporate registry shows shared officers or addresses with the issuer; fires when any shared-control match exists; action referral to FDA and customer notification.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Normita Sierra (owner/operator of Golden Meadows Hospice Inc. and D'Alexandria Hospice Inc.); Rowena Elegado; Carl Bernardo (marketer); Relyndo Salcedo (nurse practitioner); Golden Meadows Hospice Inc.; D'Alexandria Hospice Inc.
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Sierra's two hospices billed Medicare over $4.8 million (paid ~$3.8M) for hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill; marketers were paid kickbacks of up to $1,300 per patient per month (code-named 'girl scout cookies') to recruit patients, and a nurse practitioner falsified assessments exaggerating patient conditions so hospice physicians would certify them as terminally ill. Patients were typically discharged around six months, sometimes to Sierra's home health company or other hospice. Two co-participants (Bernardo and Salcedo) have pleaded guilty and await sentencing; Sierra and Elegado were arrested on indictment.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, hospice election periods end near six months with live discharge, visible in the revocation and discharge status codes. A single nurse practitioner NPI signs the face-to-face encounter for beneficiaries whose diagnoses lack any supporting hospitalisation or treatment claims. Beneficiaries discharged from hospice appear immediately on home health claims from a commonly owned NPI shown in CMS-855A ownership fields. Marketer payments appear as per-patient monthly amounts in the provider's own books, matching admission counts obtained on site visit. Beneficiaries show no prior narcotic, oxygen or hospital claims consistent with a six-month terminal prognosis.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Live-discharge rate: on hospice NPI x quarter, compute the share of elections ending in live discharge and the median length of stay from election and discharge dates; fires when the live-discharge share is above the calibrated percentile versus peer hospices; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Certifier concentration: on certifying NPI x hospice NPI, compute the count of certifications and the share of the hospice's admissions signed by that one clinician; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit on new elections. 3) Common-ownership recycling: on beneficiary, compute days between hospice discharge date and the next home health start of care from an NPI sharing an owner TIN in PECOS; fires when the gap is under one billing cycle; action postpay audit and site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida; Justice Department Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: Marek Rex Vernon Harrison (true beneficial owner and manager of CTD Network LLC); CTD Network LLC (purported telemedicine company)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Harrison allegedly ran telemedicine company CTD Network, whose providers conducted sham telehealth consultations to approve medically unnecessary genetic (cancer-risk) testing orders for Medicare beneficiaries referred by marketing companies and labs, with no treatment relationship or use of results; CTD billed Medicare over $2.7 million for the telehealth services and was paid over $600,000. CTD also allegedly filed false Medicare enrollment forms naming other people as owners/managers to hide Harrison's control and his 2019 bank fraud conviction.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, telehealth E/M claims cluster on beneficiaries whose only companion claims are hereditary cancer panel CPT 81162 and 8140x lines. The ordering NPI has no prior or subsequent encounter with the beneficiary in the payer's remittance history. One telehealth NPI orders genetic panels for beneficiaries spread across dozens of states within a single week. Telehealth encounter durations billed as 99442 or 99443 are implausible against the clinician's daily total minutes. The CMS-855B enrolment names owners and managers who do not match ownership records or hide a person with a bank fraud conviction.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Consult-to-panel coupling: on ordering NPI x week, compute the share of that NPI's telehealth encounters followed within 14 days by a hereditary cancer panel 81162 or 8140x order; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) No-treatment-relationship gap: on beneficiary x ordering NPI, compute the count of prior and subsequent E/M claims between them outside the single telehealth date; fires when that count is zero; action prepay edit. 3) Enrolment identity mismatch: on TIN x CMS-855 record, compute the count of listed owners and managing employees not matching PECOS, NPPES or LEIE identity and exclusion records; fires on exact registry mismatch; action site visit, then payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Insys Therapeutics, Inc.; John N. Kapoor (founder and former Executive Chairman); Richard M. Simon (former National Director of Sales); Sunrise Lee (former Regional Sales Director); Joseph A. Rowan (former Regional Sales Director); Michael J. Gurry (former VP of Managed Markets); Michael Babich (former CEO and President); Alec Burlakoff (former VP of Sales)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Insys founder and executives used pharmacy data to identify high-volume rapid-onset opioid prescribers and paid them bribes/kickbacks (via sham speaker programs and similar inducements) to write more and higher-dose prescriptions of Subsys, a fentanyl spray approved only for breakthrough cancer pain, and then misled Medicare and private insurers about patients' diagnoses to obtain prior authorization and payment for medically unnecessary prescriptions. The $48,344,036 restitution figure is the total ordered across the seven convicted/pleading executives, now collected in full.
WaysToIdentify: At prior authorization, the submitted cancer diagnosis code is absent from every other claim in the beneficiary's history. At adjudication, the transmucosal fentanyl NDC is billed for beneficiaries with no oncology encounter or chemotherapy claim. A small set of prescriber NPIs accounts for an outsized share of that NDC's paid volume in Part D PDE data. Those same prescriber NPIs appear as paid speaker-program recipients in Open Payments records for the labeling manufacturer. Dose escalation per beneficiary rises across successive fills faster than the prescriber's own trailing baseline for the same NDC.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Off-label indication mismatch: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the count of claims carrying an active malignancy diagnosis in the 12-month claim history across all payers; fires when the count is zero for a REMS cancer-pain-only NDC; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Prescriber concentration plus payments: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the paid volume share of the rapid-onset fentanyl NDC and the summed Open Payments dollars from its manufacturer; fires when both are above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Dose escalation slope: on beneficiary x prescriber NPI, compute the change in daily morphine-milligram-equivalent across consecutive fills of the same NDC; fires when the slope exceeds the prescriber's trailing baseline for the same NDC; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Raytheon Company; Teva Pharmaceuticals; Kabbage, Inc.
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Other - Unknown
SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement rather than a single scheme: the office collected $60.17 million in FY2024 ($19.56 million criminal, $40.6 million civil) plus $14.87 million jointly, and over $1 billion in calendar year 2024, including a $575 million Raytheon procurement fraud resolution ($147 million criminal/$428 million civil), a $425 million Teva Pharmaceuticals settlement for paying kickbacks through two co-pay assistance foundations in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and False Claims Act, and a $120 million settlement with lender Kabbage, Inc. for submitting false PPP loan forgiveness, guarantee and processing-fee claims to the SBA.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections round-up rather than a single scheme, so there is no single claim stream and no adjudication point. The nearest detection routes are co-pay foundation data reconciliation and SBA loan-forgiveness file review outside the claims system. Manufacturer donations to patient assistance foundations matched against the foundation's grant lists reveal drug-specific steering.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on manufacturer x foundation fund, compute the correlation between donation amounts and grants awarded to patients using that manufacturer's drug; fires when the fund is effectively single-product; action referral for False Claims Act review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Dakota
FraudEntity: Dunes Surgical Hospital; two unnamed physician groups
SchemeSummary: Annual debt-collection release noting that, in addition to $3,496,288.47 collected in FY2024, the office obtained a $12.7 million settlement resolving alleged False Claims Act violations arising from improper financial relationships between Dunes Surgical Hospital and two physician groups, plus $1.4 million in restitution in a separate pandemic fraud prosecution.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, the CMS-855A ownership and Stark disclosure fields list physician-group owners whose referrals dominate the hospital's inpatient and surgical claim volume. Hospital claims show rendering NPIs from two group TINs accounting for an outsized share of designated health services. Physician-group compensation reported in the hospital's cost report exceeds fair-market-value benchmarks for the same specialty and region. Referral volume from those two TINs rises sharply in the quarter following the dated financial arrangement in the ownership file. The pandemic relief attestation on file names a payroll figure inconsistent with the TIN's reported wages.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Owner-referral concentration: on hospital NPI x referring TIN, compute the share of designated-health-service claim lines whose referring NPI maps to a disclosed owner in CMS-855A; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-size peer hospitals; action postpay audit. 2) Compensation-to-referral ratio: on physician NPI, compute the ratio of hospital-paid compensation reported on the cost report to that physician's referred DHS payments; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Post-arrangement referral step change: on referring NPI x quarter, compute referred inpatient claim counts to the disclosing hospital against the referrer's own trailing baseline; fires when the post-arrangement quarter exceeds baseline beyond the calibrated percentile; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
SchemeSummary: Annual collections announcement rather than a single fraud case: the office reported collecting $104.8 million in Fiscal Year 2024, comprising $9,239,721.20 in criminal restitution, $95,604,774.97 in civil actions (mostly False Claims Act recoveries), and $2,441,761 in asset forfeiture, with recoveries stemming from matters including crop insurance fraud, employee-related theft, and health care fraud.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections announcement covering unrelated matters, so there is no identifiable claim, provider or adjudication point. The nearest detection route is program-level recovery reporting rather than a prepay control.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of North Carolina
SchemeSummary: No specific fraud scheme described; the release announces the annual meeting of the Western District of North Carolina's Health Care Fraud Working Group, a multi-agency partnership (FBI, HHS-OIG, IRS-CI, VA-OIG, DCIS, NC and SC Medicaid units) focused on detecting health care fraud, and provides fraud reporting contacts.
