FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Nevada
FraudEntity: Paulino Gonzalez (registered nurse); Mary Huntly (nurse practitioner)
SchemeSummary: Two Las Vegas nurses were charged by information for applying amniotic wound allografts—some medically unnecessary—to Medicare beneficiaries in exchange for illegal kickbacks from an allograft distributor; Gonzalez received about $7,391,584 in kickbacks while a wound care company billed Medicare over $94 million (paid over $54 million) for allografts he and others applied (Oct 2021–Apr 2024), and Huntly's wound care company billed Medicare about $14,333,550 (paid about $9,105,563) from Sept 2022 through Apr 2024. Figures span both defendants; part of the 2025 national takedown involving 324 defendants and $14.6 billion in intended loss.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, skin-substitute Q-code units billed per beneficiary encounter far exceed the wound surface area documented in the paired CPT application code. Application CPT 15271-15278 is billed in place of service 12 or 32 rather than a facility wound clinic. A single rendering nurse NPI applies allografts to more beneficiaries per day than working hours physically allow. Nearly all allograft product NDCs and Q-codes trace to one distributor per wholesaler pedigree data despite multiple billing TINs. Beneficiaries have no prior wound-care evaluation claim from any ordering NPI before the first graft date of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Units-to-wound-area mismatch: on claim line, compute billed square centimetres on the Q-code against the wound area implied by the paired 152xx application CPT; fires when billed centimetres exceed the coded area band; action prepay edit. 2) Applier day capacity: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries with allograft application CPTs multiplied by the code's typical service minutes; fires when the product exceeds 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Distributor-applier concentration: on rendering NPI, compute the distinct-value count of allograft manufacturers and the share of paid dollars tied to one distributor's Q-codes; fires when the share is above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: Gilead Sciences, Inc. (pharmaceutical manufacturer)
State_County: New York - New York County (Manhattan); nationwide
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (New York Medicaid among state programs); TRICARE
SchemeSummary: Gilead used 'HIV Speaker Programs' to funnel kickbacks - over $20 million in honoraria plus lavish meals at high-end restaurants (e.g., 157 events at the James Beard House) and travel to destinations like Hawaii and Miami - to high-volume prescribers of its HIV drugs (Stribild, Genvoya, Complera, Odefsey, Descovy, Biktarvy), inducing prescriptions that resulted in tainted claims paid by Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE; one speaker paid over $300,000 generated over $6 million in federal program payments. Resolved by a $202 million False Claims Act settlement ($176,927,889.28 to the U.S.) arising from an intervened whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, prescriber-level Part D volume for the branded HIV NDCs rises sharply in the quarters after the first Open Payments speaker honorarium. The same prescriber NPI appears as a paid speaker on hundreds of events with repeat attendee rosters in the manufacturer's transparency file. Honoraria and meal transfers of value per prescriber exceed same-specialty peer distributions in Open Payments general-payment records. Branded NDC share versus generic alternatives for the prescriber exceeds peer infectious-disease prescribers in the payer's remittance history. Event locations reported in the transparency file are resort destinations rather than clinical venues.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Honorarium-to-prescribing lift: on prescriber NPI x quarter, compute paid claim counts for the manufacturer's HIV NDCs against the prescriber's own pre-honorarium trailing baseline using Open Payments dates; fires when the post-payment quarter exceeds baseline above the calibrated percentile; action postpay audit. 2) Transfer-of-value outlier: on prescriber NPI x year, compute summed speaker honoraria plus meal and travel value from Open Payments divided by the prescriber's total transfers; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Branded-share concentration: on prescriber NPI x drug class, compute the ratio of branded manufacturer NDC claims to all HIV-regimen claims in the payer's remittance history; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit on subsequent claims.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: CVS Pharmacy, Inc. (national retail pharmacy chain)
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; TRICARE; Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
SchemeSummary: CVS dispensed full five-pen insulin cartons that exceeded plan days-of-supply limits and, instead of obtaining overrides and reporting the true days-of-supply, instructed staff to report only the maximum days-of-supply allowed; because its dispensing/auto-refill software calculated refill dates from that understated data, CVS repeatedly refilled prescriptions prematurely and billed Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and FEHBP for refills ineligible for reimbursement. Resolved by a $37.76 million False Claims Act settlement ($24,446,240 to the United States, remainder to states) after the Government joined five whistleblower suits.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the days-of-supply field on the insulin NDC claim equals the plan's benefit maximum exactly rather than the metric quantity dispensed divided by the sig daily dose. Metric decimal quantity on the claim reflects a full five-pen carton while reported days-of-supply is capped below it. The refill claim's date of service falls before the prior fill's quantity would have been exhausted at the prescribed daily dose. Repeated fills for the same beneficiary and NDC show identical truncated days-of-supply values across many pharmacy NPIs in one chain TIN. No plan override or prior-authorisation record exists for the quantity exceeding the days-of-supply limit.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Days-supply arithmetic mismatch: on claim line, compute metric decimal quantity divided by the sig daily dose and subtract the reported days-of-supply field; fires when the difference is positive and the reported value equals the plan maximum; action prepay edit. 2) Premature refill gap: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the gap in days between consecutive fill dates of service minus the quantity-derived true days-of-supply; fires when the gap is negative without a documented override record; action claim suspension. 3) Chain truncation rate: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of insulin NDC lines whose reported days-of-supply exactly equals the plan cap while quantity implies more; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-chain peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York
FraudEntity: New York-Presbyterian Hudson Valley Hospital (hospital, formerly Hudson Valley Hospital Center)
SchemeSummary: The hospital entered three 2011-2012 agreements (melanoma center medical directorship, breast center medical directorship, and IORT service line management) paying a Westchester oncology practice hundreds of thousands of dollars per year; over $4 million was paid between 2011 and 2019 for work that was not performed, not performed as required, or undocumented by time records, continuing even after the agreements expired in 2016, in order to induce oncology patient referrals that the hospital then billed to Medicare and Medicaid in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute, Stark Law and False Claims Act. Resolved by a $6,836,764.30 settlement ($6,469,410.32 to the United States, remainder to New York State), arising from a whistleblower qui tam suit the Government joined.
WaysToIdentify: At claim adjudication, oncology claims cite a referring NPI whose group holds a hospital medical-directorship contract lacking supporting time records. The hospital's disclosed financial relationships on its Stark self-disclosure and contract register show payment dates after the written agreement expiry date. Referral concentration from one oncology TIN to one hospital TIN rises sharply in the payer's own remittance history after the contract start date. Directorship compensation per hour on the contract file exceeds fair-market-value benchmarks for that specialty and locality. Physician-owned entity disclosures on the hospital's CMS-855A ownership fields omit the paid oncology practice as a financial relationship.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Expired-arrangement referral flow: on referring NPI x hospital TIN, compute the count of paid inpatient and outpatient oncology claims with dates of service after the contract expiry date on the disclosed arrangement register; fires when that count exceeds zero; action postpay audit. 2) Referral concentration shift: on referring NPI x hospital TIN x quarter, compute the share of that physician's total referrals going to the contracted hospital versus his pre-contract trailing baseline; fires when the share rises above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Undocumented directorship pay: on physician TIN x month, compute the ratio of directorship dollars paid to logged director hours on submitted time records; fires when logged hours are zero or the implied hourly rate exceeds the fair-market benchmark; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Texas
FraudEntity: Walgreens (retail pharmacy chain)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Drug_Prescriptions; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: In a departure announcement summarizing office accomplishments, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Texas described a $97 million False Claims Act settlement with Walgreens for billing government health care payors for prescriptions that were never actually dispensed to patients. The same release also references separate resolutions not part of this settlement: $21.75 million with Medisca, Inc. for submitting false and inflated average wholesale prices for compounding ingredients, and $5.3 million paid by a Texas hospital CEO over illegal payments to physicians for laboratory referrals.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the pharmacy's paid NDC claims lack a matching dispensing event in the pharmacy management system fill and pickup logs. Prescriptions billed then reversed and rebilled without a new fill show refill-too-soon patterns in the payer's own remittance history. Dispensed quantity summed by NDC exceeds the pharmacy's wholesaler acquisition volume in pedigree and ARCOS purchase data. Ingredient average wholesale prices reported by the compounding supplier exceed published pricing compendia benchmarks for the same NDC. Laboratory referral volume from one physician group rises after payments recorded in the hospital's disclosed financial arrangement register.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dispense-without-pickup: on beneficiary x NDC x fill date, compute the gap in days between the paid claim date of service and the recorded pickup or delivery confirmation in the pharmacy dispensing log; fires when no pickup record exists within the return-to-stock window; action prepay edit. 2) Purchase-to-dispense reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x quarter, compute the ratio of units billed to units acquired per wholesaler pedigree and ARCOS data; fires when billed units exceed acquired units; action payment suspension. 3) AWP outlier: on NDC x reporting supplier, compute the ratio of reported average wholesale price to the compendia median for the same ingredient; fires when the ratio is above the calibrated percentile versus peer ingredients; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Jawad Bhatti (pain management physician); Keri Ayres (owner, Ability Unlimited); Lori Adcock (operations manager, Ability Unlimited); Kevin White (owner, Ithiel Group residential group homes); Yvoune Kara Petrie (president/COO, Virginia Integrative Health); Cristina Schasse (Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist)
State_County: Virginia - Richmond; Virginia - Fauquier County (Warrenton); Virginia - Loudoun County (Leesburg); Virginia - Henrico County (Glen Allen); North Carolina - Pender County (Hampstead)
PayerName: Medicare; Virginia Medicaid; CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; Device, DME; IdentityFraud; Drug_Prescriptions; FakeEncounter; Other - FDA Submission Fraud
SchemeSummary: Six defendants charged in separate EDVA schemes: Bhatti allegedly used FDA-unapproved ozone gas devices and billed Medicare/Medicaid for the injections as nerve blocks and for ultrasound guidance not actually used (over $5.2M claimed); Ayres and Adcock of Ability Unlimited allegedly hid arbitrary profit margins in subcontractor costs for Medicaid home/vehicle environmental modifications (approx. $245,000 and $213,210 respectively); White billed Medicaid over $1,000,000 (paid $461,704) for group home residents who were hospitalized, incarcerated or away; Petrie billed CareFirst about $1.9M for hyperbaric oxygen therapy never provided or prescribed, using recruited family/friends as patients and four physicians' NPIs without permission; Schasse allegedly diverted fentanyl and Versed from a Pyxis machine and substituted mislabeled saline/Precedex syringes given to patients.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, nerve-block CPT lines carry a drug or device with no FDA-approved NDC or HCPCS, visible in the claim's drug fields. Ultrasound-guidance CPT is billed on nearly every procedure line by one rendering NPI without a stored image report. Group-home residential day claims overlap inpatient hospital stay dates for the same beneficiary in the payer's other claims. Rendering NPIs listed on hyperbaric therapy claims have no NPPES address or credentialing link to the billing TIN. Controlled-substance waste and administration records in the automated dispensing cabinet log do not reconcile with the fentanyl units billed on patient accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Non-covered device masquerade: on rendering NPI x CPT, compute the share of procedure lines whose paired drug NDC or device HCPCS is absent from the FDA approved product file; fires when the share exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 2) Residential-inpatient overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of residential or group-home per-diem units billed on dates falling inside a paid inpatient, incarceration or hospice claim span; fires when that count exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 3) Unauthorised rendering identity: on rendering NPI x billing TIN, compute the count of paid claims where no credentialing or CMS-855 reassignment link exists between that NPI and the TIN; fires on exact registry mismatch in PECOS; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Charles Adams, M.D. (physician); Adams' medical practice
SchemeSummary: A federal jury found that Dr. Charles Adams and his medical practice violated the False Claims Act by submitting false claims to Medicare for chelation therapy (drugs to remove heavy metals) that was not medically necessary; Medicare reimbursed more than $1.1 million, and post-trial penalties brought total liability to over $27 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, chelation J-code and infusion CPT lines lack any claim-history diagnosis of heavy-metal poisoning for that beneficiary. No laboratory claim for blood or urine heavy-metal testing precedes the chelation administration date for the same beneficiary. One rendering NPI's chelation infusion units per beneficiary per year exceed the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers. Repeat chelation sessions continue for months with no interval toxic-level laboratory result in the beneficiary's other claims. The practice's share of total billing concentrated in chelation drug and infusion codes far exceeds its own trailing baseline.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Missing toxicity indication: on claim line, compute the count of heavy-metal poisoning diagnosis codes on the chelation claim and in the beneficiary's 12-month diagnosis history; fires when that count is zero; action prepay edit. 2) Pre-treatment lab absence: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the gap in days between the chelation date of service and the most recent paid heavy-metal laboratory test; fires when no such test exists in the lookback window; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Chelation intensity outlier: on rendering NPI x year, compute chelation infusion units per treated beneficiary over J-code and CPT units; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Michael L. Riggins
FraudTypeAll: Device, DME; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: Riggins paid for doctors' orders for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment and tricked physicians into signing DME orders and certificates of medical necessity, then submitted over $3.8 million in fraudulent claims to Medicare (reimbursed over $1.8 million) despite hundreds of victim complaints about fraudulent orders; he was sentenced to 57 months and roughly $1.8 million restitution. (The press release also lists unrelated non-health-care prosecutions.)
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, DMEPOS claims name an ordering NPI with no prior evaluation-and-management encounter with that beneficiary in claim history. A small set of ordering NPIs signs certificates of medical necessity for an implausibly large distinct-beneficiary count in one week. Beneficiary complaint records in the payer's contact-center file name the same supplier NPI repeatedly before payment. Beneficiary residence ZIPs sit far outside the service area declared on the supplier's CMS-855S enrolment record. Signature dates on submitted certificates of medical necessity precede the recorded physician-beneficiary encounter date on any claim.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the days between the DMEPOS date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) CMN signer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the distinct-beneficiary count and distinct supplier-NPI count on signed certificates of medical necessity; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Complaint-linked supplier: on supplier NPI x month, compute the count of beneficiary complaints in the contact-center file per hundred paid DMEPOS claims; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Mexico
FraudEntity: William Monford Wood (former Los Alamos National Laboratory employee)
State_County: New Mexico - Los Alamos County; California - Alameda County (Oakland, Livermore); California - Santa Barbara County (Santa Barbara)
SchemeSummary: A former Los Alamos National Laboratory employee submitted 23 false claims for payment between July 2016 and December 2017 relating to business trips to California, claiming time he did not actually work and expenses he did not incur or that lacked a legitimate business purpose; he agreed to pay $67,500 (including $38,549.83 restitution) and to never again work on federally funded contracts.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point, because the false submissions were employee travel and time vouchers on a federal contract. The nearest detection route is contractor expense-voucher auditing against badge access, hotel folios and airline records. Claimed labour hours can be reconciled against timekeeping and facility entry logs.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on employee ID x travel voucher, compute claimed work hours and expense dates against badge-access and receipt records; fires when claimed hours occur on dates with no corroborating record; action contractor audit and suspension of reimbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Kentucky
FraudEntity: Ashley Barnett (doctor of veterinary medicine); Laura Webb (doctor of veterinary medicine); Rachel Goldstein; Kristina Coomer (retail pharmacy employee); Matthew Ryan Elkins (advanced practice registered nurse-certified registered nurse anesthetist)
State_County: Kentucky - Jefferson County (Louisville); Kentucky - Washington County (Springfield); Kentucky - Oldham County (Crestwood); Indiana - Clark County (Jeffersonville)
SchemeSummary: Five defendants charged in Western Kentucky with controlled-substance diversion: two veterinarians allegedly used another's DEA registration number and, with a co-conspirator, issued prescriptions for over 25,000 Schedule II pills (oxycodone, hydrocodone) in the names of canines, including deceased and fictitious dogs, with the drugs actually going to the defendants; one defendant had a co-conspirator fill her own dextroamphetamine prescription and bill Medicaid, and other defendants stole oxycodone, buprenorphine and fentanyl from pharmacy/medical supply chains and tampered with a patient's fentanyl syringe.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the prescribing DEA number on the Schedule II claim belongs to a veterinarian not enrolled to treat human beneficiaries in PECOS. The patient name on the pharmacy claim has no matching Medicaid member ID or date of birth in eligibility files. Fill dates fall after the beneficiary's date of death in the Death Master File. The dispensing pharmacy's controlled-substance acquisitions in ARCOS fall short of the Schedule II quantities dispensed under that DEA number. The same beneficiary's stimulant prescription is filled and billed by a pharmacist NPI who is also the listed patient.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber-scope mismatch: on claim line, compare the prescriber DEA registration business activity and state licence board file specialty against human-patient eligibility; fires on exact registry mismatch for a veterinary registrant; action prepay edit. 2) Ghost patient identity: on claim line, compute the match rate of billed patient name, date of birth and member ID against the Medicaid eligibility and Death Master File records; fires when no exact match exists or fill date follows date of death; action claim suspension. 3) Dispenser self-fill and inventory gap: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x month, compute dispensed units minus ARCOS wholesaler acquisition units, plus the count of fills where dispensing pharmacist equals the patient; fires when the difference is positive or that count is above zero; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Terry Hill, Jr. (owner/operator of Recovery Street Central); Recovery Street Central (substance abuse treatment recovery facility)
SchemeSummary: Hill, excluded from Medicare and Medicaid in 2021 after a Medicaid fraud conviction, allegedly continued to secretly own and operate a Dayton substance abuse recovery facility that billed Medicaid more than $4 million for counseling services that were never provided or were provided in violation of Medicaid rules.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment, an owner or managing employee listed on the facility's CMS-855A ownership fields matches an individual on the OIG LEIE exclusion file. Bank account and pay-to address on the CMS-588 EFT record match those previously used by an excluded provider's prior entity. PECOS shows the excluded individual's home address or phone reused as the new entity's correspondence contact. At adjudication, counseling H-code units billed per rendering NPI per day exceed the hours available in a 24-hour workday. Beneficiary rosters overlap heavily with the excluded owner's prior billing entity in the payer's own remittance history.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Exclusion graph match: on TIN x owner SSN, compute the count of CMS-855A owners, managing employees and authorized officials matching OIG LEIE or state exclusion records; fires on any exact registry match; action payment suspension. 2) Shared-identifier successor: on bank account, compute the distinct count of billing TINs sharing that EFT account, address or phone with a previously excluded entity; fires when that count exceeds one; action site visit. 3) Counselor day impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total billed counseling minutes from H0004/H0015 units; fires when total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania
FraudEntity: Penn State Health (multi-hospital health system)
SchemeSummary: Penn State Health self-disclosed in 2023 that between December 2015 and November 2022 it submitted Medicare claims for Annual Wellness Visits that were not supported by the wellness record; it entered a February 2024 settlement agreeing to pay $11,712,336. (The same collections release also noted an unrelated non-health-care SNAP benefit-for-cash scheme by Jimmy Tran of Asia Market, Harrisburg, PA, involving $1,843,534 in benefits and $299,174.60 in forfeiture/restoration.)
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, G0438 or G0439 is billed without any documented health risk assessment element in the encounter record supporting the wellness visit. The same beneficiary shows G0438 initial wellness visits billed more than once in a lifetime across the payer's claim history. G0439 subsequent wellness visits appear at intervals shorter than the 11 full months required by the benefit rule. Wellness visit volume per rendering NPI per day exceeds the visit minutes physically available in that provider's scheduled hours. The rendering NPI on the wellness claim is a non-physician whose specialty in PECOS was not supervised or enrolled during the service period.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Lifetime and interval rule: on beneficiary x HCPCS, compute the count of paid G0438 lines lifetime and the month gap between consecutive G0439 dates of service; fires when G0438 count exceeds one or the gap is under 11 months; action prepay edit. 2) Wellness visit day capacity: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the count of G0438/G0439 lines multiplied by the typical visit minutes; fires when the product exceeds 24 hours; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Wellness billing rate outlier: on provider NPI, compute the ratio of G0438/G0439 lines to total E/M lines against the provider's trailing 24-month baseline; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Edward William Salko, D.O. (physician); Jackson & Coker LocumTenens, LLC (health care staffing company); Justin Leland (owner of Spokane Valley medical supply company)
State_County: Washington - Benton County (Richland); Washington - Spokane County (Spokane Valley)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Device, DME; FakeEncounter
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the office reported health care recoveries including $700,000 in civil collections from physician Edward William Salko and Jackson & Coker LocumTenens, LLC, and $224,620 from Justin Leland, based on allegations they took part in kickback schemes in which Medicare was billed for medically unnecessary durable medical equipment and diagnostic laboratory testing (figures span multiple defendants and separate settlements).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on DMEPOS and diagnostic lab claims has no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One staffing-agency-placed ordering physician signs orders for beneficiaries across many states within a single week. The same beneficiary receives an identical L-code brace and a large panel lab test ordered by the same NPI on the same date. Ordering volume for a physician jumps from near-zero to peer-top-decile immediately after a locum tenens contract start recorded in PECOS reassignment fields. Multiple unrelated supplier and laboratory NPIs submit claims citing the identical ordering NPI and identical diagnosis code strings.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and beneficiary; fires when no encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the distinct count of beneficiary states, supplier NPIs and laboratory NPIs on ordered claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Paired DME-lab bundle: on beneficiary x ordering NPI x date of service, compute the count of DMEPOS L-code lines co-occurring with high-value diagnostic panel lines; fires when that count exceeds the provider's trailing baseline rate; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Unnamed network of healthcare companies (telehealth psychological care providers); Unnamed operators of Connecticut dental practices
SchemeSummary: Annual collections release noting two health care civil recoveries: approximately $4.5 million from a network of healthcare companies alleged to have submitted false claims to Medicare and Connecticut Medicaid for telehealth psychological care services, and more than $1 million from operators of Connecticut dental practices alleged to have paid patient recruiters to steer Connecticut Medicaid patients to their practice. Figures span multiple unnamed defendants.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, telehealth psychotherapy units billed per rendering NPI per date of service exceed the minutes available in 24 hours. Psychotherapy CPT 90837 lines lack any documented session start and stop times in the encounter record supporting the 60-minute threshold. The same beneficiary receives duplicate telehealth counseling claims from several unrelated group TINs on the same date of service. Dental claims cluster around a small set of beneficiary addresses and phone numbers repeated across unrelated NPPES beneficiary records, indicating recruiter steering. Marketing or recruiter payments appear as contracted managing entities on the practice's CMS-855 ownership and managing-employee fields.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Telehealth minute impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total psychotherapy minutes implied by 90832/90834/90837 units plus place-of-service 02/10 lines; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 2) Duplicate session overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlapping billed session minutes across distinct rendering NPIs and TINs; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero; action claim suspension. 3) Recruiter address concentration: on dental practice NPI, compute the distinct-beneficiary count sharing a single address or phone number in claim demographic fields divided by total beneficiaries; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action site visit.

SchemeSummary: In a debt-collection recap press release, the office noted that Keven Ellis Partin pleaded guilty to offering or paying health care kickbacks and was ordered to pay $338,805 in restitution to the Department of Labor, TRICARE, the Department of Veterans Affairs and Medicare; the district recovered $287,521.53 of that in FY2024 through liens and other enforcement tools (other collections listed in the release involve non-health-care bank fraud and drug cases).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Shephard Spruill
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the office reported recovering over $800,000 that criminal defendant Shephard Spruill had transferred and concealed; Spruill had participated in fraudulent billings to Medicaid by abusing his access to patient information. (The release also notes an unrelated $500,000 recovery from Michael Robinson for USDA farm assistance program fraud.)
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claims cite beneficiary IDs whose access came from an employee account with no corresponding encounter in the practice's other claims history. A single rendering NPI shows a sudden burst of new beneficiaries never previously seen in the payer's remittance history. Billed beneficiaries' residence ZIPs on the eligibility file lie far outside the billing provider's service area. Payment goes to a bank account on the CMS-855 EFT page that recently changed and is shared with unrelated billing TINs. Beneficiaries deny service when surveyed, and no ordering NPI or prior-auth record supports the dates of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) New-beneficiary burst: on provider NPI x week, compute the count of beneficiaries with no prior paid claim to that NPI divided by total beneficiaries billed; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action claim suspension. 2) Shared payee account: on bank account number from the CMS-855 EFT record, compute the distinct count of billing TINs receiving remittance; fires when that count exceeds one without documented common ownership; action payment suspension. 3) Orphan-encounter check: on claim line, compute the days between date of service and the nearest other claim for that beneficiary with the same TIN; fires when no supporting encounter exists in the lookback window; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
FraudEntity: Riverpark Operations, LLC (operator of Avamere Riverpark of Eugene skilled nursing facility); Avamere Group, LLC (parent company)
SchemeSummary: Riverpark billed Medicare and Oregon Medicaid for skilled nursing facility services at its 119-bed Eugene facility that were allegedly grossly substandard because staffing fell below minimum requirements, leading to preventable urinary tract infections, pressure sores and falls; Riverpark and parent Avamere paid $2 million and entered a five-year Quality-of-Care Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, Payroll-Based Journal nurse hours per resident day fall below the state minimum for the facility CCN's census on the same dates billed as skilled RUG/PDPM days. MDS assessments record new Stage 2+ pressure ulcers, UTIs and falls acquired after admission at rates above same-state peers. The PDPM nursing case-mix component billed implies staffing intensity the PBJ file cannot support for those dates of service. Hospital claims for the same beneficiaries show emergency transfers for sepsis or fracture within days of the billed SNF days. State survey deficiency citations for staffing overlap the same billing periods on the CMS-2567 record.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staffing-to-billing mismatch: on facility CCN x day, compute PBJ total nurse hours divided by resident census and compare to the state minimum hours per resident day; fires when the ratio falls below the regulatory minimum on days billed as skilled; action prepay edit. 2) Acquired-harm rate: on facility CCN x quarter, compute the count of MDS-coded facility-acquired pressure ulcers, UTIs and falls divided by resident days; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action postpay audit. 3) Case-mix versus hours: on facility CCN x month, compute mean PDPM nursing component index minus PBJ-implied staffing index; fires when the gap is above the facility's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Amstrong Chapajong (personal care aide and community support worker); Michelle Shropshire (WMATA employee); Harlisha Jones (WMATA employee); Sharon Washington (WMATA employee); Selethia Blake (WMATA employee); Brady Turner (WMATA employee); Lushawn Foreman (WMATA employee); Margot Jackson (WMATA employee)
State_County: District of Columbia (Washington, DC); Maryland; Virginia
PayerName: Medicaid (District of Columbia Medicaid program); American Family Life Assurance Company of Columbus (AFLAC)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Wire Fraud; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Two D.C. cases charged as part of the 2025 national takedown: Chapajong, working as both a personal care aide and community support worker, billed D.C. Medicaid for in-home personal care and behavioral health services to multiple clients in different places at the same time, with EVV data showing he was not near clients' homes (Medicaid paid $461,369); separately, WMATA employees Shropshire and Jones and other co-workers submitted fraudulent AFLAC health care and short-term disability claims using forged medical excuse notes and physician statements for injuries and treatments that never occurred, with Jones kicking back about 20% of the roughly $58,750 she received to Shropshire (AFLAC paid at least $362,035 on the other employees' false claims). Figures span multiple defendants; Shropshire was later sentenced to 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, EVV visit records place the rendering aide's GPS location away from the client's address on the billed dates of service. Two personal care or community support claim lines for the same rendering NPI show overlapping service minutes for different beneficiaries. Summed billed units per rendering NPI per day exceed the hours physically available in 24 hours. Disability and medical-excuse documentation carries a physician NPI that never submitted any claim for that patient on the stated treatment dates. The same attending physician signature and note template appear across unrelated claimants in the same employer group.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) EVV geofence mismatch: on claim line, compute the distance between the EVV check-in coordinates and the beneficiary's address on the eligibility file; fires when the distance exceeds the geofence radius for that visit; action prepay edit. 2) Aide overlap: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total overlapping billed service minutes across distinct beneficiaries; fires when overlapping minutes exceed zero or daily units exceed 24 hours; action claim suspension. 3) Phantom-certifier check: on certifying physician NPI x claimant, compute the count of that physician's paid encounter claims for the claimant within the certified treatment window; fires when that count is zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas
FraudEntity: Medisca, Inc.; Booz Allen Hamilton; Elara Caring and subsidiaries (hospice provider); Ma Acupuncture Center and Dr. Dongxin Ma; Five Point Enterprises LLC; Lafayette RE Management LLC and Thibault Adrien; Freedom Solar LLC; Oncology San Antonio and Dr. Jayasree Rao; Dr. Alfonso Luevano; Shrieve Chemical Company LLC; Sachnikumar Patel, RPh., Medical Arts Pharmacy, and Express Pharmacy
State_County: Texas - Western District of Texas (San Antonio; El Paso)
FraudTypeAll: Drug_Prescriptions; Upcoding; FakeEncounter; kickback_Bribery For Referral; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Falsify certificate; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Annual roundup of over 25 civil enforcement recoveries totaling $55,969,678.60 by the Western District of Texas in 2024, spanning multiple defendants: Medisca allegedly reported false and inflated Average Wholesale Prices for compounding ingredients ($21.75M); Elara Caring allegedly billed hospice services for patients who were not terminally ill ($4.2M); Ma Acupuncture Center/Dr. Ma allegedly submitted inflated acupuncture bills to the VA ($2.3M judgment); Oncology San Antonio/Dr. Rao allegedly paid unlawful kickbacks and billed medically unnecessary tests and treatments ($1.3M); Dr. Luevano and pharmacy defendants allegedly issued/dispensed unlawful controlled-substance prescriptions; and PPP borrowers allegedly made false certifications to obtain or have loans forgiven. Figures span multiple unrelated defendants.

The nearest non-claims route is tracking each settlement separately through the district's civil recovery and debt files. Individual mechanics such as inflated price reporting and non-terminal hospice would each need their own control if pursued as separate cases.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: David A. Parks (physician); James M. Bilderback (clinical manager and clinical research coordinator); Michelle J. Scheer (front desk assistant)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; private health insurers
SchemeSummary: Indictment alleges a St. Louis clinic physician, clinical manager and front desk assistant conspired to prescribe controlled substances outside the usual course of professional practice to maximize patient volume and profit, and that Parks and Bilderback billed Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and private insurers for services falsely identifying Parks as the rendering provider, including while he was out of the country.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, E/M and procedure claims list a rendering NPI on dates when passport or travel records place that physician outside the country. Rendering NPI daily billed time across all payers exceeds the hours available in 24 hours at that place of service. Controlled-substance prescriptions under one prescriber DEA number show high-dose opioid and benzodiazepine combinations across a wide beneficiary radius in PDMP data. Visit intervals per beneficiary cluster at the minimum refill spacing with identical CPT levels every encounter. Incident-to claims lack any supervising-physician presence documented in the practice's schedule or timesheets.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Impossible-day rendering: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute total CPT-implied service minutes summed across all claim lines and payers; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours or falls on documented absence dates; action claim suspension. 2) Prescriber concentration: on prescriber DEA/NPI x month, compute the count of beneficiaries receiving opioid plus benzodiazepine on overlapping days divided by panel size; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Cloned-visit ratio: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the share of E/M claims at a single CPT level with identical diagnosis code sets; fires when above the provider's own trailing baseline; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky
SchemeSummary: Annual statistical press release rather than a single fraud case: the Eastern District of Kentucky reported collecting over $20 million for crime victims and taxpayers in FY2024 (including $14,299,361.43 through its Financial Litigation Program and asset forfeitures) and obtaining $20,078,263.98 in civil settlements and judgments, of which over $19.7 million came from False Claims Act enforcement and more than $300,000 from civil penalties paid by healthcare providers who violated the Controlled Substances Act. No individual defendant, payer, or scheme is identified.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual statistical release of district collection totals with no named defendant, payer or billing scheme. There is no claim and no adjudication point to control. The nearest non-claims route is case-level tracking of the underlying False Claims Act and Controlled Substances Act penalty matters as they are individually resolved.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on each resolved provider judgment, compute remaining balance and enrolment status to trigger revalidation review.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Graciela Venegas, aka "Graciela Salgado" (U.S. Postal Service employee)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Labor (federal workers' compensation program); U.S. Postal Service
SchemeSummary: Venegas, a USPS employee receiving federal workers' compensation benefits since 2012, allegedly continued to claim her spouse as a dependent after their 2013 divorce and his 2014 death, thereby collecting augmented monthly benefits equal to an extra 8 1/3 percent of her pre-injury pay and pocketing $51,776 in unentitled payments from 2013 to 2024. Charged with five counts of wire fraud and one false statement to the U.S. Department of Labor.
WaysToIdentify: At each compensation payment cycle, match the claimed dependent spouse SSN on Form CA-1032 against the Social Security Death Master File. Compare the dependent's name on the augmented-rate benefit record to state vital-records divorce decree files. Check whether the dependent spouse appears on any beneficiary's other claims or tax filings after the stated marriage date. Compute the elapsed years since the last signed CA-1032 dependency recertification on the claimant's case file. Flag augmented-rate cases where no dependent has appeared as an enrolled dependent in the payer's own health-benefit enrolment file.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Dependent death match: on beneficiary x payment cycle, compute a match of the dependent SSN and date of birth on Form CA-1032 against the Death Master File; fires when an exact registry match with a death date before the payment date exists; action payment suspension. 2) Augmentation recertification gap: on beneficiary, compute the days between the payment date and the most recent signed CA-1032 dependency attestation; fires when the gap exceeds the program's annual recertification interval; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Marital-status conflict: on beneficiary, compute the count of state vital-records divorce or remarriage events dated after the dependency attestation date; fires when that count is at least one; action claim suspension, then postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Unified Care Services LLC (skilled nursing facility chain); Emmanual David (owner); Casa Montana LLC; Geri-Care Inc.; Geri Care V LLC; Pacific Palms Healthcare LLC; Foothill Care Center Inc.; Mount Megiddo LLC; Canyon Properties III LLC; Cloverleaf Enterprises Inc.; Foothill Care Center LLC; Foothill Care Center II LLC; David Kleis III LLC; David Kleis II LLC; Miramonte Enterprises LLC; Washington Enterprises III LLC
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: A chain of skilled nursing facilities and its owner allegedly falsely certified on PPP loan and loan-forgiveness applications in 2020 that each applying entity was a small business with fewer than 500 employees, concealing that the entities were part of a larger commonly owned and controlled chain that made them ineligible for PPP loans; they agreed to pay $18 million to resolve the qui tam FCA suit, with $2,070,000 going to the whistleblower.
WaysToIdentify: This is a loan-eligibility certification scheme, so there is no health care claim and no adjudication point in the payer's system. The nearest non-claims route is comparing each applicant entity's certified headcount to commonly owned affiliate structures. CMS-855A ownership and managing-control disclosures identify the affiliated chain that defeats the small-business certification.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on applicant EIN, compute the total employee count across all entities sharing owners, officers or managing control in CMS-855A and state licence filings, and fires when the affiliated total exceeds the program size standard.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: People's Rx, Inc., d/b/a The People's Pharmacy Shoppe (pharmacy)
PayerName: Medicare Part D; New Jersey Medicaid
SchemeSummary: The pharmacy submitted claims to Medicare Part D and New Jersey Medicaid for prescription drugs never dispensed to beneficiaries; wholesaler inventory records showed it had not purchased enough of the medications to fill the prescriptions it billed. It agreed to pay $995,420 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, billed units of an NDC exceed the pharmacy's wholesaler pedigree and ARCOS acquisition quantities for the same period. Refill intervals on chronic NDCs are shorter than the prior fill's days supply for many beneficiaries. Beneficiaries billed by the pharmacy have no matching prescriber encounter claim from the listed prescriber NPI. High-cost NDC volume jumps far above the pharmacy's own trailing baseline without any change in unique beneficiary count. Beneficiary ZIP codes on paid claims cluster far outside the pharmacy's CMS-855B service area.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Inventory reconciliation: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x month, compute billed dispensed units minus purchased units from wholesaler pedigree and 340B or ARCOS records; fires when billed exceeds purchased; action payment suspension. 2) Early refill accumulation: on beneficiary x NDC, compute the gap in days between consecutive fill dates minus the prior days supply; fires when the gap is negative on a count of fills above the calibrated percentile versus peer pharmacies; action prepay edit. 3) Orphan prescription: on claim line, compute the count of encounter claims between the listed prescriber NPI and the beneficiary in the lookback window; fires when that count is zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina
FraudEntity: Premier Medical, Inc. (clinical laboratory); Kevin S. Murdock (former CEO and owner of Premier Medical); Michael Conroy (former Vice President of Compliance, Premier Medical); Freedom Medical Labs, LLC (marketing/referral entity); Robert Alan Richardson (Freedom Medical); Edward Burch (Freedom Medical)
PayerName: Medicaid (Georgia Medicaid; Colorado Medicaid; South Carolina Medicaid)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Premier Medical and its owner paid kickbacks to Freedom Medical marketers who set up tables at bus stops, dollar stores and street corners in low-income areas of GA, CO and SC, paid Medicaid beneficiaries up to $20 for DNA swabs, and bought telemedicine physician orders from providers with no treating relationship; Premier then billed state Medicaid programs up to roughly $12,000 per cancer genetic (CGX) test. Judgments/settlements total over $114 million across all defendants (Premier default judgment $71,015,255.70; Murdock consent judgment $27,544,460; Richardson and Freedom Medical $8 million; Burch $8 million; Conroy $15,000), against actual program losses of about $13.77 million.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on CGX panel CPT codes has no prior treating encounter claim with that beneficiary. The ordering telehealth NPI submits CGX orders for beneficiaries across multiple state Medicaid programs in one week. Beneficiary residence ZIPs cluster far outside the laboratory's CMS-855B service area on file. The same beneficiary receives duplicate hereditary cancer panel CPT codes from unrelated laboratory NPIs within a short window. No oncology or family-history diagnosis appears anywhere in the beneficiary's claim history supporting the panel.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the days between the CGX date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Telehealth orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute the count of distinct beneficiary states and distinct laboratory NPIs on ordered molecular pathology CPT lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Germline panel duplication: on beneficiary x CPT, compute the count of distinct laboratory NPIs paid for hereditary cancer panels in the member's lifetime; fires when that count exceeds one; action prior-authorisation requirement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee
SchemeSummary: Annual statistical announcement rather than a single case: the Middle District of Tennessee U.S. Attorney's Office reported collecting $137,054,515 in FY2024, including $135,738,858 in civil recoveries largely under the False Claims Act (including Medicare and TennCare fraud) and over $59 million in Controlled Substances Act civil penalties, about $4,130,000 in criminal money judgments, and $939,718 in forfeited assets.
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual statistical collections announcement with no named defendant, no claim and no adjudication point. The reported totals aggregate many unrelated civil and criminal matters. The nearest non-claims route is per-case tracking of False Claims Act and Controlled Substances Act resolutions in the district's debt files.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Nearest control outside the claims system: on each resolved provider TIN, compute open judgment balance against current enrolment status and refer active billers to integrity-agreement monitoring.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana
FraudEntity: Lafayette Physical Rehabilitation Hospital; Acadiana Management Group (parent company); Dr. Carolyn Smith (physician)
SchemeSummary: In a False Claims Act settlement announced among the district's notable cases, Lafayette Physical Rehabilitation Hospital and its parent Acadiana Management Group paid $1.2 million and Dr. Carolyn Smith agreed to pay $575,000 to resolve allegations that they submitted claims to Medicare for inpatient rehabilitation services that were not medically necessary.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, inpatient rehabilitation facility claims lack a documented IRF-PAI showing the required intensive therapy tolerance and multidisciplinary need. Compare the beneficiary's prior claims: admissions arriving directly from the same acute hospital under common ownership suggest routing rather than clinical need. The certifying physician NPI on the IRF preadmission screen signs a share of admissions far above same-specialty peers. Case-mix group distribution on the facility's claims skews to high-weight CMGs relative to state IRF peers. Short lengths of stay with rapid discharge home contradict the certified need for hospital-level rehabilitation.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) IRF certification concentration: on certifying physician NPI x quarter, compute the count of IRF admissions certified and the share lacking a prior 3-day acute stay or qualifying condition in the 60% rule list; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Therapy intensity shortfall: on claim (IRF stay), compute total therapy minutes from the IRF-PAI divided by length of stay in days; fires when below the intensive-therapy threshold in the coverage rule; action prepay edit. 3) Referral funnel: on referring hospital NPI x IRF NPI, compute the share of that IRF's admissions originating from one commonly owned hospital per CMS-855A ownership fields; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer IRFs; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

No dates of service, HCPCS codes, or provider NPIs are identified, so no edit can be written. The nearest non-claims route is tracking case outcomes into the payer's provider-sanction and OIG LEIE screening feed.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Vermont
SchemeSummary: Not a fraud case document: this is a press release announcing the resignation of U.S. Attorney Nikolas Kerest for the District of Vermont, summarizing office accomplishments including a Controlled Substances Act settlement with eBay and recoveries from NextGen (electronic health records) and Vermont defense contractors, without describing any specific health care fraud scheme.
WaysToIdentify: This is a resignation press release with no billing conduct, no claim line, and no adjudication point. The recoveries mentioned involve contractors and software vendors rather than payer-adjudicated claims. The nearest non-claims route is contract and grant oversight by the awarding agency's inspector general.
