FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Maintain a standing referral pipeline from payer program-integrity analytics to the prosecuting office.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division (Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section) and U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California
FraudEntity: Barco Uniforms Inc. (apparel seller/importer); Kenny Chan (operator of supplier companies); David Chan (operator of supplier companies); Able Allied Limited; Nathan Global Direct Inc.; J&K Garment Inc.; Mega Goodwill Ltd.; JS Garment Co.; Superway Import & Export Inc.
SchemeSummary: The United States intervened in a qui tam False Claims Act suit alleging that Barco Uniforms and Chan-controlled supplier companies used a double-invoicing scheme, submitting false entry summaries to U.S. Customs and Border Protection that undervalued garments imported from China and elsewhere, thereby reducing and underpaying customs duties owed; the underpayment allegedly continued after a third-party auditor warned Barco about duty-calculation risks.
WaysToIdentify: This is customs duty underpayment on imported goods, with no health care claim and no adjudication point. The relevant record is the CBP entry summary and commercial invoice, not a remittance file. The nearest detection route is CBP reconciliation of declared entered value against the importer's paid-invoice and wire-transfer records. Prior auditor warnings to the importer create a documented knowledge trail for penalty exposure.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. CBP can compare declared value per entry summary against the importer's ledgered payments to the supplier and open a focused assessment on divergence.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Aetna, Inc. and affiliates (Medicare Advantage insurer); Elevance Health, Inc. (formerly Anthem) (Medicare Advantage insurer); Humana Inc. (Medicare Advantage insurer); eHealth, Inc. and an affiliate (insurance broker); GoHealth, Inc. (insurance broker); SelectQuote, Inc. (insurance broker)
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: The United States intervened in a qui tam False Claims Act suit alleging that Aetna, Elevance/Anthem and Humana paid hundreds of millions of dollars in kickbacks, disguised as marketing or other payments, to broker organizations eHealth, GoHealth and SelectQuote in exchange for steering Medicare beneficiaries into their Medicare Advantage plans regardless of suitability; Aetna and Humana also allegedly threatened to withhold these payments to pressure brokers to enroll fewer disabled beneficiaries perceived as less profitable.
WaysToIdentify: At enrolment reconciliation, compare the plan's broker compensation payments against CMS broker compensation caps in the plan bid and marketing files. Payments labeled as marketing, co-op, or data fees to a field marketing organization exceed per-enrollee caps in the same period. Enrollment files show one broker NPN steering a dominant share of members into a single contract despite multi-carrier appointment. Disenrollment within 90 days of a broker-sourced enrollment runs far above the contract's own trailing baseline. Enrollment rates for beneficiaries with disability-based original entitlement fall below plan-service-area demographics in the CMS enrollment data.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Broker payment cap test: on broker organization TIN x contract x year, compute total payments of all types divided by enrollments produced; fires when the quotient exceeds the CMS compensation cap for that year; action payment suspension. 2) Steering concentration: on broker NPN x quarter, compute the share of enrollments going to one parent-organization contract; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers appointed with the same carrier set; action postpay audit. 3) Disability enrollment shortfall: on contract x county, compute the ratio of disabled-entitlement enrollees to the county's Medicare disabled share; fires when below the calibrated percentile versus peer contracts in the same market; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Delaware
FraudEntity: Dr. Shayasta S. Mufti (physician)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleges Dr. Mufti referred more than 100 Medicare beneficiaries for expensive, medically unnecessary genetic laboratory tests based on brief telemedicine consultations or no consultation at all, without any treating relationship, examination, or use of results to manage patients' conditions, causing Medicare to pay claims of thousands of dollars per patient.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on high-cost molecular CPT claims has no prior office or telehealth E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One ordering NPI's beneficiaries span many states outside the ordering physician's licensed state per the state licence board file. Ordered panels repeat the same CPT set for nearly every beneficiary, indicating a template rather than clinical selection. No downstream treatment, drug NDC, or follow-up E/M claim appears in the beneficiary's claim history after the result date. The telehealth E/M that does exist is a minimal-duration code billed on the same day as the order for dozens of patients.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between the specimen date of service and the most recent E/M claim between that ordering NPI and beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Orderer panel uniformity: on ordering NPI x month, compute the distinct-value count of molecular CPT combinations divided by the count of beneficiaries ordered for; fires when below the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) Result non-use: on beneficiary x molecular CPT, compute the count of subsequent E/M, drug, or procedure claims by the ordering NPI within 180 days; fires when that count is zero for a provider whose zero-rate is above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia; U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: Vohra Wound Physicians Management LLC; Dr. Ameet Vohra (founder and majority owner); VHS Holdings, PA
SchemeSummary: DOJ alleges Vohra, a nationwide bedside wound care provider serving nursing homes and skilled nursing facilities, programmed its proprietary EMR to bill nonsurgical debridements as higher-paying surgical debridements, hired physicians without wound care expertise and trained them with misleading Medicare rules, and set revenue-driven debridement targets, causing medically unnecessary and upcoded Medicare claims. The EMR also automatically appended Modifier 25 to E&M claims so exams already included in the global surgical debridement package were separately billed.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the group's ratio of surgical debridement CPT 11042-11047 to nonsurgical CPT 97597-97598 sits far above same-specialty peers. Rendering NPIs show no wound care or surgical specialty in NPPES taxonomy or board certification files. Modifier 25 appears on nearly every E/M line paired with a same-day debridement by the same rendering NPI. Debridement counts per rendering NPI per date of service across multiple nursing facilities imply impossible travel and service minutes. Serial debridements recur on the same beneficiary and wound site at fixed intervals regardless of MDS-documented wound status.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Surgical debridement mix: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute surgical debridement lines divided by all debridement lines using CPT 11042-11047 and 97597-97598; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action prepay edit on the surgical codes. 2) Modifier 25 saturation: on rendering NPI x month, compute the share of E/M lines carrying Modifier 25 with a same-day global-period procedure by that NPI; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action claim suspension pending documentation request (ADR). 3) Per-day service feasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of CMS time or work-value proxies for all debridement and E/M lines plus travel between distinct facility addresses; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida
FraudEntity: AIMA Business and Medical Support, LLC (medical billing and compliance company); Aaron Liston (CEO); Excellent Laboratories Inc. d/b/a Selecta Laboratory (diagnostic laboratory)
SchemeSummary: The government alleges AIMA, a billing and compliance company with a UK-based CEO and India-based staff, submitted approximately $15.18 million in Medicare Part B claims for genetic tests on behalf of Miami lab Excellent Laboratories (d/b/a Selecta Laboratory) despite knowing the tests were not medically necessary and were not ordered by beneficiaries' treating physicians; Selecta collected Medicare funds and paid AIMA for its billing services.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on the lab's molecular claims has no prior claim history with the beneficiary establishing a treating relationship. A single billing agent's submitter ID files claims for multiple lab NPIs with identical panel composition and coding patterns. Beneficiary residence ZIPs cluster far outside the lab's CLIA site and service area on the CMS-855B enrolment record. Ordering NPIs are concentrated in a handful of physicians producing volumes above same-specialty peers. The lab's paid volume rises from near-zero to top decile within weeks of a new billing submitter ID being registered.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Submitter fan-out: on billing submitter ID x month, compute the distinct count of billing lab NPIs and the correlation of their CPT mix; fires when distinct NPIs and mix similarity are both above the calibrated percentile versus peer submitters; action prepay edit. 2) Treating-relationship test: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute the count of E/M claims between that ordering NPI and beneficiary in the prior 12 months; fires when the count is zero; action claim suspension. 3) Geographic dispersion: on lab NPI x month, compute the share of beneficiaries whose residence state differs from the CLIA laboratory state; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer labs; action site visit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Local Initiative Health Authority for Inland Empire Health Plan d/b/a Inland Empire Health Plan (IEHP) (California Local Initiative Medi-Cal managed care health plan)
State_County: California - San Bernardino County (Rancho Cucamonga); California - Riverside County
SchemeSummary: The United States alleges IEHP, which received Medi-Cal Expansion funding required to be spent at least 85% on allowed medical expenses, avoided repaying surplus funds by creating sham provider 'incentive programs' and an extra-contractual retroactive rate increase - funneling payments for consultants, technology services, administrative costs and other patient populations through providers and backdating spending - and made false statements to DHCS (relayed to the federal government) about the nature, timing and purpose of those payments so it could retain the overpayment rather than return it.
WaysToIdentify: At MLR reconciliation, compare the plan's reported allowed medical expenses in the DHCS financial template against claim-level paid detail by provider NPI. Large lump-sum provider payments lacking encounter records or member attribution indicate non-claims spending booked as medical. Payment issue dates fall after the contract period close but are booked to the prior period, visible in the general ledger date fields. Retroactive rate increases appear in provider remittance history without a corresponding amended contract in the contract file. Payments trace to consultant and technology vendors downstream of the provider, visible in the provider's own subcontractor disclosures.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Unmatched medical expense: on plan contract x rate year, compute reported allowed medical expense minus the sum of adjudicated claim and encounter payments tied to member IDs; fires when the residual exceeds the plan's own trailing baseline residual share; action postpay audit with documentation request (ADR). 2) Backdated booking: on payment transaction, compute days between check issue date and the end of the accounting period credited; fires when the gap exceeds the contractual accrual window; action payment suspension of the reconciliation settlement. 3) Incentive lump-sum test: on provider NPI x payment, compute the ratio of non-claim incentive dollars to that provider's adjudicated claim dollars in the same period; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer providers in the network; action prepay edit on the settlement release.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California
FraudEntity: Local Initiative Health Authority for Inland Empire Health Plan d/b/a Inland Empire Health Plan (IEHP) (California Local Initiative Medi-Cal managed care health plan)
State_County: California - Riverside County and San Bernardino County (Rancho Cucamonga)
SchemeSummary: The United States alleges IEHP, which received Medi-Cal Expansion funding requiring at least 85% be spent on allowed medical expenses or refunded, misspent surplus funds through sham provider 'incentive' programs and an extra-contractual retroactive rate increase, disguising administrative, consultant and technology spending as incentive payments funneled through providers and backdating spending, while making false statements to DHCS (relayed to the federal government) to avoid repaying the difference.
WaysToIdentify: At MLR reconciliation, reported allowed medical expenses exceed the sum of member-attributable adjudicated claims in the encounter file. Bulk incentive payments to network providers carry no encounter records or quality-measure numerators in the quality reporting file. Ledger entries show service dates backdated into the closing rate year while checks issued afterwards. A retroactive rate increase appears in remittance history without an executed contract amendment on file with DHCS. Funds paid to providers are re-routed to consultants and IT vendors, traceable in subcontractor disclosure forms.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Encounter-backed expense ratio: on plan contract x rate year, compute adjudicated claim dollars tied to member IDs divided by reported allowed medical expense; fires when below the 85% floor stated in the funding rule; action payment suspension of the reconciliation. 2) Incentive without measure: on provider NPI x incentive payment, compute the count of linked quality-measure numerators or encounters; fires when the count is zero; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Period-shifting: on payment transaction, compute the gap in days between the credited period end and the actual disbursement date in the bank account record; fires when the gap exceeds the contractual accrual window; action postpay audit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania; DOJ Civil Division
FraudEntity: ProMedica Health System, Inc. (owner/operator); HCR ManorCare Inc. (affiliate); ProMedica Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation - Pottstown; ProMedica Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation - Riverview; ProMedica Skilled Nursing, Rehabilitation - Greenville East; ProMedica Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation - Imperial
State_County: Pennsylvania - Pottstown; Ohio; South Carolina - Greenville; Virginia
SchemeSummary: The United States intervened in a qui tam FCA suit alleging four ProMedica/HCR ManorCare skilled nursing facilities billed federal health care programs for non-existent or grossly substandard nursing care from 2017-2023, failing to develop or follow individualized care plans (inadequate wound care, hygiene/showers, and feeding assistance causing severe weight loss), and falsely documented in resident medical records that services had been provided when they had not.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, facility payroll-based journal nurse-hours per resident day fall far below the CMS staffing expectation for the billed RUG or PDPM level. MDS assessments report wound care and feeding assistance at frequencies unsupported by the PBJ staffing hours filed for the same days. Resident weight-loss and pressure-ulcer quality measures in MDS worsen while high-acuity per-diem billing rises. Charted service entries carry timestamps clustered in bulk after shift end, visible in EHR audit-log exports. State survey deficiency citations for care planning coincide with the billed dates of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staffing-to-acuity mismatch: on facility CCN x quarter, compute PBJ nurse hours per resident day divided by the case-mix-expected hours implied by billed PDPM components; fires when the ratio falls below the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action documentation request (ADR) then payment suspension. 2) Charting burst: on facility CCN x date of service, compute the share of clinical entries whose EHR audit-log creation timestamp is more than one shift after the documented care time; fires when above the facility's own trailing baseline; action postpay audit. 3) Outcome divergence: on facility CCN x quarter, compute the change in MDS-derived unplanned weight loss and new pressure ulcer rates alongside the change in high-acuity per-diem share; fires when outcomes worsen while acuity billing rises above the calibrated percentile versus peers; action site visit.
FeatureCategory: Cost Report and Risk Adjustment Audit

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland; U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland
FraudEntity: Dr. Richard Akoto, M.D. (family medical doctor); Richard O. Akoto, M.D. PC (his medical practice)
SchemeSummary: Akoto treated patients' pain with non-invasive auricular electro-acupuncture (P-Stim) devices taped behind the ear, a service Medicare does not cover, but billed Medicare using the code for surgical implantation of an implantable neurostimulator, a complex neurosurgical procedure, resulting in a $1,407,493.23 False Claims Act judgment against him and his practice.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, implantable neurostimulator CPT 64553/64555 is billed with an office place of service rather than a facility operating room. No corresponding implantable pulse generator HCPCS or device NDC appears on any claim for that beneficiary. No facility, anesthesia, or imaging claim exists on the same date of service for a purported surgical implantation. The rendering NPI's NPPES taxonomy carries no neurosurgical or pain-implant privileges in the state licence board file. Beneficiaries receive repeat implantation codes at short intervals, which is impossible for a single implanted device.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Device-absent implant: on claim line, compute the count of matching implantable device HCPCS or facility claims for the same beneficiary within the implant date window; fires when the count is zero for CPT 64553-64595; action prepay edit. 2) Place-of-service impossibility: on claim line, compare the place-of-service code against the CMS facility-only list for the billed implantation CPT; fires on exact mismatch; action claim suspension. 3) Repeat implantation: on beneficiary x implant CPT, compute the count of paid implantation events in a rolling 12 months; fires when the count exceeds one without a documented revision or removal code; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Missouri
FraudEntity: Dr. Mohd Azfar Malik (psychiatrist, part-owner of Behavioral Health Services, LLC, which owned and operated Psych Care Consultants)
PayerName: Medicare; Missouri Medicaid; private health insurers
SchemeSummary: Psychiatrist billed Medicare, Missouri Medicaid and private insurers for face-to-face psychotherapy sessions he did not personally provide, including claims submitted while he was out of state or out of the country and for services actually rendered by other practitioners; resolved by a $501,556 FCA settlement (double the $250,778 restitution) alongside an April 2025 guilty plea to making false statements in health care matters.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, total billed psychotherapy minutes from timed CPT 90832-90838 for a rendering NPI on one date exceed 24 hours. Dates of service overlap periods when the rendering NPI has no in-state activity, testable against travel or hotel records obtained on audit. Claims list the supervising psychiatrist as rendering while shift schedules show other practitioners delivered the sessions. Face-to-face place-of-service 11 is billed on days the provider filed no other local claims across any payer in remittance history. The same rendering NPI appears on claims from multiple distant practice addresses on identical dates of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Minutes-per-day feasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of CPT-defined service minutes for all timed psychotherapy and E/M lines; fires when the sum exceeds 24 hours or exceeds the calibrated percentile of peer psychiatrists; action prepay edit. 2) Geographic impossibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the maximum straight-line distance between billed service addresses; fires when travel between them is infeasible within the same day; action claim suspension. 3) Incident-to substitution: on rendering NPI x week, compute the count of face-to-face lines billed under that NPI divided by documented on-site hours from facility timesheets; fires when the quotient exceeds one; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: RegalCare Management Group, LLC; RegalCare Management 2.0, LLC (management companies); 19 skilled nursing facilities in Massachusetts and Connecticut; Eliyahu Mirlis (owner); Hector Caraballo (executive); Stern Therapy Consultants (therapy consultant)
State_County: Massachusetts - Amesbury; Massachusetts - Danvers; Massachusetts - Greenfield; Massachusetts - Harwich; Massachusetts - Holyoke; Massachusetts - Lowell; Massachusetts - Quincy; Massachusetts - Saugus; Massachusetts - Taunton; Massachusetts - Worcester; Connecticut
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid (MassHealth and its managed care organizations)
SchemeSummary: Civil False Claims Act complaint (government intervention in a qui tam suit) alleging that RegalCare's skilled nursing facilities systematically billed Medicare for the highest level of skilled rehabilitation therapy and MassHealth for inflated long-term care services that patients did not clinically need, with an executive altering patient records beyond his licensing level to support the billing and the therapy consultant scheduling unnecessary therapy and pressuring therapists to deliver it; claims were also submitted before supporting clinical documentation was complete.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the facility's share of ultra-high therapy RUG or highest PDPM case-mix levels far exceeds same-state SNF peers. Therapy minutes on the MDS cluster just above the threshold for the top payment tier. EHR audit logs show MDS and assessment fields edited by a user whose licence in the state board file does not permit clinical documentation. Claims are submitted before the assessment reference date documentation is finalised, visible in the gap between claim receipt date and record completion timestamp. Therapy volume per resident rises without corresponding change in admission diagnosis mix on the claim header.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Threshold clustering: on facility CCN x quarter, compute the share of MDS therapy-minute values falling within a narrow band just above the top payment tier cut-point; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-state peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Unlicensed record edit: on MDS assessment record, compute the count of clinical field edits by user IDs whose credential in the state licence board file lacks clinical scope; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Claim-before-documentation: on claim, compute days between claim submission date and the completion timestamp of the supporting assessment; fires when the value is negative; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Idaho
FraudEntity: Bloom Care LLC (urgent care operator); its owners
PayerName: Medicare; Medicaid; Department of Veterans Affairs
SchemeSummary: Bloom Care allegedly used the COVID-19 pandemic as a pretext to bill federal health care programs for medically unnecessary strep and influenza tests on asymptomatic patients at its Idaho and New Mexico urgent care centers, and billed high-level evaluation and management codes for COVID-19 patients by exaggerating time spent and complexity when lower-paying codes were warranted; settled for $3,000,000 with no admission of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, rapid strep CPT 87880 and influenza CPT 87804 are billed without any symptom-bearing ICD-10 diagnosis on the same claim. Testing rate per E/M visit at the clinic NPI far exceeds same-specialty urgent-care peers. Level 4 and 5 E/M code share for respiratory diagnoses sits above the clinic's own pre-pandemic trailing baseline. Documented visit time on the record falls below the minimum time floor for the billed time-based E/M code. Positivity rate on the billed rapid tests is far below the regional public health reporting rate, indicating untargeted testing.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Test-without-indication: on claim line, compute whether any ICD-10 code on the claim appears in the coverage-approved indication list for CPT 87880 or 87804; fires on exact mismatch with the covered-diagnosis file; action prepay edit. 2) E/M level drift: on billing NPI x quarter, compute the share of E/M lines at levels 4-5 for respiratory diagnoses; fires when above the provider's own trailing pre-period baseline and above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 3) Reflex testing rate: on clinic NPI x month, compute rapid antigen test lines divided by distinct E/M visits; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus urgent-care peers; action documentation request (ADR).
FeatureCategory: Coverage, Indication and Prior Auth Edits

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio
FraudEntity: Matthew Maluchnik
FraudTypeAll: Other - Unknown; Tax, Payroll or Coupon Fraud
SchemeSummary: In an annual collections announcement, the USAO noted that Matthew Maluchnik was sentenced in October 2023 for health care fraud and making false statements on his tax returns, and was ordered to pay $941,068.50 in restitution; in April 2024 the office transferred $715,979.50 in forfeited funds to the court for payment to his victims. The release does not describe the billing mechanics or payer. (The same release also listed a separate $7.6 million False Claims Act settlement with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation over federal grant applications and progress reports.)
WaysToIdentify: This is an annual collections round-up that names no billing mechanic, code, payer, or conduct period. Without a claim type or provider NPI, no adjudication-point edit can be specified. The nearest non-claims route is matching restitution and forfeiture judgments to the payer's overpayment recovery ledger and to grant-award oversight.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. Reconcile court-ordered restitution judgments against the payer's accounts-receivable file so recovered amounts offset outstanding overpayments.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Richard Hyland (Department of Veterans Affairs firefighter)
State_County: New Jersey - Lyons (Lyons VA Medical Center)
PayerName: U.S. Department of Labor (federal workers' compensation program)
SchemeSummary: Hyland, a VA firefighter who began receiving federal workers' compensation benefits after a 2014 back injury, falsely certified annually to the U.S. Department of Labor that he was not working or volunteering elsewhere while in fact working as a tow truck and long-haul truck driver and volunteering at his local fire department, collecting $479,341.26 in benefits from March 2017 through December 2024.
WaysToIdentify: At benefit recertification, the claimant's sworn EN-1032 earnings certification reports no work while state wage-reporting records show covered employment. Commercial driver licence and DOT medical certification records show an active CDL held during the disability period. Employer quarterly wage filings under the claimant's SSN identify a trucking employer during certified non-work months. Public volunteer fire department rosters list the claimant during the same benefit period. Medical restrictions on file conflict with the physical demands documented in the CDL medical examiner certificate.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Earnings certification match: on claimant SSN x certification period, compute wages reported in state new-hire and quarterly wage files during months certified as no-work on the EN-1032; fires when reported wages exceed zero; action payment suspension. 2) Licence activity conflict: on claimant SSN, compute whether an active CDL and DOT medical certificate exist with issue dates inside the disability period; fires on exact registry match; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Duration outlier: on claimant x injury code, compute total benefit months paid versus the same injury-code cohort; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peers with equivalent impairment ratings; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: Vault Medical Services, P.A.; Vault Medical Services of New Jersey, P.C.
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud
SchemeSummary: Vault provided COVID-19 specimen collection and vaccine administration via telehealth and in-person sites and billed the HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program for patients who actually had active health insurance, allegedly ignoring verified insurance information on file and failing to correct known patient data-integrity gaps; resolved for $8 million with no determination of liability.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, HRSA Uninsured Program claims carry patient identifiers that match an active commercial or Medicaid coverage record in the eligibility clearinghouse. The submitter's own intake file already contains a payer name and member ID for the same patient encounter. Duplicate paid claims exist for the same beneficiary and date of service in a commercial payer's remittance history. The share of claims submitted with missing or placeholder demographic fields is far above peer submitters. Eligibility verification transaction logs show a 271 response confirming coverage before the uninsured claim was filed.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Coverage crossmatch: on claim line, compute whether the patient identifier matches an active coverage segment in the eligibility file on the date of service; fires on exact match; action prepay edit. 2) Verification contradiction: on claim, compute the count of 270/271 eligibility transactions by that submitter for the same patient returning active coverage before submission; fires when the count exceeds zero; action claim suspension. 3) Data-integrity rate: on submitter NPI x month, compute the share of claims with missing SSN, date of birth, or address fields; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer uninsured-program submitters; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington
FraudEntity: Omnicell (Delaware-based VA contractor selling/leasing medical device hardware and software)
SchemeSummary: Omnicell held a federal contract to sell and lease medical device hardware and software to the VA at set or negotiated discounted prices but did not always charge the correct contract prices; although it issued credits when specific customers raised pricing concerns, it failed to systemically correct known pricing-system errors or identify and refund other federal customers it had overcharged. Resolved under the False Claims Act following a qui tam complaint by a former employee, with $4,366,660 paid ($2,183,330 as restitution to VA; $785,998.80 to the relator).
WaysToIdentify: At invoice adjudication, the unit price billed exceeds the ceiling price on the contract line item in the federal supply schedule file. Price variance for the same part number differs across federal customers within the same period. Credit memos issued to complaining customers exist without matching corrective credits to other customers who bought at the same wrong price. Contract modification effective dates precede invoices still charging the superseded higher price. Discount terms in the pricing agreement are absent from the vendor's order-entry system extract.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Contract price mismatch: on invoice line, compute billed unit price minus the contract ceiling price for that part number and effective date; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit. 2) Cross-customer price dispersion: on part number x quarter, compute the distinct-value count and range of unit prices charged across federal customers; fires when the range exceeds the contracted discount band; action postpay audit. 3) Unremediated credit: on part number x overcharge event, compute the count of customers charged the erroneous price minus the count receiving credits; fires when the difference exceeds zero; action payment suspension pending refund.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section
FraudEntity: Gregory Schreck (vice president of the company that operated DMERx); DMERx (internet-based platform)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care benefit programs; other insurers
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; Falsify certificate; Device, DME; FakeEncounter; Drug_Prescriptions; IdentityFraud
SchemeSummary: Schreck and co-conspirators used misleading mailers, TV ads and offshore call centers to harvest Medicare beneficiaries' personal information and consent to unnecessary orthotic braces and pain creams, then used the DMERx platform to generate signed doctors' orders from telemedicine companies that paid doctors to sign without examining patients; DME suppliers and pharmacies paid kickbacks for the orders and billed Medicare and other insurers over $1 billion, of which more than $360 million was paid.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the ordering NPI on L-code brace and compounded pain cream claims has no prior E/M encounter with that beneficiary. One telemedicine ordering NPI signs orders for beneficiaries across dozens of states within a single week. Beneficiary ZIPs sit far outside the service area declared on the supplier's CMS-855S enrolment. The same beneficiary receives duplicate L-code braces from several unrelated supplier NPIs and pharmacy NPIs within 30 days. Supplier and pharmacy claim volume jumps from near-zero to peer-top-decile shortly after a PECOS ownership change.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Order-encounter gap: on claim line x ordering NPI, compute days between date of service and the most recent E/M claim linking that ordering NPI to the beneficiary; fires when no such encounter exists in the lookback window; action prepay edit. 2) Telemedicine orderer dispersion: on ordering NPI x week, compute distinct beneficiary states and distinct billing supplier or pharmacy NPIs on ordered DMEPOS and topical analgesic claims; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension. 3) Duplicate device saturation: on beneficiary x HCPCS, compute count of distinct supplier NPIs paid in rolling 30 days; fires when count exceeds one absent documented replacement reason; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Mississippi
FraudEntity: Laron Evans (organizer, purported owner/manager of fake companies); Travious Quinshad Jackson (co-defendant)
State_County: Mississippi - Warren County (Vicksburg); Mississippi - Forrest County; Maryland; Minnesota; Florida - Orlando
PayerName: Third-party Health Savings Account administrator companies (Maryland and Minnesota)
FraudTypeAll: IdentityFraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Evans sent stolen personal identifying information for 57 real people to a Maryland third-party benefits administrator, falsely claiming they were employees of a fictitious company, so the administrator created and pre-funded Health Savings Account debit cards mailed to Vicksburg addresses; Evans and Jackson drained the cards on gift cards and goods, and Evans used proceeds to buy a $44,335 Suburban, then repeated the scheme with a Minnesota administrator (seeking $91,000 in HSA funding) while on bond in violation of court order. Restitution figures span both defendants ($1,917,231.26 for Evans and $302,099.34 for Jackson); Jackson received 2 years.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no adjudication point here; funding flowed through an employer-sponsored HSA account-opening process. At enrolment, the employer TIN submitted to the third-party administrator has no wage filings and no state employer registration on record. Dozens of enrolled 'employees' share a small set of mailing addresses in one city unrelated to the employer's stated location. The nearest detection route is the administrator's account-opening KYC and card-shipping address controls.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Employer verification mismatch: on employer TIN at account setup, compute a match indicator between the submitted TIN and state unemployment-insurance wage filings and IRS TIN-name records; fires on exact registry mismatch; action claim suspension of card funding pending verification. 2) Address concentration: on mailing address x employer TIN, compute count of distinct enrollee SSNs shipped cards to the same street address; fires when count exceeds the calibrated percentile versus peer employer groups of similar size; action documentation request (ADR) before card activation. 3) Funding velocity: on employer TIN x week, compute sum of pre-funded HSA dollars and share of cards drawn to zero within 14 days; fires when above the administrator's trailing baseline for comparable groups; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Dr. Scott Saffold (physician); Chesapeake Bay, ENT, P.C. (his medical practice)
State_County: Virginia - Virginia Beach; Virginia - Belle Haven (Accomack County)
SchemeSummary: Government alleged the doctor and his ENT practice billed federal and state health programs for medically unnecessary balloon sinus dilations - performing the procedure on six sinuses even absent medical indication - and staged the procedures side-by-side at separate times to increase reimbursement, while also billing CPT 31235 (endoscopy with sphenoid sinusoscopy) for services not actually performed. Resolved for $625,000 following a qui tam whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, claim lines show balloon sinus dilation CPT codes billed for six sinuses on the same beneficiary across staggered dates. The rendering NPI's rate of sinus dilation per unique beneficiary sits far above same-specialty otolaryngology peers in the payer's claims history. CPT 31235 sphenoid sinusoscopy is billed alongside dilation codes at a rate inconsistent with operative report availability. Prior imaging claims (sinus CT) are absent or show no obstructive disease before the dilation dates of service. The same beneficiary returns for additional sinus dilation lines within a short interval, indicating splitting rather than a single session.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Sinus site saturation: on beneficiary x rendering NPI, compute the count of distinct dilated sinus CPT/modifier sites billed within 180 days; fires when the count reaches all six sinuses without a documented CT indication claim; action prior-authorisation requirement. 2) Session splitting: on rendering NPI x beneficiary, compute the gap in days between successive balloon dilation dates of service and the count of such sessions per beneficiary; fires when multiple sessions occur within a window shorter than the provider's own trailing median; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Add-on endoscopy ratio: on rendering NPI x quarter, compute the ratio of CPT 31235 lines to total sinus dilation lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey
FraudEntity: NEXT Bio-Research Services LLC, d/b/a NEXT Molecular Analytics (clinical laboratory)
SchemeSummary: NEXT allegedly paid doctors in Texas and Arkansas thousands of dollars disguised as consulting and medical director fees to induce them to order NEXT laboratory tests, and paid independent contractor marketers commissions based on the volume and value of referrals, then billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE for the resulting lab tests. Resolved for $758,000 under the False Claims Act following a qui tam suit; relators receive $113,700.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, a small set of ordering NPIs accounts for a dominant share of one laboratory's total test volume across Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE. Those same ordering NPIs appear as medical directors or consultants in the lab's CMS-855B ownership and managing-employee fields or in Open Payments records. Test volume per ordering NPI rises sharply in the months after the first consulting payment date in Open Payments. Marketer-linked referral clusters show identical panel composition across unrelated beneficiaries and practices. Ordering physicians' specialty in NPPES is unrelated to the panels they order at that laboratory.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Orderer concentration: on laboratory NPI x quarter, compute the share of paid test dollars attributable to the top ordering NPIs and the Herfindahl index over ordering NPIs; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty laboratory peers; action postpay audit. 2) Payment-referral coupling: on ordering NPI x laboratory NPI, compute the change in monthly ordered test dollars before versus after the first Open Payments consulting or medical-director payment date; fires when the post-payment rate exceeds the orderer's own trailing baseline; action prepay edit on that pair. 3) Ownership overlap: on ordering NPI, compute an exact match against the laboratory's CMS-855B owner, officer and managing-employee fields; fires on exact registry match without a disclosed safe-harbour arrangement; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida; U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia
FraudEntity: Dr. Ameet Vohra (owner); Vohra Wound Physicians Management LLC
FraudTypeAll: Upcoding; FakeEncounter; Falsify certificate; Phantom Claims; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Vohra, a nationwide bedside wound-care provider for nursing home and skilled nursing facility patients, allegedly pressured, trained and financially incentivized its physicians to perform debridements at as many visits as possible regardless of medical need, and programmed its EHR/billing software so Medicare was always billed for the higher-reimbursed surgical excisional debridement (even when only routine non-surgical wound management or no procedure occurred) with false supporting documentation, plus non-billable evaluation and management services; resolved for $45 million plus a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the rendering NPI bills surgical excisional debridement CPT 11042-11047 on nearly every nursing-facility visit for the same beneficiary. Debridement-per-visit ratio for the group TIN sits far above same-specialty wound-care peers in remittance history. Repeat excisional debridements recur at intervals shorter than plausible wound healing on the beneficiary's claim timeline. Facility MDS assessments for those beneficiaries record no pressure ulcer stage consistent with excisional debridement. Separately billed E/M lines accompany debridement lines at a rate above the practice's own trailing baseline, without modifier-25 support.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Debridement-per-visit ratio: on rendering NPI x month, compute paid excisional debridement lines divided by total nursing-facility visit lines; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Repeat-debridement interval: on beneficiary x wound site, compute the gap in days between successive excisional debridement dates of service; fires when the median gap falls below clinically plausible healing intervals; action prepay edit. 3) Assessment corroboration: on beneficiary x date of service, compute a match between the billed debridement depth code and the wound stage recorded on the nearest MDS assessment; fires on exact registry mismatch or absent ulcer coding; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida
FraudEntity: VRA Enterprises, LLC dba Precision Rx (pharmacy)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Retention of Overpayment; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: Under the CMS OTC COVID-19 Test Demonstration Project (which reimbursed $12 per test, up to eight tests per beneficiary per month), the Tampa pharmacy billed Medicare Part B for over-the-counter COVID-19 tests it never shipped to beneficiaries, including roughly 136,491 January 2023 claims for tests not shipped until April 2023, and despite internally acknowledging it should refund Medicare for unshipped tests, it retained the payments.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, OTC COVID test claims carry dates of service preceding the carrier's first shipment scan in the pharmacy's fulfilment records. Monthly test units per beneficiary approach the eight-test program cap for nearly the entire beneficiary panel. Claim counts for a single pharmacy NPI spike far above its own trailing baseline within days. Beneficiaries billed have no other claim history with that pharmacy NPI, indicating no dispensing relationship. Wholesaler acquisition invoices show test kit inventory far below the units billed for that month.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Ship-date reconciliation: on claim line, compute the gap in days between billed date of service and the earliest tracking-number ship date supplied by the pharmacy; fires when no ship record exists or the ship date follows the service date; action prepay edit. 2) Inventory-to-billing ratio: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute billed test units divided by units acquired per wholesaler invoice or pedigree data; fires when the ratio exceeds one; action payment suspension. 3) Cap saturation: on pharmacy NPI x month, compute the share of its beneficiaries billed at the full eight-test monthly maximum; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus pharmacy peers; action postpay audit and refund demand.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina
FraudEntity: Sonya Lenise Davis (owner of Sonya's Braiding)
FraudTypeAll: Covid or General Loan Fraud; Wire Fraud; Falsify certificate
SchemeSummary: Davis submitted a PPP loan application to the SBA for her business, Sonya's Braiding, inflating employee count and income, and helped co-conspirators submit fake IRS wage forms and fake bank statements to support their own PPP applications, obtaining more than $85,000 in COVID relief loan funds.
WaysToIdentify: No health care claim exists and there is no payer adjudication point in this loan scheme. The nearest detection route is SBA lender underwriting cross-checking the applicant's IRS Form 941 and W-2 filings against the payroll figures claimed. Bank statements submitted as support can be verified through direct account-data feeds rather than uploaded PDFs. Repeated applications sharing one preparer IP address, phone number or bank routing account reveal coordinated filings.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Payroll attestation match: on loan application EIN, compute the difference between claimed annual payroll and IRS-transcript wage totals for the same tax year; fires on any mismatch beyond rounding; action documentation request before disbursement.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
FraudEntity: Walgreen Co. (national pharmacy chain)
SchemeSummary: Walgreens pharmacies allegedly reported inflated 'usual and customary' prices for certain generic medications to MassHealth and Georgia Medicaid, which reimburse at the lowest of four price points, causing the programs to pay more than they should have for those generics; resolved for over $2.8 million following a qui tam whistleblower suit.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, the usual-and-customary price submitted on the claim exceeds the pharmacy's own cash discount-program price for the same NDC and quantity. The reported U&C for a generic NDC sits far above the chain's median U&C across its other store NPIs. U&C fields stay static while the pharmacy's advertised discount-club price schedule shows a lower posted price. Reimbursement lands on the U&C price point rather than the lower MAC or FUL benchmark on the state's four-point pricing rule. Only Medicaid claims carry the higher U&C while commercial remittance history for the same NDC shows lower submitted prices.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) U&C versus cash price: on claim line, compute submitted usual-and-customary price minus the pharmacy's posted discount-program cash price for the same NDC and quantity; fires when the difference is positive; action prepay edit. 2) Chain U&C outlier: on pharmacy NPI x NDC x month, compute the ratio of reported U&C to the chain TIN median U&C for that NDC; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-chain peer stores; action claim suspension. 3) Payer-selective pricing: on NDC x pharmacy TIN, compute the difference between mean U&C on Medicaid claims and mean U&C on commercial claims from remittance history; fires when the difference is positive beyond the trailing baseline; action postpay audit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance; Walgreen Co. and subsidiaries (national pharmacy chain)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care programs
SchemeSummary: Walgreens pharmacists allegedly filled millions of invalid controlled substance prescriptions - excessive opioid quantities, early refills, and 'trinity' drug combinations - despite clear red flags, and then billed Medicare and other federal health programs for those unlawful prescriptions. Walgreens agreed to pay $300 million (plus an additional $50 million if sold/merged before FY2032) and entered DEA and HHS-OIG compliance agreements; relators receive 17.25% of the FCA recovery.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, controlled substance claims show refills dispensed before the prior fill's day supply has elapsed for the same beneficiary and NDC. Concurrent active claims for an opioid, a benzodiazepine and a muscle relaxant overlap in days supply for the same beneficiary. Daily morphine milligram equivalents computed from NDC, quantity and day supply exceed guideline ceilings without a prior-authorisation record. Beneficiaries fill the same controlled NDC across multiple pharmacy NPIs and multiple prescriber NPIs within one month. Prescriber NPIs concentrated at one store show controlled-substance shares far above same-specialty peers in PDMP and claims data.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Early refill gap: on beneficiary x NDC, compute days between fill date and the prior fill date minus prior day supply; fires when the gap is negative beyond the allowed tolerance; action prepay edit. 2) Trinity overlap: on beneficiary x date, compute overlapping days supply across opioid, benzodiazepine and carisoprodol NDC classes; fires when all three overlap on the same day; action prior-authorisation requirement. 3) MME ceiling: on beneficiary x day, compute total morphine milligram equivalents from quantity, strength and day supply across all pharmacy NPIs; fires when above the guideline ceiling without documented cancer or hospice status; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs; U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois; U.S. Attorney's Offices for the Northern District of Illinois, Middle District of Florida, District of Maryland, Eastern District of New York, and Eastern District of Virginia
FraudEntity: Walgreens Boots Alliance; Walgreen Co. and various subsidiaries (national retail pharmacy chain)
PayerName: Medicare; other federal health care programs (TRICARE/Defense Health Agency; OPM FEHB; Department of Veterans Affairs; Department of Labor programs)
SchemeSummary: DOJ alleged Walgreens pharmacists knowingly filled millions of invalid controlled substance prescriptions (excessive opioid quantities, early refills, 'trinity' drug combinations) despite red flags, while the company pressured pharmacists to fill quickly and withheld prescriber data from them, then billed Medicare and other federal health programs for those unlawful prescriptions. Walgreens agreed to pay $300 million (based on ability to pay) plus an additional $50 million if sold, merged or transferred before fiscal year 2032, with whistleblower relators receiving 17.25% of the FCA recovery, and entered into a DEA memorandum of agreement and a five-year HHS-OIG Corporate Integrity Agreement.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, controlled substance claims show refills before the prior day supply is exhausted for the same beneficiary and NDC. Opioid, benzodiazepine and muscle-relaxant claims overlap in days supply for the same beneficiary across the chain. Computed daily morphine milligram equivalents exceed guideline ceilings without any prior-authorisation record on file. Single prescriber NPIs supply an outsized share of one store's controlled-substance dispensing volume relative to peers. Beneficiaries fill the same controlled NDC at multiple store NPIs within the same chain in one month.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Early refill gap: on beneficiary x NDC, compute fill date minus prior fill date minus prior day supply; fires when negative beyond tolerance; action prepay edit. 2) Prescriber concentration at store: on pharmacy NPI x prescriber NPI x quarter, compute the share of that store's controlled-substance claim dollars from one prescriber; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-region pharmacy peers; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Cross-store duplication: on beneficiary x NDC x month, compute distinct dispensing pharmacy NPIs with overlapping days supply; fires when the count exceeds one; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Marlenin Vito (Medicaid Coordinator at assisted living facility; later bookkeeper)
State_County: Connecticut - Stamford (Fairfield County); Connecticut - Hartford; New York - White Plains (Westchester County)
FraudTypeAll: Wire Fraud; Covid or General Loan Fraud
SchemeSummary: As Medicaid Coordinator at a Stamford assisted living facility, Vito generated roughly 500 checks from the facility's system, forged a coworker's signature, cashed them as if disbursing cash to residents, kept about $310,820, and falsified ledger entries debiting residents' patient trust accounts; she also pocketed residents' COVID-19 Economic Impact Payments and continued deducting for cancelled supplemental insurance. After termination she stole about $23,558 from an alarm company (false overtime and personal orders) and about $27,179 from a Hartford law firm via forged 'Petty Cash' checks.
WaysToIdentify: There is no payer claim adjudication point; the theft ran through the facility's resident trust accounts and check-writing system. Resident trust ledgers show cash disbursements to residents at frequencies and amounts far above the facility's own baseline, all authorised by one staff login. Cancelled checks bear a signature that does not match the on-file signature card for the named signer. Deductions continued for a supplemental insurance policy after the policy's termination date in the carrier file.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Trust disbursement anomaly: on facility x preparer user ID x month, compute the count and dollar sum of cash disbursements from resident trust accounts and the share signed by a single signer; fires when above the facility's trailing baseline or when signer differs from the preparer's authorised signature card; action postpay audit by the state survey agency.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Michele Devine (executive director of Southeastern Regional Action Council on Substance Abuse, Inc. (SERAC))
FraudType: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds
FraudTypeAll: Other - Embezzlement of federal grant funds; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: As executive director of SERAC, a Connecticut nonprofit funded by state DMHAS and federal HHS/SAMHSA grants for substance abuse, gambling and mental health services, Devine used organization funds beginning around 2008 for personal expenses including home appliances, travel, timeshare fees, spa stays and private school donations; she pleaded guilty to wire fraud and was ordered to pay $397,064.93 restitution and a $2,000 fine plus 24 months in prison.
WaysToIdentify: There is no health care claim and no payer adjudication point; the loss was grant funds spent on personal items. The nearest detection route is grantor-side review of the Federal Financial Report and the annual Single Audit against the general ledger. Vendor-level ledger analysis shows disbursements to merchant categories such as appliances, resorts and timeshares that are unallowable under the grant cost principles. Corporate card and check payees can be matched to the executive's home address and personal accounts.
FeaturesToCreate: No payer-side control applies. 1) Unallowable vendor spend: on grantee EIN x quarter, compute the dollar sum of general-ledger disbursements to merchant category codes outside allowable grant cost categories divided by total federal draw; fires when the ratio exceeds zero beyond a documented exception; action grantor documentation request and drawdown suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Ashley Jackson (sole owner of Roc City Transport); Roc City Transport
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Upcoding; kickback_Bribery For Referral
SchemeSummary: Jackson, sole owner of Roc City Transport, billed Medicaid for non-emergency medical transportation trips that were never performed, billed individual rides as higher-paying group rides, and paid kickbacks to Medicaid recipients (mostly traveling to Rochester methadone clinics) to drive themselves instead of using Roc City; approximately $40,123.29 in fraudulent billing.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, NEMT trip claims carry group-ride modifiers while only one beneficiary is billed for that vehicle, date and time. Trip claims exist on dates with no corresponding treatment encounter claim at the destination methadone clinic for that beneficiary. GPS or trip-log records submitted with the broker file show no vehicle movement matching the billed pickup times. Total billed loaded miles and trip counts per driver NPI exceed feasible hours in a 24-hour day. Beneficiaries billed for transport concurrently receive mileage reimbursement or self-transport payments in the same program records.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Destination encounter match: on claim line, compute whether a same-day service claim exists for the beneficiary at the billed destination provider NPI; fires when no such encounter claim exists; action prepay edit. 2) Group-ride integrity: on vehicle or driver NPI x date x trip time window, compute the count of distinct beneficiaries billed with a group modifier; fires when the count equals one; action prepay edit and recoupment. 3) Driver-hours feasibility: on driver NPI x date of service, compute the sum of billed trip durations plus estimated drive time between successive pickup and drop-off addresses; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Suhail Aponte (sole principal and registered agent of Minds Cornerstone LLC dba Minds Cornerstone Behavior Therapy Services); Minds Cornerstone LLC
PayerName: Medicaid (Connecticut Medical Assistance Program / HUSKY, Connecticut Department of Social Services)
SchemeSummary: Aponte, an unlicensed owner of an autism services company, and a co-conspirator billed Connecticut Medicaid roughly $1.88 million for applied behavior analysis services to children with autism that were never rendered - including services on dates when payroll records show employees were not paid, BCBA supervision billed without the corresponding technician code, services for patients who were hospitalized inpatient, and visits parents and former employees confirmed never occurred. She agreed to forfeit about $459,000 in seized funds plus additional accounts and two Hartford land parcels.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, ABA claim dates of service fall on days when no staff member appears on the agency's payroll or EVV records. BCBA supervision codes are billed without any paired technician direct-service line for the same beneficiary and date. Billed outpatient ABA dates overlap inpatient hospital claim spans in the beneficiary's other claims. Rendering staff identifiers on claims do not match any credentialed BCBA or RBT in the state licence and certification registry. Billed service hours per rendering staff member exceed 24 hours on individual dates of service.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Payroll-claim reconciliation: on rendering staff x date of service, compute billed service units against hours recorded in payroll and EVV visit records; fires when billed units exist with zero corresponding paid or verified hours; action claim suspension. 2) Supervision pairing: on beneficiary x date of service, compute the count of BCBA supervision lines lacking a same-day technician direct-service line; fires when the count exceeds zero; action prepay edit. 3) Inpatient overlap: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlap in days between outpatient ABA lines and inpatient facility claim spans; fires when overlap is greater than zero; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia
FraudEntity: Michelle Shropshire (WMATA train operator, scheme organizer); Harlisha Jones (WMATA train operator); Sharon Washington (WMATA employee); Selethia Blake (WMATA employee); Brady Turner (WMATA employee); Lushawn Foreman (WMATA employee); Margot Jackson (WMATA employee)
PayerName: American Family Life Assurance Company of Columbus (AFLAC)
FraudTypeAll: Phantom Claims; Falsify certificate; kickback_Bribery For Referral; IdentityFraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: WMATA train operators submitted fraudulent health care and short-term disability insurance claims to AFLAC under Jones's policies for injuries, treatments and disability periods that never occurred, supporting them with forged medical excuse notes and physician's statements bearing real doctors' identities and forged signatures; after AFLAC paid, claimants kicked back about 20% of the proceeds to Shropshire, who also helped numerous other WMATA employees file similar false claims (AFLAC paid ~$58,750 to Jones and at least $362,035.14 across all participants). Five co-participants pleaded guilty and Shropshire was later sentenced to 24 months.
WaysToIdentify: At claim intake, disability and indemnity claims from many policyholders share one employer, one fax number and identical medical excuse note templates. The attending physician's statement bears an NPI whose NPPES address and specialty do not match the treating relationship claimed. No corresponding medical claim exists in the health plan's history for the treatment dates asserted on the disability form. A small set of claimants recur as witnesses, referrers or payees across otherwise unrelated claim files. Bank deposit data shows repeated transfers of a fixed percentage of paid benefits from claimants to one recipient account.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Prescriber attestation verification: on claim, compute an exact match of the signing physician NPI, licence number and signature against NPPES and the state licence board file, plus a callback confirmation; fires on registry mismatch or unconfirmed signature; action claim suspension. 2) Submission cluster degree: on employer group x 90 days, compute the count of disability claims sharing the same submitting fax, IP, document template hash or attending NPI; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus peer employer groups; action documentation request (ADR). 3) Payout kickback pattern: on payee bank account, compute the count of distinct claimants transferring a similar fixed share of benefit payments within 30 days of disbursement; fires when the distinct-claimant count exceeds one; action payment suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of New York
FraudEntity: Western New York Medical P.C. (WNY Medical) (health care provider)
State_County: New York - Erie County; New York - Niagara County
SchemeSummary: WNY Medical billed Medicare for Chronic Care Management encounters under CPT codes requiring at least 20 minutes of clinical staff time per month, but for a portion of those encounters clinical staff did not actually provide the required 20 minutes during the billed month; the provider agreed to pay $251,477 to resolve the False Claims Act allegations.
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, chronic care management CPT 99490 lines lack any time-stamped care-management contact log for the billed month. Total CCM minutes attributable to a single clinical staff member across beneficiaries exceed feasible working hours in the month. The practice bills CCM for nearly its entire eligible panel each month, above same-specialty peer rates. No documented patient consent or care plan claim history precedes the first CCM billing month for the beneficiary. Beneficiaries billed CCM show no chronic-condition diagnosis pair on any claim in the prior year.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Staff-minute feasibility: on clinical staff identifier x month, compute the sum of billed CCM minutes implied by CCM code thresholds across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds available paid working hours for that staff member; action documentation request (ADR). 2) Panel saturation: on practice TIN x month, compute the share of attributed beneficiaries with a CCM line billed; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action postpay audit. 3) Eligibility precondition: on beneficiary x month, compute the count of distinct qualifying chronic conditions in the prior 12 months of claims; fires when fewer than two conditions are present; action prepay edit.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut
FraudEntity: Jessica Stuart (unlicensed provider impersonating a Board Certified Behavior Analyst); Helping Hands Academy, LLC (ABA services provider)
SchemeSummary: Stuart, who had no degree, license, or BCBA certification, stole the professional identity of a legitimate Board Certified Behavior Analyst so that Helping Hands Academy could bill Medicaid for applied behavior analysis services she performed but was not qualified to provide; over 1,900 fraudulent claims for 12 autistic children caused about $369,439 in Medicaid losses while Stuart was paid at least $146,000. She was originally sentenced to 27 months, and on Feb 26, 2025 received an additional 10 months for supervised release violations involving misuse of a SNAP card and false unemployment benefit certifications.
WaysToIdentify: At credentialing, the BCBA certification number submitted by the agency is already linked to a different individual and employer in the BACB registry. The supervising BCBA's home address and other claim activity place her in a different state from the billed service locations. Billed rendering-provider hours for the credentialed BCBA exceed 24 hours on individual dates of service. Payroll and agency personnel files list a service deliverer whose name never appears on any submitted claim line. The credentialed BCBA has no remittance or direct-deposit relationship with the billing agency's TIN.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Credential identity match: on rendering NPI x billing TIN at enrolment, compute an exact match of certification number, name and date of birth against the BACB registry and state licence board file; fires on any registry mismatch; action claim suspension pending site visit. 2) Rendering-hours feasibility: on rendering NPI x date of service, compute the sum of billed service units converted to hours across all beneficiaries; fires when the total exceeds 24 hours; action prepay edit. 3) Staff-claim reconciliation: on billing TIN x month, compute the count of claim-line rendering identifiers with no matching name in payroll or personnel records; fires when the count exceeds zero; action documentation request (ADR).

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Fraud Section; U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California
FraudEntity: Lourdes Navarro (co-owner of Matias Clinical Laboratory d/b/a Health Care Providers Laboratory); Imran Shams (co-owner); Matias Clinical Laboratory d/b/a Health Care Providers Laboratory (HCPL)
PayerName: Medicare; HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program; private health insurance company (unnamed)
FraudTypeAll: FakeEncounter; Covid or General Loan Fraud; Benefit & Eligibility Fraud; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Owners of a clinical lab obtained nasal swab specimens and COVID-19 test orders from nursing homes, assisted living/rehab facilities and schools, then ran expensive respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests on most specimens although only COVID-19 screening had been ordered and RPP tests were not medically justified for asymptomatic individuals; approximately $369 million was billed to Medicare, the HRSA COVID-19 Uninsured Program and a private insurer, yielding about $46.7 million in reimbursements. Figures span both co-owners: Navarro received 9 years and forfeited $11,662,939 (total seized/forfeited from both defendants $14,518,485) plus $46,735,400 restitution, while Shams was sentenced to 10 years (and a separate 5-year sentence in EDNY).
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, respiratory pathogen panel CPT codes are billed on specimens whose accompanying order lists only a SARS-CoV-2 test code. The share of RPP claims to total COVID test claims for the laboratory NPI far exceeds same-specialty laboratory peers. Beneficiaries billed carry no symptomatic respiratory diagnosis code on any claim near the specimen collection date. A single ordering NPI or facility supplies thousands of specimens per week from congregate settings and schools. HRSA Uninsured Program submissions duplicate beneficiaries who also have active Medicare or commercial coverage on eligibility files.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Panel-to-order match: on claim line, compute whether the billed RPP CPT is present on the electronic order or requisition record tied to that accession; fires on exact mismatch between ordered and billed test codes; action prepay edit. 2) Reflex ratio: on laboratory NPI x month, compute paid RPP lines divided by COVID-19 test lines from the same accessions; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty laboratory peers; action payment suspension. 3) Coverage duplication: on beneficiary x date of service, compute whether an HRSA Uninsured Program claim coexists with active Medicare or commercial eligibility; fires on exact eligibility-file mismatch; action claim suspension.

JurisdictionName: U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division Fraud Section (National Rapid Response Strike Force) and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona
FraudEntity: Alexandra Gehrke (owner of wound graft companies, incl. Apex Medical LLC); Jeffrey King (co-owner of wound graft company, Gehrke's husband)
PayerName: Medicare; TRICARE; CHAMPVA; commercial health insurers
FraudTypeAll: kickback_Bribery For Referral; FakeEncounter; Phantom Claims; Wire Fraud
SchemeSummary: Gehrke and King used medically untrained 'sales representatives' to canvass elderly Arizona Medicare beneficiaries (many in hospice) for wounds of any kind and to order the largest available amniotic membrane skin-substitute allografts, then had contracted nurse practitioners apply whatever was ordered regardless of medical necessity - including large grafts on small wounds, multiple grafts per wound, grafts on non-existent wounds and on dying palliative patients - and billed roughly $1.21 billion to Medicare, TRICARE, CHAMPVA and commercial insurers (paid $614.9 million). Gehrke's companies took over $279 million and King's company $130 million in kickbacks from the wholesale graft distributor for ordering its grafts, and she paid kickbacks onward to the sales reps; figures and payments span both defendants (restitution, forfeiture and separate False Claims Act settlements of $279.9 million and $30 million).</thinking>
WaysToIdentify: At adjudication, skin-substitute Q-code units billed far exceed the documented wound surface area in square centimeters on the same claim. Beneficiaries with an active hospice election receive high-cost graft applications during the hospice period. Applications repeat on the same wound at intervals shorter than the product's labelled treatment schedule. A handful of nurse practitioner rendering NPIs generate graft dollars above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers. The billing entity's ownership on CMS-855B overlaps with distributor entities receiving the ordering volume, and Open Payments shows large distributor transfers.
FeaturesToCreate: 1) Graft size versus wound area: on claim line, compute billed Q-code square centimeters minus documented wound area from the wound measurement field or attached note; fires when billed units exceed documented area beyond allowed wastage; action prepay edit. 2) Hospice concurrency: on beneficiary x date of service, compute overlap in days between the hospice election period and skin-substitute application dates; fires when overlap is greater than zero without a documented unrelated-condition attestation; action claim suspension. 3) Applier intensity: on rendering NPI x month, compute total paid skin-substitute dollars and distinct beneficiaries receiving repeat applications within the labelled interval; fires when above the calibrated percentile versus same-specialty peers; action payment suspension and postpay audit.
